author: nekwo
message:
Let an agent dispatch work and keep going

Agent-to-agent chat had exactly one shape: block until they answer. That capped
everything two agents can do together at whatever fits in a conversational
window, and it made the most useful request in this runtime -- "run the suite
and tell me what broke" -- inexpressible. An agent that asked it either sat
blocked for the whole run or never asked.

`agent_chat_send(wait=false)` returns a dispatch handle immediately, the
target's turn runs on a background executor with its own 30-minute budget
(`agent_runtime.mission_chat.dispatch_max_seconds`), and a drain inside serve
forges their answer back into the sender's own thread as a new turn once the
sender is idle. `agent_chat_dispatches` lists what is still in flight, and the
rows join the Activity projection as its sixth lane.

The payload seam had to land first, and it retires real debt.

The relay invoked the mission-chat handler in-process under
`contextlib.redirect_stdout` and parsed the captured text back into JSON.
`redirect_stdout` rebinds `sys.stdout` PROCESS-GLOBALLY, so every other thread
in a serve process wrote into that buffer for the duration -- tolerable while
relays were strictly one-at-a-time, and unshippable the moment two dispatches
can overlap. All 23 terminal emissions in the turn body now go through one
`_mission_chat_emit` seam: with no sink installed it prints byte-for-byte what
each site printed before (the CLI and the serve bridge are untouched), and with
a sink the payload dict is handed over and NOTHING is printed, so a nested reply
can never land in the outer turn's stdout capture.

Ordering, because a lost answer is the only failure that matters.

The durable row is written BEFORE the turn is queued and before the caller is
told anything. Written after, a process that died early would leave work whose
result has nowhere to go; a caller told `dispatched: true` for a row that failed
to persist would wait forever for a delivery nobody would attempt. A store
failure therefore refuses the dispatch instead of running it blind, and a queue
failure settles the row rather than stranding it `running` in the operator's HUD.

The store reuses the async_delegation protocol wholesale rather than growing a
second one: expiring claims, an attempt cap that converges to `dropped`, owner
PID plus start-time identity, and a boot sweep that turns a dispatch whose owner
provably died into a deliverable "the outcome is unknown" instead of silence. It
resolves through `get_hermes_background_work_home` -- a dispatch is made from
inside a persona turn, where HERMES_HOME is flipped process-globally, and the
ambient home is not the home the drain and the HUD read.

Delivery is a real turn, taken when the sender is idle.

Completions surface as a NEW turn through the same handler an operator message
goes through, never spliced mid-flight: role alternation stays legal and past
context is never mutated. Idle is proven twice -- the turn journal AND a
zero-timeout lease probe, because a turn whose executor died leaves the lease
free while the journal still shows it running. The probe releases before forging
(the handler takes the same lease, and holding it across would deadlock), so the
handler's own acquisition remains the real guard and a busy sender simply waits.
The delivery turn's `client_message_id` is derived from the dispatch id, so a
retried delivery converges on one turn rather than doubling the message.

Relay ruling (operator-approved): a detached dispatch is a new chain root with
its own deadline, and the chain is still forwarded. The shared deadline exists so
a synchronous hop cannot outlive the caller blocked on it, and nobody is blocked
here; forwarding the chain is what keeps that from being a loophole, since depth
and cycle detection read the chain, not the clock. A cycle is still refused at
the same chokepoint -- detaching only changes when the sender hears about it.

Capability honesty, and the lane it unlocks.

`async_delivery_supported()` answered True on this lane for the worst possible
reason: nothing had ever bound the contextvar, while nothing in serve drained the
completion queue at all. Every `terminal(notify_on_complete)` and
`delegate_task(background=true)` promise it granted was unkeepable. It is now
bound to a fact -- True for serve-hosted turns because the drain runs there,
False for cold one-shot CLI turns because the process exits with the turn -- and
with the drain live those completions are consumed for sessions whose ownership
can be positively proven, delivered through the same forged-turn path.

Contract 52 is KEPT, deliberately. The ledger's stated reason for bumping on an
addition is that the consumer would otherwise not see it at all; 52 itself
published `dispatch` in RUNNING_WORK_KINDS so the vocabulary would be complete
before the lane arrived, and what lands is a sixth key in a health map plus rows
carrying a kind string the version already declares. The ruling is recorded in
the ledger with the constraint it places on the Launcher: parse `sources` as a
map and `kind` as an open string.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
Let a delivered result read as a delivered result

A dispatch delivery turn is forged into the SENDER's own chat session as a
role="user" row. At rest that is byte-identical to a message the operator
typed, so every consumer attributed the harness's work to the human. The
`requested_by="harness-delivery"` provenance the forge stamped went nowhere:
the one site that types a persisted user row only recognised the relay lane's
`agent:<session>` prefix, so a delivery persisted unmarked and projected as
`operator_message` — the same attribution defect the relay marker retired, one
lane over, with a comment in the forge already asserting the fix existed.

It gets its own marker rather than borrowing `relay_from:`. A delivery is not
a relay: no agent sent it, there is no sending persona to name, and grouping
the two would attribute a machine delivery to whichever persona happened to be
encoded. What it carries instead is the identity of the dispatch it settles
and whether the dispatching agent flagged the operator — both read off the
marker because by the time anything reads the thread, the dispatch has left
every live projection (`running_work` reports RUNNING dispatches only, and
carries no notify flag), so a consumer has nothing left to join against.

Same column, same typed-marker-in-finish_reason precedent, same
single-authority rule: relay_policy builds and parses, nothing else
pattern-matches the string. A pre-attribution `harness-delivery` with no
suffix still reads as a delivery with no id and no flag, and an unreadable
flag reads as NOT flagged — notifying on corruption would manufacture
operator interrupts.

Contract stays 52. Nothing left the wire (the row still projects
role="operator" with the same id, text and timestamps, so a consumer that
ignores the kind renders what it renders today), and this is not "invisible
rather than merely unread": the Launcher's conversation adapter falls through
unknown kinds to a generic bubble by design and parses this one in the same
wave. The constraint that buys is the one the dispatch lane already imposed —
conversation `kind` stays an OPEN string.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
Give a detached dispatch its own process

The dispatch lane shipped running its detached turns in-process, on a daemon
executor. Review found that unshippable, and the reason is not subtle: every
persona turn executes under `profile_runner._WORKDIR_LOCK`, a PROCESS-WIDE
RLock held for the whole model turn. Serve handles requests concurrently, but
persona turns serialize on that lock.

So one 30-minute dispatch froze every foreground operator turn -- and froze it
AFTER the journal's `executing` transition, which is the worst possible place:
the console shows a running turn with no typed refusal, no timeout, and nothing
to expire it, because the wall budget only starts ticking INSIDE the lock. It
froze the SENDER's own next turn, inverting the feature outright. It made
`dispatch_max_concurrent` a fiction -- three dispatches meant three thirty-minute
waits in series. Queued waiters held the TARGET's chat-root lease while blocked,
so an operator messaging that agent got `chat_busy` for hours. It froze the
delivery drain, whose forge takes the same lock. And a nested dispatch deadlocked
outright, the parent holding the lock its child needed.

A child process has its own `_WORKDIR_LOCK`, its own HERMES_HOME override and
its own cwd. The supervisor thread now spawns `hermes harness mission-chat
message` and WAITS -- holding no lock while it waits, which is the entire point.
The cost is a cold start per dispatch, which is the right trade for work budgeted
in minutes, and it buys a second property worth as much: a dispatch that wedges
or explodes can no longer take serve down with it. The regression test holds the
lock on another thread and runs a dispatch to completion through it.

Two things had to be added for a turn to survive an argv boundary. The sender's
chat-root session id had no CLI spelling, so a child would have resolved bare
persona targets against the wrong workspace scope. And the tri-state
`new_session` has no argparse spelling at all -- absent means False, not unset --
so every dispatch would have quietly stopped opening its own task thread and
piled back into one sticky per-pair thread. `--defer-thread-policy` states the
unset case rather than changing `--new-session`'s default, which would have
started minting a fresh thread for every bare CLI send that omits the flag.

The relay deadline is now minted when the CHILD starts, not when the dispatch is
enqueued. Queuing behind the concurrency cap used to burn wall budget, so the
budget the sender was told about and the budget the turn actually got drifted
apart with nothing reporting it.

Refuse what cannot be delivered, instead of running it anyway

Two admission checks, both before any work starts. `wait:false` on a lane whose
process ends with the turn is refused: accepting it would leave an orphaned child
writing into a chat thread with no recorder left to settle its row. That is the
same ruling `delegate_task` already follows on the same signal -- fall back to
the inline path and return the result inside the turn that asked for it -- and
the tool that makes the promise now enforces it. Separately, a sender root the
delivery drain cannot resolve to a persona is refused through the drain's OWN
resolver, so the run-and-drop case (work executed, answer discarded as
`sender_session_unresolvable`) cannot happen: what could not be delivered never
runs.

The capability itself stops being a proxy. It answered True for "this is serve",
but the drain starts best-effort, so a serve whose drain failed went on promising
deliveries nothing would perform -- the same dishonesty the binding was
introduced to retire, one level down. It now reads the drain's actual liveness.

Orphans surface within a minute, not a reboot

The sweep ran only before the `ready` frame. Serve stays up for days, so a
dispatch whose process died at 09:00 sat `running` -- in the HUD and in the
sender's mental model -- until the next restart. It now runs on the drain's own
slower cadence, and the projection stops hiding what it has not yet settled: a
dead-owner dispatch row is REPORTED as unknown/unverified rather than dropped.
That is a deliberate divergence from the terminal and delegation lanes and it is
a property of the store, not a relaxed rule -- there a dead PID means the work is
over and nobody is owed anything, here it means a sender is still waiting. Hiding
it would make the one dispatch most worth looking at the only invisible one, and
its disappearance would read as "it finished". Because the row's owner is stamped
to the CHILD once it spawns, that question stays answerable even when the
supervisor that was waiting on it is gone.

Attempts count failures only

A `chat_busy` refusal at forge time burned a delivery attempt. Nothing failed
there -- the sender simply took its lease between the drain's idle probe and the
forge, which is a race with a live operator and is the system working. Eight
unlucky races would have marched a perfectly deliverable completion to a terminal
`dropped` with no failure anywhere in its history. The attempt is now refunded.
The queue-backed lane gained the cap it never had: with no durable row to count
on, a persistently-failing completion re-queued every five seconds forever,
invisibly, blocking the queue behind it. It converges and ends with a named log
line, because a silently-abandoned completion is the exact failure class this
lane exists to retire.

Also: typed refusals are rewritten for the lane they will be READ on.
`relay_budget_exhausted` ends "answer your caller with what you have", which is
sound mid-turn and nonsense in a delivered error turn arriving minutes later to
an agent with no caller waiting.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
Stop the dispatch lane reporting confident wrong answers

Four defects in the detached-dispatch bookkeeping, all of the same shape: the
runtime told the sender something specific and wrong, and nothing anywhere could
tell that from the truth.

The stream bound kept the wrong end. A child's payload is the LAST thing it
prints, and the 512KB cap discarded every line after the threshold — so a chatty
turn lost its own answer. Reproduced at 583,070 characters in, 512,033 captured,
payload gone: `parse_child_payload` returned None and a SUCCESSFUL thirty-minute
dispatch was recorded `unknown`, with an empty stderr excerpt because all the
noise had been on stdout. The buffer now keeps the tail and drops the head, with
a running total rather than re-summing the sink per line (that was O(n^2), and a
child printing past the cap pinned a pump thread to a core for the rest of a
half-hour run inside a long-lived serve).

"Last JSON object wins" picked whatever was printed last. A shutdown notice
after a successful turn (`{"event":"mcp_shutdown","ok":false}`) made it an
error; a trailing `{}` made it a success with an EMPTY reply, which reads to an
agent as "they had nothing to report". Every mission-chat payload carries
`capability_id` on every exit path, so the producer's own marker decides now and
ordering does not.

The sweep and the supervisor were two writers, and the guess could win. Making
the orphan sweep periodic in the previous commit turned a theoretical race into
a live one: from the instant a child exits until the supervisor's
`record_completion` lands -- across `proc.wait()` and two pump joins -- the sweep
sees a dead PID on a `running` row and settles it `unknown`. The 5s drain then
delivers "the outcome is unknown" for a dispatch that COMPLETED, and the real
answer written moments later is absorbed by the delivery-turn replay dedup: the
sender is told nothing is known and never receives the answer sitting in the
row. A row still supervised in this process is not an orphan by definition, so
the sweep skips it; its write is additionally scoped to rows still in flight, so
an inference can never overwrite an observation. And `record_completion` no
longer re-arms a row already marked `delivered` -- the only thing that had been
standing between a re-armed row and a duplicate message was a replay cache that
can rotate or be compressed away.

"Never raises" was a docstring claim rather than a property. `_run_dispatch` ran
unguarded, so a raise before the spawn left the row `running` and owned by the
sender's still-live serve PID -- which the orphan sweep can therefore never
settle -- and nobody noticed, because `executor.submit` discards the Future. The
body is wrapped; every exit records a terminal state. The same key is also read
one way now (`spec["max_seconds"]`, not `.get(...) or 1800` in one place and a
subscript in another, which is how a spec-shape bug hides behind a default that
looks deliberate).

Smaller, same theme: a positive capability declaration is now required before
this lane will promise delivery, because `async_delivery_supported()` returns
True for an unbound session and the binding has one call site -- so silence was
being read as consent. The drain's teardown only clears the registration when it
is still the registered drain (an unconditional clear let an old loop null a
restarted one, after which every dispatch was refused by a runtime perfectly able
to deliver). Pump threads are forced loose after their join rather than leaking
two per dispatch on a pipe a grandchild holds open -- which is exactly what "go
run the suite" spawns.

Two documentation corrections, both of things the code does not do. A nested
`wait: false` does NOT spawn a grandchild: the child is a cold CLI, its delivery
capability is False, and the nested dispatch is REFUSED. That is the honest
outcome -- the child's process ends with its turn, so a grandchild would outlive
the only thing that could record what happened to it -- but the note claimed
otherwise. And the `HERMES_HOME` handed to a child is the SENDER PERSONA's
profile home, not the operator's: it is read inside the sender's
`persona_profile_context`. That matches the synchronous relay lane and is
arguably right, but it was undocumented and it is a real change from the old
in-process lane.

Finally, the orphan message names the thread. After the subprocess move the
dominant orphan is a serve recycled while a healthy child ran to completion --
the reply exists, in the target's own thread, and only the bookkeeping row was
lost. "Re-send if you still need it" invited duplicated work in exactly that
case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
Stop losing the answers this lane exists to deliver

Review of the WP-L2 attribution wave found three ways a delivered result
could be wrong or absent on the hermes side. All are the same failure in
different clothes: work ran, an answer came back, and nothing downstream
could tell.

**An errored dispatch was indistinguishable from a successful one.**
`pending_deliveries` selects `state != running`, so `error` and `unknown`
dispatches are delivered exactly like completions — but the marker carried
only the dispatch id and the notify flag, leaving the outcome recoverable
only from the prose body. Any consumer phrasing an honest notification
would have had to sentence-match, which is precisely what the typed marker
was introduced to retire. The outcome now rides the marker, the
`requested_by` provenance, the history row and the projected `delivery`
block. It is appended LAST in both encodings so a parser written against
the earlier shape still reads the earlier fields, and an absent segment
decodes to `unknown` — never to success, because a build that predates the
field genuinely does not know how the work ended.

**Housekeeping deleted answers nobody had received.** `_prune` bounded
terminal history by deleting "delivered first, then whatever is oldest",
counting across ALL terminal rows. Once the excess exceeded the number of
delivered rows it fell straight through to `pending` ones — and a
permanently-busy sender never drains (the idle probe requeues without
burning an attempt, so its row never converges to `dropped` either), so
the rows most likely to be deleted were exactly the answers still owed.
No event, no log line, nothing left to notice it by: the lane's own
collector manufacturing the silence the lane exists to retire. Pruning is
now restricted to rows whose DELIVERY has settled. Exempting them would
trade one silent failure for another if nobody ever looked, so a backlog
past the cap is counted, logged and evented instead of trimmed.

This composes with the re-arm guard that landed in a0dbdd02c rather than
contradicting it, and the pairing is pinned by a test: that change makes
`delivered` a stable terminal state (a late write can no longer re-arm it
to `pending`), which is what makes `pending` safe to key a collector on at
all. Together they give `delivery_state` a meaning worth trusting —
`pending` is exactly "an answer someone is still owed", and it is the only
state never collected.

**An abandoned delivery was invisible.** Three paths give up on a finished
dispatch without forging a turn — no sender session, an unresolvable
sender, the attempt cap — and each left only an EventLog row that no
consumer reads. So the operator got no delivery, no notification, and a
HUD reporting that all was well. Dropped rows now surface in the
`running_work` dispatch lane for a day as terminal `error` rows carrying
the drop REASON (persisted on the row, migrated onto existing stores,
since "could not be delivered" is useless without "because"). They are
`error` rather than `unknown`: nothing about them is uncertain.

**And the greppable mirror could not tell either.** `_relay_sender_fields`
parsed only the relay marker, so a forged delivery line in
`chat_live_logs/` was structurally identical to an operator message. That
is worse there than in the UI, because the mirror exists for machine
consumption: a head agent grepping a teammate's thread had nothing in the
line to distinguish the runtime's own delivery from the human. Both live
append and backfill now carry typed origin fields, translated rather than
copied — the projection names these facts `delivery_*` and the mirror
names them `origin`/`dispatch_*`, so a key-for-key copy would have
silently written nothing.

Contract stays 52; the ledger records why. Both additions land on blocks a
consumer already parses, under a `kind` it already knows, and the Launcher
consumes them in the same wave. The event-count gate went red on
`dispatch.delivery_backlog` and was moved deliberately, which is the gate
working.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
Say why the answer was abandoned

Final review of the dispatch delivery wave. Three ways the lane still kept
something from the party that needed it, and one way the alarm was worse
than the condition.

**The attempt-cap drop persisted no reason — the one drop where "because"
matters most.** `drop_delivery` recorded its reason on the row; the
cap-drop inside `claim_delivery` wrote every other delivery column and
skipped that one. So the Activity panel rendered `delivery abandoned:
undelivered` for the drop an operator is most likely to be reading, since
it is the one that follows eight visible failures. Row and event now read
the same constant, so they cannot drift.

Which surfaced the next thing: re-arming a cap-dropped row left its
exhausted counter and its stale reason in place, so the first claim on the
fresh answer tripped the cap instantly and the operator read `attempt_cap`
against a delivery that never got an attempt. Re-arming now clears both —
scoped, so the delivered-row guard is untouched.

**The dispatching agent could see THAT its answer was abandoned but never
why.** `agent_chat_dispatches` exposed `delivery_state` alone, and the
agent's whole recourse is deciding whether to re-dispatch: a vanished chat
root means re-sending is pointless, an exhausted cap means it is exactly
right. Same information, same lane, one bounded field.

**The backlog alarm stormed.** `_prune` runs on every completion, so once
the backlog passed the cap it emitted an EventLog row and a warning per
completion — noise manufactured by the alarm for a quiet failure, in the
state where the log is most needed for something else. Throttled to new
highs plus an interval floor.

The first throttle keyed on "the count changed", and its own test caught
that this is not enough: the two lanes interleave, so pending oscillates as
rows drain and new ones land, and 3 -> 4 -> 3 -> 4 reproduced the storm
exactly. A high-water mark ignores the oscillation while still reporting
genuine growth. The test that caught it then exposed a second thing worth
keeping: the throttle state is process-global (right in production, wrong
in a test process, where one test's mark silently suppresses the next), so
it is reset per test rather than inherited.

Also here: a `dispatch.outcome_superseded` event for a second writer
landing a DIFFERENT outcome on an already-delivered row. The re-arm guard
makes that harmless to the sender, which is exactly why it would otherwise
leave no trace — and it is the observable symptom of the supervised-id
registry being process-local, so it gets a name rather than being absorbed.
The event-count gate went red and was moved deliberately, twice now.

Smaller, all recorded where the next reader will meet them: the live-log
mirror's live path now matches its backfill path's `unknown` fallback (the
two vocabularies are identical on purpose, so a fallback on one side only
is a real divergence); `_run_dispatch` releases its supervised id from one
site instead of two; `parse_child_payload`'s fallback is documented as NOT
the ordering inversion it reads like (it is overwritten by every unmarked
object while none is marked, so in the only case it is returned it holds
the last object, as before); `_BoundedTail` states what `limit` actually
bounds, since a single oversized line is kept whole on purpose and the real
ceiling is `max(limit, longest line)` inside a long-lived serve; and the
Activity panel's 24h undeliverable window states its own bound, so an empty
dispatch lane is not read as "nothing was ever abandoned".

author: nekwo
message:
fix(runtime): context-scope HERMES_HOME readers; pin process-home contract

Audit of every in-process direct HERMES_HOME reader against the
persona_profile_context ContextVar override (the env write at
profile_context.py:276 mirrors the override process-globally, so any
reader on the wrong resolver is exposed the moment turns stop being
fully serialized — and background gateway threads are exposed today).

- agent_runtime/profile_readiness.py: the _provider_issue memo key now
  resolves its home component through get_hermes_home() (ContextVar-
  first) instead of reading os.environ directly. With the env mirror
  held constant, two persona scopes previously collapsed onto one memo
  key and leaked the first profile's readiness verdict to the second.
- gateway/lifecycle_ledger.py, gateway/shutdown_watchdog.py: the local
  _process_hermes_home copies fell back to get_hermes_home() when the
  env var was unset — that resolver honors the profile override, so a
  lifecycle/heartbeat write landing mid persona-turn could route into
  the wrong profile directory (issue #56986 class). Both now delegate
  to the canonical get_process_hermes_home().
- gateway/status.py: same delegation (behavior identical; one owner).
- agent_runtime/profile_context.py: documented exactly which live
  readers pin each remaining os.environ write (openviking plugin +
  ambient-inheriting spawns for HERMES_HOME; hermes_cli/auth.py for

author: nekwo
message:
feat(runtime): make unbounded the default tool-access posture

Operator ruling 2026-08-09 (docs/agent-runtime-harness/
UNBOUNDED_DEFAULT_PLAN_2026-08-09.md): every persona in this runtime gets full
tool access by default, with no per-session escalation ritual.

The default was hardcoded twice in tool_permissions.py and liftable only by an
operator grant. It now flows from one config knob through the one chokepoint:

* permission_modes.py - new dependency-free leaf owning the mode vocabulary, so
  config / runtime_config / terminal_envelope can read it without closing an
  import cycle through tool_permissions -> tool_visibility. Adds the explicit
  PERMISSION_MODE_BOUNDED restriction tier (plan section 3.5 option (a)).
* runtime_config.ToolPermissionConfig + config._tool_permission_config -
  agent_runtime.tool_permissions.default_mode, shipping `unbounded`. An unknown
  value is a typed issue and falls back to profile_default: a config fault must
  never resolve to MORE capability than the operator wrote. migrations surfaces
  that issue so the narrowing is never silent.
* tool_permissions - the session store is INVERTED into the restriction lane. A
  stored profile_default reads as "no opinion" (the live store is full of expiry
  writebacks that would otherwise pin those sessions bounded forever); a
  corrupt/unknown stored mode clamps to `bounded`, never to the sentinel.
  consume_turn decrements for any opinionated mode, fixing the latent
  turns-bounded read_only that never expired.
* terminal_envelope - schema-plane "full access" was hollow while the execution
  plane still refused `git push`. envelope_decision now grants
  GRANTABLE_COMMAND_CLASSES under `unbounded`, stamped from the same resolve the
  schema plane uses. Every such command still writes a receipt naming the mode:
  the ruling trades a preventive control for a detective one, so the receipt IS
  the compensating control. The hard floor and ungoverned lanes are untouched.
* Honest surfaces - the HUD states the posture instead of falling silent;
  blocked_tools_count reads 22 -> 17 (registry hygiene never yields to a mode,
  and the old empty answer was a preview lie); tool-diff previews and the
  envelope explanation are mode-aware; CLI help is reworded around restriction.
* READ_ONLY_BLOCKS is now the ONE mutating-tool definition; tool_visibility
  reads it instead of keeping a second copy of the same 7 names.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(harness): release the chat-root lease before the turn's finalization tail

The 2026-08-09 incident: an operator's follow-up was refused `chat_busy`
56 seconds AFTER the reply he was answering was already on his screen. The
refusal was correct -- the root really was leased -- but ~46s of that lease
was a finalization tail that writes nothing to the root: the session
auto-title's synchronous auxiliary-LLM round trip, which resolved the whole
provider chain, lazily pip-installed `provider.anthropic`, and retried a 401
on a revoked OAuth token.

The title was already placed after the terminal frame was emitted (F4). That
is a different boundary from after the lease releases, and the operator
experiences the second one. `_mission_chat_commit_turn` now PACKAGES the
title into a `MissionChatDeferredFinalization` instead of running it;
`_cmd_mission_chat_message` runs it once the `with persona_chat_root_lease`
block has exited. The title-change metadata event travels with the title it
reports. Everything that writes turn/transcript state stays under the lease.

Failure semantics change and are documented in code: a deferred failure now
happens strictly after the exit code is decided, so it can no longer mark the
turn -- the intended direction, since the turn was complete, durable and
reported before the title was ever attempted.

Second half: refused sends were durably recorded NOWHERE. Every durable write
in the lane lives inside the lease, so a send refused on the way to it wrote
no operator row, no turn record and no event -- the investigation looked for a
message the operator had definitely sent and found it in zero persistence
surfaces. `persona_chat.send_refused` is the counter-record: root session,
client_message_id, error_kind, refusing lease pid/kind/acquired_at, and the
envelope's ts. It deliberately carries NO message text -- operator prose has
two sanitising chokepoints and both are inside the lease a refusal never
takes, while events.jsonl feeds the snapshot/read-model pipeline.
SURVIVING_EVENT_COUNT 57 -> 58, moved deliberately.

Refs: docs/mission_control/CHAT_SEND_RELIABILITY_INVESTIGATION_2026-08-09.md (R0)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(harness): let a granted command see its own audit receipt

The 2026-08-09 unbounded-default ruling traded the preventive refusal for a
detective control: every formerly-refused command writes a receipt to
terminal_envelope_decisions.jsonl. That trade only holds if the fact is
checkable, and the one party who could never check it was the party the
receipt is about.

Live 2026-08-09: the QA agent ran `curl https://example.com` (a formerly
refused network_egress command), was asked to confirm the mechanism, and
reported "the terminal receipt did not expose an audit record or
permission_mode provenance, so the required unbounded audit proof is
missing" — an honest BLOCKED verdict on facts that were all fine. It was
right about what it could see: _harness_envelope_block's granted branch
returned None and the tool result carried the ordinary output/exit_code
shape. The runtime knew; its subject was structurally blind.

No new authority and no new decision. envelope_provenance() surfaces what
envelope_decision() already resolved and record_envelope_decision() already
wrote: command_class, decision, granted_by, grant_source, permission_mode,
plus the bare receipt-log filename and whether a row actually landed. It
rides ONLY grants — OUTCOME_ALLOW and ungoverned lanes return None, so the
commands an agent runs all day pay exactly zero. ~63 tokens on a gated
command.

Two supporting changes, both about not asserting what we did not verify:
_append_jsonl and record_envelope_decision now return whether the write
landed, so `receipted` is the write's real answer rather than an assumption
— a receipt that silently failed is exactly what an agent must not cite as
proof.

terminal_tool becomes a thin wrapper over _terminal_tool_run so the gate and
the merge each happen once, ahead of that body's dozen-plus json.dumps
exits; attaching provenance per-exit would be a hand-maintained list a new
exit falls out of silently. The wrapper fails closed on a gate fault, in the
same shape the body's own handler returns.

Live-proven end to end: real curl reached example.com under an unbounded
mission-chat scope, the result carried the account, and the receipt on disk
matched it field-for-field.

Tests are red-first proven by sabotage — all five mechanisms (the merge, the
not-a-grant guard, the honest receipted flag, the bare-filename rule, the
never-damage-the-output rule) were reverted individually and each took the
suite red.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(runtime): never mutate the venv from inside a live turn

On 2026-08-09 Mission Control refused to open behind a destructive-repair
gate. Root cause was one corrupt package in the runtime venv: jiter's
compiled single-file extension sat inside a jiter/ directory with no
__init__.py (so it resolved as an empty namespace package), alongside THREE
conflicting dist-info dirs whose invalid metadata made pip silently no-op
every --force-reinstall. That is the signature of concurrent/interrupted
installs racing into one venv — and this runtime generated exactly that
traffic: a lazy `provider.anthropic` pip install ran mid-turn, inside the
chat-root lease, during a live operator conversation.

Three changes, each closing a different half of the class:

1. Venv-mutation barrier at the lazy-install chokepoint
   (tools/lazy_deps.py). `deny_venv_installs(reason)` refuses venv-scoped
   installs process-wide; ProfileAgentRunner.run arms it for the whole turn,
   covering every harness lane. Refusals raise RuntimeInstallDenied, a
   FeatureUnavailable subclass, so all ~40 existing call sites degrade to
   "feature unavailable" with the exact install command instead of raising
   something new. Durable-target (--target) installs stay allowed: they are
   append-only on sys.path and cannot corrupt the running venv, so sealed
   Docker deployments and the LSP server store are unaffected.

2. Provider SDKs are DECLARED, not discovered mid-turn
   (hermes_cli/runtime_environment.py). anthropic / boto3 / google-auth join
   openai in the requirement table, so preflight names a missing SDK before
   token spend. Requirements are distribution names with an import-name map,
   which also fixes the dotted-probe crash (find_spec("azure.identity") raises
   when the parent is absent) and keeps the launcher's reinstall target right.

3. Venv-integrity detection (hermes_cli/venv_integrity.py). Names the CAUSE,
   not just the symptom: conflicting dist-info dirs for one distribution,
   unreadable/invalid metadata (pip's "invalid metadata entry 'name'"), and a
   package directory shadowing a same-named extension module. Emitted shape
   stays {kind, package, summary} with a runtime_dependency_* kind, so the
   launcher classifies and renders them with its copy button; summaries carry
   the exact command, including the "delete these dirs first, reinstall alone
   does nothing" fact that was the whole trap.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
refactor(snapshot): prune the writer-less persona-instance wire fields at contract 54

Lands the deferred-debt ledger's parked S70 batch (5). Six keys leave every
`persona_instances` row and the snapshot contract moves 53 -> 54; the Launcher
pin moves in the same wave.

Two were duplicate ALIASES that projected byte-identical values to the canonical
key beside them: `current_work_assignment_id` (= `current_assignment_id`) and
`attached_task_id` (= `current_task_id`). Four were writer-less since the
worker/goal lanes died, with no consumer past a Launcher model copy:

`watchdog_warning_count`. Those four also leave `PersonaInstance` itself and the
configured/idle reset that was their only assignment; that is safe against

and ignores keys it does not know.

Three corrections to the ledger entry, all recorded in doc 19:

- `attached_task_id` was NOT writer-less. `current_task_id` is written live by
  the steer/`goal_id` lane, so the cut is justified by redundancy — the value
  still ships under the canonical key — not by deadness.

  by `state_patches`, and the Launcher folds patch fields with no allowlist, so

- `token_budget_used` and `last_heartbeat_at` are equally writer-less but STAY:

`test_s57_unruled_config_debt_removal` and `test_stage19_visibility` had all been

author: nekwo
message:
perf(serve): attribute the boot timeline and prewarm the read model

Two startup items from the 2026-08-09 Mission Control startup analysis
(docs/mission_control/PERF_STARTUP_ANALYSIS_2026-08-09.md in the launcher):

T5/T9 — the boot measures itself. A cold serve boot has been recorded at
>25s and cannot be reproduced on demand (any machine that just ran the
launcher has every relevant file cached), so instead of a repro the boot
stamps its own phases into the frames the supervisor already reads:
`booting` carries the interpreter + CLI import tax, `ready` carries the
per-phase breakdown (chat registry, head publish, store root, orphaned-turn
sweep, dispatch restore), and the same line goes to agent.log. Measured on
the live install: interpreter_ms 1.2-3.2s, every post-import phase <=32ms —
i.e. the cold-boot term is entirely import, which is now recorded rather
than assumed.

T2 — serve prewarms one read-model core right after boot. A fresh child's
first build costs ~6.1s against ~2.1s warm; ~4s of that is per-process
cache fill. The warmup runs on its own daemon thread started just BEFORE
the ready frame, because only the build that started first can be shared:
the launcher's first request lands milliseconds after ready.

Sharing needed a new opt-in. build_snapshot coalescing deliberately refuses
to hand a caller a build that started before it arrived; under that rule a
prewarm would make the boot hydrate wait for it AND then pay a second
build — strictly worse than no prewarm. `accept_inflight=True` lets a
caller ride the running build, and the stream hydrate is the one caller
that may: its watermark comes out of the core it carries and the stream
tails from exactly that offset, so nothing is skipped, it only arrives as
the first delta.

Measured (live install, base profile, hydrate over a fresh serve child):
hydrate 15s after ready 3.61s -> 2.13s (build_ms 3486 -> 2011); hydrate
immediately after ready 6.74s -> 6.54s median of 3, i.e. unchanged — the
prewarm is shared, not doubled. The boot-path win from T2 alone is small
by construction and stays that way until the launcher stops serializing
first paint behind serve (T6).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
perf(vision): answer the capability check without building a client

T4a of the 2026-08-09 Mission Control startup analysis. `check_vision_
requirements` is a registry check_fn: one cold snapshot build runs it ~1,050
times (once per gated toolset per persona), and it answered by resolving a
REAL provider client — lazy openai SDK import, keepalive httpx client, TLS
context, Codex OAuth token handshake. cProfile put 1.5s of provider-client
construction inside a read-only projection. Same disease the 2026-07-08
chat-lane fix retired (shared_ssl_context, per-turn client rebuilds), one
layer down; recurrence is the finding.

The resolution authority does not move. A probe runs the same resolver,
the same fallback chain including the auto step #31179 added, inside
`capability_probe_scope()`; only the terminal construction is replaced by
an inert stand-in. Attribute access on the stand-in yields the stand-in
(thin wrappers read .api_key/.base_url while they construct, and a probe
that raised there would report "unavailable" for a backend that IS
available — the exact false negative #31179 fixed); CALLING anything
raises, so one that ever escaped into a request path fails loudly instead
of hanging. Nothing resolved during a probe may enter the shared client
cache — guarded twice, since the resolver wraps what it built.

Pinned structurally, not by wall clock: `client_construction_count()` is a
counter on the construction seams, and the pins assert a zero DELTA across
the check on a fixture that deliberately routes into the branch that DOES
construct (Codex credentials present), plus a guard-on-the-guard test
proving that route constructs when not probing.

Measured (live install, base profile): check_vision_requirements 1.96s ->
1.47s cold with 0 constructions (1 before); cold build_snapshot 6.08s ->
5.54s median. The 1.5s in the analysis was cProfile-inflated; the honest
figure is ~0.5s per cold build, and the invariant is what stops it
returning.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo

test(vision): pin the probe's HTTP-client seam separately

The probe has two sufficient mechanisms (the SDK-construction proxy and

left the suite green. This pins the second one on its own guarantee: a

author: nekwo
message:
fix(send): bound the operator turn per envelope, record the wire, drop the wasted construct

Four items from PERF_SEND_ANALYSIS_2026-08-09 (launcher f587e841).

T4 - record the WIRE, not the composition. `final_model_input` captured
`request.user_message`, the text the turn COMPOSED, while the persona-chat
persistence boundary rewrote the live actor's row in place before the first
provider call. The record therefore showed a 56 KB user turn the provider
metered at 4.2k tokens, which is how T1 below ran live and invisible. The
capture now reads the agent's own current-turn row and carries a typed
`user_message_wire` receipt (source / composed_chars / wire_chars / bounded,
or a named unavailable_reason) so a fallback to the composed copy is never
silent. `context_budget` gains two typed alarm rows that ride the existing
`chat.final` frame: `estimate_drift_alarm` (the drift ratio existed and
nothing read it - 5.48 sat in the record on the 200k turn) and `wire_drift`,
the exact companion, raised when composed and wire chars disagree.

T1 - one flat 20,000-char cap was applied to a COMPOSED row whose three parts
have three different contracts (message . skill_preload . runtime_context),
and it mutilated all three: the model received 37% of a required skill cut
mid-sentence, the runtime HUD never arrived at all on big-preload personas,
and the amputated `</skill_preload>` closing tag made the `unchanged` dedupe
structurally unreachable, re-shipping ~3.7k tokens every turn forever. The
row is now bounded PER PART under one 256 KiB ceiling, served in priority
order: HUD first (smallest, load-bearing), operator text second (never cut
without the explicit in-band marker), preload last (largest, and the only
part with its own re-delivery machinery, so it absorbs the remainder). An
over-budget envelope is shrunk through its BODY via a codec that owns the
grammar, so tags and attributes stay byte-exact and the dedupe keeps working;
a part that cannot survive at all is dropped and reported, never mangled.
Rows carrying no envelope are bounded exactly as before.

T3 - `profile_runner` constructed an agent unconditionally (~1.4-1.8s, tool
setup dominated) and then threw it away whenever the resident registry reused
one, because `factory=lambda: agent` was not lazy. The seven turn-scoped
values `_prepare_resident_persona_chat_agent` wanted from that throwaway are
resolved from the REQUEST instead, so construction now happens only on a miss
or rebuild. On reuse `agent_construct_ms` is absent rather than reporting
discarded work; `resident_actor_reused` says why.

T6 - memoize the runtime resolution for an unchanged (profile, provider,
model, config) tuple. The TTL is a safety bound, not a tuning knob: the
resolver refreshes OAuth tokens within a 120s skew, so a 30s TTL guarantees
any handed-out token still has >=90s of validity. config.yaml/.env stamps
join the key so an operator edit invalidates immediately.

Not implemented here (operator decides personally): T2 MCP admission reuse,
T5 compaction default, T7 tool-schema budget.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(send): pin the wire row, the per-envelope bound, and the two reuse seams

Written against the completed implementation and red-proved by reverting each
covered line, per the repo's implement-then-test discipline.

Fixtures are chosen so broken and correct genuinely differ. Every T1 fixture
uses a 54,114-char preload (the measured qa `launcher-stagec-mcp-screenshot`
size) inside a well-formed envelope with a distinctive tail marker, because a
fixture under the retired 20,000-char cap makes the amputating boundary and
the fixed one identical and would pass either way.

The T3 refresh pin asserts the OUTCOME (turn 2's listener receives turn 2's
tool event) rather than the wiring: `_finish_resident_persona_chat_agent`
detaches every callback after a run, so a resident holding turn 1's stale
handle would still read non-None from outside and a "a callback is attached"
assertion would pass against exactly the bug it is meant to catch.

The T6 TTL-under-refresh-skew invariant is pinned structurally, not
behaviourally: the credential is opaque at this layer, so no unit test can
observe a token going stale. Pin the rule instead.

conftest gains an autouse reset for the new runtime-resolve memo. It keys on
(profile home, provider, model, config stamps), none of which distinguish one
test's monkeypatched resolver from the next test's — without the reset a suite
that patches two resolvers for the same provider/model silently reads the
first one's answer.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(harness): stop gating wait=false dispatch on the hot-sessions cache flag

agent_chat_send(wait=false) has refused every dispatch on the serve lane
since the day it shipped (2026-08-03): the mission-chat capability binding
required persona_chat_runtime_registry() to be non-None, believing the
registry "tells serve from CLI". It does not — the registry exists only
when agent_runtime.persona_chat.hot_sessions_enabled is set, an unrelated
resident-agent cache policy that defaults to False and is off in the live
root config. So every default-config serve bound declare_stateless_channel()
and the tool returned async_delivery_unavailable with the drain alive and
perfectly able to deliver. Zero dispatches were ever recorded on the live
install outside ship-day probes; none was ever delivered.

The capability now gates on the one fact it promises: delivery_drain_is_live().
The drain starts in exactly one place (the serve loop), so its liveness
already distinguishes serve from a one-shot CLI; the registry conjunct
added nothing but the false refusal.

Also: a drain that fails to start now logs at WARNING, naming the lane it
disables — at debug it was invisible in every live log, which is why this
took an operator incident to find.

Live incident: 2026-08-09 Mission Control operator turn, Neko Mission Lead
-> personainst_backend_dev_agent_29fdd71a. Investigation doc lands in the
launcher repo (docs/mission_control/DISPATCH_LANE_INVESTIGATION_2026-08-09.md).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(harness): read mission-chat lease provenance from the serve request id, not the cache flag

Second instance of the proxy retired in 506e16272, and recurrence is the
finding: the message-turn root lease labelled its observer
"serve" if persona_chat_runtime_registry() is not None else "cli" — the
hot-sessions cache flag again, default off and off in production — so every
live serve turn wrote observer_kind=cli into the lease owner file, the exact
forensics a chat_busy incident reads (and 2026-08-09 had one). The same line
also read args.serve_request_id for the lease owner id, an attribute nothing
in the tree has ever set, so every owner file carried the pid-<n> fallback
instead of the request correlation the name promised.

Both fields now come from one authority: serve's per-request ContextVar,
exposed as current_serve_request_id(). Non-None is direct provenance that
the turn arrived as a serve frame request — a serve whose delivery drain
died is still a serve, which is why this reads the request id and not
delivery_drain_is_live(); provenance and capability are different questions.
The request id doubles as the lease owner_id, so a chat_busy refusal's
lease_owner block now names the frame that holds the root.

Decision extracted to _mission_chat_lease_provenance() and pinned red-first:
serve turn observed as serve with hot_sessions_enabled=False (registry has
no vote), and a cache-enabled CLI turn still reads cli.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
perf(send): chat-lane compaction default + measured MCP admission attribution

T5 gives the mission-chat lane a compaction threshold it can reach. The lane
inherited `compaction_ratio x window` = 892,500 tokens on a 1.05M model, a
bound a chat root reaches approximately never, so long roots grew linearly and
one tool-heavy turn on a 200k root metered ~826k prompt tokens against the
subscription's weekly limit where a fresh thread meters ~50k.

`agent_runtime.mission_chat.compaction_threshold_tokens` (default 150,000) is
applied through `ContextCompressor.threshold_tokens_cap`, so it can only make
compaction fire EARLIER: a small-window model keeps its own, already lower,
threshold. `0` disables it and is honoured verbatim rather than being folded
back into the default by `_clamped_positive_int`. An explicit
`--compression-threshold-tokens` still wins in both directions, through the
same single write path.

The receipt is fixed alongside it: `context_budget.compaction_tokens` was a
`window x ratio` derivation that could not see the cap, so it would have
rendered "compaction at 892,500" for a root the compressor compacts at
150,000. The turn now records what the live compressor holds and the budget
prefers that reading, labelled by `compaction_basis`.

T2 asked for an admission-outcome cache on the premise that per-turn
re-registration costs 2.35-3.4s. Measured against a real 60-tool stdio MCP
server: a WARM re-registration of all 60 tools is 6-8ms and teardown is
0.2-0.3ms; a COLD admission (spawn + handshake + tools/list) is 3,197ms. The
analysis' three probe turns each ran in a fresh CLI process, so all three paid
a cold spawn and reported turn-1 numbers as steady state. A cache of tool
definitions cannot remove a spawn, so it would buy ~6ms in exchange for a new
leak surface on the cross-persona isolation chokepoint. Not built.

Built instead: the attribution that makes the claim checkable in production.
`McpAdmissionOutcome.transport_paths` records warm/cold per server, observed
under the admission mutex before anything is registered, and the turn's
profile_timing carries `mcp_admission_transport` /
`mcp_admission_cold_servers`. Nothing persisted this before, which is why the
live 3.4s could only ever be inferred.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
docs(send): record the T2/T5/T7 decisions and the measurements behind them

T2's cache was refused on measurement (warm re-registration 6-8ms vs a 3,197ms
cold spawn), so the reasoning belongs where the next session will look: the
admission design doc's performance section, next to the consequence that
already predicted it ("persistent-within-serve, not per-turn").

T7 built nothing, which means the reasoning IS the deliverable. A registry
census says 74% of the lane's schema bytes are core tools that
tools/tool_search.py refuses to defer by design, and that deferral machinery
already ships enabled by default -- so the mechanism T7 proposed is running on
everything it is allowed to touch. Deferring further costs a discovery round
trip that re-meters the whole prompt, which is net negative on the persona that
has the tools; the only remaining lever is per-persona tool restriction, the
thing tonight's ruling removed.

Also refines the T5 receipt: `applied` now describes whether the cap GOVERNS
the root rather than whether this call moved a number, because a resident actor
is reused across turns and the did-it-change reading reported the cap as
inactive -- and blamed the model -- on every turn after the first.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(runtime): arm the venv barrier at the turn loop so the CLI lane is covered

ProfileAgentRunner.run armed deny_venv_installs for every HARNESS lane, but the
CLI-interactive lane (hermes chat -> HermesCLI.chat -> AIAgent.run_conversation)
never routes through that runner, so it ran live turns with lazy installs still
permitted — the exact shape of the 2026-08-09 incident, where a mid-turn pip
install of a provider SDK rewrote the interpreter the turn was executing in and
took Mission Control down.

agent.conversation_loop.run_conversation IS the turn loop and is the one
function every lane reaches (AIAgent.run_conversation is its only non-test
caller, and harness / CLI REPL / gateway / ACP / one-shot / delegation /
background review all go through that forwarder), so it becomes the arming
site. The body moves to _run_conversation unchanged; the public name is now a
thin barrier wrapper.

Two details that are not incidental:

- The reason string is INHERITED when an outer scope already named one. The
  barrier reports the innermost reason, so a generic inner scope would erase
  "profile='base'" from the operator-facing refusal. Re-using the outer string
  rather than SKIPPING the inner scope is deliberate: skipping would leave a
  turn on another thread unprotected the moment the outer scope exited.
- The barrier stays per-TURN. hermes tools / setup / doctor --fix / postinstall
  are top-level commands with no turn on the stack and keep installing, and
  durable-target installs stay allowed even under the barrier.

Tests: the wrapper arms and releases (including on a raising turn), the outer
reason survives both the inner arm and the inner release, every turn argument
is forwarded and the two signatures stay in lockstep, operator installs reach
the real installer before and after a turn while the same call during one is
refused, and two AST pins — that _run_conversation has exactly one caller (no
future bypass of the wrapper) and that AIAgent.run_conversation still delegates
here (the claim that makes this site cover the CLI lane).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent): point the Nous OAuth-401 guidance gate at the whole turn loop

`run_conversation` became a thin venv-barrier wrapper and the loop body moved
to `_run_conversation`, so two gates that assert guidance strings via
`inspect.getsource(conversation_loop.run_conversation)` went red on a pure
refactor — the strings never moved out of the turn loop, only out of that one

Worth naming: a gate that greps a function's own source proves the text exists,
not that the branch runs, and it breaks on any restructuring of the function it
watches. These two survive because the guidance really is a literal, but the
class is fragile — a behavioural assertion on the 401 path would be the durable
version.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(runtime): name the persona-chat wire boundary, and give the contract version an owner

Three weakness escalations raised on 2026-08-09, all the same shape: a guarantee
pinned at the wrong level, so the pin rotted while the guarantee held.

WIRE BOUNDARY. `persona_chat_continuity._MAX_CONTENT` read as a persistence bound
and silently governed the wire: the crash-resilience flush in `run_agent` hands
each row through the boundary and writes the result BACK into the live actor's
message list, before the first provider call of the turn. The per-part fix landed
in 23c684cb3; what did not land was an invariant, so every future change to a
bound could still change the prompt silently.

`safe_native_message` is promoted to a named boundary, `native_wire_row`,
returning a typed `WireBoundaryRow` carrying submitted / redacted / wire lengths
and the notes explaining every character between them. The invariant is
`unaccounted_loss == 0` — NOT "wire == submitted", which could never hold because
shortening is the boundary's job, and which is exactly why the previous receipt
could report drift and never prevent it.

Three of the four roles were still losing content silently: assistant, tool and
system rows took a flat 20k cut with no note, no log, no receipt. So did every
tool-call argument blob at 4k. Both are now accounted. Argument loss is reported
separately and never netted into the content arithmetic — summing them would let a
truncated argument cancel a real content residue and drive the residue to zero, a
check that hides what it exists to find.

Production reports through `record_wire_boundary_drift` (typed row + logger.error)
rather than asserting: the flush runs on the live turn loop, and raising would
convert an accounting bug into a lost turn on a healthy conversation. The hard
assertions live in the new unit tests over the pure boundary, where they cost
nothing. `safe_native_message` survives as the plain-row wrapper, so no existing
caller changes.

CONTRACT VERSION. The snapshot contract version had no owner: restated in eight
places, and the restatements rotted on a schedule — the 52->53 landing moved two
of six literals and left four red on main for five days; the 53->54 sweep found
eleven more still at 52. Every one was a NEGATIVE gate ("this cut did not move the
contract") written as an absolute number, so unrelated bumps made true statements
go red and taught readers that a contract failure is routine noise. A gate readers
re-baseline is not a gate.

`agent_runtime.snapshot.SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION` is now the single producer-side
authority. Thirteen sites across twelve test files derive from it (eight genuinely
red at 52). Exactly one test states the literal, deliberately, with the cross-repo
checklist attached — the Launcher's `kSupportedMissionContractVersion` requires
exact equality, so a one-sided bump makes every live frame read stale. An AST gate
fails if any other module states it; substring matching would not do, since the
number appears in prose in a dozen docstrings and inside assertions that are
themselves gates.

FIXTURE GATE. `test_response_contract_fixture` hashed each fixture against a
manifest generated from those same bytes and checked four structurally-invariant
scalars — so `work_list_empty.json` advertised the `mcp_server` running-work source
through the whole of contract 53's removal of it, gate green, while its sibling
stream gate went red in the same window for the one reason that matters: the stream
gate re-runs the producer. This one now does too, via the generator's own
`_parser`/`_run` so gate and regeneration path cannot disagree. The manifest check
survives, demoted and labelled as the hand-edit tripwire it always was.

One real finding while wiring it: `running_work` mixes contract with ambient
filesystem state in its `detail` prose ("head_home=hermes; no state.db"), and
whether the suffix appears depends on whether a module that opens a state.db was
imported before the home was isolated — same producer, same contract, two outputs
decided by test import order. The suffix vocabulary is pinned rather than
regex-stripped, so an unknown suffix fails instead of being swallowed. The
underlying mixing is filed, not fixed here.

S55 WITNESS. The gate was already AST-based; its WITNESS matched source text, and
a cosmetic reformat broke it (ec1dd3498 kept three calls on one line to appease
it). The guarantee is real — the runner supplies the label, the sink never writes
it, which is why the resolver cannot see these three types — but line layout was
never part of it. Converted to AST, plus a permanent red-proof driving the same
helpers over deliberately reflowed source and over prose that must NOT satisfy
them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(harness): re-aim four gates from a function's neighbourhood to its guarantee

All four asserted on `inspect.getsource(<one function>)` and a substring. Each
guarantee was intact; each gate was measuring where a line of text happens to
sit, and three were red on `main` because a refactor moved the code one function
over.

`test_s56_config_block_removal::test_the_roster_section_is_emitted_unconditionally`
calls itself a COUNTERFACTUAL PROOF that six live profiles gain the roster, and
inspected `snapshot._build_snapshot_uncoalesced` — but the emission now lives in
`_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope`. It proved nothing about the roster. The
counterfactual is now RUN: a config with no `enterprise_worker_sessions` block at
all (the shape those six profiles carry) must still produce `persona_instances`
and a truthful `persona_instance_runtime`.

`test_s47_wire_constant_field_removal::test_status_no_longer_forwards_a_task_list_to_the_channel_projection`
had the identical break: it required an `operator_channel_summary` call inside
`status.build_status`, and the call moved to `_build_status_in_runtime_scope`.
Re-aimed at the module AST, which is strictly stronger than the old scan — a
forwarding call added to a sibling function was previously invisible — plus a
behavioural assertion that the projection still happens.

`test_s56_worker_session_lane_removal::test_the_snapshot_contract_version_moved`
parsed `int()` out of source lines. This one broke on the contract-version
authority landing in the previous commit: the envelope now reads a named
constant, and the parse blew up on `SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION` — a false red
against a version that had not moved. Both halves survive, each asserted against
what it is about: the FLOOR on the number and on a built frame, and "not a second
copy" on the AST (the envelope must reference a Name, never restate a literal).

Also narrows the previous commit's contract-version gate from all comparisons to
EQUALITY comparisons. An equality pin rots at the next bump; an ordering floor
("never regressed below 47") stays true across every bump and is a guarantee the
removal-contract tests legitimately own. Flagging floors would have pushed their
authors toward allowlist entries for literals that were never a hazard — the gate
found this itself, on the re-aimed s56 assertion above.

SWEEP. 62 `inspect.getsource` uses across 32 files in tests/agent_runtime: 31
module-scoped (a move within the module is invisible to them, so low risk) and 22
function-scoped across 13 files. A scan for "asserted literal absent from the
inspected function but present elsewhere in its module" flags 16 sites; all but
the ones fixed here are NEGATIVE assertions (`not in`), which absence correctly
satisfies — `test_s48_cli_entity_row_consolidation` is green for that reason.

RED-PROOF, sabotage-verified with file backups (never `git checkout --`), each
reverted:

* roster gate — regressing the runtime block to `{"enabled": False}` fails the
  new assertion; deleting the emission from the runtime-scope function fails it
  too. The old text gate was falsely RED on pristine `main` while the behaviour
  was intact (verified on a detached worktree at ec1dd3498), and by construction
  would have stayed GREEN had the emission been deleted while a matching string
  survived in the inspected function.
* contract authority — bumping `SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION` 54 -> 55 fails exactly
  ONE test, the deliberate pin, while 56 others including every consumer travel
  for free. Planting `== 52` back into `test_stage19_visibility` fails the AST
  gate naming that file and line.
* s47 — the re-aimed assertion is green on the restored tree and the module-wide
  scan covers strictly more call sites than before.

NOT FIXED, and reported rather than touched: `test_s55` is red on `main` for
`persona_assignment.created` — a registered event type with no production
emitter. `6b9a27a74` (s70, retire the free-floating assignment lane) deleted the
emitter and left the registration, which is precisely the S24->S25 / S43->S44
pattern that gate exists to catch, so the gate is correct and the defect is real.
De-registering moves `contract_hash()`, which is stamped on every live persona
instance, and `persona_chat_history` still reads the type in two places — a
contract-affecting change in the dispatch lane's owner's territory, needing its
own ruling.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(harness): derive the snapshot reachability roots instead of restating them

Three red gates, one root cause each, all in the same family as `a20973d03`: a
test that froze an answer instead of asking the question.

`test_s27_snapshot_orphan_tree_removal::test_no_module_level_name_is_unreachable_from_the_external_surface`
and
`test_s29_snapshot_dead_local_removal::test_the_reachability_roots_are_back_to_the_real_external_surface`
both walked reachability over `agent_runtime/snapshot.py` from a HARDCODED
five-name `roots` set — the module's external surface as hand-verified once, at
S27. `hermes_cli/harness_parts/serve.py:629` later grew a function-local
`from agent_runtime.snapshot import snapshot_build_context_scope`, used at :631,
and both gates began naming that live, called context manager as an unreachable
module-level orphan. The helper is not unreachable; the root set was stale by
construction, and a cut driven by that verdict would have deleted production
code with a caller.

The surface is now DERIVED from the production tree. An `ast` walk over
`agent_runtime`, `hermes_cli`, `gateway`, `agent`, `tools`, `cron`, `providers`,
`scripts`, `apps` and the repo-root modules (852 files; `tests/` excluded on
purpose — a test pin is not a caller, which is S29's own thesis) collects every
`from agent_runtime.snapshot import X` and `from .snapshot import X` at any
depth, function bodies included, plus `snapshot.X` attribute loads in files that
bind the module. It resolves 13 external names where five were written down:
the five, `snapshot_build_context_scope`, `SnapshotBuildContext`,
`_board_card_row`, `board_summary_row`, `office_summary_row`,
`_office_actor_summary_row`, `_realm_summary`, `_workspace_summary`. A consumer
added tomorrow roots itself.

ANTI-VACUITY, because an over-approximated root set can only hide an orphan and
"assert the empty list is empty" is the shape that passes forever after the
machinery under it dies:

* the derived set must be non-empty and must contain `build_snapshot`;
* the hand-verified five survive as a separately-asserted FLOOR (they were a
  ceiling before, and that ceiling is what produced the false accusation) —
  `test_the_verified_external_surface_is_still_external`, plus s29's pin that
  neither helper IT removed (`_open_incidents_frame`, `snapshot_section_bytes`)
  has re-acquired a production consumer;
* `test_the_reachability_walk_names_a_planted_orphan` runs the walk against a
  synthetic module carrying a genuine two-node island and requires it to name
  both, and to stop naming them once a root reaches one.

`test_s29::test_the_lookalike_live_locals_survive` is the third failure and a
straight repeat of `a20973d03`: it asserted
`"ensure_for_personas(agents)" in ast.get_source_segment(...)` of
`_build_snapshot_uncoalesced`, and the call moved one function over into
`_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope` (snapshot.py:497). The roster was untouched.
Re-aiming it at the new function name would reproduce the defect at the next
refactor, so the whole test is module-scoped and structural now: no call
anywhere in the module passes `tasks=` or `run_summaries=`; nothing binds
`tasks` / `workers` / `run_rows`; `derive_from_workers` is called nowhere; and
`ensure_for_personas` is still called with exactly one positional persona list
and no keywords — a second argument IS the retired worker seed returning, under
any name, in any function. Plus a behavioural half: a built frame still carries
`persona_instances`. The negative halves are strictly stronger than before —
a seed reintroduced in a sibling function was previously invisible to all of them.

RED-PROOF, sabotage-verified with file backups (`cp`, never `git checkout --`
or `git stash`), each restored and `git status` confirmed clean afterwards:

* PLANTED ORPHAN — a genuine two-function island appended to `snapshot.py` is
  named by BOTH re-aimed gates, by name:
  `['_planted_orphan_head', '_planted_orphan_tail']`. The walk resolves.
* ROSTER DELETED — replacing both `ensure_for_personas(agents)` call sites fails
  `test_the_lookalike_live_locals_survive` with "the persona-instance roster
  projection has left agent_runtime.snapshot entirely". Note the gate now
  requires ALL call sites to go, where the old one only watched one function.
* WORKER SEED RETURNS — `ensure_for_personas(agents, workers)` fails the
  arity assertion (`2 == 1`), which the old substring gate could not see at all.
* THE DERIVATION IS LIVE, NOT PERMISSIVE — deleting serve.py's import outright
  makes `snapshot_build_context_scope` a real orphan and both the floor pin and
  the reachability gate go red naming it. A gate that merely rooted everything
  would have stayed green. (First attempt at this sabotage renamed the binding
  with `as _gone`, which left the import intact — correctly still green; the
  sabotage was wrong, not the gate.)
* ANTI-VACUITY — pointing `_PRODUCTION_PACKAGES` at a nonexistent package makes
  the derivation resolve nothing, and three gates go RED ("the roots are empty
  and this gate would pass vacuously") instead of passing on an empty diff.

The synthetic-orphan fixture found one bug in itself on first run: a module-level
`ALIAS = _helper` binding is an unreferenced module-level name and the walk
flagged it, correctly. The fixture was wrong, not the walk; it now uses a bare
module-level call for the same purpose.

Per-file after: 6 passed / 6 passed. No production file is touched by this commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(harness): green main via a witnessed read-back exemption, and retire two zero-information gates

GREEN MAIN. `test_s55_registered_events_have_emitters` has been red on `main`
for `persona_assignment.created`. Ruling: do NOT de-register.

The investigation supports the exemption rather than the cut. `contract_hash()`
is stamped on every live persona instance, so de-registering invalidates stamps
across the install to satisfy a test. More decisively, the type is still READ:
`persona_chat_history` resolves it in the `_TRACE_EVENT_TYPES` fetch filter
(:563, :582, :626) and the `_trace_entry` mapping (:1551), which renders it as an
`assignment_created` harness-trace row. Both feed `persona_chat_trace_summary`,
which ships on the live snapshot AND status wire (`data['persona_chat_trace']`)
and reaches the Launcher. Rows written before `6b9a27a74` (S70, retire the
free-floating assignment lane) still carry it, so de-registering would break
reading real historical data.

Clinching it: the sibling `persona_assignment.closed` is STILL emitted
(`persona_assignments.py:1795`) and travels the identical reader. The two types
are read as a pair, so the consumer path is exercised in production today — this
is not a lane kept alive only by the argument for keeping it.

So: a retired producer with a live consumer, which is the inverse of the debt the
gate was built for (a shape the contract advertises that NO reader will ever
see). It goes in a SEPARATE allowlist, `RETIRED_PRODUCER_LIVE_CONSUMER_ALLOWLIST`,
because the existing one claims "the type arrives as data at the sink" and
folding these in would make the entry assert something untrue about itself.

The witness proves the CONSUMER, not the registration — registration is what is
being excused, so it cannot also be the evidence. It drives `_trace_entry` on a
historical row and asserts it resolves to `assignment_created`, checks the fetch
filter still admits the type, and asserts the sibling still has an emitter. Plus
`test_a_retired_producer_entry_is_dropped_once_an_emitter_returns`, so the
exemption self-destructs if a writer comes back, and an anti-overlap test.

TWO ZERO-INFORMATION GATES REPLACED. Neither was a weak test; each was an
assertion that could not fail, sitting where the real one goes and reading as
coverage to every audit that walked past.

`test_s54_individual_dead_symbols`: `assert "worktree" in
getsource(reap_orphan_worktrees)` — the substring is in the function's own `def`
line. Now runs the janitor with `dry_run=True` against an isolated root and
asserts its typed result, including that `capture_dir` still lands at
`wt_reaped_patches` (the "nothing is deleted with an uncaptured diff" guarantee
the two live incidents bought).

`tests/gateway/test_update_command`: `'"update"' in
getsource(GatewayRunner._handle_message)` — 71.8 KB of source containing that
literal many times over. Its comment also described a mechanism that no longer
exists: `_known_commands` is not a local of `_handle_message` any more, and the
function imports `GATEWAY_KNOWN_COMMANDS` from `hermes_cli.commands`. The test
was grepping a haystack as a proxy for a variable gone long enough for nobody to
notice. That registry is importable and `tests/cli/test_version_command.py`
already imports it, so there was never a reason to grep.

APPROVAL BYPASS GATE RE-AIMED (the worst offender on the ranked list).
`test_execute_code_approval_cluster` proved the approval PLUMBING was spelled a
certain way in source and proved nothing about whether unapproved code executes —
the exact change it must catch leaves the watched strings untouched. Added

author: nekwo
message:
test(quality): stop the source-grep test class from growing

A test that reads a function's TEXT and asserts a substring appears in it
proves the characters exist and nothing more. It never proves the branch
runs, and the class fails in both directions on this tree: three gates fired
FALSE RED on pure renames/code-moves (the test_s56 roster gate, two in
tests/agent/test_nous_oauth_401_guidance.py), and replaying a real collector
removal left an old positive gate FALSE GREEN while a correctly-aimed gate
went red.

The ruling, enforced here: ban inspect.getsource in tests unless the result
is fed to ast.parse and asserted against a resolved AST node, and forbid any
POSITIVE `in`-assertion over getsource output. The asymmetry is the point --
`not in` tombstone gates are untouched, because text absence is exactly the
guarantee they claim.

The gate walks tests/ with ast (it does not commit the sin it gates) and
models three things, because getting any of them wrong would make it the
disease it treats:

* TEXT vs TREE. ast.parse converts text to a resolved tree; ast.unparse
  converts it straight back, so a parse/re-render helper hands back text and
  its greps are greps. Helpers are classified kind-preservingly, which is
  what separates test_terminal_config_env_sync's _extract_dict_keys (parses,
  launders) from its _terminal_tool_env_var_names (regex-scrapes, does not).
* Scope-local taint. A module-wide taint set condemns every unrelated
  `result`/`src` in the file.
* Claim polarity. `if "x" in src: pytest.fail(...)` is a NEGATIVE claim
  wearing `in`; `if "x" not in src: pytest.fail(...)` is a POSITIVE one
  wearing `not in`. The ban is on direction, not syntax.

Existing violations are NOT migrated. 83 of them across 35 files are
ledgered in tests/source_grep_debt.txt, keyed path::qualname::assertion so
that editing a grandfathered file cannot re-bless a new violation in it, and
carrying no line numbers so unrelated edits never churn the register. The
ledger is closed to additions -- a new grep is a red build, not a new line --
and a paid-off entry left behind fails the gate, so the register cannot rot
the way the pins it retires did.
