author: nekwo
message:
fix(security): make TIRITH_FAIL_OPEN bind at all five readers, not one

hermes_cli/tips.py promises operators that TIRITH_FAIL_OPEN overrides the
tirith_fail_open config -- "a quick toggle without editing config.yaml".
Four of the five decision points that read the tirith flags could not see
it. Only tools/tirith_security.py::_load_security_config honoured the
override; cli.py, gateway/run.py and both tools/approval.py ImportError
lanes read hermes_cli.config directly. So the documented toggle bound in
one place and was inert in four -- and the two approval.py lanes, the ones
that actually gate a command, were among the inert ones.

Filed as future work in the commit body of 186ee3108, which fixed the
sibling honesty bug on the unsupported-platform arm. This is that seam.

hermes_cli/tirith_config.py states the three facts ONCE -- the default,
the tirith_enabled interaction, and the env override -- and all five sites
read it. Three named resolvers rather than one blob, because the callers
ask two different questions: tirith_enabled() / tirith_fail_open() are the
raw flags (tirith_security checks them independently), and
fail_open_when_scanner_unavailable() is the question approval.py's two
except-ImportError branches actually ask, named once instead of re-derived
twice.

Where it lives is a constraint, not a preference. Both approval.py readers
run precisely when `from tools.tirith_security import ...` failed, so the
seam cannot live there. It equally cannot live in hermes_cli/config.py:
measured, that module costs ~3.5s and ~199 transitive imports (urllib,
http.client, agent.*), and tools/__init__.py warns that subsystems load
tools while it is still initializing. The accessor therefore imports only
hermes_cli.config_defaults (pure data, +2 modules) and keeps the config
load lazy inside the resolvers. A subprocess test pins that importing it
does not pull in hermes_cli.config, and proves that pin is non-vacuous by
measuring both costs in the same probe.

Defaults are read from DEFAULT_CONFIG["security"] rather than re-typed, so
this is an accessor and not a fourth copy of the defaults. The truthy set
is deliberately {"1","true","yes"} -- narrower than utils.TRUTHY_STRINGS,
which also accepts "on" -- because that is the set the only binding reader
has always used; widening it would silently re-decide an operator's
existing value.

WHAT THIS CHANGES, precisely. With neither env var set, every site decides
exactly what it decided before; that is pinned by test. The live runtime is
in that state (no TIRITH_* in the environment, no `security:` section in
config.yaml), so nothing about the operator's current behaviour moves. Both
deltas require an env var to be set:

  * TIRITH_FAIL_OPEN=false + config fail-open + tirith unimportable: the
    two approval.py lanes now fail closed. That is the promise being kept,
    and it is what tirith_security already did for the same operator.

  * TIRITH_ENABLED=false + config tirith_fail_open: false + tirith
    unimportable: approval.py now ALLOWS where it used to block. This one
    is a loosening and is called out rather than buried. It removes an
    arbitrary asymmetry -- check_command_security already returns "allow"
    up front when scanning is disabled, so the *less* capable state (module
    missing) was the *stricter* one. Disabled now means disabled on both
    paths.

That second delta is why two existing tests needed a one-line change.
tests/conftest.py sets TIRITH_ENABLED=false for the entire suite to keep
tirith's auto-install off the network. That variable was previously
invisible to approval.py; now it is not, so it reached two tests whose
subject is the CONFIG value and forced fail-open. Both now delenv it, which
preserves their intent exactly. The hazard is worth naming: a global
fixture set for a network reason now has reach into approval decisions
across the suite.

gateway/run.py's startup heads-up was a bare condition ~250 lines inside
GatewayRunner.__init__ with no reachable seam, so its predicate is
extracted to a module-level pure _needs_risk_assessor_warning(config). The
decision is unchanged; a test pins the other two conditions to prove the
extraction did not re-decide anything.

Every site test pairs its override assertion with a near-miss run under the
same config and no env var, so a passing verdict has to come from the
override binding rather than from the config already agreeing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): make serve settle the delegation row it just delivered

`delegate_task` completions are persisted to `async_delegations` before they
are ever queued, and that row carries the whole delivery protocol:
`delivery_state`, `delivery_attempts`, `delivery_claim`, `delivered_at`. The
gateway (`gateway/run.py`), the interactive CLI (`cli.py`) and the TUI gateway
have always driven it through `claim_event_delivery` /
`complete_event_delivery` / `release_event_delivery`. Serve was the one
consumer that did not: `drain_background_completions` worked off the in-memory
`process_registry.completion_queue`, forged a real turn, and wrote NOTHING
back - counting attempts in a process-local dict instead.

So a serve-delivered delegation stays `pending / 0 / None` FOREVER, and the
durable row reports a delivery that demonstrably happened as one that was never
attempted.

That is not cosmetic. Live specimen, 2026-08-10: delegation `deleg_1f53b4be`
was delivered into the operator's own thread 8 seconds after it completed -
turn journal record `bg-completion-async_delegation:deleg_1f53b4be` with
`provider_submitted` / `native_committed` / `projection_committed` all true, the
`user` + `assistant` rows in `messages`, and a `persona_chat.projected` event at
14:03:39.8 - while its row read `delivery_attempts: 0`. An entire incident
investigation was routed by that row into concluding the drain had never run.
The forensics did not merely omit the truth; they asserted its opposite.

Two more things followed from the same missing write:

* Every serve delivery was re-armed for replay. `restore_undelivered_completions`
  selects exactly `state != 'running' AND delivery_state = 'pending'`, so serve's
  own successful deliveries are re-queued at the next boot and re-forged.
  Reproduced against a COPY of the live store: the boot restore re-enqueues
  `deleg_1f53b4be`, carrying the operator's live chat root. Only the chat lane's
  `client_message_id` replay dedup has been absorbing them - an idempotency
  guard silently doing a ledger's job, and only while the journal retains the
  record.
* Retention could not do its job. `_prune_durable_records` deletes
  `delivery_state='delivered'` rows first and otherwise evicts the OLDEST
  pending ones, so with nothing ever marked delivered the fallback is the only
  path and undelivered work is what gets dropped.

The fix consumes the EXISTING authority rather than adding a fourth spelling of
it. `tools/async_delegation` is upstream and is untouched here; the claim is
taken after the idle probe (never before - a burnt attempt for losing a race
with a live operator is the failure class the dispatch lane already had to fix)
and before the forge, and the outcome is written back to the row that owns it. A
claim this process cannot take means another consumer holds it or the row
already settled: the event leaves the queue rather than spinning on work
somebody else owns.

`MAX_BACKGROUND_DELIVERY_ATTEMPTS` now covers only the LEDGERLESS half of the
lane - `terminal` notifications and completions whose producer never persisted a
row. A durable row counts its own attempts, and two counters for one completion
is the second ledger this change exists to retire.

Tests were written after the implementation and watched fail against the
unfixed module first: acknowledgement on the row, no re-enqueue by the next
boot restore, no double delivery of a completion another consumer holds, and an
honest release-with-attempt on failure.

NOT yet in effect on the live runtime: the drain is a serve-process thread, so
this binds only at the next serve start. No restart was performed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): name the agent that owns a delegation, so its work can be seen

`running_work`'s delegation and terminal lanes built their rows with only a
`session_id`, so every one of them shipped
`owner: {persona_id: null, persona_instance_id: null}`. Mission Control's
Activity surface groups BY owner and discards rows whose owner key is empty --
so a background `delegate_task` could not appear there. Not late: never. The
chat-turn and dispatch lanes had always populated the block; these two simply
never asked.

They ask now, through the resolver that already existed. The
session -> owning instance -> persona_id derivation was open-coded inside
`dispatch_delivery._sender_persona`; it moves to
`persona_assignments.chat_session_owner_persona` and both callers defer to it,
so the delivery lane and the projection can never answer "whose work is this"
two different ways. `_sender_persona` stays as the delivery lane's local name.

An unresolvable session leaves the owner EMPTY. Fabricating one -- the parent's
persona, the active instance, anything plausible -- would be worse than the
original bug: a consumer can render "no owning agent", but it cannot un-believe
a name. That is now rule 5 in the module's honesty contract, and it cuts both
ways by construction.

The lookup takes a build-scoped memo (siblings from one conversation share a
chat root) and deliberately no process-lifetime cache, which would keep naming
a retired instance.

Proven across the repo boundary, because both sides were green while only the
join was broken: `hydrate_running_work_owner.json` is a new generated golden --
a real hydrate frame over a seeded root carrying one owned and one deliberately
unowned delegation -- mirrored byte-identically into the Launcher, which parses
it through its real read model. Reverting the producer line reddens the Dart
test; that round trip was run.

Contract 54 is unchanged: `owner.persona_id` / `owner.persona_instance_id` are
existing wire fields that stopped being null, so this is additive-compatible.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): make harness doctor derive its verdict from every section

`ok` was a hardcoded `True` on every path and `needs_fix` came from two of the
five sections the report ships, so a payload documenting a broken event log, an
unreadable model-authority config, or diverged persona bindings still announced
`ok: true, needs_fix: false`. That is the worst shape in this class: `harness
doctor` is the triage tool, so a false all-clear here terminates the
investigation that would have found the real defect.

Both flags are now derived from a `summary.section_health` map every section
contributes to. A section whose probe RAISED reports `health: "unknown"` plus
its error and clears `ok` without claiming a defect it never observed - the
orphan-sweep precedent in `cron/executions.py` (`status='unknown'`, "whether
side effects ran is unknown"). Model-authority notices stay informational and
move neither flag, as before.

The worktree sweep and `event_log_health()` ran unguarded and could crash the
whole doctor; both now report `unknown` instead. A `finding_counts` value is
`None` when its class was not observed, never `0`.

`_snapshot_null_id_defects` returned a snapshot build CRASH as one
`snapshot_null_id_rows` defect - the counter naming a defect class nobody
observed, sending an investigator hunting null ids in a frame that never built.
The build outcome now rides its own `findings.snapshot_build` section.

Text mode printed two counts and an event-log size, so three of the five
examined sections never reached the operator on the default path. It now leads
with the verdict and renders every non-ok section, the diverged-binding
remediation, and model-authority notices. `--json` gains a top-level `healthy`
mirror so `jq .ok` (command status, also spent on a refused invocation) cannot
be read as an all-clear.

Report `schema_version` 2 -> 3. This is the CLI doctor report, not the snapshot
wire: the Mission Control snapshot contract (54) and its launcher pin are
untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): stop reporting an unreadable chat as a successful empty one

`_safe_curated_messages` answered both a missing SessionDB and a raised read
with `[], "safe"` - byte-identical to a genuinely empty conversation, right
down to a `redaction_status` certifying content that was never loaded. The
reader packaged that as `ok: true, count: 0, total_count: 0, has_more: false,
redaction_status: "safe", messages: []`, so an unreadable transcript and an
empty chat were indistinguishable envelopes.

That is reachable against live SQLite under a running serve - lock contention,
corruption, schema drift - and it is confidently wrong in the worst direction:
an operator sees an empty chat and concludes messages were lost, and an agent
hunting a missing turn is told authoritatively there are none.

The helpers now return a third element: `None` when the transcript was READ,
otherwise a typed `{error_kind, detail}` block. The vocabulary is the one
`persona_assignments.py` already uses for this condition
(`session_db_unavailable`), plus `session_db_read_failed` when the read raised.
The redaction status of an unread body is `"unknown"`, never `"safe"` - a
verdict nobody was in a position to give. Shape follows the orphan sweep in
`cron/executions.py`: a typed unknown, never a plausible default.

Propagated at all three consumers, each of which would otherwise re-flatten
the failure into success:

- `persona_chat_session_messages` returns `ok: false` + `error_kind` and drops
  the success vocabulary entirely. The launcher's page collector already
  returns any `ok == false` envelope, and its refusal classifier defaults
  unknown `error_kind`s honestly.
- `harness persona chat history` (text mode) prints the read failure instead
  of "no messages for <session>" - the exact sentence that reads as data loss.
- `agent_chat_open` refuses instead of handing the calling agent `count: 0`
  over an unread thread.

Snapshot chat rows gain `messages_unavailable` (present ONLY when the tail
could not be read; the healthy frame is byte-for-byte unchanged) and no longer
fold an unread tail into a row-level `redaction_status: "safe"`. Both are
additive on an error path: the launcher tests for exactly 'redacted'/'unsafe'
with a safe fallback, so `"unknown"` degrades to "render normally" over an
empty body. Snapshot contract stays 54 and the launcher pin does not move;
surfacing `messages_unavailable` in Mission Control is owed follow-up.

Test-only churn: `_safe_recent_messages` / `_safe_curated_messages` gained a
third return value, so 27 existing unpack sites widen by one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): stop minting "caught up at byte 0" from an unreadable log

`events_watermark` swallowed `OSError` into `offset = 0` and shipped it as
`{"event_offset": 0}` - indistinguishable from a genuinely empty log, and
reachable on this runtime's platform under AV scanning or a share violation.

Zero is the single most damaging value that field can carry, because every
reader treats it as a real position:

- `read_model.read_projection` answers "no new rows" to every cursor, since 0
  is <= any `since_offset`.
- `read_model.apply_full_rebuild` persists 0 as the stored projection
  watermark.
- `stream_frames` resumes a tailer from byte 0 - a full log replay rendered as
  fresh activity at the root of every Mission Control surface.

`read_model.snapshot_watermark` documents this exact trap in its own docstring
while this producer was still minting one.

An unreadable log now yields `event_offset: None` plus `event_offset_error`,
and the parity envelope carries an `event_offset_unknown` warning on its
existing warnings channel. Each reader branches on the unknown rather than
guessing:

- `snapshot_watermark`'s fallback is `None`, not 0. Unknown stays unknown.
- `apply_full_rebuild` DELETEs the watermark row instead of storing 0. The
  absent row is already this table's typed unknown (`projection_watermark`
  answers `None`), and the column is NOT NULL, so 0 was the only alternative.
- `read_projection` will only claim "caught up" from a recorded position.
- `stream_frames` takes the resync lane it already has. `or 0` there also
  folded a MISSING watermark key into 0; `_resume_offset` separates both
  absences from "the head of the log". With no readable tail it emits liveness
  with an honestly null position and retries. When the tail becomes readable it
  re-baselines with a fresh full core tailed from THAT frame's own offset -
  resuming from the newly measured tail alone would silently drop whatever
  landed during the outage, and resuming from 0 would re-render the whole log.
  `heartbeat_frame` accordingly accepts `offset=None`.

Wire impact: additive on an error path. `watermark.event_offset` widens from
int to int|null and `event_offset_error` / the `event_offset_unknown` warning
code are new; the healthy frame is byte-identical. The launcher already reads
the field through `_intOrNull` and its `shouldApplySequence(null)` accepts the
frame, so a null degrades to "apply, do not order" rather than wedging. The
snapshot contract stays 54 and the launcher pin does not move.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): make background work visible to the stream and its completions deliverable

Two producer-side defects behind the 2026-08-11 Mission Control Activity
incident (a 20s terminal task rendered 'Terminal - running' minutes after
exit, and its notify_on_complete output never arrived anywhere):

1. stream watchdog blind spot: a background process start/exit rewrites
   processes.json (and a delegation dispatch/finalize writes
   async_delegations) with NO EventLog event, and _scope_fingerprint never
   statted those stores - so the last pre-exit running_work frame was never
   superseded and stream consumers rendered it indefinitely. The serve
   read-model cache adopted these stores on 2026-08-03; the push path now
   adopts them through the same one path authority
   (running_work_store_paths), including the SQLite WAL/journal siblings.
   Same class as the 2026-07-25 Chat History freeze the watchdog exists to
   prevent.

2. undeliverable terminal completions: a terminal spawned from a
   mission-chat turn wrote session_key '' (nothing ever bound
   tools.approval's session key on this lane), so its completion event
   resolved to no persona chat root, was re-queued by every 5s drain pass,
   and evaporated - ledgerless - on the next serve restart, taking the
   output tail with it. The same absence left the running_work row
   unattributable ('NO OWNING AGENT'), exactly as 1c0e95bc3 predicted.
   New chat_root_session_key_scope binds the run's root chat session id
   into upstream's own public set_current_session_key surface for the
   whole persona run (positive knowledge at spawn time - the drain's
   #64484 no-guessing rule stays intact). No upstream file is edited;
   ContextVar propagation to tool worker threads rides the existing
   propagate_context_to_thread copy_context mechanism.

Wire shape is unchanged: values only (session_key now resolvable, rows
now owned), so SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION stays 54.

Tests pin both halves and the join: the drain-side specimen event is
built by the REAL producer (_move_to_finished) keyed exactly as the
spawn-side test proves the terminal tool stamps it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent_runtime): pin the runner-level chat-root session-key binding

The scope unit test and the terminal-tool spawn test can both stay green
while the runner never enters the scope - this pins the join at
_execute_agent_run itself.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): make the delivery drain name the gate that bounced a completion

On 2026-08-11 a background completion (proc_379e2ddbbc4f) sat undeliverable
for ~5 consecutive drain passes while the operator's chat was provably idle,
and the gate that bounced it was structurally unknowable afterwards: the
per-pass tally was returned and discarded, every requeue logged nothing, and
no store recorded a considered-and-bounced event.

This adds accounting AROUND the decisions and changes none of them. Every
existing if / continue / completion_queue.put / claim / forge line still
executes on exactly the values it executed on before; the new call sites are
tagged [A] in-line so the split stays legible.

* `_probe_sender_idle` carries the typed reason behind `_sender_is_idle`'s
  bool - journal_inflight / journal_unreadable / lease_busy_owned /
  lease_busy_ownerless / lease_probe_error. The last is the discriminator this
  slice exists for: a lease held with NO readable owner file, repeated across
  passes, is the stale Windows byte-range-lock fingerprint.
* `_sender_is_idle` KEEPS its name, signature and semantics and stays the only
  function the decision consults - the drain's tests override that exact
  attribute, and re-routing the decision would have made ~11 of them vacuous
  while still printing green. Accounting reads a ContextVar stash after the
  fact and records `sender_busy:unprobed` when a test has overridden it.
* `_owns_event_with_accounting` replaces the ownership lambda so `not_owned` is
  visible: upstream re-queues a rejected event inside `drain_notifications`,
  where the caller cannot see it, and that closure is ours. No upstream file is
  touched.
* Bounded telemetry (<=32 outcome rows keyed by (event_key, reason), truncated
  details) plus a durable mirror at `<store_root>/dispatch_delivery_drain.json`
  - required, because the launcher's visibility probe runs `harness status
  --json` as a freshly spawned process where in-memory state does not exist.
  Written atomically, only on an outcome change or a 60s heartbeat, path frozen
  once at drain start so a HERMES_HOME flip mid-pass cannot scatter it. It is
  deliberately NOT in any freshness fingerprint: a file changing every <=60s
  there would hold the read-model cache permanently cold.
* `harness status --json` gains one additive `delivery_drain` key. Status is not
  the snapshot contract, so SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION does not move; the
  launcher's two status consumers read `runtime_health` / `agents` by name.
* The chat-root lease's release `finally` now WARNS on both swallowed OSErrors
  instead of `pass`. Control flow, ordering and exception disposition are
  byte-identical; this is the producer-side half of the stale-lock
  discriminator.

This slice SEES. It deliberately does not fix the stall.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent_runtime): pin the drain's accounting, and that it did not become the decision

Written after the implementation and red-proven one revert at a time, per the
repo rule: a test authored green-first in the same commit as the code encodes
the author's belief rather than the behaviour.

The load-bearing one is the decision-not-changed guard. ~11 tests in
test_dispatch_delivery.py override `_sender_is_idle` BY NAME; if the drain's
decision stopped routing through that exact attribute they would all pass
vacuously while still printing green. That test asserts BOTH halves — the
override still requeues the event, AND accounting recorded
`sender_busy:unprobed` rather than quietly re-probing.

Two corrections against the design's expectations, both verified in
`process_registry.drain_notifications`:

* `owns_event` is consulted ONLY for events that carry routing metadata
  (`session_key` / `origin_ui_session_id`) or are async_delegation. A
  `session_key: ""` completion — the pre-c5d11f5cf live shape — is therefore
  handed over as a legacy ownerless event and bounces one layer further in, at
  the loop's own re-check, as `no_root`. `not_owned` needs a NON-EMPTY but
  unresolvable key. Both are pinned, each on the input that can actually reach
  it.
* The JOIN test asserts the delivery marker at `mission_chat_reply`'s
  `relay_sender_marker`, not on a persisted SessionDB row: since native session
  continuity landed, the mission-chat lane does not append the user row itself
  — the runtime persists it and `stage_persona_chat_user_row_marker` types it
  from exactly that value. With the provider stubbed (the only stub in that
  test) the persisted row is not written at all, so asserting on it would have
  pinned nothing.

The JOIN test otherwise runs the whole road in one process: a REAL persona
instance, a REAL `sleep 1` spawned through the process registry inside
`chat_root_session_key_scope`, the real queue, the real
`_chat_root_of_completion` / `_sender_persona` / `_sender_is_idle`, and the
real `forge_delivery_turn`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent_runtime): hand the process-global registry back exactly as found

The JOIN test spawns a REAL background process, and `process_registry` is a
module singleton whose `_running`/`_finished` maps outlive any tmp home. The
finished session left behind became a row in every projection this process
built afterwards, which reddened `test_response_contract_fixture` seven test
files later in a full-package run while every focused run stayed green — the
worst shape of test pollution, because the failure names an innocent module.

Snapshot-and-restore in a fixture rather than a trailing cleanup call, so it
still runs when the test fails.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): stop reporting a delivery nobody could see as a delivery

A forged turn coming back `ok` proves the TURN ran, not that the operator saw
an answer. On 2026-08-11 a completion notice landed in the operator's thread and
the delivery turn's model returned no content three retries deep, so the reply
was empty — while the log line, `last_delivery` and `harness status` all
reported a clean delivery. The mechanism worked perfectly and only the report
was false, which is the harder failure to catch: everything upstream succeeded.

Both drain lanes now classify a successful forge and record `delivered_silent`
when the reply is empty, logged at WARNING and carried on `last_delivery.reason`
so the field a human reads first cannot mislead. Settlement is deliberately
unchanged — re-queuing would re-forge into the very transcript that produced the
silence, once per pass, with a duplicate notice per lap.

Missing evidence is not evidence of silence: a payload with no `reply` key stays
`delivered`, because a caller-supplied forge may not report one and inventing
silence would be the same lie pointed the other way.

Known weakness left in place, deliberately: the mission-chat payload exposes no
typed "this turn produced visible content" signal, so the classification is
re-derived from reply text here and would be re-derived again by the next
consumer that needs it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): give "did this turn produce visible content" one owner

`ok: True` never meant "the operator saw an answer" — the mission-chat handler
returns exactly that with an empty `reply` when the model produces no content.
Nothing in the runtime had a NAME for that difference, so every lane that
needed it re-derived it from whatever evidence was in reach: the delivery drain
compared reply text to the empty string, cron treats an empty final_response as
a soft failure and writes an English sentence into `error`, cron-health reads
that sentence back with `if "empty response" in text`, the error classifier
keeps five phrasings of it, and the gateway has both a predicate and a prose
filter. Three of those match on prose, and they disagree about whether an empty
turn is an error, normal traffic, or something to suppress.

`agent_runtime/turn_visibility.py` computes it ONCE, from the strongest
evidence the runtime already produces — reply text, the final assistant
message's `finish_reason` (provider-derived and already persisted), and the run
result's failed/error keys. Nothing upstream is edited; this only reads what is
there. The handler stamps the typed block on every payload that carries a
reply — live turn, both idempotent replays, projection failure — and the drain
becomes a CONSUMER of it rather than a second derivation.

Unknown is a first-class state, not a bool's third case: a payload from a serve
that predates the block, or a forge that reports no reply at all, is `unknown`,
and unknown is neither visible nor silent. Only proven silence is reported as
silence. Truncation modifies emptiness and never overrides content — a cut-off
turn that still produced words is a short answer, not a silence.

Found while testing, and fixed here because it is the same defect one layer
down: the turn store could not RECORD a silent turn. `_safe_journal_metadata`
drops empty text for every field, which is right for an id or a fingerprint and
wrong for `stored_reply` — "replied with nothing" and "no reply recorded" are
different facts. The replay branch admits a settled turn on `stored_reply is
not None`, so a resent silent turn missed its own record, fell through to the
live provider path and died there as `chat_turn_not_submitted /
rejected_stale_transition`. The drain derives its client_message_id from the
dispatch id precisely so a retry converges on one turn; for silent turns that
convergence was broken. Absent still stays absent — the exemption is one field,
by name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): tell a dispatching agent WHICH kind of nothing came back

The detached-dispatch supervisor is the last process holding the child's
payload, and it recorded `ok` plus an empty reply the same way whether the
teammate answered with nothing or their answer never made it back. The sender
then read one blank for both, from a delivery block that could only shrug:
"They returned no reply text. Read the thread above, or re-dispatch." One of
those situations is worth re-dispatching and the other runs the same silent
turn again.

The supervisor now records the typed verdict it alone can see, read from
`agent_runtime.turn_visibility` rather than re-derived, and the delivery block
names the cause when it knows one — keeping the honest shrug when it does not,
because a row written by an older process carries no verdict and must not be
given one.

The verdict rides the completion's existing result blob, so there is no schema
to migrate and absent stays absent: the error paths, which never held a
payload, record nothing at all rather than claiming `unknown`.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): project the turn that ended without saying anything

A turn can settle in a state nothing calls terminal — it ran, it finished,
the store calls it completed — and still produce no printable text. Its
assistant row IS persisted, with a finish_reason explaining why, and
_curate_chat_message_text then dropped it. The transcript projected the
operator's message and nothing after it. Reopening the conversation showed
the same nothing, and a forged dispatch DELIVERY turn that ended this way
was never rendered at all, so a completion notice appeared to have been
answered.

Dropping empty assistant rows was not itself wrong. Across the operator's
live profiles 22,179 of them are intermediate tool-call rounds and 5 are a
real silence; rendering the majority would put a blank bubble under every
tool call. The defect was that nothing typed on the row separated the two,
so the 5 went out with the 22,179.

classify_persisted_turn_row reads the three columns the flush persisted and
answers with the existing verdict vocabulary, sharing the reason ladder with
the live classifier so a turn cannot be described one way live and another
on reload. A tool-call round gets None — not silent, not unknown, the
question does not apply — and an unexpected input gets None too, which is
exactly today's behaviour rather than a marker over a turn nobody proved
was silent.

The projection then synthesizes a typed turn_silent marker row, keyed per
LOGICAL turn (the live incident persists three empty rows for one turn and
two for the next), and only when the turn produced no visible reply at all
— a turn whose retry spoke is a turn the operator SAW.

Verified against the incident itself, profiles/base rows 2750-2758: the
same session projects 2 rows before and 4 after, each turn now followed by
its marker.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): the chat scope gains a per-conversation INSTANCE_RECORDED rung

The chat head is a PER-CONVERSATION fact — different personas legitimately
live in different profile DBs — so no machine-level pointer can answer it
alone. PersonaInstance now records the chat head home its conversation was
bound against (stamped by open_chat under any AUTHORITATIVE scope, re-affirmed
every turn because the send path re-enters open_chat per turn), and
resolve_chat_session_scope(session_id=...) consults that record between the
explicit env/relay rungs and the shared-root pointer.

The rung does double duty — resolve AND verify. A disagreeing AUTHORITY
(explicit head above, pointer below) yields a typed ChatScopeMismatch on the
scope instead of a silent preference for either side; the ambient guess
disagreeing with the record is NOT a mismatch — that rescue is the point.
Absence is modeled explicitly (UNRECORDED / NO_INSTANCE / UNRESOLVABLE /
RECORDED_HOME_MISSING) and falls through to the pointer exactly as before,
so pre-stamp rows and ambient-only binds are byte-identical to today.

Newly viable because the machine root anchor landed: finding the instance
requires store_root, which ambient processes now resolve via the anchored
config rung (verified live: an ambient probe from this worktree resolved the
shared-root pointer).

The stamp stays OFF the snapshot/patch wire (both are explicit allowlists)
and is safe on persisted rows in both directions (serde ignores unknown keys).

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): ambient_home stops being an answer for chat reads

Reaching the AMBIENT rung on a chat-history read means 'I do not know where
to look'; returning ok:true, count:0 from whichever state.db ambient
resolution produced is the whole silent-empty class (2026-08-12 incident:
one lost operator day, three investigations, two wrong root causes — every
probe that resolved its own root confirmed health).

persona_chat_session_messages now, when it self-resolves (session_db=None):

* resolves the PER-CONVERSATION scope (the new INSTANCE_RECORDED rung);
* refuses a typed chat_scope_mismatch when two authorities disagree about
  where the conversation lives, naming both heads — never a silent
  preference for either side;
* refuses a typed chat_scope_unresolved instead of reading the ambient
  guess, with the resolved chat_scope block riding the refusal so the caller
  learns WHY. Escape hatch for a deliberately single-root, serve-less setup:
  HERMES_ALLOW_AMBIENT_CHAT_READS=1 (plus a WARNING log on every allowed
  ambient read);
* stamps the ACTUAL conversation scope onto every envelope it returns —
  success and refusal — so an empty page always says which state.db answered
  (attach_root_observability at the verb never overwrites it).

Refusal placed at the read FUNCTION, not the verb or the resolver: the
resolver is shared with mint/write postures whose ambient semantics are
pre-existing and out of scope, while the verb-level-only alternative would
leave agent_chat_open and the live-log backfill consuming silent empties.
Consumer enumeration (CLI verb prints + exit 2; agent_chat_tool propagates a
typed refusal; chat_live_log backfill stops; the Launcher fetch lane maps
exit 2 to a retryable-error tile and always names an explicit head anyway)
shows every consumer degrades honestly, so the refusal ships default-ON.
Callers that pass their own session_db own the acquisition and are
byte-identical to before.

author: nekwo
message:
refactor(chat-scope): make the conversation an INPUT, and gate root re-derivation

`resolve_chat_session_scope(session_id=None)` defaulted the conversation away,
which made the wrong answer the one you got by typing less: a caller holding a
session id could omit it and resolve a different frame of reference. Because a
wrong root answers `ok: true, count: 0` rather than failing, the omission was
invisible at every layer above — the shape behind three 2026-08 incidents and
the fourth populated shadow runtime nothing pointed at.

`session_id` is now REQUIRED, and callers with no conversation in hand say so
by name through a new `resolve_process_chat_scope()`. Same ladder underneath;
what changes is that a session-less resolution is a decision you can grep for
instead of an omission nobody can tell apart from an oversight. A blank id
takes the process lane rather than falling through to the instance rung, so it
can never adopt some other conversation's recorded head.

Each of the six session-less sites now records WHY it is one. The binder in
`persona_assignments` is the interesting one: it holds `normalized_session`
right there, so omitting it would read as a bug. It is deliberate — that site
WRITES the INSTANCE_RECORDED rung, and a writer consulting its own rung would
let a stale head re-affirm itself forever instead of being corrected by the
pointer beneath it.

The CI gate (`test_hermes_home_env_gate.py`) fails on any fork-owned module
outside a justified allowlist that reads HERMES_HOME/HERMES_HEAD_HOME from the
process environment. AST, not grep — an earlier gate here matched the comments
describing what it forbade. It deliberately does NOT flag `.get()` on an
INJECTED mapping: `_hermes_home(env)` and the codex spawn builder take the
environment as a parameter, which is the remedy, not the defect. Three tests:
the offender check, an anti-vacuity check that a scan finding nothing fails,
and an anti-rot check that a stale exemption fails.

Also fixes `test_boot_timeline`, which failed this run. Two assertions read
`>= 15` after `sleep(0.02)`; Windows' ~15.6ms timer granularity returns 14ms of
monotonic time often enough to be a real flake. One now measures the sleep it
compares against. The other was worse than flaky — it was VACUOUS, passing just
as happily under an implementation that overwrote instead of accumulating; it
now sleeps twice so the two behaviours differ by 2x, proved by sabotaging
`phases()` to overwrite.

Red-proofed: an unsanctioned env read added to running_work.py turns the gate
red; a bogus allowlist entry turns the anti-rot test red; both restores verified
byte-identical by sha256.

tests/agent_runtime: 4842 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed (13 deselected: the
pre-existing slow test_s55). Affected hermes_cli suites: 15 passed.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): service foundations — version handshake, drain, auth token, discovery

Slice 2 of the durable runtime-root service (Launcher
docs/mission_control/DESIGN.md §10, settled 2026-08-12). All four land
BEFORE any socket exists, so the transport slice starts safe rather than
retrofitting.

The three costs that settled direction priced in, and what pays them:

1. A DURABLE SERVICE PINS STALE CODE. Today serve is a per-client child, so
   every launcher restart picks up landed fixes for free and nobody ever had
   to ask which code a runtime is on. A surviving service silently runs last
   week's — the shape of the dispatch dead-flag-proxy incident, which ran
   green for a week. agent_runtime/build_stamp.py resolves repo root (walking
   to a `.git` FILE too, because every agent works in a linked worktree),
   commit, tracked-only dirty state, and a monotonic-safe boot baseline, once
   per process and cached. It never raises: no repo, no git, a 2s timeout each
   yield a TYPED unknown carrying the reason. Absent means not measured —
   never a fabricated `dirty: false`, which would read exactly like a measured
   one and tell an operator "you are current" about a service that is not.
   Surfaced additively on the `ready` frame as `build`, re-askable at any time
   via the new `version` op, and in `harness status --json` as `runtime_build`
   — stamped with `answered_by` (cli|serve, from current_serve_request_id, the
   one honest serve-provenance fact), because the whole point is that the two
   readings disagreeing IS the staleness signal.

2. THE SECURITY ENVELOPE CHANGES. An inherited stdio pipe is effectively
   unforgeable; a named pipe/localhost socket is reachable by any local
   process, and this runtime executes agents with tools.
   agent_runtime/serve_auth.py mints a per-root 256-bit token at boot iff
   absent (O_EXCL, so a boot race adopts the winner rather than locking out
   its clients), takes the root as an INPUT, and fails CLOSED in `verify`.
   The value never enters a frame, a log, or an event — `ready` carries only
   `auth: {token_file: present|minted|error:<reason>}`. Unwired to any
   transport. The Windows ACL gap is documented honestly in the module
   docstring rather than papered over with a chmod that only toggles the
   read-only attribute.

3. DISCOVERY ACROSS ROOTS. QA lanes, isolated worktree roots and dev profiles
   legitimately coexist here, and "how many serves run against this root, on
   what code" had no answer at all. agent_runtime/serve_registry.py writes
   <store_root>/serve_instances/<pid>.json atomically at boot and removes it on
   every clean exit (shutdown AND drain). A crash leaves it — deliberately, so
   liveness is proven at READ time: alive + start-time identity + a serve-like
   command line, classified live | stale_dead_pid | stale_recycled_pid |
   unknown, with unknown as the fail-safe direction and never collapsed into
   live. Listing REPORTS; only `harness status --json --prune-stale` deletes,
   and only provably-dead entries, naming each one.

Plus the drain verb the same section demanded alongside the handshake:
`{"op":"drain"}` refuses new requests with a typed `draining` frame (and a
terminal exit 75 so clients predating the event cannot hang), lets in-flight
work land, and emits `drain_complete` with requests_refused / requests_completed
/ drain_ms before exiting 0. A bounded deadline emits `drain_timeout` naming the
stuck request ids and exits nonzero — a drain that can hang forever is not a
drain. The timeout path pulls a process-level lever on purpose: concurrent
futures' atexit hook JOINS worker threads, so a plain return would restore the
same "forever". Both process levers (`hard_exit`, `drain_wakeup`) are injected
and OFF by default, the same contract as snapshot_prewarm/root_anchor, so unit
tests observe frames and exit codes without exiting the test process.

Contract discipline: every frame change is additive (verified against the
Launcher's own frame switch, which ignores unknown events and unknown keys); no
EventLog event types were added; `serve_instances/` and `serve_auth_token` are
deliberately kept OUT of every freshness fingerprint — they churn at boot and
would hold the read-model cache cold, the same standing precedent as
dispatch_delivery.DRAIN_STATE_FILENAME.

Tests: 78 new across five files, written after the implementation and
red-proofed — 10 sabotage→RED→restore (sha256-verified byte-identical)→GREEN
passes covering -uno, the non-fabricated unknown stamp, verify's fail-closed
branch, mint-never-rewrites, the unknown classification, prune's dead-only
rule, the drain refusal actually blocking dispatch, the timeout lever, the
drained registry cleanup, and the --prune-stale wiring.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(root-anchor): the runtime declares its own head home

Slice one of the durable runtime-root service: "runtime owns its identity"
precedes "runtime owns its lifecycle".

`HERMES_HEAD_HOME=<root>\profiles\base` was a MACHINE fact recorded as a
string literal in a Dart client (`mission_control_settings.dart`). Only
launcher-spawned processes ever learned it; everything else degraded down the
chat-scope ladder — which is how a populated shadow runtime under
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` accumulated for a month with nothing pointing at it
(2026-08-12).

So `harness serve` now declares its own head, the same way it already anchors
its store root:

* `root_anchor` writes `agent_runtime.head_home` into the PLATFORM DEFAULT
  config.yaml when — and only when — this serve was started with an EXPLICIT
  head (env or relay, via the chat-scope authority's `explicitly_named`
  posture). A head resolved from the pointer, from a prior declaration, or
  from the ambient guess is NOT this process's own fact and is refused under
  its own name (`no_explicit_head`, carrying the rung it degraded to), because
  laundering a guess into a machine-wide declaration is the defect class this
  whole workstream retires. Same discipline as the store root: write only
  while absent, typed outcome on every exit path, re-parse verification, and
  a text-level merge that preserves the operator's bytes and line endings —
  both keys now share ONE `_merge_key` editor rather than two chances to get
  the operator's file wrong.
* New ladder rung `CONFIG_DECLARED`, below SHARED_ROOT_POINTER and above
  AMBIENT_HOME, reads it. It is AUTHORITATIVE (a recorded machine fact, not a
  guess) and earns its place by being reachable where the pointer is not: the
  pointer requires a resolvable store root — that is exactly how the shadow
  runtime hid — while the declaration sits in the config an environment-less
  process already opens. In the INSTANCE_RECORDED verification it is treated
  exactly like the pointer: a recorded instance head disagreeing with it is a
  typed ChatScopeMismatch, never a silent preference.
* The rung is SKIPPED when the process pins `HERMES_AGENT_RUNTIME_ROOT`. That
  is the rung's real domain, not a hedge: a pinned root can always reach the
  pointer above it, and an explicitly pinned root is a deliberate alternate
  resolution (tests, probes, persona isolation) that must not inherit a
  machine-DEFAULT fact. It is also what keeps this machine's own declaration
  out of every other test in the repo.
* The `root_anchor` serve frame carries the head outcome additively under
  `head`, so one line says what was declared vs found-already-present vs
  declined and why; a report without a head declaration emits the previous
  frame byte-for-byte.
* `harness status --json` now stamps `chat_scope`. Status is the ORIENTATION
  verb, and a runtime that declares its own head must be able to show which
  rung named it; the AST gate requires it from here on.

No new environment read: the head comes from `resolve_process_chat_scope()`,
the one allowlisted authority, so the HERMES_HOME env gate is untouched.

Tests written after the implementation and red-proofed by sabotage (8 lines:
the explicit-head guard, the key-parameterized never-overwrite, the rung
itself, the stale-declaration check, the pinned-root skip, the instance
mismatch branch, the frame block, and the status stamp) — each confirmed RED,
restored byte-identical by sha256, confirmed GREEN.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(root-anchor): declare what the MACHINE records, in one verified write

Three defects in the head-home declaration, all the same shape: a report that
reads as success without measuring anything.

1. The head block carried only `head_home` - the serve child's OWN head, which
   for a launcher-spawned child is the client's HERMES_HEAD_HOME pin travelling
   back through the environment. The Launcher's consistency check compared that
   against the pin, i.e. against itself, and confirmed. A config already
   declaring a SHADOW head under %LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes read as CONFIRMED
   (reproduced 2026-08-13), as did every outcome that wrote nothing. The block
   now carries `recorded_head_home`: what the machine-wide config actually holds
   after the attempt (ours on a publish, the operator's on operator_value_kept,
   the winner's on lost_race, null when nothing landed). Additive; `head_home`
   is unchanged.

2. `_merge_key` ran twice sequentially, once per key, each with a fresh read.
   Atomic rename prevents torn files, not LOST UPDATES: two serves booting
   together could land runtime A's store_root beside runtime B's head_home with
   both reporting `published`. The keys now merge in ONE read-modify-write
   (`_merge_keys`), and the file is re-read from DISK afterwards - a value that
   is not ours reports the new typed `lost_race` outcome instead of a publish.
   The old re-parse check verified the text we composed, never what landed. A
   best-effort O_EXCL lock beside config.yaml (stale-bounded, never blocking
   boot) narrows the window; the post-write read is what makes the report true.

3. The head lane checked `probe_isolation_required` but not the probe ROOT
   prefix the store lane refuses on. A serve on an isolated
   agent-runtime-probe-* root carrying an explicit HERMES_HEAD_HOME wrote a
   QA/worktree head into the operator's machine config - write-once, so
   permanently. The guard is now mirrored exactly. The reader's `layer == "env"`
   skip is deliberately NOT mirrored, with the reasoning in a comment: the
   Launcher pins HERMES_AGENT_RUNTIME_ROOT on every serve child, so refusing
   there would ship the declaration dead.

The two lanes now decide independently (`_store_plan` / `_head_plan`) and write
together, which is what makes the single pass possible.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(chat-scope): surface the declaration the pointer beat

When the SHARED_ROOT_POINTER rung wins, a CONFIG_DECLARED value naming a
DIFFERENT directory was never compared against anything and never reported:
ChatScopeMismatch models instance-record vs resolving rung only. The two
recorded authorities drift apart BY DESIGN - the pointer is rewritten on every
explicitly-headed serve boot, the declaration is write-once - so a machine whose
declaration has gone stale looks identical to one where both agree, right up
until the pointer stops answering and every chat read silently moves.

The losing declaration now rides the scope as `declared_head_home` with a
`declaration_diverges` flag, so `harness status --json`'s chat_scope block says
so. Both fields appear together or not at all: a bare `declaration_diverges:
false` with nothing behind it would read as a check that ran and passed.

Which rung WINS is unchanged - the pointer is the fresher fact and stays on top.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve-auth): a zero-byte token file self-heals instead of wedging the root

A process killed between the O_EXCL create and the write leaves an empty token
file. Under mint-iff-absent nothing ever repaired it: every later boot saw a
file that exists, reported `error:empty_token_file`, and every `verify` failed
closed against a token nobody could hold. Permanent, per root, and silent apart
from one status string.

An empty file's value is held by nobody, so replacing it cannot lock out a
reconnecting client the way rotating a real token would - which is exactly what
makes healing safe here and unsafe for a populated file. `_heal_empty` writes a
fresh secret to an O_EXCL temp and os.replace()s it, then RE-READS the file and
returns what is actually there, so two concurrent healers converge on one token
and neither reports a value it does not hold. The typed `error:empty_token_file`
state remains for the boot that cannot heal (an unwritable root) - the report
was right, only its permanence was wrong.

Public signatures unchanged (the socket lane is consuming this module).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(harness-status): stop rendering serves=0/0 for a read that never happened

When the serve-registry read throws, `_attach_runtime_service_blocks` sets
`serve_instances = []` plus a typed `serve_instances_error`. The --json consumer
sees both; the human line rendered `serves=0/0` off the empty list - not a
degraded measurement but a measurement that never ran, reporting the most
reassuring value available ("no serves, all accounted for"). An operator chasing
a serve that will not appear would read the failure as an empty registry.

It now renders `serves=unavailable(<error_kind>)`. This is S28's own rule
applied to a field that arrived after it: no constant dressed as a count.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve): a drain that ends quietly is the crash it exists to replace

Three defects on the drain lane, all of them silence where the design
promises an accounting. Two came from an independent review of slice 2;
the third was found live, by the first end-to-end drain this stack has
ever run against a real serve child.

1. A drain terminated by `shutdown` or by pipe EOF exited with NO
   terminal frame: both break the reader loop, which fell straight to
   `return drain_exit_code`, skipping `drain_complete`/`drain_timeout`,
   skipping `_unregister_instance`, and returning 0 even when the drain
   had TIMED OUT. `drain_finished` was declared and set and never
   awaited. The reader now waits a bounded moment for the monitor (the
   pool is already joined, so it is normally one poll away) and, failing
   that, publishes `drain_abandoned` — counters, elapsed, and a nonzero
   code — then unregisters. A supervisor can tell "drained" from "gave
   up"; it could not before.

2. `drain_complete.requests_completed` could UNDER-COUNT. The pop from
   `inflight` and the completion increment were separate critical
   sections, so a request could be in neither at once; the monitor,
   seeing an empty pending set, published fewer completions than the
   exits it had let land (reviewer: 5 reported for 8, 2 trials in 40).
   The counters are the drain's only evidence, and an under-count reads
   as work the restart dropped. Pop and count are now one critical
   section, lock order inflight_lock -> _DrainState.lock.

3. The forced exit sat BEHIND the wakeup, and the wakeup can block. On
   Windows, closing the protocol descriptor a reader is parked on does
   not return until that read does, so `hard_exit` was never reached: a
   child published `drain_complete`, released its lane, removed its
   registry entry — and then ran forever. The watchdog is now armed on
   its own thread before the wakeup is attempted, so nothing on the path
   to the exit can block. Measured: the child now exits 0 ~5.5s after
   `drain_complete`, where it previously never exited at all.

Plus the bookkeeping half of the same handover: `unregister_serve_instance`
now retries a transiently locked entry. On Windows a file created seconds
ago in a scanned directory is routinely held by the AV/indexer, `unlink`
fails with WinError 32, and the drain left the registry advertising a
serve that had just gone. Measured at ~16ms; one retry cleared it.
`FileNotFoundError` is not retried — already gone is a state.

Tests are red-proofed: each fix was reverted, its test observed RED, the
file restored and verified byte-identical by sha256, and the test observed
GREEN again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): the socket lane — one durable, multi-client service per root

Slice 3 of the durable runtime-root service. `serve_loop` stops being a
per-client stdio child and becomes a service other processes can find,
authenticate to, subscribe to, and restart — with the stdio lane
byte-identical for the Launcher, which migrates later.

ONE dispatcher, N transports. The op table moved out of the reader loop
into `_handle_line`/`_handle_message`; stdio passes `frames` and no
connection, so its frames, their order, and its exit codes are unchanged.
A second copy of the op table is the duplicated-authority shape this
stack keeps retiring.

Auth is first, and it is the only thing that is first. The FIRST line on
a socket must be `{"op":"hello","token":…}`, verified through slice 2's
`serve_auth.verify` (constant-time, fails closed). Before it is verified
a connection can do NOTHING: a wrong token gets one typed
`hello_rejected` and a close, proven by a test that pipelines a `version`
op and a request behind the bad hello and asserts the peer received
exactly one frame and no build block, no runtime root, no boot id.
Repeated failures trip a sliding-window rate limit. The token appears in
no frame, log, error, or registry entry.

One owner per root, decided by an OS-held exclusive lock (the locks.py
msvcrt/fcntl pattern) held for process lifetime. The loser does not fail
and does not retry: it runs stdio-only and SAYS so on `ready` —
`socket: {"outcome":"lock_held_by","pid":…}`. The winner publishes its
port into its `serve_instances/<pid>.json` entry (`transport`,
`port`, `socket_started_at` — always present, null on stdio-only, so
"no socket" is distinguishable from "predates the lane").

Subscriptions run ONE producer fanned out to N subscribers, never one
generator per client: a delta batch rebuilds a full snapshot core, so
per-client generators multiply the stream's dominant cost by the number
of clients. Each subscriber owns a bounded buffer and its own pump, so a
socket write that blocks blocks only that subscriber; overflow yields a
typed `subscription_dropped` (reason `backpressure`) and an unsubscribe.
Subscribing RE-BASELINES the lane so every subscriber — including a late
joiner — opens on a hydrate rather than folding deltas onto nothing.

Observability as acceptance, not polish: a `connections` block on the
`version` reply and its own `{"op":"connections"}` op (count, per client
name/build/subscribed/connected_at, frames and bytes pushed), one
structured stderr line per connection open/close/reject carrying boot_id
and client name, and `build_mismatch` on `hello_ok` when a client's build
disagrees with the code answering it — visible, never fatal.

`harness serve connect [--probe] [--drain]` is the first real client: it
resolves the root's live socket from the registry, performs the hello,
and prints the reply as JSON. `--drain` is the durable service's restart
verb from the outside, and it is what finally exercised the drain path
end to end — a proof slice 2 could not run, because over stdio the drain
ends the only connection that could watch it. That live run is a test
here, against a real spawned child in a sandboxed HOME/LOCALAPPDATA, and
it is what surfaced the blocking-wakeup defect fixed in the previous
commit.

Nothing new enters any freshness fingerprint: `serve_socket.lock` and
`serve_socket.owner.json` are excluded by the same standing precedent as
`DRAIN_STATE_FILENAME`, pinned by a test that fails if either is added.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
WIP(serve-socket): socket-lane hardening — implementation only, TESTS NOT UPDATED

DO NOT LAND. Committed to preserve an agent's work that was interrupted before
it could update tests or self-verify. The implementation reads complete and
parses clean; nothing about it has been proven.

State at this commit: 7 failed, 33 passed across test_serve_socket_lane.py,
test_serve_stream_hub.py, test_serve_drain_accounting.py. Every failure is a
test pinning the OLD hello contract (wrong-token rejection, malformed hello,
rate-limit hammering, connection log lines, socket drain, drain-refuses-new)
plus one renamed constant (`_DRAIN_EXIT_GRACE_SECONDS`). That is the expected
shape for a wire-contract change whose tests have not been rewritten — it is
NOT evidence the fixes work, and no red-proof has been run on any of them.

What appears implemented (unverified, read from the diff):
- F1 challenge-response: server speaks first with `server_hello` carrying a
  32-byte nonce + `hello_contract: 2` + `algorithm: hmac-sha256`; the client
  answers with an HMAC proof. The raw token no longer traverses the wire.
  `resolve_socket_target` gains `allow_stale` (default False) so a
  dead-classified registry row is no longer returned by default.
- F3: a separate `_timeout_limiter` appears, splitting non-auth rejections off
  the auth-failure window.
- F5/F8: substantial stream-hub rework (~360 lines).
- Remaining findings (F2 drain gating, F4 pre-auth bound + accept-loop death,
  F6 teardown watchdog ordering, F7 drain_state lock, F9 POSIX unlink) are
  NOT confirmed present — verify each against the review before trusting.

Next session: read the handoff doc, verify finding by finding, rewrite the
contract tests, then red-proof F1/F2/F3/F5 before landing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve): the drain floor belongs to the SOCKET lane, and a drop must name its bound

Two corrections to the interrupted hardening, both found by auditing the WIP
against the review findings rather than by trusting it.

F2 was over-applied. The 30s minimum deadline was installed as a global floor,
so it also floored `drain` over STDIO — which is not the lane the finding is
about. The stdio asker is the PARENT that spawned this process and owns its
stdin; it can end the runtime with a signal whether or not the drain
cooperates, so a floor there buys no safety, and it silently rewrote a contract
the socket slice promised to leave byte-identical (four pre-existing stdio
tests in test_serve_service_foundations.py pinned exactly that and went red).
The floor now applies on the transport the threat lives on: `max(ask, 30s)` for
a socket client, the long-standing 0.05s sanity floor for stdio. The second
half of F2 — never `hard_exit` while `chat_turns > 0` — stays on BOTH lanes,
because recording safety is a property of the work, not of the asker.

F8 was implemented in the hub and dropped at the join. `StreamSubscription`
measures `drop_bound`, `bytes_discarded` and `byte_limit`, and the
`subscription_dropped` frame threw all three away — reporting a frame count
against a `buffer_limit` read from the CONFIG, which is None whenever it was
left at the default. A client told only `backpressure` cannot tell one that
fell 256 heartbeats behind from one that pinned 32 MiB. The frame and the
service log line now carry which bound tripped and both bounds' numbers, and
`stream_byte_limit` is a `serve_loop` knob like the frame bound beside it.

Both are the shape this workstream keeps finding: the halves were right and the
join between them was not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(serve): rewrite the socket-lane tests onto the new handshake, and pin the joins

The hardening changed the wire contract, so seven tests were pinning a hello
that no longer exists. They were testing the right BEHAVIOURS — an impostor
learns nothing, a malformed hello is refused by name, the rate limit bites, the
lane's lifecycle is logged, a socket drain reaches every client — so they are
rewritten to the challenge-response contract rather than reverted.

Anti-vacuity, because two prior reviews of this workstream found proofs that
passed for the wrong reason:

- the wrong-proof test asserts the impostor received EXACTLY ONE frame after
  the challenge and then end-of-stream, not that a rejection appeared somewhere;
- a wire-tap on the reference client captures the actual bytes and checks them
  against the actual secret, in-process AND against a real spawned child;
- an IMPOSTOR-SERVER test stands up a plain listener, points the client at it,
  and asserts the client sends only a proof — and, for five malformed
  greetings, that it sends ZERO BYTES rather than adapting;
- the rate-limit test proves RECOVERY on an injected clock: blocked, then let
  back in once the real failures age out, which is the half the defect made
  impossible (a `rate_limited` rejection re-armed its own window);
- the hub test asserts the producer count does not GROW per subscribe and
  RETURNS TO ZERO when the room empties — and cross-checks against the
  factory's own set of running generator bodies, since either half alone passes
  vacuously;
- the F2 test proves a live chat turn SURVIVES a socket drain by watching it
  land, with its own exit frame, after two deadline lapses it outlived.

New coverage for the findings the WIP had implemented but nothing exercised:
the pre-auth bound (F4), the accept loop announcing how it ended (F4), the
byte bound tripping before the frame bound and naming which (F8), stop()
joining superseded producers (F5), the exit watchdog covering the teardown that
parked (F6), a completed drain never being relabelled abandoned (F6), and two
connections racing to drain starting exactly one (F7).

Also: the lock file now survives release by design (F9), so the assertions that
demanded its absence now demand its presence AND that it is immediately
re-lockable — the property the unlink was wrongly thought to provide.

The two child-e2e tests carry an explicit 300s timeout. They boot a real serve
and spawn the CLI verb two or three more times; measured at ~25s, they sat
inside the suite's 30s global cap only by luck, and the file already declared
180s budgets of its own that the cap silently contradicted.

160 passed, 1 skipped across the socket/hub/drain/e2e files plus the serve
registry, foundations, harness-serve, auth, env-gate and status-block suites.
Baseline at the WIP commit was 11 failed, 119 passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(serve): harden four proofs the red-proof caught passing against the defect

Sixteen sabotages were applied to the implementation and each was expected to
turn a named test red. Four did not, and every one of them was a test that was
true, useful-looking, and unable to fail:

F3b — charging `rate_limited` to the auth limiter left ONE record inside a
limit of three, so the single blocked retry recovered anyway. The live repro
was twelve polite retries; the test now makes three, which is what refills the
window and is what made the lockout self-sustaining.

F5a/F5b — both hub lifecycle tests used fakes that yield every 5ms, so
whatever the hub failed to do the producer noticed on its own next lap. The
guarantee had two independent mechanisms and removing either left the test
green. The unsubscribe half now uses a source that PARKS on its stop event, so
being told is the only way out; the stop() half uses uninterruptible producers
whose parks get SHORTER per generation — with a uniform delay, joining the
newest waited long enough for the older ones to finish by themselves, which is
exactly how a stop() that ignored them looked correct. It now also compares
every producer's exit timestamp against the moment stop() RETURNED, because
"they were gone afterwards" is not the claim.

F8 — the byte-bound test lived entirely inside the hub, and the defect was in
the JOIN: the `subscription_dropped` frame that reaches a client threw the
bound away. Sabotaging serve.py could not move a hub test. There is now a test
that subscribes over the real loop against a stdout that parks mid-write, and
reads the bound off the frame the client actually receives.

That is the recurring finding of this workstream, three more times: both halves
of a seam correct, the join between them untested.

Ledger: 16/16 sabotages now produce the named RED, restore byte-identical by
sha256, and return GREEN. 162 passed, 1 skipped across the ten target files.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve): the pre-auth path had one uncaught call, and one drain frame never left stdio

Independent review of the hardening branch found two more defects, both the
shape that has now produced every defect in this program: two halves each
correct, and the JOIN between them untested.

[HIGH] One non-ASCII byte in `proof` escaped the handshake as an unhandled
TypeError. `hmac.compare_digest` REFUSES to compare non-ASCII str, and the
comparison sat on a path an unauthenticated peer drives with no try around it.
The peer therefore got no rejection frame, the attempt was counted nowhere,
the rate limiter was never charged — the pre-auth bound bypassed by one byte —
and the traceback was written to a stderr that `serve_loop` has redirected onto
the NDJSON protocol stream, complete with source paths.

Fixed by comparing BYTES. But the specific call was not the defect: the defect
was that a single uncaught call existed there at all, so any exception escaping
the handshake is now converted into a refusal, charged like one, and counted as
`handshake_errors` / `last_handshake_error` — because the finding was that the
attempt left no trace. `serve_auth.verify` carried an identical latent copy and
is fixed too; it has no production caller, which is exactly why the copy left
lying around is the one that comes back.

[MED-HIGH] `drain_progress` was emitted to stdout and nowhere else — the only
drain frame not broadcast. Its stated purpose is that a draining service never
looks dead to a watchdog, and the socket client IS such a watchdog: it reads
with a 10s timeout and reports `transport_failed`. With the socket lane's 30s
minimum deadline, a drain holding a chat turn open put the first socket-visible
frame half a minute out, so a healthy drain that completed reported a transport
failure and exit 6.

Also, from the same review's weaker findings:

- The proof is now bound to the DIALLED PORT, and the docstring claiming an
  impostor learns "nothing anywhere" is corrected. A fresh nonce stops replay
  but not a live RELAY: an impostor dials the real service, adopts its nonce as
  its own challenge, and forwards the answer. Binding to anything the greeting
  merely asserts would bind to a number the impostor echoes; the dialled port is
  the one value each end knows from its own socket. hello_contract 2 -> 3,
  bumped rather than shimmed while the cost is still zero — no client speaks
  this handshake yet, and it becomes permanent the moment one does.
- A 1 MiB flood was classified `hello_timeout`, spending the budget reserved for
  peers that presented nothing. It gets its own reason.
- `record_success` was wired to the auth limiter but not the timeout limiter, so
  the silence throttle cleared only by time — the same "the server's own state
  locks out a good client" shape F3 set out to retire, applied to the other half.

Red-proof: 6/6. Each fix reverted byte-wise, its test named RED, restored in a
finally with sha256 verified identical. The impostor test now harvests a proof
over the REAL service's live nonce using the REAL token and proves it is still
refused there — an arbitrary secret would have failed for the wrong reason and
passed without the binding existing. The silence-throttle test staggers its two
abandoned connections 30s apart, because two that age out together cannot
distinguish "the window emptied itself" from "the handshake cleared it".

202 passed, 1 skipped across the ten serve suites (C:\Python312\python.exe --
the live venv has no pytest).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(doctor): a root-only key set in a profile is inert, and nothing said so

Four agent_runtime keys resolve through harness_root_config_path() and never
consult the active profile: read_model.delta_patches, mcp_admission, and the
per-persona chat_lane_restore_toolsets / workdir. YAML accepts them anywhere and
profile-aware surfaces report them back, so a value written one layer below its
reader looks applied and does nothing.

This class has now landed twice in three weeks, in both directions. 2026-07-23:
the ruling lived in the ROOT while the reader used the profile, so
chat_lane_restore_toolsets resolved off profiles/alice and the operator's ruling
was dead on arrival — that is why harness_root_config_path exists. 2026-08-13:
the mirror image. read_model.delta_patches: true sat in profiles/base and
profiles/alice while the reader correctly used the root, which carried no
read_model block at all.

Cost of the second one, measured live rather than argued: the S7-A patch
producer stayed dark for its entire life. One field change on one persona
instance shipped an 822,671-byte delta carrying an 864,241-byte full snapshot
core, where the patch frame the lane was built for is 486 bytes — ~1,693x. The
whole time, harness status reported delta_patches: true, because status reads
profile-aware.

The table keys on LEAVES, not blocks: read_model is split across both loaders
(read_model.enabled is profile-aware, read_model.delta_patches is root-only), so
a block-level rule would false-positive on nearly every profile and train
operators to ignore the finding.

Severity splits on whether the root also carries the key. Profile-only is a
defect (the instruction is inert). Set in both is a notice (the live value is
correct; the copy is a leftover) — grading that a defect would leave harness
doctor permanently red over a cosmetic duplicate, which is the "a gate that is
always red is not a gate" failure this repo has already shipped once.

On the operator's machine it finds 9 misplaced keys across 7 profiles, all
correctly graded notice; each was verified against the root YAML independently
of the new code.

Tests cover all three branches plus the two subtleties that would silently
weaken it: read_model.enabled must not be flagged, and a root pin for
personas.neko.workdir must not excuse personas.qa.workdir. One test asserts every
table entry still names a reader that exists, so the table cannot outlive the
readers it protects.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(stream): a patch for an entity the client cannot fold is worse than the core it replaced

The patch lane decided promotion purely on the OP (upsert/remove fold,
refresh does not). Nothing looked at the ENTITY -- but the consumer's fold
table is the narrower half: mission_read_model.dart maps exactly two entity
classes to core sections (persona_instance, incident) and an unknown entity
makes its fold return needsResync, i.e. "re-hydrate from a fresh checkpoint".
So the first patch emitted for a third entity (office_actor, running_work)
would have cost every connected launcher a FULL re-hydrate per frame --
strictly worse than the full-core delta the patch replaced, because the
client pays the patch and then a core anyway.

The producer cannot know that unilaterally, so the CLIENT declares what it
folds and the producer promotes only within the declared set. One undeclared
entity demotes the WHOLE batch onto the honest-fallback full core that
already exists; the op rules run first and are unchanged.

Absence means the HISTORICAL {persona_instance, incident}, never the empty
set. Absence is what every client in the field sends, and the historical set
is exactly today's wire, so an un-updated launcher is byte-for-byte
unaffected. Defaulting to empty would have been the safe-LOOKING choice that
silently demoted every connected client to full cores the day this landed --
486 bytes replaced by 822,671 -- which is how this lane already lost its
whole life once, to a config that resolved where nobody read.

Both lanes declare:
  stdio   harness stream --fold-entities persona_instance,incident
  socket  {"op":"subscribe","lane":"stream","fold_entities":[...]}

The socket producer is SHARED (one generator, N subscribers), so a
declaration is a request, not a setting: the accepted set is the
INTERSECTION over every attached subscriber, because a promoted frame is
fanned out to all of them and a union would aim the original bug at the
client sitting next door. The accepted set is echoed on the subscribed ack
and on the hydrate beside delta_patches -- the handshake's missing direction,
and not a restatement of the request, since a client can be honoured for
less than it asked. A malformed declaration is refused
(subscribe_denied/invalid_fold_entities) rather than read as absent, which
would widen a client that meant to narrow.

Additive and inert by construction: no new entity is enabled, no chokepoint
changed, and the echo only exists on a hydrate that already carries
delta_patches, so the flag-off wire and every stream golden are untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): argv on the wire cannot be versioned, so the first method carries its own manifest

Increment 1 of the CALL half (launcher DECISION_push_and_rpc_2026-08-13 §3):
`runtime.office.get`, one typed JSON-RPC 2.0 read method, built as the template
the remaining 37 capability ids copy.

Everything structural is MIRRORED from `tui_gateway/server.py` rather than
re-decided, per launcher fa2226750 — the request/result/error frames, the
`@method` registry, the request normalizer, and the error-code vocabulary
(-32600/-32601/-32602/-32000, plus 4001 reused verbatim for not-found rather
than renumbered). A fork that renumbers "not found" turns a future union of the
two dispatchers into a translation layer.

The lane sits BESIDE the argv lane, never over it. A frame is claimed only when
it names `jsonrpc` or `method`, neither of which an argv request has ever sent,
so the fallback keeps its frames and exit codes — asserted by running the same
argv request with and without method calls interleaved and comparing the emitted
LINES character for character, because "additive" is a claim, not a proof. It is
answered inline on the transport's own thread like `ping`/`version`, and for the
same reason is still answered while draining: a drain refuses new WORK, and a
bounded read that holds nothing is not what it is protecting.

The result is the canvas-shaped projection Stage 2b ruled — the runtime owns who
exists, where it sits, and a POINTER to the character class (`persona_id`); the
launcher owns what that class looks like. So the surface's append-only
`archived_actor_keys` ledger, and every actor's `updated_by` / `created_at` /
`state` / `backing_profile`, stay off the wire; a truncation past the snapshot's
own MAX_OFFICE_ACTORS_PROJECTED is ACCOUNTED rather than silent. Both live
workspaces project under 2 KB.

How a client learns the surface follows `hello_contract` rather than inventing a
parallel scheme: `{"contract":N,"methods":[...]}` rides the greeting each
transport already reads (`ready` on stdio, `hello_ok` on the socket) and is
restated on the re-askable `version` reply, because a durable service outlives
the install it was started from. It is a SET plus an integer, not an integer
alone — the integer moves when a method's shape changes, the set grows when one
is added, so methods are adoptable one at a time exactly as `fold_entities` is.
