author: nekwo
message:
docs(serve): the design doc spent five weeks saying "not yet implemented" about a thing that shipped

`harness-serve-design.md` was frozen at 2026-07-08 and still opened with
"settled with Tony, not yet implemented" — while the Launcher-side note cited
it as the canonical design doc and correctly said the feature shipped both
sides that same day. Anyone following that pointer got a contradiction, and
three of its stated non-goals had since become features.

Scored the original decisions instead of deleting them, because a design record
whose predictions can be checked is worth more than one that only describes
today. All five decisions settled with Tony held; two grew. The three non-goals
that flipped — no network listener, no auth, no cancel — each flipped for a
reason worth keeping:

  * "local stdio child IS the security model" stopped being true when a second
    client wanted the same warm runtime, so there is a socket lane;
  * a listener needs auth, so there is an HMAC hello handshake bound to the
    dialled port at contract 3, designed in rather than bolted on;
  * "Launcher timeout -> kill + respawn covers hangs" contradicted decision 5,
    which forbids killing serve mid-chat-turn. `cancel` resolves that, and
    `cancel_denied` is its honest half.

Also corrected: two ops documented, ten in the code (`ping`, `hello`, `version`,
`connections`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `drain`, `stacks`, `shutdown`,
`cancel`); `SERVE_SCHEMA_VERSION` is still 1 because the envelope never broke —
which is precisely why an integer was the wrong tool for a growing op surface
and the method lane carries a manifest instead. The 2026-08-14 method lane
(contract 1) is now described here at all.

The structural fix is the pointer at the top: frame shapes live in serve.py's
module docstring, which is maintained in the same commits that change them, and
this file keeps the durable why. Prose that duplicates a wire format rots; prose
that explains a constraint does not.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): the office wire named the class but never which one of it was placed

`runtime.office.get` carried `persona_id` — a POINTER to the character class —
and deliberately dropped `persona_instance_id` as "not renderable". That was
right about rendering and wrong about identity: the launcher can draw the right
sprite for `backend_dev` and still have no idea WHICH backend_dev is sitting
there. The store has keyed instance-bound actors by
`canonical_persona_instance_id` since day one (`office_store.py` header, plan
§4.3); nothing downstream could see it.

So the item object grows a 9th key, the owning actor's binding, `null` when the
actor is class-keyed. It is the ACTOR's and not the item's, repeated onto each
flattened item because the wire shape is flat. And it is explicit `null`, never
an omission — the rule desks already follow for `display_name` / `pet_slug`.

The contract integer did NOT move, and a reader will expect it to. It moves when
a client that folds v1 must REFUSE v2. The launcher's item decoder gates on
required-key PRESENCE (`containsKey`, `mission_office_rpc.dart:484`) and never
on a key count, so the client already shipped folds a 9-key item and ignores the
new key. Bumping would have made that shipped client refuse a payload it can
already read — the version would have been a lie about compatibility.

The snapshot lane needed nothing: `_office_actor_summary_row`
(`snapshot.py:1232`) has carried `persona_instance_id` since it was written. The
field was visible on one of the launcher's two office lanes and invisible on the
other, which is the divergence this closes. A test now pins both lanes together
so neither can drop it alone.

`scripts/office_actor_rekey_to_instance.py` is the DATA half, unrun. Every one
of the 8 live actors is class-keyed because every placement was authored without
an instance id, not because the schema lacked one. The script re-keys each actor
onto the canonical instance id read from its `agent`-kind item, and refuses
rather than guesses at all three places the derivation can fail: no agent item
or more than one, an id that will not canonicalize, an id with no
`persona_instances/*.json` behind it. It defaults to dry run and has been run
only that way.

Read its RESURRECTION GUARD section before `--apply`. Archiving `backend_dev`
and upserting `personainst_backend_dev_agent_29fdd71a` does not collide — the
guard is keyed by actor key and the two are different strings — but any later
class-keyed write re-creates the old actor AND clears the guard entry
(`office_store.py:345-350`), leaving the same agent placed twice. The migration
is not durable until every writer sends the instance id.

Mutation-proofed: 11 mutations on the projection, 12 on the script. Three stayed
GREEN and were the point of the exercise — the write ORDER (new key before
archiving the old, so a crash leaves a duplicate and never a gap), the
already-bound shortcut (an actor bound to instance A whose item names instance B
must be left alone, not re-homed), and the minted-key mismatch guard. All three
now have tests.

message:
docs(envelope): the module docstring explained one of the two doors

`terminal_envelope.py` opens with "Deny by default, no wildcard, no
inheritance… Nothing here weakens the envelope for a class that has no grant."
Every word of that is true of the grants table. It is also beside the point,
because `resolve()` grants any class in GRANTABLE_COMMAND_CLASSES on
`resolved.unbounded` alone, 600 lines below, without consulting the grants
table at all — and `unbounded` is the shipped default. R-2 removed the last
hard floors, so with no stanza written anywhere, all four classes run.

That is the intended posture, confirmed with the operator today: R-2 traded a
preventive control for a detective one, and a mode grant is receipted through
`record_envelope_decision` exactly like a config grant, so nothing runs
unaudited.

The problem was never the posture, it was that a careful reader starting at
the top of this file concluded the opposite of it — which is exactly what
happened to `mission-chat-terminal-envelope-grants.md`, corrected earlier
today. That doc quoted rule 2 accurately and still told operators every
envelope-gated class on mission-chat was a typed refusal. A docstring that
sends its most careful readers to the wrong conclusion is not a documentation
nit; it is the mechanism by which the safety story drifted.

So the mode door is named first, and the grants section says which door it
describes.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office): the migration archived the old key, and the two writers that could hand it back

The class -> instance re-key archives every class key and records it in the
surface's resurrection guard. upsert_actor then reads an explicit upsert of an
archived key as intent to re-add and CLEARS that entry, so one surviving
class-keyed write re-creates the old actor ACTIVE beside the instance-keyed
one -- same agent placed twice, duplicate item_ids on one canvas, and no
conflict warning anywhere, because every guard in the store keys on the actor
key and the two keys are different strings.

The store's contract is right for a caller that holds operator intent. Two
callers do not, so the predicate lives outside the store, at them:

- workspace_template: REFUSES the copy per-actor. No escape hatch -- nobody is
  in the loop at copy time to own the double placement. Bound source actors
  already copied as bound payloads; only an unbound source actor writes a class
  key. Bound actors now copy FIRST so the guard is order-independent.
- harness office actor-upsert (also the launcher's save path): refuses with
  duplicate_conflict. --persona-instance-id is OPTIONAL, not required --
  class-keyed placements are a supported shape, and a hard requirement would
  outlaw a legal canvas. Warn-and-proceed was the other wrong answer: this
  verb's output is machine-read, so the warning would go to nobody.
  --allow-class-key forces it and puts the override on the record.

The guard is conditional, not a ban: archived class key, or item ids already
owned by an active instance-keyed sibling. A template landing on a fresh
workspace and an operator placing a class-keyed actor on a clean canvas are
untouched, and both are pinned.

Three of the tests exist because a mutation stayed green: the guard scanning
archived actors, comparing a stored persona_id un-normalized (reachable --
resolve_conflict --take remote writes a peer's spelling straight to disk), and
skipping _safe_id on incoming item ids.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(mcp): the denial line sent agents to a lane deleted three weeks earlier

`stagec_mcp_visual_provider.py` went in 5a1267ef60. `VisualProofRunner` has
zero matches; there is no `request_screenshot` row in `_EVENT_CONTRACTS`. The
admission lane never noticed: on every denial it still told the agent, in
band, to "use the server's harness-side contract (for launcher_qa: the
qa.request_screenshot decision contract)". Naming a sanctioned alternative was
the whole mechanism for retiring W3 — an agent that hears "no tools" and no
plan invents `pwsh -File`. Pointing it at a contract that does not exist is
not a weaker version of that mechanism, it is the failure the sentence was
written to prevent, with the runtime's own authority behind it.

There is no replacement contract and none is planned, so the honest wording is
that the route is closed: no fallback to try, report the denial and what went
unverified, finish the turn, and only an operator can lift it (the per-code
fix_hints already name which config key). Seven emitter sites, not the four
the grep found — two fix_hints and the flag-off `mcp_lane` hint never spell
the contract's name, and one test pinned the old tail by its last sentence.

Tests keep the guidance pinned rather than dropping the assertion, plus a
fence that `request_screenshot` appears in no emitted text on any denial code.
Mutation-proofed: 13 mutations, 3 initially GREEN (the two admission fix_hints
and the `mcp_lane` requirement-failure hint were unpinned entirely) — guards
added, all 13 now red.

The design doc argued in six places that denial is cheap *because* the
fallback exists. Corrected in place; §D3's W3-retirement and §8's "rollback is
free" are withdrawn rather than reworded, because both rested entirely on the
deleted lane.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(read-model): the whole patch lane hung on a flag in one untracked file on one machine

`read_model.delta_patches` defaulted False, so a fresh clone against a fresh
runtime root got the S7-A patch lane DARK and said nothing about it. The only
place the flag existed was the operator's `X:/Eternia/.hermes/config.yaml`,
which is in no repository. Reimage that machine and every field change goes
back to re-shipping a full snapshot core -- measured live 2026-08-13, ONE field
change on ONE persona instance shipped an 822,671-byte delta carrying an
864,241-byte core where the patch frame is 486 bytes -- with nothing in any repo
recording that the flag existed or why it mattered.

Scaffolding it into a generated config was not a hypothetical alternative: that
mechanism already exists and already lost. The Launcher installer's
`kMissionControlBaseSeedConfigYaml` stamps `delta_patches: true` into the fresh
`base` PROFILE, and the key is ROOT-ONLY -- the only reader resolves
`harness_root_config_path()` and never consults the active profile -- so every
fresh install reproduced the exact defect the seed was trying to prevent. A
value that must land in one specific file is a value a writer can put in the
wrong file. Reporting the absence from `harness doctor` was the other option and
helps only an operator who runs the doctor, which a lane that costs bytes rather
than failing anything never sends one to do.

So the default SHIPS. `SHIPPED_DELTA_PATCHES` is the `ReadModelConfig` default
and `config._read_model_config` applies it for an ABSENT key, mirroring
`permission_modes.SHIPPED_DEFAULT_PERMISSION_MODE`: it reaches a fresh install
and an existing one identically, cannot be written to the wrong file, and needs
no init or upgrade step to have run. An operator's explicit root-config `false`
still wins; only silence resolves to the shipped value. The precondition the
False default was born under -- "dark until the launcher fold exists" -- expired:
`mission_read_model.dart` folds, the stream promotes coverable batches to v2
`patch` frames, and 79fc7fb7 landed the fold-entity handshake, so a batch naming
an entity the client did not declare is demoted to the honest full core rather
than shipped as a patch nobody can apply.

Shipping a default ON forces a distinction the loader cannot make. Every
agent_runtime config read goes through `parse_cache.cached_yaml_file(path,
default=None)`, and `cached_by_mtime` returns that default for a PARSE failure
exactly as it does for a missing file -- so a root config.yaml full of broken
YAML does not raise, it silently produces an empty config and every key resolves
to its shipped default. That was harmless while this default was False (absent
and broken agreed on the answer). At True they stop agreeing and the loader
answers the wrong one: measured directly, an unparseable root config resolved
`delta_patches_enabled()` to True, in silence, in the very file an operator may
have written `false` into. `_root_config_fault` now separates the cases -- an
ABSENT root is a fresh root and resolves ON, an existing file that does not parse
into a mapping is a fault -- at zero cost on the happy path, since it hits the
same mtime cache entry the loader is about to use.

The remaining off-paths are LOUD. `delta_patches_enabled` warned about none of
them: an unparseable config, a load that raised, and a config object carrying no
such field all returned a bare False. All three are non-observations, all three
keep landing on `FALLBACK_DELTA_PATCHES` (deliberately not the shipped value --
a config the runtime could not parse has told it nothing, and that must not be
read as "start emitting a new event class from every store chokepoint"), and all
three now say so. An operator's explicit `false` is an answer, not a fault, and
stays silent -- a warning on every deliberately-full-core install is how a
warning stops being read. An empty config.yaml is silence too, not damage.
Silent-off is the failure mode being retired; it does not get to survive as a
fault path.

Profile-level copies are left alone and still reported: they are inert and worth
deleting, they just no longer decide whether the lane runs. The Launcher seed
template is the durable half of that and is a separate repo.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): the read leg published a revision, but not the one the write leg guards

`runtime.office.upsert` is the WRITE half of the office RPC pilot and the first
place client prediction + server reconciliation is actually exercised: the
launcher draws a drag immediately, sends it, and the server acks LIGHT —
`{actor_key, revision}` — rather than re-projecting the actor onto the hot path
of a drag. Those two fields are the two facts the client provably cannot
compute: the store canonicalizes the identity triple at its own boundary (drift
aliases collapse), and the revision is the token the NEXT write must present.

The contract integer does NOT move, and a reader will expect it to. The manifest
is a set plus an integer: the integer moves only when a client that folds v1
must REFUSE v2. A client only ever calls a method it found in the SET, so
publishing one more cannot break it; and `runtime.office.get`'s new key is
additive to a decoder that gates on required-key presence and never on a count
(`mission_office_rpc.dart:260`). Bumping would have made the shipped launcher
refuse a payload it can read.

That new key is the reason this commit touches the read leg at all. Items now
carry the OWNING ACTOR's `revision` — the token `expect_revision` is checked
against. Before this, a client had no honest source for it: the surface-level
`revision` sitting right beside `items` is the SURFACE's, and
`OfficeStore.upsert_actor` rewrites the actor file and leaves `office.json`
alone, so it does not move when an actor moves. A client could only ever write
unguarded, which is precisely the lost update the guard exists to prevent. The
reconciliation loop was open at the seam; this closes it.

Concurrency is the store's `expect_revision` / `_guard_no_conflict`, passed
through and translated, never re-implemented. A mismatch is 4090 with
`data.reason: "stale_revision"`, whose `data` deliberately omits the current
revision — handing back a bare integer invites a retry with it, and the
prescribed cure is to refetch and rebase onto server truth. An unresolved
realm-sync sidecar shares the code with its own reason `sync_conflict`, because
retrying never clears that one and a client that conflated them would spin.

4090 had to be minted; upstream has no concurrency code because its domain
never contends. The number matters: upstream allocates 4xxx sequentially and has
reached 4020, and `4002` — the obvious guess — is already spent there on
"invalid value", so it would have collided on day one.

Unlike the CLI verb beside it, the method REFUSES an unknown workspace rather
than letting `ensure_surface` lazily author one. The read leg already refuses a
typo so a blank canvas cannot render for one; a write that silently authored a
whole office for the same typo is the worse half of that pair, because a
mis-rendered canvas is repainted on the next poll and a mis-authored one is on
disk forever. Surface authoring stays on the argv lane, which is untouched.

The dispatch-site comment justified answering the lane during a drain by saying
it was a read. It isn't anymore, and the real invariant is different: a drain
protects work that can be cut off half-done, and an inline handler cannot be —
the actor file is written atomically and the lock released before the ack is
emitted. Refusing would fail an operator's drag during a restart to protect
against a loss that cannot occur. Pinned by a test so it reads as a decision.

Red-proofed by 28 mutations. Two came back GREEN and are fixed here: a
projection that stamped `projected[0].revision` on every row survived a
single-actor seed, and nothing at all asserted that `updated_by` reached the
store — a handler that accepted the param and dropped it would have attributed
every launcher drag to `operator`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve): the third writer through the class-key hole was the one on the wire

`office_class_key_guard` fenced the two writers that could hand back an archived
class key. `runtime.office.upsert` is the third, and the only one reachable from
the network — so the fence runs before the store here too. A collision is 4090
with its own `data.reason: "class_key_collision"`, carrying the guard's
structured facts including the key it collided WITH.

Its own reason, because the remedy is a third thing. Not `stale_revision`: the
client is not behind and refetching tells it nothing new. Not `actor_invalid`:
the payload is well-formed and was legal before the re-key. The cure is "name
WHICH instance you are placing", so it gets its own branch. The guard's two
narrow reasons ride beside it as a list rather than as the branch point — they
share that one remedy, and a client decoder switches on a single stable string.

There is NO wire equivalent of the CLI's `--allow-class-key`, and the asymmetry
is the decision rather than an omission. A flag is consent: an operator read the
refusal, typed the override, and owns the double placement. A wire PARAMETER is
not consent — it becomes a constant in a client build, set once by whoever was
debugging the day drags started failing, and sent forever by every install with
no human in any loop. The wire client also needs it least: the read projection
hands it `persona_instance_id` on every item, so its remedy is to send back the
binding it was already given. The operator-intent paths are untouched — `harness
office actor-restore`, and the CLI's own override.

`refusal_message` is deliberately not reused; it ends by offering
`--allow-class-key`, which does not exist on this lane, and advice a caller
cannot follow is worse than none. The message written here also stops claiming
"this would place the agent twice" on the archived-key branch, where that is
simply not what happens — it clears the resurrection guard.

The fence is CONDITIONAL, and a test pins that a class-keyed write onto a clean
canvas still goes through. Class-keyed placements are a supported shape; a guard
that refused every unbound write would outlaw a legal canvas and would have
passed every other test here.

Red-proofed by 9 further mutations, all red: the fence uncalled, computed and
ignored, run after the write, reusing the revision-conflict reason, honouring an
`allow_class_key` param, fencing only one of the two reasons (each way), banning
every class-keyed write, and dropping the conflicting key from the refusal.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent-runtime): the root config was already sandboxed; the head home, which is written to, was not

The reported defect does not exist. `tests/conftest.py::_hermetic_environment`
has pinned `HERMES_HOME` to a per-test tmpdir since 2026-04-17 (d404849351), and
`config.harness_root_config_path()` resolves through it, so no agent-runtime
test has been reading `X:/Eternia/.hermes/config.yaml`. Measured: the resolved
root config does not even exist during a test, and `delta_patches_enabled()`
returns the SHIPPED default rather than the operator's value.

What WAS unpinned is `HERMES_HEAD_HOME`, one variable over and strictly worse.
`get_hermes_head_home()` returns it verbatim and only falls back to the
sandboxed `get_hermes_home()` when unset; the Launcher's serve exports it
(`<root>/profiles/base`); and it does not select a file to read but the
SessionDB the Mission Control transcript store WRITES to, while also flipping
`hermes_head_home_is_authoritative()` and with it which branch the fail-closed
guards in persona_chat_history take. A suite run from a Launcher-shaped shell
wrote test rows into the operator's live profile. Deleted rather than re-pinned:
unset is what CI has, and unset degrades to the already-sandboxed HERMES_HOME.

The agent-runtime guard is an ASSERTION, not a third pin. The pin exists and
works; what was missing is any statement that it is load-bearing for the four
ROOT_ONLY_CONFIG_KEYS readers, every one of which would silently start
answering out of an operator's config.yaml — with the suite still green — if it
regressed. A second setenv for the same variable would just be an authority
that can drift from the first.

Two mutations survived and were fixed rather than reported as clean:

* Replacing `load_root_runtime_config`'s body with the profile-aware loader —
  the exact 2026-07-23 defect `harness_root_config_path` exists to kill — left
  everything green, because a sandbox that pins HERMES_HOME at a plain
  directory makes root and profile the same file. The new test puts
  HERMES_HOME in the `<root>/profiles/<name>` shape the CLI bootstrap leaves it
  in, writes opposite values to the two configs, and requires the root to win.
* Repointing the guard's head-home leg at the root resolver while leaving its
  `what=` label unchanged kept every token a source grep looks for, removed the
  check entirely, and stayed green under a poisoned HERMES_HEAD_HOME. The wiring
  assertion now reads the call arguments off the AST instead of the source text.

/1 failed -> 5109 passed/1 failed, +9 new tests, zero tests changed state. The
two pre-existing reds are unrelated and reproduce on main:
test_snapshot_contract_version_authority::test_no_other_module_states_the_contract_version,
and test_s55_registered_events_have_emitters, which trips the 30s per-test cap.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office): the conflict-resolution door was the one the migration's fence could not reach

The class→instance re-key migration is durable at three writers and porous at
a fourth. ``OfficeStore.resolve_conflict(take="remote")`` does not go through
``upsert_actor`` at all — it deserializes the peer's actor out of the conflict
sidecar and calls ``_write_actor`` directly — so no caller-side guard is even
reachable from it. On a migrated office that meant one ``--take remote`` could
write an archived CLASS key back as ACTIVE beside its instance-keyed sibling:
the same agent placed twice, duplicate item ids on one canvas, no warning.
Worse than the unfenced upsert it mirrors, in fact: ``upsert_actor`` at least
clears the resurrection ledger and deletes the archive copy, while this path
touches neither and leaves an active actor whose key is still listed archived.

The fence therefore lives in the store, not at the CLI. The hazard is intrinsic
to the method (peer-authored bytes, past the chokepoint), not to any one
caller, so a future second caller inherits the guard instead of having to
remember it — the mirror image of why ``upsert_actor``'s guard sits at ITS
callers, where the payload is the caller's own intent.

Refusal with consent, not a flat refusal and not an auto re-key. A realm-sync
resolution has a human in the loop, so ``--allow-class-key`` mirrors
``actor-upsert``'s hatch and puts the decision on the record; the refusal names
``--take local`` because that is the exit an operator under conflict pressure
actually needs. Re-keying the incoming actor onto the instance binding was
rejected: it rewrites what the peer published into an identity the peer never
had, and in the duplicate-item case it lands ON TOP of the migrated actor —
trading a visible double placement for a silent clobber.

Both sides of the class-key test are normalized. This is the one path whose
input never met ``_normalize_persona_id``, so a peer's ``Backend_Dev`` arrives
verbatim and a raw comparison reads it as instance-keyed.

Red-proofed by 16 mutations. Two stayed green and were closed: keying the fence
on ``resolve_conflict``'s ``actor_key`` argument instead of the remote record's
own ``actor_key`` (every fixture had them agree, but ``_write_actor`` routes on
the record — "payload is truth, the filename is routing only"), and hard-coding
the class-key test to the flagship fixture's persona (every case re-used
``backend_dev``; the live canvas carries four archived class keys).

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office): a drag moves one actor, so the wire should carry one actor

The office read and write legs landed at ~2.5KB and a light ack; the push
leg still made every drag cost a full core. Office was absent from the S7-A
producer, so an actor write fell through to the honest full-core fallback.

The entity is `office_actor`, keyed `<workspace_id>/<actor_key>`, and both
halves of that were forced rather than chosen. Measured against a copy of
the live canvas: the whole office row is 3158 bytes against a 3584-byte
per-value budget, so surface granularity blows the 4KB cap and degrades to
`refresh` at roughly the seventh desk on a surface bounded at 200. One
actor row is 663-764. And an `actor_key` is unique only inside its
workspace -- actor files live at office/<ws>/actors/<token>.json -- so a
bare key would let a drag in one office move a desk in another.

The watermark question has two answers because there are two watermarks.
The stream's is the EventLog offset, unchanged. The entity's is
`actor.revision`, and it only agrees with the offset order because the
emit happens INSIDE `office_lock` from the object just written: append
after the release and two writers can land rev 3 at the lower offset and
rev 2 at the higher, leaving a folded core older than disk with no gap for
`base_offset` to catch.

A patch describes ONE actor row, so any write that also moves the parent
office row takes an accounted `refresh` instead -- a create moves
`actor_count`, a re-add of an archived key rewrites the resurrection
ledger. Removes and surface writes stay uncovered entirely, which routes
them down the lane they already took.

Nothing here widens what an un-updated client receives: `office_actor` is
not in HISTORICAL_FOLD_ENTITIES, so a launcher that declares nothing keeps
getting the byte-identical full core -- verified through the real stream
generator, not inferred from the classifier.

Two tests exist because mutation testing found them missing. The
`surface_rewritten` arm was never independently exercised (every path to
it went through remove_actor, which unlinks the actor file, so the create
arm answered first), and flag-off inertness was only checked for silence,
not for the projection cost the early return exists to avoid.

message:
test(conftest): a var that leaks on one machine is still a var the suite branches on

`HERMES_GATEWAY_DETACHED=1` is exported in the operator's live environment and
was not blanked. It is not a tint on a default — it SHORT-CIRCUITS one:
`_windows_gateway_should_absorb_console_controls` (hermes_cli/gateway.py:1737)
returns True on any truthy word and never reaches the `sys.stdin.isatty()`
branch under it, so `gateway.py:4924` installed `SIG_IGN` for SIGINT/SIGBREAK
and called `SetConsoleCtrlHandler(NULL, TRUE)` in whichever direction the shell
pointed. The Windows service wrappers export it verbatim
(gateway_windows.py:413, :498, :816, :883), which is how it came to be set on
the machine that found this. Deleted rather than re-pinned, per the
HERMES_HEAD_HOME ruling in 5a0db7bad3: unset is what CI has, and unset degrades
to the isatty() fallback, which under pytest's captured stdin is the sandboxed
answer. Both branches are already covered by tests that set it explicitly
(tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway.py:259 deletes it, :289 sets it).

The twelve path-shaped names are blanked in the same commit rather than left
latent, and the argument is that "currently unset" is a fact about one shell on
one day, not a property of the code. HERMES_HEAD_HOME was also unset until the
Launcher's serve started exporting it, and it took a live incident — test rows
written into the operator's profile — to notice. Every one of the twelve
redirects a lookup at an operator-controlled path: the active profile and
default author name (agent_runtime/profile_context.py:129,
hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:9450, tools/kanban_tools.py:877), the auth home and
shared-secret dir (hermes_cli/auth.py:940, :5137), the skill / MCP / plugin
discovery roots (hermes_constants.py:318, :334, :350, :380,
hermes_cli/plugins.py:62), the `hermes` binary dispatched workers are spawned
with (kanban_db.py:9258), the TUI bundle and web dist (main.py:1973, :10219),
and the home an ACP child inherits (hermes_constants.py:871). Four test files
already hand-roll a private defence against exactly these names arriving from
the ambient env — test_realm_sync_skill_inbox.py:56 and test_skill_promotion.py:35
pop HERMES_SHARED_SKILLS with the comment "a stray ... would break isolation",
tests/agent/test_external_skills.py:88 pops the same one, and
test_copilot_acp_client.py:200 names an "ambient HERMES_REAL_HOME". Four
independent workarounds for one missing central blank is the argument for
blanking centrally. Unset is what CI has for all thirteen: run_tests.sh forwards
only HERMES_RUN_SLOW_PET_TESTS and HERMES_E2E_BROWSER (:182-183), and
tests.yml sets none of them.

The guard asserts the property from INSIDE a running test — `name not in
os.environ`, on the same os.environ production calls os.getenv on — rather than
asserting that a frozenset contains a string, which would pass just as happily
with the fixture deleted or switched from delenv to setenv. Three checks that
fail in three directions: the absence gate (red wherever the var is exported), a
statement of WHY it is absent (red everywhere if the frozenset is hollowed), and
a per-var witness that the production reader still exists (red when an entry
becomes decoration), AST-based because hermes_constants.py:332 names
HERMES_OPTIONAL_MCPS in prose one line above the real read.

Five mutations, all red as designed, none survived: dropping
HERMES_GATEWAY_DETACHED from the frozenset with the var live-exported (2 red);
exporting HERMES_BIN with its entry present (green — the control, the blank
absorbs it); exporting HERMES_BIN with its entry dropped (2 red); switching the
fixture from delenv to setenv("") (14 red); repointing one witness at the wrong
module (1 red).

Verified: 14 affected test files, 260 passed / 8 skipped. The 5 reds in
test_install_sh_acp_launcher.py and test_install_sh_pythonpath_sanitization.py
are pre-existing and reproduce identically with tests/conftest.py reverted to
HEAD — they are install.sh shell tests, unrelated to env blanking.

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent-runtime): three wires version independently, so the gate must exempt a pair, never a name

`test_no_other_module_states_the_contract_version` has been red on main since
the two lane contracts landed. It matches on the name suffix CONTRACT_VERSION,
which is the right net for the defect it was built for — six restatements of ONE
number, four of which went red for five days after the 52->53 landing — but this
repo versions more than one wire, and two of them are not the snapshot frame:

* serve_rpc.py:120 `RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION = 1`, the METHOD-SURFACE contract
  published at :178 as `{"contract": ..., "methods": method_names()}`. It
  versions request/result shapes for a manifest argv on the wire cannot version
  for itself; adding a method deliberately does not move it.
* serve_socket.py:217 `HELLO_CONTRACT_VERSION = 3`, the handshake stamped on
  every server_hello (:913, :1093) and folded into the HMAC proof preimage at
  :527. It gates whether a client can answer the challenge frame at all — a
  connection concern settled before any snapshot is sent.

Neither reaches `parity.contract_version`, and neither may drag contract_hash —
stamped on every live persona instance — along when it moves. Three independent
numbers is the design, not the debt, and the gate predates two of them.

WHAT THE EXEMPTION DOES NOT GIVE AWAY. Entries are keyed on the exact
(filename, symbol) PAIR, never a filename and never a name pattern, so an
exemption covers one declaration in one module. A module redeclaring
SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION = 54 matches no pair and is still flagged. That alone
would be an absence-based argument, so the refusal is also structural: the
authority symbol is derived from DEFINITION_SITE and the lane lookup refuses it
outright, which makes "no exemption can ever cover the snapshot version" a
property of the code instead of a property of what happens to be in the dict.
`test_no_lane_exemption_can_ever_cover_the_snapshot_version` INSTALLS the lie —
a lane entry naming SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION, in the worst spelling — and
requires the detector to flag it anyway. A gate that merely lacked the entry
would pass that by accident.

Each entry is witnessed on its own module rather than trusted: the symbol must
still be a singular module-scope int literal, and the module must not reference
SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION anywhere — a lane deriving from the snapshot authority
is not independent, and the honest response would be deleting the second number
rather than exempting it. A fourth test states the basename uniqueness the
exemption silently depends on, since a future tests/agent_runtime/serve_rpc.py
would inherit the exemption for free.

Six mutations, all red, none survived. Three on the detector: dropping the
authority-symbol refusal (1 red); widening the key to filename only (1 red);
widening it to symbol only (1 red). Three on production, reverted after: planting
SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION = 54 in serve_socket.py — THE genuine duplicate this
gate exists for — fails the main gate naming `serve_socket.py:218` (2 red);
adding an un-exempted WIRE_CONTRACT_VERSION = 7 to serve_rpc.py fails it too
(1 red); making serve_rpc.py import SNAPSHOT_CONTRACT_VERSION fails the
independence witness (1 red).

`_scanned_modules` is now session-cached, matching the pattern in
test_s55_registered_events_have_emitters. Three tests parse the scanned roots
and this commit added the third; uncached, the file ran 31.6s, cached it runs
11-16s with the slowest test at 8.0s against the 30s cap.

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent-runtime): a per-TEST budget was billed for a per-SESSION walk, and the walk was doing it eight times

This file made the default single-process suite invocation impossible. Six tests
share one resolver through the caches at the top, so exactly ONE of them pays for
it — and which one is decided by collection order, which none of them chose.
`--timeout=30` is a per-test budget; this is a per-session cost. Charging a
shared setup to whichever item ran first made a passing test fail for a reason
unrelated to what it asserts, and because `--timeout-method=thread` KILLS the
process rather than failing the item, `pytest tests/agent_runtime/` collected
nothing after this file.

MEASURED, and the reported figure was the timeout, not the cost. 33.5s is what a
30s cap plus teardown looks like; the actual walk is 10-17s to parse 934
production modules plus 25-43s to resolve, i.e. 50-60s on this box — roughly 2x
the cap, so nothing marginal would have fixed it.

NOT MARKED `integration`, and this is the load-bearing part of the choice.
`addopts` filters `-m 'not integration'` in EVERY pytest invocation, including
each per-file subprocess `scripts/run_tests_parallel.py` spawns (which is
acknowledged at run_tests_parallel.py:333). There is no integration lane to catch
it: `.github/workflows/tests.yml` runs `scripts/run_tests.sh --files ...` and
neither it nor ci.yml mentions the marker anywhere — grep returns zero hits. The
marker would have deleted this gate from every run on every machine, which is
strictly worse than a slow gate, and the suggestion to use it should be treated
as refuted rather than deferred.

Two changes instead:

1. THE COST. `_production_call_index` flattens every production function and its
   calls ONCE. The resolver is a fixed point — it discovers wrapper sinks, then
   re-scans for what those wrappers are called with — and it used to re-walk all
   934 ASTs on each of up to eight rounds, with `ast.walk(func)` inside
   `ast.walk(tree)` re-walking each nested function once per enclosing function
   on top. Nothing about the trees changes between rounds, only the sink set, so
   every round after the first recomputed an answer that could not have moved.
   Sinks are now indexed by callee name too, so a call is matched by one dict
   lookup instead of a scan over every sink found so far.

   Output is IDENTICAL, and that was proven rather than assumed: HEAD's resolver
   and this one were loaded side by side in one interpreter over the same tree —
   same 111 types, same site lists, `sorted(set(...))` equal per key. Resolve
   time 42.6s -> 8.2s; with the index warm a re-resolve is 0.33s.

2. THE ATTRIBUTION. Both caches are warmed at module import, so the remaining
   ~25s lands in collection, which pytest-timeout does not clock. Verified
   directly, not assumed: a module that sleeps 35s at import passes under
   `--timeout=30`. No test is excluded and no marker is involved.

The guard pins the cause, not the symptom. `_CACHE_SIZES_AT_IMPORT` snapshots
cache occupancy at import so deleting the warm fails deterministically instead of
depending on collection order, and the builders are asserted to have run exactly
once via `cache_info().misses` rather than a wall clock — a timing assertion on a
box that measured this same walk at anywhere from 8s to 43s under load is a flake
generator, and it would be asserting the symptom anyway.

ONE MUTATION SURVIVED AND IS REPORTED RATHER THAN GATED. Making
`emitted_event_types()` bypass `_emitted_event_types_cached` entirely stays
GREEN. A first draft of the guard was aimed at exactly that and asserted a
wall-clock budget over repeated calls; the mutation exposed that its premise was
wrong. With the index cached, an extra full resolve costs 0.33s, not 8s — the
whole cost lives in the two builders, so that is where the guard now points. A
gate on the third-of-a-second path would have been ceremony.

Six mutations red, none of them silently: deleting the module warm reproduces the
ORIGINAL symptom exactly (process killed, `+++ Timeout +++`, mid-parse);
dropping `@lru_cache` from `_production_call_index` (1 red, file 98s); reverting
the resolver to HEAD's re-walk-every-round form (1 red, file 80s); failing to
rebuild the sink index after the sink set grows, which kills idiom 3 (42 types
lost); indexing only the first call per function (54 types lost); dropping idiom
4 (`state.patched`, `persona.profile_rebound` lost).

File: 13 passed with one test over the cap -> 15 passed, slowest test 1.84s.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent-runtime): three session-scoped walks in one file, each billed to one test item

`test_tombstone_registry.py` is the next blocker to a completing single-process
`pytest tests/agent_runtime/`, and the interesting part is that it does not fail
reliably. It sits a few seconds under the 30s per-test cap, so whether it trips
depends on page-cache warmth and machine load:

  cold, this machine:  exit 1, `+++ Timeout +++`, no summary line (observed twice)
  warm, this machine:  exit 0, 915 passed in 103s
  coordinator, main:   exit 1, 34.7s; and 32.2s with `-p no:randomly`
  a parallel agent:    "passes standalone, 915 passed in 296s"
  another:             "timeout-shaped, no tests ran"

That is worse than a clean failure, not better: `--timeout-method=thread` KILLS
the process, so on the runs where it does trip it takes every test after this
file with it — at random, in CI, where it reads as flake and gets re-run rather
than fixed.

THREE independent session-scoped computations were each billed to whichever test
item reached them first. Measured before, warm:

  test_the_scanner_is_not_vacuous                          17.3s / 21.2s
  test_round4_deleted_tests_left_no_live_production_...    21.2s / 18.5s

1. The production render — `ast.parse` 27.6s plus `ast.unparse` 12.4s over 934
   files. `_CODE_CACHE` already shared it between scans; what it lacked was an
   owner.
2. A SECOND, larger walk hiding one screen down: 2880 files under `tests/`, 43.9s
   to parse, inline in the round-4 coverage test. Fixing (1) alone just moved the
   process death here, which is why the guard for it exists separately.
3. The round-4 diff itself: a `git show` SUBPROCESS per test file changed since a
   PINNED base. 21.4s once (2) was hoisted off it. Never over the cap on the day
   it was written, and included anyway because its cost grows with every commit
   to `tests/` while its base stays fixed — leaving it was scheduling the same
   kill for later.

All three are now warmed at module import, where pytest-timeout does not clock
them (verified: a module that sleeps 35s at import passes under `--timeout=30`).
Separately, `code_offenders` re-resolved `Path(__file__)` inside its per-file
loop — 934 files x 156 scans, 1.04s of pure `resolve()` per scan — and re-globbed
the tree per row. Both are hoisted into a cached `_scan_paths`.

NOT marked `integration`: `addopts` filters `-m 'not integration'` in every
invocation including the per-file subprocesses `run_tests_parallel.py` spawns,
and there is no integration lane (`tests.yml` runs `scripts/run_tests.sh`; the
marker appears nowhere in `.github/workflows/`). The marker deletes the gate
rather than fixing it.

The unparse is KEPT, though it is the obvious thing to cut.
`test_no_production_file_failed_to_parse` treats a file the scanner cannot RENDER
as a hole rather than a pass, and `_code_only`'s own docstring records that S46's
cheaper token-join turned `card.title` into three tokens so no dotted assertion
could match — a gate that passed vacuously. The cheap version was already tried
and already failed, so nothing about what is compared changed here. Proven rather
than asserted: all 154 CODE rows produce byte-identical offender lists before and
after the `_scan_paths` refactor.

AFTER, twice, warm: exit 0, 920 passed in 66.9s / 62.1s. Both former hot tests
fall out of the top five entirely; the slowest test in the file is now 0.95s, a
31x margin under the cap instead of a 1.4x one. Whole-file wall clock also drops
from 103s to 62-67s, because the per-row `resolve()` syscalls are gone.

ONE MUTATION SURVIVED AND WAS FIXED RATHER THAN REPORTED CLEAN. The first
cache-key guard drove all 154 rows twice and required the second pass to add no
misses. Mixing the row's own text into the scan key — the exact regression it was

bounds the number of ENTRIES by the number of distinct scopes, and the same

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve-rpc): the emitter was never missing — the handler had no name for its caller

`runtime.office.subscribe` could not be written against `fn(rid, params)`, and
the reason was not the one I had been giving. The push machinery has shipped
for as long as the socket lane has: `SocketConnection.emit` writes one frame to
one connection, `ServeSocketServer.broadcast` fans out to all of them, and
`serve.py`'s dispatcher already holds the stable per-connection `sink` in scope
at the very line that answers a method call. What a handler could not do was
NAME the caller it would push to later, so a subscription had nothing to
register. This is that argument, and deliberately nothing else.

`RpcContext` carries three facts and no behaviour beyond `push`: the caller's
own frame sink (None when there is no push channel — the honest state for a
test or a future non-duplex transport, and a method that needs one must refuse
rather than assume), the transport name, and `connection_key`. The key is the
SUBSCRIPTION identity: it is the only token the teardown path can name, so a
registry keyed on it can be swept when `connection_sinks.pop` fires on drop.
On stdio there is no key, and that is a real difference rather than a missing
value — a stdio subscribe has one implicit caller.

`notification()` is the frame: a request object minus `id`, per spec §4.1,
with `id` an ABSENT KEY and not `null`. Our own launcher is tolerant here on
purpose (`mission_control_serve_session_io.dart:691` treats `"id": null` as a
notification because a sloppy encoder is likelier than a runtime awaiting an
uncorrelatable reply), so this is a contract choice for the next client rather
than a fix for the current one. A strict client correlating on key presence
would file the push into its pending-call table and leak the entry.

`push` does not swallow. A push raised inside a handler is still inside
`handle_request`'s boundary, so it becomes a typed -32000 on the call that
tried it — the one moment a dead channel is reportable, since a notification
has no reply to carry an error. Fan-out to OTHER subscribers is a different
path with a different answer (drop, account, close) and must not borrow this.

`context` defaults to an EMPTY context rather than None so handlers can ask
`context.emit is None` instead of guarding the argument; the two live handlers
take it with a default so direct-call sites (the rekey script's end-to-end
test) keep working. One test stub grew the third parameter.

The method set and RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION do not move — asserted, because this
leaking into the CALL contract would make the version integer wrong.

Red-proofed both ways: `emit=None` in serve.py turns the end-to-end wiring test
red, and `"id": None` in notification() turns three red. 525 passed across the
serve/rpc/contract selection.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve-rpc): runtime.office.subscribe — one baseline, one derivation, one lane

Operator ruling: option (A), RE-ENVELOPE. The office delta lane already exists
and works — `emit_office_actor_patch` writes an `office_actor` upsert into the
event log and `stream.patch_batch_frame` assembles the batch. The only thing
wrong with it was the ENVELOPE: a bare frame with no correlation rule, which is
how a push could arrive and be dropped on the floor with nothing to say so.

So this adds no derivation. `serve_office_subscriptions` registers with the
SAME StreamHub every stream client uses, under a sink that re-wraps what it
cares about as JSON-RPC notifications. `StreamHub.subscribe` already takes an
arbitrary sink callable, so this is a use of the seam rather than a new one.

The consequence that decided it: an RPC subscriber COUNTS as a hub subscriber.
The hub stops producing when its room empties, so a fan-out that merely
OBSERVED the hub would — the moment the launcher stops joining the legacy
stream, which is the entire point of the ruling — observe a producer that had
already exited, and the office would silently stop updating.

The sink is ADDRESSED where a frame is broadcast: only `office_actor` rows
whose id sits under this subscription's workspace cross, which is what
`office_actor_patch_id`'s "<workspace_id>/" prefix was built for. A batch with
nothing for this workspace sends NOTHING rather than an envelope the client
opens and discards. A hydrate/delta means the batch was not patch-coverable, so
it becomes `runtime.office.resync`; an UNKNOWN frame type takes the same exit
deliberately, because a type this module has not been taught is by definition a
change it cannot express as a patch, and a resync is recoverable where a
dropped change is not. Heartbeats carry no state and are skipped.

ONE offset comparison absorbs two different seams, which is why it is stated as
a comparison and not as two guards: `StreamHub.subscribe` restarts the producer
so a late joiner's first frame is a hydrate (we do not want it — the reply
carried the baseline), and the dispatcher emits a reply AFTER the handler
returns (so a patch published in between lands BEFORE the baseline it rebases
on). Both are "at or behind what the client already has".

`runtime.office.subscribe` returns the baseline AND the offset it was read at,
both under `office_lock`, because a get-then-join is two reads of one truth
with an unreportable window between them. The projection is EXTRACTED into
`_office_projection` and shared with `runtime.office.get` — a subscribe whose
baseline could disagree with a get would restore the two-readers-of-one-truth
state this lane exists to end, and the test asserts the two results are equal
rather than checking fields.

Refusals are typed because the cures differ: `push_channel_unavailable` (this
caller has no channel — the reason RpcContext.emit may be None),
`push_lane_unavailable` (no hub bound, a runtime fact), `already_subscribed`
(4090, idempotent with a receipt rather than a silent re-register that would
leak a subscriber per retry).

Teardown is NOT free and is wired explicitly. `_release_subscription` already
unsubscribes the stream lane's bare connection key; the office keys are
namespaced (`rpc:office:<conn>:<ws>`) precisely so the two cannot take each
other's subscription, so the release path had to grow a second sweep. Without
it a disconnect leaks a subscriber, and a leaked subscriber keeps a producer
alive for nobody. The registry is also unbound FIRST on lane close, so a
subscribe racing the drain is refused typed instead of registering against a
hub about to stop.

CORRECTION to 6317c5bcd4's message: it called `SocketConnection.subscribed` a
declared-and-never-assigned bool and the natural slot for a topic set. Both
halves are wrong — my grep was scoped to agent_runtime/ and missed hermes_cli/.
serve.py:1752 assigns it and the stream lane sets it True; the field is LIVE
and belongs to the stream lane, so this commit does not touch it. (That
commit's other claim — that the emitter machinery existed and only the handler
argument was missing — stands.)

Red-proofed: dropping the workspace filter turns 3 red, and `<` for `<=` on the
baseline turns the boundary case red. 929 passed across the
serve/rpc/stream/patch selection.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(office-push): the lane had never met a producer, and it does not survive one

Every one of the 23 tests behind runtime.office.subscribe runs against a
_FakeHub and hand-built frames. That is the right shape for the sink's
filtering rules — an integration test that happened to produce no frame looks
identical to a filter that drops everything — but it left the whole lane
unproven where it actually runs: nothing had ever shown that an office write
reaches a subscriber at all. This adds that proof against a real StreamHub
over the real stream_frames producer, the real EventLog and the real
OfficeStore, and the proof came back negative in two independent places.

The first is an ordering bug in office_patch_sink. StreamHub.subscribe
deliberately restarts the producer so a late joiner opens on a hydrate, and
serve_office_subscriptions' docstring answers that by declaring the hydrate
at-or-below the baseline and therefore dropped — "both are answered by
dropping any frame whose watermark.event_offset does not exceed the offset
captured with the baseline". The code branches on the frame TYPE first, so a
hydrate takes the full_core resync exit before any offset is compared. The
first thing a freshly subscribed client is told is to subscribe again, which
restarts the producer, which emits another hydrate. Only a real hub can
deliver a frame nobody asked for, which is exactly why the fake-hub file could
not see it.

The second is that the producer never promotes office_actor. Promotion is
entity-negotiated, and serve.py's _accepted_fold_entities intersects the
declarations of the STREAM lane's subscribers; an RPC office subscriber
contributes none, so a room holding only office subscribers — the room the
ruling creates when the launcher stops joining the legacy stream — resolves to
HISTORICAL_FOLD_ENTITIES and demotes every office write to a full core. The
push lane therefore emits nothing but resync in production, which is worse
than the legacy lane rather than merely no better: the client pays a resync
round trip per write, and each re-subscribe costs every other subscriber on
that shared producer a fresh core.

Both are recorded as xfail(strict=True) stating the intended behaviour rather
than as assertions blessing today's output. A pinned-defect test and a strict
xfail both go red when the defect is fixed, but only the xfail says which
direction is correct, and an XPASS names the test that must lose its marker.
Asserting the observed behaviour as if it were the contract was rejected: it
would read as an endorsement of a lane that does not work, and this file
exists precisely because a fake made a broken lane look tested.

What the remaining tests prove is that nothing else is in the way. Given a
producer that does declare office_actor — a one-word change to a set — a real
upsert_actor arrives as runtime.office.patch carrying the actor's moved row;
the subscribe reply's baseline is byte-equal to the base_offset the producer
chains its batch from, which nothing in the code forces and which a gap
detector would reject if it drifted by one; an RPC subscription alone sustains
the producer across more than one frame; release genuinely unsubscribes from
the hub and the producer then stops; a create that moves the surface row
degrades to a resync rather than to silence; and another workspace's real
write reaches this subscriber's sink and is discarded there.

Every wait is a bounded poll on a condition, and on frames_delivered rather
than frames_produced. That distinction was itself a bug caught mid-work: the
hub increments frames_produced while OFFERING a frame into a bounded queue
under its own lock, and the sink runs later on the subscriber's pump thread,
so waiting on the produced count proved only that a frame was queued. Two
tests were passing on thread scheduling, and the drain that clears the
hydrate's spurious resync could let it land afterwards and be mistaken for the
notification the test's own write produced.

Anti-vacuity: ten mutations were run against production. The baseline
comparison widened and narrowed by one each kills the boundary test; silencing
the patch branch kills three; degrading a non-patch frame to silence kills the
resync test and flips the rehydrate xfail to XPASS; registering a subscription
without joining the hub kills all six live tests; a release that prunes its
index without unsubscribing kills the teardown test; a zero baseline in the
subscribe reply kills the offset-identity test; removing the workspace address
filter killed nothing until the cross-workspace test was added, and kills it
now. The two xfails were confirmed non-vacuous the same way, in reverse:
comparing the baseline before the type branch turns the first green, and
adding office_actor to the negotiated default turns the second green, each
without disturbing the other.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-push): the baseline gate ran AFTER the type branch, so every subscribe answered itself

Found by putting the lane behind a real StreamHub for the first time
(cd1bec9ef6). The 23 fake-hub tests could not see it, and the reason is worth
keeping: a fake only ever hands the sink a frame the test chose. A real hub
delivers a frame nobody asked for — `StreamHub.subscribe` deliberately restarts
the producer so a late joiner opens on a hydrate — and that is precisely the
frame this got wrong.

`office_patch_sink` classified by frame TYPE first, so the hydrate took the
`full_core` resync exit unconditionally; the offset comparison sat inside the
patch branch and never saw it. The module docstring three lines up claimed the
opposite — that one comparison absorbs both the hub's re-baselining hydrate and
the reply-after-push ordering. The code disagreed with its own stated rule, and
the rule was the correct one.

The consequence is a LOOP, not a wasted frame: the client is told to resync,
re-subscribes, the hub restarts the producer, the new hydrate resyncs it again —
and every other subscriber on that shared producer pays a fresh full core each
lap. A lane that answers "subscribe again" to every subscribe is worse than no
lane, because it also taxes the room.

The gate now runs above the type branch, which is what the docstring described:
a frame at or behind what the subscribe reply already carried has nothing to
tell this client, WHATEVER its type. Only genuinely-new frames get classified.

One thing this fix must not do is silently swallow a frame it cannot place, so
`_event_offset_of` returns None as a THIRD answer rather than coercing a missing
watermark to 0. An unplaceable frame is exactly the case where a resync is the
honest reply; treating it as ancient history would turn the one recoverable
outcome into the unrecoverable one.

`test_the_baseline_rule_should_absorb_the_hubs_mandatory_rehydrate` was landed
`xfail(strict=True)` stating the intended behaviour. It XPASSed on this fix, so
the marker is retired and the test renamed to the indicative. That XPASS is the
red-proof: the test was red before this change and green after, by construction.

The SECOND defect that run found is NOT fixed here and its xfail stays: the
producer never promotes `office_actor` at all, because `_accepted_fold_entities`
intersects the STREAM lane's declarations and an RPC subscriber contributes
none. That is a cross-stack change and gets its own commit.

31 passed, 1 xfailed across the two subscribe suites.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-push): the office lane was a subscriber the negotiation never counted

The office delta lane has never carried a single patch in production, on any
transport, for its entire life. Not a config gate, not a dark feature: the
producer was never permitted to promote `office_actor` at all, so every office
write took the full-core lane and the push lane could emit nothing but resync.

Promotion is entity-NEGOTIATED. A batch ships as a `patch` frame only when every
`state.patched` in it names an entity the ROOM declared it can fold, and the
accepted set is the intersection over everyone attached to the shared producer.
`serve.py`'s `_accepted_fold_entities` derived that intersection from
`stream_fold_entities` — the table only the STREAM lane's `{"op":"subscribe"}`
writes. An RPC office subscriber registers against the SAME `StreamHub`, is
fanned exactly the same frames, and counts as a subscriber for every other
purpose in this file (it is what keeps the producer alive once the launcher
stops joining the legacy stream), but it contributed no declaration. So an
office-only room resolved to `HISTORICAL_FOLD_ENTITIES` and demoted itself.

The fix is a declaration, not a widening. `OfficeSubscriptions` now hands one
`OFFICE_FOLD_ENTITIES` per live subscription to `_accepted_fold_entities`, which
intersects over both lanes.

`OFFICE_FOLD_ENTITIES` is the historical set UNION `office_actor`, and the union
half is the part that matters. Declaring `{office_actor}` alone — the obvious
one-word change, and the one this file's own xfail suggested — intersects to the
EMPTY SET against any legacy stream client in the room: nothing promotable for
anybody, and the persona-instance patch lane that works today would go dark the
instant an office subscriber existed. That is a regression wearing a fix's
clothes, and it would have looked correct in every office-only test. The
superset is also honest rather than merely safe: `office_patch_sink` discards
every row that is not an `office_actor` under its own workspace, and a discard
IS a correct fold for an entity a subscriber does not track — the office lane
projects one workspace's actors, not the whole core.

Widening `HISTORICAL_FOLD_ENTITIES` was rejected for the reason its own comment
gives: that constant is what a client which said NOTHING is taken to fold, so
widening it would declare `office_actor` on behalf of every un-updated client in
the field. It is untouched, and a silent client is answered exactly as before.

The declaration is recorded BEFORE `hub.subscribe`, because that call bumps the
generation and starts a producer thread which immediately asks what it may
promote; an index written afterwards races it, and the mutation confirms three
tests go red when the two are swapped. Recording early then makes a REFUSED
subscribe able to leak, so the withdraw is guarded — and guarded on whether this
call was the one that declared, because a duplicate subscribe adds nothing and
must not withdraw the live subscription's declaration on its way out. That last
bug was written and then caught by the duplicate test in this commit.

The launcher half of this cross-stack change needs no code: it landed yesterday
in 92ff1f045, which taught `mission_read_model.dart` to fold `office_actor`
nested into `offices[<workspace_id>].actors[]` and declared
`--fold-entities persona_instance,incident,office_actor` on its stream subscribe.
`patch_coverage`'s module docstring still asserted the launcher's fold was a
hardcoded table of exactly two entries and that a third entity would cost a
re-hydrate; that is now false and actively misleading, so it is corrected here
rather than left to mislead the next reader of this negotiation.

`test_a_real_office_write_should_reach_a_default_wired_subscriber_as_a_patch`
was landed `xfail(strict=True)` naming this defect. It XPASSes on this change,
so the marker is retired and the test renamed to the indicative — and its
fixture now DERIVES the fold set per producer generation the way `_stream_source`
does, instead of hard-coding "told nothing", or the assertion would have been
about the fixture rather than about the negotiation.

Anti-vacuity, six mutations: singleton declaration → the empty-intersection trap
red; serve.py dropping the office declarations → both serve-level tests red;
recording the index after `hub.subscribe` → three tests red; removing the
withdraw guard → the stopped-hub test red; withdrawing unconditionally → the
duplicate test red; the fixture reverted to a hard-coded None → the default-wired
test red. A seventh (removing the withdraw guard before the stopped-hub test
existed) SURVIVED, which is why that test exists.

412 passed on `-k "fold or patch or subscribe or coverage"`, 611 passed 1 skipped
on `-k "office or stream or serve"`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office-push): subscribe re-baselines, and a client can finally give one back

`runtime.office.subscribe` registers and answers in one call, which is right:
the baseline projection and the event-log offset are taken together under
`office_lock`, because a get-then-join is two reads of one truth with an
unreportable window between them. The consequence nobody followed through on is
that the subscription is live before the client has finished parsing the reply.
A client that finds the baseline unusable — truncated, an unreadable watermark,
a crossed workspace id — is right to refuse it, since folding a knowingly-partial
office would render it as authoritative. It was then stuck: a live subscription
it would never fold against, `already_subscribed` on every retry, and no method
that could release it. Short of dropping the connection the runtime could not
reclaim that subscriber.

So a second subscribe for the same connection and workspace now REPLACES the
registration with a fresh baseline and watermark. That kills the stuck state by
construction rather than by care — the cure for a bad baseline is the same call
that produced it. The refusal it retires was only ever there to stop a
subscriber leaking per retry, and replacement prevents that leak by the same
mechanism, one key meaning one subscription, while being useful instead of
merely safe. It is not free and it must not look free: `StreamHub.subscribe`
restarts the producer, so a replace costs every other subscriber on that hub a
fresh full core, where the old refusal cost nothing at all because a duplicate
key was declined before a generation was ever bumped. It is therefore a receipt
and not a silent operation — `replaced` on the reply for the client,
`serve_office_subscription_rebaselined` on the service log for the operator.
A client in a retry loop must not be able to tax the whole room invisibly. What
was rejected here was doing the replacement quietly and letting the hub's
generation counter be the only trace, which bills a cost to a party that cannot
see the invoice.

`runtime.office.unsubscribe {workspace_id}` is the other half, for the client
that wants no baseline rather than a better one — it navigated away, or it gave
up. Releasing something already released answers `{"released": false}` rather
than erroring, because releasing what you are not sure you hold is exactly what
a recovering client does and an error there would make recovery
indistinguishable from a fault. Also rejected: taking `office_lock` and checking
that the workspace still exists. There is no baseline to pair a read with, so
the lock could only make a release wait behind a write, and refusing an unknown
workspace would strand the subscription for good — the very failure being
closed. The answer comes from the hub and never from the registry's own index,
because an index that disagreed with the hub is precisely the leak this registry
exists to make visible.

Removing `already_subscribed` also had to retire a mislabel riding with it,
which a parallel review surfaced mid-change. The old branch derived its reason
by asking `bound()`, and that is true for a hub which is DRAINING exactly as for
a live one — so a subscribe racing `_close_socket_lane` was told "already
subscribed to this workspace" while holding no subscription at all, and pointed
at the one cure that cannot work. Collapsing it into `push_lane_unavailable`
would have been nearly as wrong, since that reason says this runtime does not
push at all and a client believing it will not reconnect. A refusal now carries
`push_lane_unavailable` or `push_lane_draining`, plus `prior_subscription_released`
when the re-baseline's teardown had already run and the caller's old lane is
gone with it. The teardown must run first — the hub refuses a duplicate key, so
no atomic swap exists — and what makes that a window rather than a gap is the
caller holding `office_lock` across the projection, the watermark and the
registration alike.

Both changes are additive and `RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION` holds at 1, asserted rather
than assumed. The method set grew to four and a client only ever calls what it
found in the set; `subscribe`'s result gained a key, which is the same precedent
`runtime.office.get` set when it gained `persona_instance_id`, because the
launcher's decoder gates on required-key presence and never on a count. Bumping
would have made a client refuse a payload it can read.

Behaviour claims are pinned against the REAL hub, not the fake, because the fake
shares the registry's bookkeeping and so cannot contradict it: a re-subscribe's
watermark is required to have MOVED across an intervening write rather than
merely to have come back, the replacement sink is required to carry a later
write while the peer's delivery count is required to climb (the cost, charged
where it lands), and unsubscribe's silence is synchronised on a peer's lane
rather than on a sleep. The shape half stays with the fake. Thirty-two
mutations were run against the finished state with no survivors; three earlier
survivors each named a real hole and each is now covered — an untested
`__bool__` guard, an index prune that only a hub/index divergence can catch, and
the one keyword argument wiring `serve.py` to the receipt, which no unit test
could have missed and which is now proven over a real socket.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
merge: office fold promotion + subscribe reclaim, with their overlap resolved by hand

Two branches touched `OfficeSubscriptions.subscribe` for different reasons and
git could not reconcile them, because each moved the same lines for a rule the
other did not know about.

`fix/office-fold-promotion` records the subscription in the index BEFORE calling
`hub.subscribe`, and that order is load-bearing: the call bumps the hub's
generation and starts a producer thread, and the producer asks `declarations()`
what it may promote. An index written afterwards races that thread — the
subscription would be missing from the very producer its own subscribe created,
and the first office write after a join would demote to a full core for no
reason a reader could find.

`feat/office-subscribe-reclaim` rewrote the same body to RE-BASELINE: tear the
old registration down, then register fresh. The teardown has to go first because
the hub refuses a duplicate key, so no atomic swap exists.

The resolution keeps both, and the combination is smaller than either. The
re-baseline makes the promotion branch's `declared_here` guard unnecessary and
it is gone: that guard existed so a REFUSED duplicate could not withdraw the
LIVE subscription's declaration on its way out, and a duplicate can no longer
reach that point — the key was torn down a few lines above and the only
registration in play is this one.

Four tests then failed, all of them premise-stale rather than broken, and each
was repaired to assert what the merged behaviour actually guarantees rather than
deleted:

* two asserted `subscribe(...) is True/False` against what is now a
  `SubscribeOutcome`. They now read `.registered`, never the object's
  truthiness — `__bool__` is unconditionally true, so `assert registered` would
  have passed against every refusal those helpers exist to catch.
* `..._a_refused_duplicate_subscribe_leaves_no_declaration_behind` pinned the
  `already_subscribed` refusal that reclaim deleted. The DEFECT it guarded did
  not disappear with the refusal, it moved: a replacement that added its key
  without the teardown pruning the old one would leave two declarations for one
  live subscription. Rewritten to that.
* the stopped-hub case now also asserts `push_lane_draining`, because folding
  the drain race into `push_lane_unavailable` would tell a client that CAN
  reconnect that this runtime does not push at all.

886 passed, 1 skipped across the office/subscribe/fold/patch/coverage/serve
selection. The `office_actor` xfail is retired — the promotion branch is what
made it pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
docs(office-push): validated design + stages — the surface never needed to be an entity

The brief asked to stage 'make the office surface a fold entity'. The audit
says no: everything the two gestures move on the surface row is either
client-derivable from rows the client already folds (actor_count,
actors_truncated, the archived_actor_keys delta under the two lifecycle ops)
or read by nobody (updated_at). The staged design is two lifecycle ops on the
existing office_actor entity behind a negotiation capability token, plus the
two defects the audit found on the way: the dual-producer shared-watermark
race that arms the moment mixed batches promote, and the resubscribe that
restarts the shared producer to build a hydrate the office sink provably
discards.

Eight stages (3 launcher, 5 hermes), every mixed version pair degrading to
exactly today's wire; the first real gesture folds at six. Live evidence
read-only from the operator's running root and diag log; every claim carries
its file:line and whether it was read or run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office-push): O-H1 — creates and archives finally have a foldable op, gated

The office gestures cost two full cores each because the producer had no
vocabulary for them: a create emitted `refresh` ("a SECOND row changed and I
cannot express it"), an archive emitted no patch at all, and `chat_opened` was
a covered-looking event with no paired producer anywhere.

The 2026-08-16 validation retired the first reason rather than working around
it. Every surface field the two gestures move is either DERIVED at projection
(`actor_count`, `actors_truncated`) or has a delta the two lifecycle ops
determine exactly (`archived_actor_keys`) — so the client computes the
container state from the rows it already folds, which is the rule upstream's
project tree has always used for derived container fields. No second entity, no
second wire row, no contract move.

So:

* `upsert_actor` emits a real `upsert` for creates and re-adds, stamped
  `created: true` — the row was absent from the client's list, which is the
  only question insert-on-absent asks. `surface_rewritten` is gone.
* `_archive_actor_locked` emits the missing `remove`, inside the lock and
  before the domain event, for the `emit=False` conflict path too: the row did
  leave, and a client told nothing renders a desk the store no longer has.
* `refresh` keeps exactly one meaning — the actor list is TRUNCATED past
  `MAX_OFFICE_ACTORS_PROJECTED`, where membership is genuinely not
  client-decidable. The conflation dies with its misuse.
* `open_chat` finally emits its pair: a diffed persona-instance `upsert` on
  re-open (with `updated_at` always among the fields, so the pair can never be
  empty), an honest `refresh` on create.

And the piece without which all of the above would be a REGRESSION. This
widens the OPS of an entity every fielded launcher already declares, which the
per-entity negotiation cannot express — those clients would have the widened
rows promoted at them and answer each with a re-hydrate, paying the patch AND
the core. `office_actor_lifecycle` is a capability token in the same
declaration channel (it was only ever a set of strings), and the two widened
ops are coverable only when a client names it. A plain move upsert stays
coverable under bare `office_actor`, exactly as today.

Three tests invert, and they are spec changes, not fixes: the two "degrades to
refresh" office tests and the `surface_rewritten` arm. Their docstrings now
cite the derivability analysis that retired the premise, and the third records
the one residual — an un-updated client keeps a stale `archived_actor_keys`
mirror on the sync-convergence path, a field no widget reads.

Mutation-tested: dropping the `created` stamp, skipping the archive emit,
deleting the truncation guard, removing the coverage gate, emitting an upsert
for a create, and dropping the unconditional `updated_at` each turn a named
test red. Two survivors reported honestly in the map's own comment: the
identity-mapped store→wire rows are redundant against the projection's
same-name fallback, and the session trio is carried by either of two entries.
