author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-push): O-H2 — the office lane stopped claiming a span it did not send

Two defects, one stage, and the first is data loss rather than cost.

The sink forwarded a workspace-FILTERED subset of a batch's rows stamped with
the FULL batch's watermark. The launcher folds BOTH transports into one read
model with one sequence, so the delete gesture's batch — a persona remove
beside an office remove — arrived here as the office row alone CLAIMING the
whole span. Fold that first and the stream lane's frame at the same watermark
is dropped as stale: the persona remove never applies, the roster is silently
wrong, and no gate can recover it because the watermark says the span was
already applied. Latent only because this lane has never folded anything
(`folded 0` on every subscribe in the operator's session); it arms the moment
O-H3 promotes a mixed batch, which is why this lands first.

So a frame with anything in scope is forwarded WHOLE. "Addressed, not
broadcast" is untouched — nothing in scope still sends nothing — and the rows
are affordable by construction: each is bounded by the 4 KB payload cap and the
client's fold already handles every entity with one body for both lanes.

The second: this lane declared what an office subscriber can fold IN GENERAL,
from a server-side constant, which is a shape that can only ever report a fact
about the runtime. A launcher whose fold had been widened could therefore never
have its widened rows promoted here — the room's intersection cannot contain a
token nobody told the server about. `runtime.office.subscribe` takes an
optional `fold_entities`, fail-open to the old constant when absent, honoured
as empty when explicitly empty, refused when it is not a list, unknown members
passed through untouched. The accepted set is echoed on the reply, because a
declaration a client cannot confirm was honoured is one it learns to stop
sending.

That closes the chain: a real CREATE now promotes end to end against the
producer serve.py actually builds, asserted in the live-hub file with the
un-updated subscriber's resync beside it so neither half can be green alone.

One spec inversion, flagged: `test_a_mixed_batch_carries_only_this_workspaces_rows`
asserted the filtering this commit removes. Its docstring now carries the
watermark reasoning that inverted it.

Mutation-tested: restoring the row filter, dropping the in-scope gate, ignoring
the param, collapsing absent-to-empty, dropping the echo, and reverting
declarations() to the constant each turn a named test red. A seventh mutation —
deleting the declaration prune from _forget — survived every assertion, because
declarations() walks the owned index and can never see a stale entry; it is a
leak guard on a process-global registry, and it now has a test that says so
rather than one that pretends otherwise.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

message:
feat(office-push): O-H3 — the gestures promote

`office.actor.removed` join the live covered set, so the add and delete

both-ways partition gate holds without edits — which is the reason this is a
constant change rather than a leap of faith: a live entry cannot be invented
without a producer behind it, and O-H1 is where those producers landed.

`office.actor.removed` was deliberately absent, and its comment said why: an
archive rewrites the surface's `archived_actor_keys` ledger and `updated_at`,
which an actor-row patch could not express, so covering it would have shipped a
patch that folded the actor and silently dropped the surface change beside it.
That reasoning was correct for the wire as it stood. What retires it is the
derivability audit, not a change in the honesty rule: the ledger's delta under
the two lifecycle ops is exactly determined, the counts are derived at
projection and recomputed the same way client-side, and the surface
`updated_at` has no launcher reader. Nothing is dropped because nothing is left
that only the surface row could say. The comment is rewritten to carry that
argument rather than deleted.

Its remaining siblings stay uncovered with specific reasons rather than
residual caution: a restore un-archives from a copy the client never held, a
conflict resolution adopts a peer's row past the upsert chokepoint, and
`office.surface.*` moves `folders` and the surface's own revision.

Measured against the operator's baseline: a delete gesture went from two ~822
KB core builds plus a resubscribe whose hydrate the sink discarded, to one
sub-4 KB patch frame. The add's roster half still rides one full core on CREATE
— an honest refresh, deferred D3 — while its office half promotes, which the
live 1s split between the two halves makes the common case.

Cross-stack, and it needs the launcher's hand:
`tests/fixtures/stream_frames/patch_coverage_manifest.json` CHANGED BYTES (the
launcher pins its own copy, so it stays green while diverging), and
`patch_delete_gesture.json` is new — the milestone batch as one frame carrying
both removes at one watermark, which is the pairing O-H2's complete-batch
forwarding exists to keep intact. Both are called out in the fixture README's
outstanding-copy note.

One spec split, flagged: `test_remove_and_restore_stay_uncovered` asserted both
halves; remove's half inverts and restore's survives, so the test splits rather
than being relaxed — the surviving half is what stops the widening sliding one
event past what was argued for.

Mutation-tested: dropping any one of the three constants, ADDING
`office.actor.restored` (over-widening), and disabling either arm of the
lifecycle gate each turn a named test red.

author: nekwo
message:
perf(office-push): O-H4 — the office lane stops resyncing on other people's cores

An uncovered batch resynced EVERY office subscription runtime-wide. An agent's
turn, a board write, another workspace's office edit — each cost this lane a
full re-subscribe, and a re-subscribe restarts the shared producer, so every
other subscriber was billed a fresh ~822 KB core for a frame that carried
nothing for anyone here. The operator's session shows the backoff ladder
(250ms→500ms→1s) being walked by exactly this, which means the 5-per-60s park
threshold was reachable by background noise rather than by defects.

A coalesced delta already says what it was about: `events` carries one block per
batched event. So a delta is skipped when nothing in it is an `office.*` event
naming this workspace and nothing is a `state.patched` for an `office_actor`
under it. Both arms are needed and they are different facts — the second is an
office row that rode a batch some OTHER event demoted, so the actor moved and no
patch frame is coming for it.

Only a `delta` is scopable, and the asymmetry is the rule rather than an
optimisation: a hydrate says "here is everything" and enumerates nothing, and a
frame type this module has not been taught says nothing at all. Both keep the
unconditional resync — upstream's `full` bit under another name — as does an
office event that carries no `workspace_id`, because unplaceable must not be
read as "not mine".

Recorded in the docstring for whoever writes the stream-less client: skipping is
sound TODAY because the stream lane owns read-model currency. A client whose
only lane is this one needs a bookmark advance in the skip path first.

Mutation-tested: restoring the unconditional resync, leaking the scoping onto
hydrates, answering False where the code answers None, reading an unplaceable
office event as "not mine", dropping either scoping arm, and ignoring the
workspace prefix each turn a named test red. The conservative arm has its own
anti-vacuity test, because a scoping rule whose "I cannot tell" branch is dead
will one day skip a frame it should have resynced with nothing to notice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
perf(office-push): O-H5 — a rejoin stops billing the room for a hydrate it discards

`StreamHub.subscribe` restarts the producer by contract so a late joiner's
first frame is a hydrate. The office lane does not want that hydrate: its
baseline rides its own `runtime.office.subscribe` reply, and its sink provably
drops everything at or behind that baseline. So every office join was
manufacturing an ~822 KB core to throw away, and superseding the running
producer to do it — a cost paid by every OTHER subscriber in the room, on a
path a client walks repeatedly under the resync backoff ladder.

`subscribe` gains `restart_producer`, defaulting to True so the stream lane's
semantics are untouched. The office registry passes False only when a producer
is live for the current generation AND the joiner's declaration is a superset
of the accepted set in force — no narrowing, so the running producer is still
promoting only rows everyone can fold. Narrowing without a restart would leave
a producer emitting rows the room cannot fold, which is the regression the
negotiation exists to prevent, so it keeps the restart.

The room spans BOTH lanes and the stream lane's declaration table lives in a
serve-loop closure, so serve.py lends its own `_accepted_fold_entities` rather
than the registry re-deriving half of it — reading only one of the two tables
is the mistake this lane already made once. No probe bound, or a probe that
raises, degrades to correct-and-expensive.

Two floors, in the layer that can enforce each. The hub starts a producer
regardless when none is running, because a subscriber attached to nothing
receives nothing — silently, forever — and the caller's check cannot answer
that question anyway: a re-baseline's own teardown empties the room between the
check and the join. And the `serve_office_subscription_rebaselined` receipt now
MEASURES `producer_restarted` from the hub's generation counter instead of
asserting the constant True, so the emptied-room case reports the restart it
really caused rather than the one it asked for.

Mutation-tested, eight: always restarting, never restarting, ignoring whether a
producer is live, reporting the request instead of the outcome, letting a
broken probe take the cheap arm, dropping the hub's producer floor, counting a
superseded producer as alive, and bumping the generation on a restart-free join
each turn a named test red. `_FakeHub` models the flag and the generation
rather than accepting and ignoring them — a double that always bumped would
make the cheap path indistinguishable from the expensive one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

message:
docs(office-push): what the stages actually bought, and the two claims this plan got wrong

The eight stages landed and the operator drove real gestures against the built
runtime. Section 10 records what that measured, because the numbers move the
plan's own conclusions.

The milestone is real: archives promote, and the MIXED batch folds — one frame
carrying the roster row and the actor row, both applied. That proves the token,
the declaration, the room intersection and the launcher fold end to end against
a real runtime rather than in tests.

Deletes fold in 280-368ms. Creates still cost 6.94s, and the budget says where:
~6.3-6.6s of it is `build_snapshot()`, measured 1.17s warm / 6.92s cold on the
operator's drive, a metadata-heavy filesystem workload of ~4,000 stat calls over
~2,000 files. It is not a bandwidth problem — serialising 822KB costs 5ms.
So D3 is worth ~20x on this path, LARGER than this plan claimed rather than
smaller, and the follow-on is ordered accordingly.

Two claims in here were wrong, and both are the same shape — an assertion about
ordering in time made from thin evidence:

The "~1s apart, separate batches" bet. stream.py's 200ms is a JOIN window, not a
splitter: the producer drains, sleeps, and drains again into the SAME pending
list. The operator's two halves landed 356ms apart and coalesced, and one
`refresh` sank the batch. That claim rested on a single observation with
one-second-granularity timestamps.

The "O-L1/O-L2 are inert against every runtime" ordering note. True of O-L1,
false of O-L2, which is actively lossy without O-H2 — proven with a red probe
and then corroborated by the runtime's own STALE-dropped receipt.

Both are corrected in place rather than quietly dropped, with a standing warning
to treat the remaining timing claims here as unverified until measured.

author: nekwo
message:
obs(stream): log what build_snapshot() actually cost, and what paid for it

build_snapshot() is ~6.3-6.6s of every demoted gesture on the operator's
machine and nothing wrote it down. Establishing that number took two diagnostic
passes — subtraction from events_archive/*.jsonl byte offsets, then profiling an
isolated probe copy of the runtime root. The next such investigation should be
a grep.

Every full-core build now emits one INFO line:

    snapshot_build reason=demote elapsed_ms=234 offset=780 events=4

`reason` names the lane that paid — hydrate / demote / resync / full_core.
`demote` and `full_core` cost identical seconds and mean opposite things (a
foldable update that paid for a whole snapshot, versus the flag-off wire working
as designed), so they are classified in `_batch_frames_with_liveness`, the only
place holding all three facts. `offset` is the resulting watermark, so the cost
ties back to the events that caused it.

Timing is taken ON the build thread rather than around `job.done.wait`, whose
100ms cancel poll would round every build up.

CORRECTION to the follow-on plan's §10.3 item 2, which claimed the heartbeat's
`activity.elapsed_ms` already carries this number. It does not:

  * it is a CADENCE sample (`current - started` at heartbeat time), never the
    total — a 6.5s build against the 5s serve cadence yields ONE sample at
    ~5000;
  * a build shorter than one interval emits NOTHING — the measured 1.17s warm
    build is invisible on the wire;
  * it only exists on the uncovered-batch lane. `hydrate_frame` and
    `delta_frame` build synchronously with no liveness envelope at all, so the
    boot hydrate — a full build — never had a heartbeat.

Both emits are covered and mutation-checked: disabling either turns a named
test red.

author: nekwo
message:
perf(office-push): D3 — the create's roster row folds, and the 18KB was never true

`open_chat`'s create arm emitted `op: refresh`, and one unfoldable row demotes
its whole batch — so every Mission Office "add an agent" gesture dragged the
perfectly foldable `office_actor created:true` upsert down with it and paid a
full `build_snapshot()`: 6.3-6.6 s of a measured 6.94 s gesture.

The refresh's stated reason was that a full `persona_instance_summary` row
"cannot be assumed to fit the 4 KB cap (~18 KB)". That figure predated R2's
residue slimming, which evicted the tool-detail payloads — ~97% of the row —
behind a typed `visibility_ref`. Measured against the operator's live roster
(17 instances, read-only probe copy): largest complete row 3,012 bytes, largest
assembled payload 3,133 against 4,096, largest single value 504 against 3,584.
It was an assumption recorded as a fact, and it outlived being true.

So the create emits a COMPLETE-row `upsert` stamped `created: true`, gated on a
new `persona_instance_create` capability token in the same declaration channel
`office_actor_lifecycle` rides. Every mixed pair degrades to exactly today's
wire: an old client never declares it and keeps getting full cores; an old
runtime sees an uninterpreted string in a frozenset.

Two things this does NOT copy from the office pattern, both deliberate:

* `build_state_patch`'s oversize shrink loop is right for a SUBSET upsert and
  wrong for a create — the launcher inserts the row wholesale, so a marker would
  BECOME the roster row's value for that field. `emit_persona_instance_create`
  is therefore all-or-nothing and falls back to `refresh`, i.e. the pre-D3 wire,
  for any row that cannot be carried losslessly. The worst case is today, never
  a fabricated row.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent-create): AC-1 — one call places an agent, and a crash between its two writes resumes

`runtime.agent.create`: the fifth JSON-RPC method, beside the four
`runtime.office.*`. It composes the two chokepoints the launcher's create
already hits — `PersonaInstanceStore.add_instance` and
`OfficeStore.upsert_actor` — in a fixed durable order, under a
recorded-progress idempotency reservation.

What the two-call flow could not do, and this can:

* Both half-states become unrepresentable to the client. Today an awaited
  argv-lane instance write and a 600 ms-debounced RPC placement write can
  come apart in either direction (R#37, and the placement-naming-no-instance
  write the office store still accepts). Here a placement failure COMPENSATES
  — the just-minted instance is retired through the same chokepoint the delete
  gesture uses — and the reply names the phase and whether the rollback landed.
* A replay resumes instead of duplicating. The reservation records
  `instance_minted` -> `done`, durable BEFORE the placement is attempted, so a
  crash in the seam completes on retry rather than stranding a roster row.
* One batch by construction. Both emissions happen inside one handler
  milliseconds apart, well inside the producer's 200 ms settle, instead of
  ~356 ms apart across two transports and hoping they coalesce.

Deliberately NOT a speed change: the events are byte-for-byte the two-call
flow's (pinned by a parity test that runs both flows), which is what lets this
inherit D3's foldable `persona_instance` create instead of colliding with it.

Two things the plan got wrong, both corrected here rather than worked around:

1. AC-0 says the shared normalisation/naming layer extracts "UPWARD" into
   `persona_commands.py`. That direction does not exist: the file is exec'd
   into `harness.py`'s globals (harness.py:3667-3674) and is not importable,
   so its functions raise NameError outside that namespace. The layer lands in
   `agent_runtime/agent_create.py`, which BOTH lanes import — the CLI now calls
   down into it for the honest-default-display-name rule, so "QA Agent" (not
   the store template's "Qa") is one copy rather than two.
2. §5 says the handler holds its locks "sequentially, never nested". The office
   lock is taken inside the reservation lock. No cycle is possible — nothing
   else in the runtime takes an agent-create lock — and that is now the stated
   reason rather than an unnoticed contradiction.

Decision D-A3, forced rather than chosen: a rolled-back key REFUSES its own
replay. `retire` leaves an end-of-life tombstone and `assert_bindable` refuses
to ever re-bind that instance id, so the placement id is burned; a resume would
have to invent an id the client never predicted.

No caller exists yet — dead code against every launcher build until AC-2 lands
and gates on the manifest advertisement. `RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION` stays 1: adding
a method does not move it.

23 new tests; 15 deliberate mutations, 15 killed (see the branch report).

message:
docs(office-push): unified gesture prediction — one intent, rendered now, reconciled once

Operator ruling: prediction for both gestures as a general system, and on
release trigger the RPC.

The plan separates two things that were both being called prediction, because
building them as one without separating them first produces the wrong thing:
intent-to-RENDER (show it before any round trip) and intent-to-RECONCILE
(resolve against the server by revision). The drag has the second and not the
first. The create has neither — it is currently FAST rather than predicted,
since D3 removed the full-core build.

Root cause of the invisible drag, verified rather than assumed:
mission_office_game.dart:199 setInteractionMode writes interactionMode into
the render model and NOTHING reads it — rg returns exactly one reference, its
own setter. The game is told a node drag is in progress and does nothing with
the fact. The enum and the setter exist; the consumer never did. Confirmed
separately that this is not a regression from the 2026-08-16 commit-on-release
work: git diff shows the during-drag path byte-identical.

The design is one intent record per gesture, a canvas that renders
server-state + pending-intents, and resolution against each call's own reply.
Its consequence is the point: a drag emits ONE intent on release instead of a
mutation per frame, so there is nothing to coalesce and the 220ms and 600ms
debounces stop applying to drags — they were a repair for a problem the
per-frame streaming created, not a feature. And an explicit intent record has
nothing to infer, which is what finally lets the absence-means-delete branch
that caused R#40 be deleted rather than fenced.

Sequenced build-alongside, prove agreement, then delete — not delete-and-see —
because this refactors the code that lost data once. UP-0 (give the dead field
a consumer) ships alone and fixes the operator-visible bug by itself.

Most likely wrong, and stated as such: UP-0's size. I verified the field has no
consumer; I did NOT read how applyRenderModel seeds node positions, so "move
the node to the cursor" may need a render-model change rather than a hook.

author: nekwo
message:
docs(office-push): the invisible drag, found — the paint path retires the override mid-gesture

Root cause, verified by me on top of the scoping agent's report:

isSettled is now `!writesInFlight` (mission_office_layout_controller.dart:440).
During a drag the 220ms trailing save debounce is CANCELLED AND RE-ARMED on
every pan frame, so no write is ever staged, writesInFlight stays false, and
isSettled answers true on every frame. The retire branch in
_resolveOfficeLayoutOrNull (mission_control_page.dart:2789-2812) therefore
fires per frame: it returns the stale provider layout and microtask-clears the
override the gesture just wrote. The canvas repaints the old position all the
way through the drag. Release stages the save, the reply lands, the node pops.

The render chain is innocent: _reconcileAvatars does move existing avatars
(avatar.applyTransform assigns position unconditionally), the host rebuilds
every drag frame, and nothing shadows the layout.

REGRESSION COMMIT: 91fec5ddb, 2026-08-15 15:19 — "a state only a read could
leave was also the state that stopped every read". It changed isSettled from
full reconciliation to writes-in-flight to break a real deadlock, and its own
commit message states the safety argument: "the canvas loses nothing by
dropping the override once the ack lands, resolveLayout overlays that same
acked payload". That is true AFTER an ack. During a drag there is no write at
all, so there is no acked payload to overlay — and the override is dropped
with nothing to replace it. The drag had been riding the deadlock for six
weeks; fixing the read lane killed it as a side effect.

My two wrong calls on this, both corrected in the unified plan: I said it was
not a regression (off a one-commit diff window, when the break was the day
before), and I named the dead interactionMode field as the cause (it is dead,
and irrelevant — b2f815cd8 is a red herring; the field was dead the whole six
weeks the drag worked). The operator's "the drag used to work fine and i used
to be dragging around" is what forced the re-examination, and it was right.

Fix ordering per the plan: OR-1 is the symmetric completion of 91fec5ddb — the
paint path may not retire while the page itself holds a pending save — not a
revert of it.

message:
docs(office-push): UP-0 was aimed at the wrong layer, and the plan said so first

`UNIFIED_GESTURE_PREDICTION_PLAN_2026-08-16.md` opened UP-0 with "the smallest
change that fixes the operator-visible bug". It is not one. The invisible drag
lived in the page's paint-path resolver, which discarded its own optimistic
override on every frame of a gesture; giving `interactionMode` a consumer would
have drawn a node at the cursor in the game while the page went on throwing the
operator's gesture away one level up. A second source of truth papering over a
first that was actively lying — and the defect would then have stayed hidden
until UP-2 removed the echo again.

Three edits, and the DESIGN is untouched because the design never depended on
the wrong diagnosis.

  * §1's three open questions are answered from
    `OFFICE_OPTIMISTIC_RENDER_REGRESSION_PLAN_2026-08-16.md` and the launcher
    work that followed it: (a) the host does rebuild and nothing shadows the
    page, (b) `_reconcileAvatars` moves existing avatars unconditionally, (c)
    the regression commit is `91fec5ddb`. The render chain is innocent, and the
    dead field was dead for the six-plus weeks the drag demonstrably worked.
  * UP-0 is re-scoped to what it is genuinely for — the local-echo half of
    UP-2, which needs something to draw the node once a drag stops streaming a
    mutation per pointer move — and is explicitly no longer shippable as a bug
    fix. Its gate now tests it against UP-2's world, where the per-frame stream
    is gone, because shipping it while the stream is live buys nothing.
  * §6's "UP-0 is not as small as this plan says" is confirmed, with the
    correction that the instinct was right and the reason was wrong: reading
    the render path settled the size question in UP-0's favour. The problem was
    the layer, not the line count.

§0's table is corrected too, and this is the part worth reading. The render
half was never absent — `_officeLayoutOverride` had been doing that job for six
weeks. What broke is that the paint path started discarding it. That makes the
argument for UP-1 STRONGER than the one this plan shipped with: the distinction
was never presence, it is whether the render half is a property of the model or
a thing every gesture path remembers to poke. One predicate changed in a
different file, for a good reason, and the render half silently stopped
existing for every gesture at once with no test to say so.

UP-1 also acquires the paragraph OR-4 asked for, written before UP-1's code so
the OR-1 patch cannot fossilize: the intent ledger DELETES
`_officeLayoutOverride`, `_hasPendingOfficeSave`, the whole override branch in
`_resolveOfficeLayoutOrNull`, and `isSettled`'s only caller. If any of them
survive UP-1, UP-1 is not done. Its gate now also requires the launcher's OR-4
fence to stay green byte-unchanged through the rewrite — that group deliberately
names no predicate, so needing to edit it means UP-1 changed what the operator
sees.

Docs only. No production code in this repo is touched, and the launcher fix
lands on its own branch.

docs(providers): first-class provider logins, and the office write-verb RPC plan

Two scoping plans, docs only.

PROVIDER_LOGIN_FIRST_CLASS — designed against upstream's Electron desktop app
(apps/desktop, read from the upstream/main ref). Stages PL-0..PL-6.

The find that changes the shape: the session-based OAuth device-code machinery
where the secret never reaches the client ALREADY EXISTS IN OUR OWN FORK, at
hermes_cli/web_server.py:9714-10850 — welded to a FastAPI dashboard the
launcher does not run. So PL-2 reuses that shape over the launcher's existing
process-stream lane rather than inventing one.

Taken from upstream: backend-authoritative provider identity (which also moves
the models.dev alias map off the launcher's hardcoded switch), deferred
credential warning at submit time rather than on sight, reauth-vs-connectivity
discipline so only a confirmed 401/403 means re-auth, and — most useful — the
at-rest secret test discipline: assert the raw bytes are absent from everything
the app writes, never assert the storage mechanism.

Desktop attaches to remote gateways; for us it is the forbidden second store),
reveal-style read-back, the first-run overlay, and the fork's own tui_gateway
credential RPC methods (a third transport).

distinct copy — the point being that "never configured" and "configured but
401" must never render the same, which is what cost the operator time today.

Least sure, and gated first: A-1, whether the running serve child caches
provider clients. If it does, a successful re-auth would fix `auth list` while

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office-push): WV-H1 — runtime.office.remove, so a delete stops spawning a process

The office write leg had four verbs on the launcher and one method on the
wire. This adds the archive: `runtime.office.remove` beside
`runtime.office.upsert`, same conventions, no producer change under it —
O-H1 put the paired `office_actor` remove patch inside
`_archive_actor_locked` and O-H3 covered `office.actor.removed`, so an
archive that arrives over JSON-RPC gets both for free. A test drives one
through the RPC lane and asserts the batch is foldable, so "no producer
change needed" is pinned rather than assumed.

Three shape decisions worth naming:

* the ack is the POST-archive revision. An archived key carries its number
  forward through a restore, so the +1 is the token a later guarded write
  must present; acking the caller's number is a guard permanently behind.
* an already-archived key is an `ok`. The store is idempotent there on
  purpose and the launcher's flush re-names keys it already deleted, so
  making the repeat an error would report a failure an operator did not
  have — with a rollback behind it that puts the placement back.
* `workspace_not_found` is checked BEFORE the store, and is a different
  4001 from `actor_not_found`. Same ruling the upsert records, reached from
  the other side: the store's own NotFound names the actor, which is true
  and useless when the office was never authored.

No class-key fence: an archive cannot resurrect anything. No reservation
ledger: one store call under one `office_lock`, guarded or idempotent, so a
transport retry converges. `RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION` stays 1 — the set grows,
the integer does not — and the three tests that pin the method set as a
sorted list gain one line each.

Dead code against every launcher until WV-L1 calls it.

message:
feat(agent-create): UC-H1 — the create sequence leaves the RPC handler

`runtime.agent.create` did the whole birth atomically, and exactly one door
could reach it: a live `harness serve`. The sequence (reserve -> mint -> place
-> compensate/resume) was welded inline into the JSON-RPC handler and to its
rid/ok/err envelopes, so every scripted create still did the two-call dance
that R#37 names.

The sequence moves verbatim into `agent_create.perform_agent_create`, which
returns a typed AgentCreateOutcome instead of a wire frame;
`serve_rpc._runtime_agent_create` becomes a translation shim and nothing else.
No reply byte moves, no reason string moves, no event moves — the launcher's
`missionAgentCreateReasonFrom` decoder is the fielded consumer that pins them,
and the existing test_serve_rpc_agent_create suite passes byte-unchanged as
the fence that the shim is faithful.

Two deviations from the plan, out loud:

* The four ERR_* codes are re-spelled in agent_create rather than imported
  from serve_rpc — importing that module would drag the whole method registry
  into any CLI process that only wants to create one agent, and would invert

and conflating the two would let a caller silently re-label an agent's origin.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent-create): UC-H3 — `harness agent create`, the same call the wire makes

Until now the atomic create had exactly one door: a live `harness serve`
speaking JSON-RPC. Everything scripted — cron, skills, an operator at a prompt
— could only shell out to `persona instance create --add-instance`, which
never writes a placement (R#37's shape), or hand-roll a socket client.

The verb calls `agent_create.perform_agent_create` directly, so the reply a
script reads here is the reply it would read off the wire; a parity test pins
the key sets rather than the bytes. It needs no serve: every lock in the path
is a cross-process file lock.

Choices worth arguing with:

* Exit codes map from the JSON-RPC CODE family (-32602 -> 2, 4001 -> 3,
  4090 -> 4, -32000 -> 1), not from `ERROR_EXIT_CODES` keyed on the reason.
  So `persona_not_found` exits 2, while that table spells it 3. It arrives
  under ERR_INVALID_PARAMS because the request normaliser refuses it, and the
  two lanes agreeing about WHY beats either agreeing with a different table.
  This is the plan's stated expectation; the divergence from the table is
  deliberate and is the thing to overrule me on if it reads wrong.
* An omitted --idempotency-key mints a fresh `cli-<uuid4>`, so a re-run is a
  NEW gesture — the launcher's micros-stamp rule. A stable default would turn
  an operator's second create into a silent replay of the first.
* The payload is stamped through `attach_root_observability`. The repo's
  root-observability gate caught the omission, and it was right to: a create
  answering out of the wrong runtime root refuses just as plausibly as one
  answering out of the right one.

`persona instance create` / `open-chat` are NOT deprecated — roster-only,
placement-free creates are the browser lane's contract and the serve-absent
recovery door.

  verb routed to the add_instance-only sequence (no office write)
    -> test_the_verb_creates_both_rows_and_echoes_the_rpc_reply_shape
  reservation bypassed (fresh key every run)
    -> test_rerunning_with_the_same_idempotency_key_replays_and_writes_nothing
  default key made stable
    -> test_an_omitted_idempotency_key_makes_every_run_a_new_gesture
  workspace guard deleted (upsert_actor lazily authors the surface)
    -> test_the_verb_refuses_a_missing_workspace_before_any_write
  guard moved after the reservation AND the reservation made eager (composed)
    -> test_the_verb_refuses_a_missing_workspace_before_any_write

Measured and reported in the test: neither half of that last mutation is
lethal alone. The docstring says so rather than claiming a kill it does not
have.

coordinator callers draw ids from live roster rows and are unaffected; the
refusal is the SAME spelling and message the unified lane uses
(`agent_create.require_known_persona`), so there is one cure to teach.

  are before any store write either way.
* `open-chat`: ONLY the `--add-instance` branch. The other branches REBIND an
  instance that already exists — the 2026-07-25 incident recovery replayed ten
  bindings through one — and guarding them would refuse a repair for exactly
  the persona whose config row went away. Minting is the thing being fenced.
  A test pins that scoping, and records the measured fact that a rebind
  currently succeeds for an unknown-persona id. Whether it SHOULD is a separate
  ruling, not smuggled in here.

message:
docs(agent-create): record UC-H2's sharp edge — an unreadable config now refuses

`resolve_persona` returns None for BOTH "no such persona" and "this process
could not load the config at all"; it swallows every exception because its
original job was only to supply a display-name fallback, where a miss is
harmless. After UC-H2 it is no longer only that: a config the runtime cannot
read turns every bare-id create into `persona_not_found`, blaming the
operator's id for a fault that is not theirs. Before UC-H2 the same fault
degraded quietly to a title-cased name.

Left as-is — failing closed on an unknown roster is the defensible half — but
written down at the predicate, because this is the most likely way the stage
misbehaves in the field and the cure (distinguish the two Nones) changes
`resolve_persona`'s contract for its other caller.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent-create): an unreadable roster is a fault, not the operator's typo

Review fix on UC-H2, found by the implementing agent's own "most likely
wrong" and fixed rather than landed.

resolve_persona swallows every exception and returns None. That was
harmless while its only job was a display-name fallback — either kind of
miss produced a title-cased name and nothing depended on the difference.
UC-H2 made it load-bearing: routed through the same None, a config the
runtime could not read would have refused EVERY bare-id create on EVERY
lane with `persona_not_found`, an error naming the operator's id as the
problem when the id was fine and the runtime was not. UC-0 measured a
hermetic root's default roster as empty, so an unreadable-or-empty roster
is a reachable state, not a hypothetical one.

Split at the source:

  persona_roster()            -> the STRICT lookup; raises
                                 PersonaRosterUnavailable when the config
                                 cannot be read. An EMPTY list stays a real
                                 answer, distinct from a raise.
  resolve_persona()           -> unchanged contract, catches the raise and
                                 returns None, so the display-name caller
                                 behaves byte-for-byte as before.

Two refusals, opposite cures, neither wearing the other's costume:
`persona_not_found` means send a different id; `persona_roster_unavailable`
means send the SAME id once the runtime is healthy. Both are loud; neither
degrades to silence.

The witnesses demand DIFFERENT reason strings from the same call shape, so
a mutant collapsing the branches in either direction satisfies at most one.
Mutation run: collapsing the fault into persona_not_found kills
test_an_unreadable_roster_is_its_own_reason_not_persona_not_found; the
empty-roster test holds the other side so the fix cannot become a blanket
excuse that reopens the hole UC-H2 closed.

My first version of that test was itself vacuous — it patched
agent_create.persona_roster, above the wrapper, so the typed fault was
never minted and the raw OSError escaped. The patch now sits at the config
loader so the real wrapping runs.

Verified by me: tests/agent_runtime/ 5366 passed, 1 skipped, exit 0.

message:
merge(agent-create): the unified create call gets a CLI, and a roster that refuses

UC-0/H1/H2/H3/H4. runtime.agent.create already did the whole agent birth
atomically, but it was reachable only as an RPC through serve and only the
palette drop routed to it — so everything scripted still did the unsafe

The orchestration moves out of the JSON-RPC handler into
agent_create.perform_agent_create; serve_rpc becomes ~10 lines of envelope

serve-absent (every lock in the path is a cross-process file lock). The
legacy `persona instance create` / `open-chat --add-instance` lanes now

persona against the roster. `--persona qa_agent` minted a roster row, a
chat root and a placement bound to a persona that does not exist. I
reproduced it by hand, and the live diag log carries an accepted

the code.

Decision D-U1 is preserved and load-bearing: bare ids validate strictly,
`profile:` ids keep their synthesize semantics, because the browser lane
sends them for profiles that own no persona row and nothing else covered
that. It has its own witness now.

rather than the record — including a claimed kill that was false (a
workspace-guard reorder is invisible until composed with an eager
reservation) and a carve-out whose single-mutation witness had to move to

It also found the plan wrong in three places, including a grep-gate that

contradicts the repo's own ERROR_EXIT_CODES table.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(usage): S1 — a 401 the console could not name stops reading as "no usage data"

The Limits panel showed "no usage data" for a lane whose /usage endpoint was
returning HTTP 401. Not an empty — a swallowed one. `_fetch_usage_lane` routed
the three shared lanes through `agent.account_usage.fetch_account_usage`, whose
blanket `except Exception: return None` erased the failure class before the
harness's own honest per-lane handler — which was built to say
`usage fetch failed (<Class>)` and is tested — ever saw it. One layer's
fail-open policy starved the next layer's reporting, and the None serialized as
the unfalsifiable "no usage data".

`agent/account_usage.py` is upstream-owned, so route around it rather than
patch it: dispatch directly to the per-provider fetchers (all module-level and
importable) so the exception reaches the handler. That handler now names an
HTTP status when there is one, and appends the re-auth hint only for 401/403 —
connectivity failures are not reauthentication events. Everything else keeps
the class-name-only rule; a bare status code leaks no token and no URL.

"no usage data" survives, narrowed to its one honest meaning: a fetcher that
declined without raising.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(providers): PL-1 — the visibility payload can finally name what you COULD connect

A client that builds its provider roster from credentials-present plus
logins-present can render "this key is dead" but cannot render "you could
connect this" — both states arrive as the same absence of usable models. That
is the ambiguity the whole provider-login effort exists to end, and no field in
the payload could resolve it.

Adds a failure-isolated `catalog` block: one row per connectable provider —
id, name, flows, key_var, models_dev_id, docs_url, disconnect_command — built
from the unified provider catalog. `models_dev_id` is the lane→catalog mapping
the launcher had hardcoded and hand-verified; it now drifts with the fork that
owns the lanes instead of with the client. `disconnect_command` carries the
documented removal command for externally-owned credentials, because Hermes
does not delete what another tool owns behind a silent call.

The OAuth flow/cli/docs rows are hoisted out of web_server.py — where they were
welded to a FastAPI process the launcher does not run — into provider_catalog,
which the module docstring already named as their intended home. web_server
keeps only the part that is genuinely dashboard-local: its status_fn bindings.

Schema string stays at /v2, deliberately and out loud. Nothing branches on it
(the launcher feature-detects blocks and never reads it), while a pinned test
was left stale and red by the last bump — a version nothing reads is a
change-detector. Consumers detect `catalog` by presence, exactly as they detect
`environment`. That stale pin is corrected here.

Credential rows gain `token_preview`: last-4 only, None for anything shorter
than eight characters, None for a non-string (the Entra bearer callable is
never invoked). The payload still carries no credential value anywhere, and a
sentinel test proves it against a planted credential.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(auth): PL-2 — a credential write a GUI can drive, that names the world it landed in

`hermes auth add` is a TTY flow: it prompts, and on a piped Windows stdin its
getpass fallback warns to stderr and echoes a prompt no GUI can answer. So
`hermes auth set-key <provider> --stdin` owns the machine path instead — the
secret is read as the first line of stdin, by us, deterministically.

Three properties, each a test:

  * the secret never reaches argv. There is deliberately no --api-key flag on
    this verb (`auth add` keeps one for operators at a terminal); argv is
    visible to process listings, transport receipts and shell history, and this
    is the verb a GUI controls.
  * the secret is never echoed. The ack is JSON of key NAMES; an internal
    failure reports a class name, because an exception raised on this path had
    a credential in scope and its message is not safe to print.
  * the write NAMES its home. A credential written to the wrong Hermes home
    reads, from every surface, exactly like one that was never written — the
    operator has already lost hours to precisely that. `--profile` moves the
    write, and the ack carries the resolved home whether or not a profile was
    asked for.

Writes route through the credential_lifecycle choke point, so a GUI-driven save
cannot recreate the .env/pool/config mirror-drift bug family it exists to
prevent. The key-var lookup reads the unified catalog rather than the registry
alone, since providers like openrouter declare theirs on the provider profile.

`auth login <provider> --json` lands the NDJSON contract with no flow wrapped
behind it, and says so: every call returns `flow_not_wrapped` naming the
command to run instead. The four device-code functions each print their own UX
inline and block in their own poll loop; converting them to emitters is four
refactors of live OAuth code that cannot be proven correct without performing a
real login. A client can code against the event shapes now, and flows migrate
one at a time — an honest gap beats an untested rewrite of credential
acquisition.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office-push): WV-H2 — runtime.office.surface.update, and the echo that closes a rewrite loop

The folder taxonomy was the second of three office write verbs with no
method on the wire. This adds it beside the archive, same conventions:
`workspace_id` validated first with the shared reason string, unknown
workspace refused BEFORE the store, exceptions translated rather than
re-implemented, `RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION` unmoved.

Three shape decisions worth naming:

* the reply carries the whole NORMALIZED folder list, not a light
  `{revision}` ack. `_normalize_folders` is not identity — it prepends
  `DEFAULT_FOLDERS`, drops duplicates and blanks, and stops at 64 — and
  the launcher's flush has until now copied its OWN desired list into
  `serverFolders` on accept. Any normalization difference therefore left
  the two permanently disagreeing and the folder branch re-firing on
  every subsequent flush, forever. The echo is what closes that, so it
  is the load-bearing half of the reply and not a convenience.

* `folders` is a LIST. The capability lane comma-joins because argv has
  no other shape, and that encoding is lossy in a way nobody has hit yet
  only because folder names happen not to contain commas — `_safe_folder`
  keeps every comma it is given, so "Design, Ops" arrives as two folders.
  A typed lane must not inherit an encoding's accidents.

* the type check on `folders` lives in the handler because the store does
  not refuse: `_normalize_folders` answers a string, a number or a
  missing value with the bare DEFAULT list and no error. Passing that
  through would silently wipe an operator's taxonomy, bump the revision
  and ack it as a success. A per-element string check rides the same
  reason for the same cause — `_safe_folder` stringifies whatever it is
  handed, so a `7` would be written as the folder "7".

The unknown-workspace refusal is the upsert's ruling at its sharpest.
`update_surface` calls `ensure_surface` on its own non-dry path, so a
handler without the check does not merely answer wrongly for a typo — it
AUTHORS an office on disk, emits `office.surface.created`, and leaves it
there, while `runtime.office.get` answers the same typo with
`workspace_not_found`. The test pins the absence of `office.json`, which
no reply-shape assertion can see.

What this does NOT do: touch coverage, the producer, or any fixture. An
RPC write emits the same `office.surface.updated` and the batch carrying
it still demotes to a full core. That is WV-H3's job, and reading this
stage as the boot fix would be reading it wrong.

Dead code against every launcher until WV-L2 calls it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office-push): WV-H3 — the folder write becomes foldable, behind a third token

`office.surface.updated` was uncoverable by design, and its comment said
so for a good reason: nothing on the wire carried `folders` or the
surface's own `revision`, so a batch containing one had to demote to a
full ~822KB core. That reasoning was correct FOR THE WIRE AS IT STOOD.
This gives it a row.

`update_surface` now emits an `office_surface` patch inside `office_lock`
and before its domain event — the O-H1 placement, for the O-H1 reason:
the cross-process lock is what makes EventLog order agree with revision
order, and a patch appended after it admits the inversion where a lower
revision lands at a higher offset with nothing downstream able to see it.

The §V1 derivability standard is what licenses the coverage, not
optimism. `update_surface` moves exactly three fields — `folders`, the
surface revision, `updated_at` — and the row carries all three verbatim.
It moves no actor row, no derived count and neither key ledger. Nothing
is dropped because nothing is left that only the demoted core could say.
The whole content is `OFFICE_SURFACE_PATCH_FIELDS`, a named constant the
launcher mirrors as its merge allowlist, so widening the row is a visible
edit rather than an extra key in a dict literal.

A SUBSET merge, not a complete-row replace, and that asymmetry with
`office_actor` is the thing the two repos could most easily disagree
about in silence. Its sibling can replace because the store rewrites a
whole actor file; the office row also carries the actor list, the derived
counts and both ledgers, all owned by the actor folds. A launcher folding
this as a replace would drop the actor list on every folder rename with
nothing on this side able to notice — which is why the golden is pinned
cross-repo and the launcher asserts the untouched fields survive.

TWO arms deliberately emit nothing:

* a write that AUTHORED the office. `update_surface` calls
  `ensure_surface`, so on an unauthored workspace it is a create wearing
  an update's name, and a three-field subset has nothing to merge onto —
  a client would answer `patch_without_target` and re-hydrate, paying the
  patch AND the core. Not hypothetical: `workspace_template` clones an
  office by calling `ensure_surface` and then this, and a template clone
  is exactly the case where no client holds the row. The existence check
  is read BEFORE the ensure, because the ensure is what makes the answer
  stop being true.
* a dry run. It writes no file, so a patch would move the client to a
  revision disk never reached.

The token, `office_surface_fold`, is the third and the first that gates a
DOMAIN EVENT rather than a widened op. `office_surface` is a new entity
name, so the entity vocabulary could have expressed the row on its own —
but a covered domain event is not entity-gated anywhere in this
classifier, so an un-gated `office.surface.updated` would make a folder
batch coverable for a client that has never heard of `office_surface`,
which then answers the only row in it with a re-hydrate. Both halves ride
the token, and `TOKEN_GATED_DOMAIN_EVENT_TYPES` names the rule rather
than hiding it in a branch.

`office.surface.created` / `.restored` / `.conflict_resolved` stay
uncovered with their reasoning intact, and a test pins that declaring the
new token does not sweep any of them in.

Fixtures: `patch_office_surface.json` joins the cross-repo pin between
`patch_delete_gesture.json` and the coverage table, and the table gains
the foldable `office.surface.updated` case plus an
`office.surface.created` case for the half that stays out. Both
`MANIFEST.sha256` files move together and the ORDER moves with them —
`check_producer_contracts.py` compares line order before bytes.

Two existing assertions moved rather than broke: the "stays uncovered"
test splits again (the surface event leaves, `office.surface.created`
takes its place), and the set-folders dry-run test now counts two events
on the real write instead of one. Its dry-run count — the assertion that
test is actually about — is unchanged.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office-push): FC-H1 — the subscribe says why it came back

The launcher already knows exactly why every re-subscribe happens. One door
mints the cause (`start`, `fold:fenced`, `push:full_core`, `reconnect`,
`deferred:*`, `fold_threw`), one window counts it, one ladder prints it — and
then the string dies in the launcher's own log. The server saw N re-baselines
and had no way to tell a fold-fence storm from a demote storm, so splitting the
two classes meant joining two logs on timestamps. That is adjacency inference,
and it is the same shape that already mis-attributed this lane once.

So `runtime.office.subscribe` takes an optional `reason` and stamps it verbatim
on the `serve_office_subscription_rebaselined` receipt. It decides nothing and
must not: a cause the client chose is evidence, never authority.

Boundary-validated because it is written to an operator's tail on a path a
confused client takes repeatedly — <=64 chars over [a-z0-9_:.-], so a newline
cannot forge a log line and an unbounded echo is not a write primitive — and
refused BEFORE the office lock, the store read and the hub, so a bad param
cannot cost a producer restart on its way to a -32602. A blank is refused
rather than filed as absent: absence is already expressible by omitting the key,
so an empty cause is a bug in the client's cause plumbing and hiding it defeats
the point. Absent prints `-`, a value rather than a missing key, so "too old to
say" is visible.

The FIRST subscribe still writes nothing. A line per subscribe buries the
signal in the ordinary case, which is the same as not having it.

A-1 is now verified rather than assumed: an unknown param is ignored, so a new
launcher against an old runtime degrades to "the cause is dropped" and never to
a refused subscription.

The LAUNCHER half is deliberately not here — it edits the same builder function
as Plan E's WV-L4 and sequences after it.

Tests: 5 added to test_serve_rpc_office_subscribe.py (64 -> 69 in file).
Mutations killed:
  * stamp the receipt's reason as a constant -> two driven causes plus the
    sentinel; no constant satisfies `fold:fenced`, `push:full_core` and `-`.
  * drop the charset/length check -> the refusal cases go green, red on both
    the boundary test and the verbatim/limit test.
  * move the check after the projection -> the unseeded-workspace case answers
    `workspace_not_found` (4001) instead of -32602, which is the whole point of
    testing it unseeded.

message:
feat(profile-binding): B-1 — a gateway says which home it booted under, and why

`argv` could not answer it. main.py strips `--profile` from sys.argv after
resolving it (:697-699), so a flag-pinned boot and a bare one are byte-identical
in the `gateway.start` diag row. The live alice history proves the cost: 308 diag
rows, and not one of them can distinguish a deliberate profile choice from an
inherited one.

Three additive pieces:

1. main.py's pre-parse now records WHICH rung answered into
   HERMES_PROFILE_RESOLUTION — flag / env_profile_dir / active_profile_marker /
   default. Stamped unconditionally to "default" before any rung runs, so a
   child cannot inherit its parent's answer and present it as its own. No rung
   is reordered and no resolution changes.

2. `gateway run` emits one typed row in ProfileContextRow's
   {code, subject, summary, fix_hint} shape, carrying the home, the rung,
   env_key_count and telegram_configured. Key NAMES only — env_key_names drops
   everything right of the first `=`, and a sentinel-value test greps the whole
   serialized line. A second WARNING row fires only for the trap shape
   (env_profile_dir + no TELEGRAM_* key + another profile owns an installed
   wrapper); it warns, never refuses, because a base gateway can be legitimate.

3. The Windows wrapper generator refuses to write a wrapper for a NAMED profile
   whose argv lacks `--profile <name>`. Not hypothetical: `_profile_arg()`
   returns "" for any home that is not exactly <root>/profiles/<name>, and
   update_cmd._refresh_windows_gateway_launchers re-renders from the UPDATING
   process's home — which is how today's healthy double-pinned alice wrapper
   could regenerate into the single-pinned trap-vulnerable form.

Mutation-tested: 10 mutants, 10 killed, baseline restored green.

Does NOT claim to fix the observed alice-gateway break — B-0 refuted every
profile-resolution candidate for it (see the report). This makes the NEXT
occurrence one log line instead of an inference.

message:
merge(profile-binding): B-1/B-4/B-5 — a gateway that says where it booted; B-2 HELD

Three of four stages. B-2 is deliberately NOT here — see below.

B-1 — the resolution RUNG is recorded and a `gateway run` emits a typed
receipt naming the profile, the home, which rung answered, and whether
Telegram is configured (key NAMES only, never values). Pre-stamped
`default` so a child cannot inherit its parent's answer. The wrapper
generator now refuses a named profile that is only single-pinned.

This is the stage that pays for itself: the operator's alice gateway
"stops working" and nothing in the logs said which home it came up under.
Next occurrence is one line instead of an investigation.

B-4 — a new projection states its profile explicitly, with a backfill for
the historical nulls. Defaults to dry_run=True, refuses wholesale on busy,
never invents `base`, never overwrites a disagreeing stamp. The migration
claim was VERIFIED against live data rather than trusted — replicated in
pure stdlib with no hermes import and no writes: planned 1, busy 0,
skipped 15, and that one instance's target is what its persona already
binds.

B-5 — the gate results, including the assumption that INVERTS the plan.

WHY B-2 IS HELD, and it is not a doubt — it is a mechanism I confirmed.
B-2 injects the persona's resolved HERMES_HOME into stdio MCP children,
fixing a real defect (they were resolving a THIRD home at
`<profile>/home/.hermes`; six live profiles carry that stray dir). The
implementing agent named it as its own most-likely-wrong: blast radius
untested against a live MCP server, launcher_qa the plausible break. I
checked instead of dismissing:

  launcher_qa takes `hermes_home` as an explicit TOOL ARGUMENT
  (server.dart:1768), NOT from ambient env — so its own pinning is safe.
  BUT launch_manager.dart:1252 does `{...Platform.environment}` and
  inherits its ENTIRE parent env into every app it launches.

So injecting into that server propagates HERMES_HOME into the Launcher app
it starts — landing in exactly the layer where the inherited-value trap
lives (hermes_cli/main.py:635-647 trusts an inherited HERMES_HOME whose
parent dir is named `profiles` without consulting the active-profile
marker). Fix shape is to pin explicitly at the call rather than inject
ambiently. Tracked; the three stages here are independent of it.

WHAT B-0 REFUTED, and it matters more than what was built: the alice
gateway break is NOT a HERMES_HOME failure. No base-homed gateway has ever
run (308 diag rows, all alice; profiles/base/logs has no gateway log); the
launcher has zero gateway verbs and its reaper structurally spares them;
the active_profile marker steers bare runs TOWARD alice. What IS
established: all 13 recorded starts carry stdin_is_tty=true — the gateway
has been launched INTERACTIVELY, from three checkouts including two agent
worktrees, since at least 2026-08-01, so it dies with its shell and nothing
restarts it. That is a supervision gap, and it does NOT account for all ten
terminations. These stages do not claim to prevent the incident.

Verified by me before landing: 28 tests across the two new files;
B-2's changes provably absent (`_inject_child_hermes_home` not present,
empty diff on tools/mcp_tool.py and profile_context.py).

author: nekwo
message:
docs(boot): Plan G — the 47s boot, and five corrections to my own diagnosis

Scoping only. The headline finding is that I was wrong twice, and the plan
leads with that rather than burying it.

WHAT I CLAIMED: the health gate (25.2s) and the serve spawn (21.9s) run
serially, so overlapping them halves boot. My evidence was that 25.2+21.9
= 47.1 and `authoritative` = 47.5.

WHAT IS TRUE: the serve child was created at 05:48:23.08 — open+4s, and
21 SECONDS BEFORE the gate cleared. They already overlap. The sum is a
coincidence, because the boot contains THREE ~20s costs and two of them
happen to end together. My follow-up correction (Riverpod laziness; fix by
reading the provider early) was also wrong, on its own cited line: that
code is a presence fallback while the verdict is null, and the spawn chain
already fires pre-verdict. The stage I proposed would have been a no-op
that claimed 22 seconds.

THE REAL COLD PATH, measured off the serve child's own boot stamps in
profiles/base/logs/agent.log plus the launcher receipt, reconciling to
±0.1s:

  presence 1.0 -> sweep tail 3.0 -> serve cold bootstrap 20.5 -> ready 1.4
  -> (1.5 gap) -> hydrate build 19.9 -> authoritative   = 47.5

The third ~20s term is `snapshot_build reason=hydrate elapsed_ms=19937`,
finishing 240ms before authoritative. It hid because the receipt has NO
ready->authoritative span. That is the single biggest boot cost and it is
paid on every boot, not just cold ones.

The 20.5s bootstrap is COLD-ONLY: warm boots on 08-16 logged
interpreter_ms 1933/2062/2092 against this morning's 20421. The cold day
was caused by my own merge — the checkout changed under the boot, firing
the stale-bytecode guard, and TWO processes each cleared ~175 __pycache__
dirs with no lock between them and then recompiled in a race.

Also corrected: the "15 CLI spawns" I reported were ZERO processes — the
readiness chokepoint refuses in-process before the runner. The update
check is local-git only, 6h-cached, and absent from the serve path. The
WAL warning is a log line inside an already-counted phase.

Stages ordered by measured seconds: BW-0 (0s, FIRST — names the two opaque
numbers and adds the missing span), BW-H1 (~18s, the hydrate), BW-H2/H3
(bounded by the 18.4s cold-warm delta, attribution first), BW-L4 (3.0s),
BW-L5 (contention + the write gate), BW-L6/L7 (0 boot seconds — the
operator rulings on held writes and the stale banner).

BW-0 is first on purpose: two remaining terms are unattributed, and the
plan says so instead of guessing. I have now been wrong twice by reasoning
past a missing measurement.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(boot-window): BW-0 — the 20-second import tax gets named segments

The 2026-08-17 cold Mission Control boot reported ONE number for everything
from process creation to the serve command's first instruction:
`interpreter_ms=20421`, against a warm baseline of ~2,000 ms. Everything after
that instruction was attributed phase by phase to 1,437 ms in total. So 18.4 s
of a 47.5 s boot sat in a single opaque phase, and two of the boot-window plan's
optimisation stages aim at costs that live inside it. A phase nobody can
attribute is a phase nobody can fix, so the split lands first and alone.

Four anchors in `hermes_cli/_boot_clock.py` (stdlib-only by contract, so that
reading the clock is not part of what the clock measures) and two recorded
durations turn it into:

    interpreter_boot_ms  process creation -> main.py's first statement
    main_import_ms       main.py's own ~450 module-scope imports
    dispatch_ms          main() -> the command's own entry point
      bytecode_sweep_ms    the launch-time stale-__pycache__ guard
      harness_parser_ms    the `hermes_cli.harness` import + parser build

They ride the `boot` block of the `booting` frame `serve_loop` already emits, as
additive keys a consumer that predates them ignores by contract. The bytecode
sweep's purge line gains `swept_ms=` and the plugin-discovery completion line
gains `elapsed_ms=` — both logged a count and no duration before.

Absence means "not measured", never zero. Every segment whose two endpoints were
not both observed is simply omitted, the same contract `interpreter_ms` already
keeps for the psutil anchor it cannot always get: a fabricated 0 is
indistinguishable from a genuinely instant phase.

**Two deviations from the plan, both because the instrument disagreed with it.**

1. The plan defined `main_import_ms` as "process create -> main.py's module-scope
   capture", which would have left main.py's own import cost in no named segment
   at all — the exact gap BW-0 exists to close. That span is now
   `interpreter_boot_ms` and `main_import_ms` is the module's own execution.
2. The plan located plugin discovery "during `hermes_cli.main` import". Measured:
   `import hermes_cli.main` takes 0.33 s and imports neither `model_tools` nor
   `hermes_cli.plugins`. The real chain runs INSIDE `main()`, via the harness
   parser build — hence `harness_parser_ms`, which is 1,641 ms of a 2,150 ms warm
   import tax on this checkout. BW-H3's stage text needs the same correction.

No behaviour change: every value is a subtraction, one dict merge, and two log
format strings.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(boot-window): BW-H2 — the bytecode sweep gets exactly one winner

On 2026-08-17 the checkout changed underneath a Mission Control boot and TWO
hermes children — the health probe and the serve child — reached the launch-time
stale-bytecode guard 12 ms apart. Each walked the tree and deleted ~175
`__pycache__` directories, and each then recompiled the entire import set the
other had just deleted, writing `.pyc` files back over each other for the rest of
the boot. The guard is correct; running it N times concurrently is not, and
nothing serialized it.

An `O_EXCL` lock beside `.bytecode-fingerprint` (same directory, same
per-checkout lifetime, the `serve_auth._mint` precedent) gives the change one
sweeper. The loser waits briefly and then proceeds WITHOUT sweeping — fail-open,
because the worst case is the pre-guard behaviour for one process while the
winner's restamp closes the window for every later spawn. A lock older than 120 s
is broken, so a sweeper killed mid-walk cannot brick every future launch. The
purge line now names the outcome (`swept` / `waited_for_winner` /
`proceeded_unswept`), because "how many purge lines appeared" was never a
readable account of a multi-child boot.

The fingerprint comparison stays OUTSIDE the lock: it is two cheap file reads,
and on the overwhelmingly common path nothing touches the lock at all.

**The claim is three-valued, and that is load-bearing.** The first draft returned
`None` for both "somebody else is sweeping" and "this filesystem cannot hold a
lock" (read-only checkout root, a share without `O_EXCL`). Collapsed, the second
case takes the loser path — which on such a filesystem means NOBODY ever sweeps,
i.e. an optimisation silently reintroducing the stale-bytecode bug class (#6207,
#60242) the guard exists to close. `unavailable` therefore sweeps, and only a
`claimed` claim releases: a process holding nothing must not unlink a lock a
concurrent winner does hold.

Witnesses are COUNTS, never durations — `_CountingPurge.calls` owned by the test,
plus the pair of logged outcomes as an independent second witness. 13 mutations
run and killed, including the two that survived a first pass (an annotation
overwriting a phase; `unavailable` collapsed onto `contended`) and prompted the
extra witnesses now in the file.

**Honest value, now that BW-0 can measure it:** the sweep BODY is 14 ms on a warm
no-op path. Its cold cost and the recompile it forces on the loser are still
unmeasured — the plan's own §6.1 anticipated this and said the stage stays
correct regardless, because the double-purge race is real either way. It is NOT
the 18 s the brief hoped for; `harness_parser_ms` (BW-H3's target) is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(boot-window): BW-H3 — tool + plugin discovery leaves the import path

One module-scope line — `from model_tools import get_toolset_for_tool` in
`agent_runtime/tool_visibility.py` — was the most expensive statement in a hermes
boot. `model_tools` is not a passive module: its module scope runs
`discover_builtin_tools()` (importing every module under `tools/`) and then
`discover_plugins()` (a walk over 54 plugin manifests). And `tool_visibility` is
reachable at import time from `hermes_cli.harness`, which `hermes_cli.main`
imports while assembling the top-level argument parser — so EVERY `hermes`
invocation paid the whole walk before parsing its own argv: `hermes --version`,
the launcher's health-probe child, and the serve child, which then pays the same
tool warmup AGAIN on a background thread after `ready`, deliberately, which is
where the cost is supposed to live.

Measured with BW-0's own instrument, warm, this checkout:

    interpreter_ms  2150 -> 1229   (-921 ms, -43%)
    harness_parser_ms 1641 -> 500
    `import hermes_cli.harness` 2.219s -> 0.516s
    model_tools on the parser path: imported -> NOT imported

Paid by every hermes child in the system, not just boot. The plan claimed
">= 0.7 s warm"; measured 0.92 s.

**The plan's location for this stage was wrong, and its test would have been
vacuously green.** It said to find the chain "during `hermes_cli.main` import" and
to assert that "importing `hermes_cli.main` does not run plugin discovery".
Measured: `import hermes_cli.main` takes 0.33 s and imports neither `model_tools`
nor `hermes_cli.plugins` — that assertion passes on unmodified code. The chain is
`main.py:11228 -> hermes_cli/harness.py -> agent_runtime/continuity ->
child_events -> persona_assignments -> tool_visibility:11 -> model_tools`, all
inside `main()`. The tests drive the harness parser build in a FRESH interpreter
instead, because this test session has `model_tools` in `sys.modules` many times
over and an in-process check would report the session's history, not the boot
path's behaviour.

**An accessor, not three function-local imports, and that is the load-bearing
part.** Importing `model_tools` is also what POPULATES the `tools.registry`
singleton this module holds. The first draft called the lazy lookup inside
`_cached_tool_names_for_toolsets`'s comprehension — which reads
`registry.get_all_tool_names()` FIRST, gets an empty list from an unpopulated
registry, never reaches the lookup at all, and memoises "this persona has no
tools" for the process's lifetime. No exception, no log line: a silent wrong
answer. Every registry read in this module now goes through the accessor before
touching the registry, and the witness for it is the LENGTH of the returned tool
tuple in a fresh interpreter — the mutant is killed by the tools it fails to
return, not by a flag it could also set.

4 mutations run and killed. Deferring is safe because `discover_plugins()` is
idempotent and every other consumer already calls it defensively.

takes 0.33s and pulls in neither model_tools nor hermes_cli.plugins, so the

BW-H2 — O_EXCL single-winner lock on the bytecode sweep. Its own test caught
a design bug in the first draft: returning None for BOTH "someone else is
sweeping" and "this filesystem cannot hold a lock" means the second case
takes the loser path, NOBODY sweeps, and the stale-bytecode guard is
silently disabled — an optimisation reintroducing the incident it guards.
Now three-valued; `unavailable` sweeps, only `claimed` releases.

BW-H3 — one module-scope `from model_tools import ...` in
`agent_runtime/tool_visibility.py:11` becomes lazy. It was the only
module-scope model_tools import in agent_runtime/, hermes_cli/, tools/ or
gateway/.

measured (it claimed -1.33s / -49%):

    import hermes_cli.harness   main 2.917s -> branch 1.183s  (-1.73s, -59%)
    model_tools in sys.modules  main True   -> branch False

The structural check is the real witness; the timing is corroboration.

what POPULATES the tools registry, so a lazy lookup called inside the
visibility comprehension read an empty registry, returned no tools, and
memoised "this persona has no tools" for the process lifetime — no
exception, no log. Every registry read now goes through one accessor that
imports first.

axis. From the operator's own snapshot (`parity.build_ms=5485`, CONFIRMED BY
ME), the `events` section is 3ms — 0.1%. 87.5% is profile-directory
readiness, skill-tree walks and SQLite chat reads, none event-backed. And
the cache would go stale with NO event to detect it: `running_work.py` and
`board_sync.py` mutate durable state without appending events.

The codebase already says so, in its own words at running_work.py:454-467
(READ BY ME): "both mutate with NO EventLog event ... without a stat the 20s
cache would keep serving a HUD claiming three processes are running". Two
production incidents from exactly this are documented at stream.py:658-692.
BW-H1 would have persisted a third instance across process boundaries.

The correct key already exists one directory over —
`serve.py:401 _runtime_state_fingerprint` — and the cheaper target is

raw_decode per cold build, which is the 2,774ms that actually dominates.

six are registered in tests/mutation_claims.json. No timing assertion
appears anywhere in the new tests.

Verified by me before landing: 108 passed across all seven touched test
files. Agent measured tests/agent_runtime/ at 5415 -> 5425 (my earlier 5386
baseline was stale).

the SERVE child rather than remove it. snapshot.py:59 imports

message:
fix(tests): EG-0.1 — the test suite stops writing the operator's live store

Three tests under tests/agent_runtime called `monkeypatch.undo()` mid-body.
`monkeypatch` is ONE instance per test function, shared with every fixture, and
`undo()` takes no argument — so each of them unwound the package's autouse
`isolate_agent_runtime_root` pins along with the stub it meant to drop, and
everything after that line ran against X:/Eternia/.hermes. The leaked actor
`ws_office_patch_test` reached revision 67, climbing once per suite run; a
persona-chat root lease file was taken out there too. Nothing went red: the
hermetic guard asserts SETUP only.

- the three sites now use scoped `pytest.MonkeyPatch.context()`, which drops
  exactly one block's patches (test_office_state_patches:751,
  test_persona_chat_continuity:156, test_mcp_admission_r2:327 — the last one's
  eager drop was genuinely required and still is, on exceptions too);
- `isolate_agent_runtime_root` grows a teardown tripwire naming this incident,
  so a fourth site reddens the exact test that did it. It watches a per-test
  sentinel token, NOT `HERMES_AGENT_RUNTIME_ROOT`: re-pointing or dropping that
  variable in a body is a supported pattern here (test_profile_runner:535 sets
  it to "before_runtime", test_chat_session_scope delenvs it, and
  test_repo_context_observation:281 restores the production worktree base), and
  a fence that punished them would be weakened rather than kept;
- test_no_midtest_monkeypatch_undo.py is the structural second witness: an AST
  gate over tests/agent_runtime with a byte prefilter, driven both directions on
  synthetic source, scanning its own file without an exemption.

Both witnesses were driven on the exact historical mutation (undo() restored at
:751): the teardown errors naming the incident, the gate fails naming file and
line. Reproduced under a contained runtime root — the mutant's write landed in a
scratch office/ws_office_patch_test/, never the live tree.

Also ships the orphaned-surface exit HC §3 asks for, SHIPPED AND NOT RUN
(clearing the real surface is live-root surgery, operator's hands only):
`harness office archive-surface --workspace <id>` archive-never-deletes a
surface whose workspace no longer resolves, clearing its `orphaned_office`
parity warning; refused when the workspace still resolves, including an ARCHIVED
one (the predicate reads the same list snapshot.py:450 projects against). The
archive rides the existing `office.surface.updated` plus an accounted
`office_surface` `refresh`, so the batch demotes to a full core. A new event type
was rejected on purpose: it moves `decision_contract_hash`, which is baked into
the committed golden fixtures, and stage zero must not become a cross-stack
fixture regeneration. Without the refresh the covered domain event alone ships a
patch frame with an EMPTY patches list — proven: dropping it makes the batch

author: nekwo
message:
refactor(usage): EG-0.3 — the last route back into the upstream swallow is gone

`_fetch_usage_lane` ended with `return fetch_account_usage(provider_id)` after
its four per-provider arms. EG-0.2 §3.2 proved it unreachable, and the reap
matters because of what it was rather than what it cost: the ONE surviving route
back into `agent/account_usage.py:884-902`'s blanket `except Exception: return
None` — the swallow the S1 direct-dispatch work exists to route around. Dead code
that was also a loaded gun. A fifth id added to `_USAGE_LANE_PROVIDERS` without
its fetcher would have re-armed the original defect silently: every failure on
that lane rendered as the unfalsifiable "no usage data".

Prove-dead, re-grepped at this head (the plan's :3355-3357 was stale; the arm sat
at :3702-3704 before this commit):

    $ grep -rn "_USAGE_LANE_PROVIDERS" --include=*.py .
    hermes_cli/harness.py:164   (definition)
    hermes_cli/harness.py:3810  (_detect_usage_candidates)

    $ grep -rn "_fetch_usage_lane\b" --include=*.py .
    hermes_cli/harness.py:3668  (definition)
    hermes_cli/harness.py:3833  (pool.submit, the sole production caller)
    hermes_cli/harness.py:3677, :3781  (doc-comment references)
    tests/test_harness_usage.py  (monkeypatches only)

The tuple is the sole id producer and `_detect_usage_candidates` only FILTERS it,
so candidates ⊆ the tuple; an unknown `--provider` yields an empty tuple and
`_cmd_usage` returns at `if not candidates` before any dispatch. All four ids
return from their own arm.

The replacement is loud, not absent. `UnknownUsageLaneError(LookupError)` carries
`provider_id` as an attribute, and `_usage_failure_reason` grows its SECOND
exemption from the class-name-only discipline, on the same test the HTTP status
passes: the fact added is the dispatch key itself, already carried verbatim in
the lane's own `provider` field, so it leaks nothing not already in the envelope,
and it is the one fact that turns "a lane failed" into "lane X has no fetcher".
Read off `exc.provider_id`, never `str(exc)`. Shape:

    usage fetch failed (UnknownUsageLaneError: nous-v2)

Removal contract per RD-L6: a CODE row in the tombstone registry, scoped to
`hermes_cli` rather than repo-wide. `fetch_account_usage` is an upstream-owned
public entry point with live readers in `cli.py` and `gateway/slash_commands.py`
— the fork rule is route around it, never delete it — so what is tombstoned is
this fork's harness calling it. CODE and not IMPORT because the reaped import was
function-local and the IMPORT scanner only reads top-level bindings. Filed as
wave s71 because `test_every_row_carries_a_wave_a_commit_and_a_reason` makes the
`sNN` spelling an invariant of that table; the stage id lives in the reason.

Two witnesses, deliberately different in kind, because either alone passes over a
partially-restored fall-through:

(a) `test_usage_lane_with_no_fetcher_raises_typed_failure_naming_the_provider` —
    pinned at both ends: the raise itself (a caller must be able to branch on the
    TYPE, not parse a string) and the operator-facing reason the lane handler
    turns it into.
(b) `test_no_usage_lane_routes_through_fetch_account_usage` — a recorder on
    `agent.account_usage.fetch_account_usage` asserts ZERO calls across a full
    four-lane `_fetch_usage_lanes` run with every per-provider fetcher stubbed.
    The absence is proved on the path that WORKS, not only on an error path. No
    network: the nous portal call is stubbed too.

Both killing mutations driven. Restoring the fall-through and feeding an unknown
