author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): MC-1 / P1 — the exclusion set names the files their writers name, and a boot's own writes no longer flip the key

The core cache's store-root walk is a DENYLIST: everything not named in
_EXCLUDED_STORE_ENTRIES is fingerprinted. The set was hand-spelled, and it had
drifted from the writers it claimed to track.

* "drain_state.json" sat in the set annotated "per
  dispatch_delivery.DRAIN_STATE_FILENAME" while that constant reads
  "dispatch_delivery_drain.json". The exclusion named a file that has never
  existed; the real drain mirror — rewritten every DRAIN_MIRROR_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS
  for the life of a serve — stayed inside the key.
* serve_socket.owner.json and serve_socket.lock were absent entirely, though
  serve_socket's own doctrine requires both out of every freshness fingerprint.
  That doctrine enumerated the ALLOWLIST fingerprints (serve's
  _FINGERPRINT_ROOT_FILES / _FINGERPRINT_STORE_DIRS, stream._scope_fingerprint),
  where "do not add these" is satisfied by inaction; this walk is a denylist,
  where the same words require an action nobody had taken.

Together they guaranteed a fingerprint_mismatch on every same-commit boot from
the day the lane shipped (measured 2026-08-18).

Every name a writer owns as a constant is now IMPORTED, never spelled. The drain
mirror's staging file moves with it: it staged path.with_suffix(".tmp") —
"dispatch_delivery_drain.tmp", which the walk's ".<stem>_*.tmp" skip does not
match — so it now writes through utils.atomic_json_write, the one atomic-write
authority, whose staging name the walk already skips.

serve_socket's doctrine paragraph now names core_cache._EXCLUDED_STORE_ENTRIES
as the second obligation, and says why one sentence written for an allowlist
does not bind a denylist.

Gates (tests/agent_runtime/test_core_cache_exclusions.py, new — 9 cases): the
load-bearing one DRIVES THE REAL WRITERS (drain mirror, socket owner lock,
serve_registry, serve_auth, a harness lock) against a tmp store root and asserts
every top-level name they produce is excluded — the names under test come from
the writers, never from a restated list. Key-stability is parametrized one
writer per case so a dropped exclusion reds exactly one claim, plus the
cumulative boot shape, plus a probe that runs INSIDE os.replace to catch the
staging transient mid-write.

Residual, stated at the constant rather than discovered later: "locks",
"snapshot.json" and the "read_model.db" trio are still literals because no
writer owns them as a constant — and read_model.db is a CONFIGURABLE default
(runtime_config's read_model.db_filename), so an install that renames it
re-opens this exact hole one config key away.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): MC-1 / P2 — reading the SessionDB is not writing it: the WAL siblings stop perturbing the key they are read under

The build OPENS the chat SessionDB and the running_work stores. An open is not a
write, but the sibling keying could not tell the difference: -wal and -shm were
both keyed on mtime, and SQLite moves both on every open.

Measured 2026-08-18 on the live root and reproduced in the fixture: with a
connection held, opening the database again moves -wal's mtime while leaving it
at SIZE 0 (the closing connection checkpoints, so the file is re-created empty
at open time) and rewrites -shm. Both moved DURING the boot build that was
reading them. The key is taken pre-build by design, so the build's own read
guaranteed the next process a fingerprint_mismatch.

The mask, with each half's ground stated at _DB_SIBLINGS:

* -shm leaves the tuple. SQLite documents it as a non-persistent shared-memory
  index, rebuilt from the WAL by whichever process opens the database and
  unlinked when the last connection closes. Its mtime is a READER's artefact,
  and anything it could indicate is already carried by -wal's frames or by the
  main file's checkpoint. stream._scope_fingerprint — the other fingerprint in
  this runtime over these siblings — has always used ("", "-wal", "-journal"),
  so this CONVERGES the two conventions rather than forking them.
* -wal is keyed as (path, size, mtime_ns if size > 0 else 0). A zero-length WAL
  holds no frames; its mtime says only when some process last opened or
  checkpointed. The instant an uncheckpointed commit lands, the file is
  non-empty and its mtime counts again in full — EG-3.1's WAL-commit
  requirement is untouched for every state the signal can actually be in. The
  mask moves the mtime and never the size, so absent (-1) and present-empty (0)
  stay different facts.

What the mask does not cover is named at the constant: a checkpoint that
truncates the WAL to zero after writing its frames into state.db moved
state.db's own mtime and size, and the main file is the first entry in the
tuple.

Gates (test_core_fingerprint_cache.py, section 4b, 6 cases): four deterministic
unit cases over _db_entries driving mtime with os.utime (NTFS ticks at ~15.6 ms
here, so a case that drove mtime by working fast enough would be measuring the
tick, not the rule), plus two integration cases through SessionDB's own
connection factory on a database forced to on-disk WAL with a connection held —
the only way to reproduce the operator's shape, because this SQLite (3.45.3,
WAL-reset bug) falls back to journal_mode=DELETE for fresh databases and a
DELETE-mode database has no -wal to mask. Every case carries a non-vacuity
assertion that the sibling really moved before asserting the key did not.

Recorded rather than shipped green: the brief's "convergence count drops" gate
is NOT here. It cannot fail in this harness — measured, build_snapshot() does
not open the chat SessionDB at all in the fixture (a build leaves -wal
untouched), so a convergence-bound assertion is green with or without the mask.
The claim it was meant to carry is instead pinned by
test_a_persisted_key_survives_the_next_process_opening_the_database, which
settles a key, drives the open explicitly, and reds with
reason='fingerprint_mismatch' when the mask is reverted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
perf(core_cache): MC-1 / P5 — one consult per boot; the riders share the leader's key instead of each walking the store

A serve boot asked this lane the same question five times inside about a second:
the stream's stale-first read, the prewarm / hub / cli riders' consults, and the
build leader's pre-build key. Five full store walks (measured ~300-355 ms each
warm on the operator's drive), four core reads, four digests — all describing one
moment, all on the boot's critical path. The count is identical on the HIT path,
where the answer is by definition the same for every asker.

They are one question, so they now get one answer. _consult_memo holds the
CacheRead the first asker computed, keyed on the STAT TRIPLES of the persisted
pair itself, and is dropped the moment the lane disarms — i.e. when the process
owns its own truth. The lock is held across the computation deliberately: riders
arrive milliseconds apart, and a lock released before the walk would let all of
them start their own.

Scope, kept narrow on purpose:

* read_persisted_core stays an unmemoised primitive — every direct caller gets a
  fresh judgement, and its docstring now says so. Only consult() and
  take_stale_first_core() reach the shared window, and a consult handed an
  explicit fingerprint bypasses it entirely.
* build_input_fingerprint is untouched and always walks.
* Each rider is handed its OWN core, re-parsed from the memoised bytes.
  label_core stamps provenance IN PLACE, so one shared dict would let the third
  rider's label land on the first rider's already-emitted frame — the same
  hazard the build coalescer deep-copies to avoid.
* snapshot's leader now calls core_cache.pre_build_fingerprint(), which returns
  the consult's key when one stands and falls through to a full walk otherwise
  (cold store, disarmed lane, moved pair). This stays on the safe side of
  write_back's direction argument: the consult's key was taken BEFORE this build
  started, so reusing it can only make the key older, which costs the next
  process a rebuild it did not strictly need — never a served core missing a
  write.

What this widens is stated at the constant rather than left to be discovered:
one asker's answer now covers the other askers in the same window. Three things
bound it — the window IS a boot and ends with the lane; the askers were already
disagreeing, which is worse (the investigation's A1-c: rider 1 served the cache
while rider 2 walked, missed and paid a full build, same store, same process);
and the shadow-validation window is untouched, so a write absorbed mid-window
still surfaces as a divergence receipt and the rebuilt core is still adopted.

Gates (7 new cases): a walk/read counter injected from outside production proves
a four-asker boot performs ONE walk and ONE read; a rewritten pair invalidates
the window by value, not by counter; two riders are proven to hold distinct core
objects; the leader's reuse and the disarmed lane's fall-through are each
counted. Every rider still emits its OWN receipt — sharing the computation must
not merge the account of it, since EG-2.1's per-caller receipts are the
instrument this lane's acceptance is measured with.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): MC-2 / P3 — the fingerprint reads the head home it resolved once, not the profile home the build exports mid-walk

The closure had a non-filesystem input, and it was the build's own doing.
Four of build_input_fingerprint's seven classes resolve home-relative, and
the ladder under them ends at os.environ["HERMES_HOME"] — which the
agents_readiness section exports per profile-bound persona through
profile_context.persona_profile_context. Measured in the field 2026-08-18:
inputs=24344 and inputs=23107 from ONE process over ONE store thirteen
seconds apart. That falsifies ledger row A6 ("non-filesystem inputs are
outside the closure by construction"), which was an argument from reading.

The home is now resolved ONCE per process (resolved_fingerprint_home) and
the four home-relative classes are taken under a context-local pin of it.
The soundness argument is written at the constant rather than here, because
it is not the obvious one: get_hermes_head_home() FALLS BACK to
get_hermes_home() with no head authority present, and the authority it
consults first is a ContextVar — which does not cross a thread boundary, so
on the very thread the divergence was measured on the recorded head is
invisible and degenerates to the flipped ambient home. Resolving through the
head is necessary and not sufficient; taking the resolution once, before any
persona scope in the process can run, is what makes the closure pure.

WHICH CLASSES WERE ACTUALLY EXPOSED (driven on a two-profile tmp root, both
shapes; P3's file list was a lead, not an inventory):

* class 1 (paths.store_root) — NOT exposed. Reads HERMES_AGENT_RUNTIME_ROOT
  then the ROOT config; unchanged across a flip on both threads. Left alone.
* class 2 (running_work_store_paths) — EXPOSED, cross-thread only. P3 said
  to leave it because running_work._head_home already asks the head
  authority. True on the same thread; on another thread it resolved the
  OTHER profile's processes.json and state.db. Pinned.
* class 3 (chat_session_db_path) — EXPOSED, cross-thread only, same cause:
  the scope ladder's first rung is a ContextVar read. Pinned.
* class 4 (hermes_cli.profiles._get_profiles_root) — NOT exposed.
  get_default_hermes_root maps <root>/profiles/<name> back to <root>, so a
  profile flip resolves the same directory. Measured stable. Left alone.
* class 5 (get_config_path) — exposed but DIGEST-INVISIBLE in the standard
  profile layout: class 4 already enumerates every profile's config.yaml, so
  the direct stat is redundant and no witness here can kill it alone. Pinned
  anyway (a closure spec must not rest on one class covering another); the
  observable half is second-order and lands in class 6.
* class 6 (get_all_skills_dirs) — EXPOSED on BOTH shapes and the source of
  the measured delta: index 0 is the ambient home's skills/, so a scoped walk
  enumerates another profile's entire tree. Pinned.
* class 7 (event_rotation) — NOT exposed; resolves off the store root.

The pin is hermes_constants.set_hermes_home_override — the same context-local
override persona_profile_context installs, in the opposite direction and only
for the length of a stat. Every class keeps resolving through its OWN path
authority, so §6.1's first mitigation ("no second list free to drift") is
preserved intact; a hand-composed home / "config.yaml" at each site would
have given exactly that up, and threading a home into get_all_skills_dirs
would have meant editing upstream agent/skill_utils.py. It is applied PER
CLASS so each states why it needs it and each is independently falsifiable.

write_back records fingerprint_home and fingerprint_home_authoritative in the
sidecar (additive), and reset_process_state drops the capture — with a
matching autouse reset in the agent_runtime conftest, because the per-test
env sandbox moves HERMES_HOME between cases and a frozen capture would answer
case 2 through a directory pytest already deleted.

Named residual, asserted rather than left as prose: a process whose FIRST
fingerprint is taken while a persona scope is already live captures that
scope's home. Not silent — the next boot judging that sidecar demotes, which
is the field signal that a capture was taken too late.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): MC-2 / P3 — a cache judged under a different home says so, and the channel table gained the row that makes it countable

Arm 1 made the closure a function of the store. This makes a closure taken
under a DIFFERENT home say so instead of wearing the same token as an
ordinary store change. Before this, a sidecar written under one home and
judged under another landed as reason=fingerprint_mismatch — the same string
an operator gets when a file legitimately moved — so the two facts, which
demand opposite responses ("go look at the store" vs "go look at who
asked"), were one number in any census. A1-b is the standing finding that a
miss names nothing.

DEMOTE_HOME_MISMATCH = "home_mismatch", and the clause sits BESIDE the
runtime_root compare and BEFORE the fingerprint-digest compare. Placement is
the whole claim, not tidiness: behind the digest compare the clause is
unreachable in exactly the case it exists for, because a pair keyed under
another home has a different digest by construction and would be swallowed as
the generic reason. The cheapest-first ordering the conjunction documents is
preserved — this is a string compare against something already in hand, the
runtime_root clause's twin.

ABSENT DOES NOT DEMOTE. Every sidecar written before this stage carries no
fingerprint_home; treating absent as mismatch would demote every install a
second time for no information — once for the closure change arm 1 already
forces, and again for a field it could not have written. The skip is stated
at the site.

THE TABLE GATE'S RED IS THE PROOF OF LIFE, and it was captured before the row
was written: with the constant added and no row,
test_core_cache_channel_table.py::test_every_token_a_writer_can_emit_is_named_in_the_table
failed with "these tokens are emitted (or emittable) by
agent_runtime/core_cache.py and no row of its channel table names them:
['home_mismatch']". Direction 2 then reddened a second time on the first
draft of the row, for naming ``fingerprint_home`` as a bare token when it is
a SIDECAR FIELD and not a receipt vocabulary word — the reverse check working
exactly as designed; the row now spells it sidecar.fingerprint_home.

The row states what the token means to a census: on a multi-home install it
is ordinary, and on a SINGLE-PROFILE operator boot it is evidence that a
persona scope was live while a build stat'd — the capture was taken too late
— which is a defect to go fix, not noise to tune out.

FINDING ABOUT THE GATE, reported rather than fixed here. The channel table's
direction-1 AST scan CANNOT catch a hand-worded demote token: it scans
logger FORMAT strings for reason=<token>, and _log_demote's format is
"reason=%s" with the token passed as an argument. Driven: replacing
DEMOTE_HOME_MISMATCH with a literal "home_mismatch_typo" at the return leaves
all 11 table cases green. Only the driven-line cases in this file catch it —
and only after they were fixed to match whole FIELDS rather than substrings,
because "reason=home_mismatch" is a substring of "reason=home_mismatch_typo"
and the first draft of that assertion passed under the mutation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(core_cache): MC-3 / P4 — the sidecar keeps the stat set it summarised, so a miss becomes diffable

CoreFingerprint.entries has always been kept in memory "so a divergence
investigation can diff two fingerprints and name the file that moved", and it
was never persisted. Measured consequence (A1-b): no process — not the serve,
not a read-only investigation — could name the file that moved between two
boots at an unchanged events offset, and the operator saw
reason=fingerprint_mismatch on every same-commit boot with nothing to act on.

entries.json now lands beside the pair, written by the SAME atomic writer, and
BOUND to the digest it describes: three files written by three os.replace calls
are three generations the moment one of them fails, so a reader that trusted
position over provenance would diff the current store against some earlier one
and name paths from a generation nobody asked about. It compares fingerprints
and refuses with its own typed reason (diff_reason=entries_unbound) instead.

The write is best effort and reports itself as entries=false reason=entries_io
rather than ok=false: the pair LANDED and the cache is usable, so wearing the
write lane's refusal spelling would tell a census a successful cache write
failed. Letting a diagnostic's failure retract a landed cache would trade the
thing this module exists for against the thing that explains it.

SIZE, PRICED (the C-7 class): measured on the operator's live tree, 22,286
entries -> 3,539,812 bytes (3.38 MiB), 159 bytes/entry against a mean path of
127 chars; ~3.5 MiB projected at the field's 23,107-entry key. That also settles
the format question in the opposite direction to P4's guess: a compact
path|mtime|size text form would spend ~153 bytes/entry, a ~4 % saving, because
the paths dominate and backslash escaping adds only ~10 bytes each. A second,
text-shaped atomic writer would buy nothing worth its own authority. The lever
is the SIZE OF THE CLOSURE, not its encoding — 18,804 of 23,107 entries are
deleted_archive/, which P12 removes.

_diff_unavailable_detail() is factored out so the two receipts that can owe a
diff word the refusal identically; two hand-written copies of a census
instruction is the C22 defect one level down.

C22 table gains the snapshot_core_cache_write entries=false row, which names
entries_io and its cross-lane consequence entries_unbound.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(core_cache): MC-3 / P4 — a fingerprint miss says which paths moved, last on the line, with its last_pair caveat

_log_demote emitted core_source=rebuilt caller=… reason=… inputs=… and nothing
else; only never_converged carried a diff=, and A2 shows that receipt cannot
fire on any boot shape. So the one line the operator sees on EVERY boot was the
one that said least — "the absence is itself the finding" (A1-b).

The tail is computed lazily and ONLY for fingerprint_mismatch. The hit path
never reaches _log_demote and so pays nothing (gated with a read counter on
entries_path over both consult shapes). The other demote reasons deliberately
grow no tail: a diff on a build_stamp_mismatch would name every file the
operator's upgrade touched and read to a census as store churn — a measurement
that is true of the wrong thing.

It reuses _changed_paths and _diff_detail, the never-converged receipt's own
helpers, so the two receipts spell ONE vocabulary and are told apart by their
family/event token exactly as the C22 table teaches. That also means the demote
inherits diff_scope= and the five-path cap for free, with changed= carrying the
full count beside the capped sample so a large drift can never read as a small
one.

diff= goes LAST, after changed=, for the reason already written at
_receipt_never_converged: it is a variable-length list and a path may contain
spaces, so nothing can be field-parsed after it. That is what makes the tail
purely additive — an existing reason= grep is unaffected.

THE CENSUS CAVEAT, on the line and in the C22 row: the scope is last_pair BY
CONSTRUCTION. A demote diff is the delta since the LAST WRITE-BACK, so on a busy
store it legitimately names files that are simply moving and the receipt is true
without naming a defect. It is self-perturbation evidence ONLY when the named
paths are runtime-owned (dispatch_delivery_drain.json, serve_socket.owner.json,
state.db-wal, serve_socket.lock). No new diff_scope token was invented for this,
per the ruling: the caveat lives in the row.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): MC-3 / P4 — the convergence streak survives a process boundary, so the shape that actually happens can fire it

_note_written_key returned early on the first write-back of a process, so
never_converged fired on the FOURTH consecutive disagreeing write-back of ONE
process. Boots write back once (07:59, 08:04) or twice (05:33 — gen 1
prewarm-led, gen 2 hub-led, streak 1). The receipt was unreachable on every boot
shape there is, and the 05:33 pair (9772c7720bef -> d525e554be44) — which IS the
self-perturbation it was written to expose — could never be reported. A process
boundary is not a convergence event.

WHAT P4'S STATED SHAPE MISSES, found by tracing it against the code rather than
by reading it: reset_process_state() zeroes _streak_length, so seeding only
_last_written_digest / _streak_entries caps EVERY boot at streak 1 and the
receipt still never fires. The streak LENGTH has to cross the boundary too. It
rides in entries.json — not the sidecar, which every consult reads on the boot
path and which must stay the cheap half of the judgement — and _note_written_key
stays the ONE authority for the number, returning it for the file to record
rather than letting a second site derive it from the same seed.

SEED ONLY ON A FINGERPRINT DISAGREEMENT. build_stamp_mismatch (the operator
upgraded), contract_mismatch (the schema moved), runtime_root_mismatch (a
different store) and home_mismatch (a different question) are legitimate
non-agreements that say nothing about convergence. Seeding on them would make a
routine upgrade look like an oscillating store and fire a WARNING at a healthy
install — the expensive direction for a diagnostic whose value is that it speaks
only when something is wrong. The judgement is asked of the read lane's own
clauses, lifted into _sidecar_answers_a_different_question so the seed and the
demote can never drift into two rules; the clause order and every reason are
preserved exactly.

A SEEDED STREAK REPORTS last_pair, NOT every_pass. The intersection this process
computed spans only the passes it observed, and C22(i) reserves every_pass for
measured self-perturbation — claiming it from one observed pass would inflate
the arm an operator is meant to act on.

The threshold stays at 3: it is the measured virgin-root convergence and its
comment explains why that number and not a round one. Retention is unchanged —
entries are held only while a streak is live and dropped when two write-backs
agree, and a seeded streak inherits that rather than being an exception to it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): MC-3b / MCF-15 — an absent WAL and an empty one are one fact, so the key stops keying them apart

MC-1 masked a zero-length WAL's mtime and deliberately kept "absent" and
"present-but-empty" distinguishable, on the general rule _stat_entry follows:
an appearing file must never look like an unchanged one. That rule is right for
every input that carries content and wrong for this one sibling, and it was the
LAST cause of a miss on a quiescent store.

SQLite deletes the WAL when the last connection closes cleanly and re-creates it
at zero length on the next open, so a quiet database alternates between the two
states for reasons that are entirely about connection lifetime. Measured on the
operator's machine 2026-08-18: two boots recorded the same events offset and the
same entry count, and the second demoted fingerprint_mismatch anyway;
state.db-wal's creation time landed 4.15 s AFTER the consult that missed. One
entry flipped and nothing else in the closure moved.

The structural consequence is worse than the flip and is now written at the
function: which state the sidecar records depends on WHICH BUILD IN THE PROCESS
WROTE LAST. A boot whose only build is the boot build keys the WAL absent and
the next boot can match; any later led build — the launcher's hydrate, any
forceFresh gesture — keys it present and the next boot is a guaranteed miss.
Perverse corollary, stated because it will mislead the first person who tests
this: a hard-killed serve leaves the WAL and converges; a clean exit deletes it
and misses.

The arm is one function. A -wal with no frames keys (path, 0, 0) whether it is
absent or zero-length; the instant a frame lands the full stat'd triple counts
again, unchanged. -shm stays excluded, and the main file and -journal are
untouched — their absence is real information. MC-3's entries.json already
persists key.entries, so the collapsed triple is what a later diff= reads and no
miss can name state.db-wal as a mover when it is not one; that binding is now
gated rather than assumed.

Renamed _empty_wal_is_content_free -> _wal_without_frames_is_content_free: the
old name says "empty", and the whole of this change is that emptiness is not the
only frameless state.

GATES (tests/agent_runtime/test_core_fingerprint_cache.py). The absent-vs-empty
case MC-1 wrote here now asserts the opposite and says why; six more join it,
each with its own killing mutation, every mutation grep-counted before and after
and restored byte-exact from a pristine copy:

* M1 restore MC-1's distinction (FingerprintEntry(entry.path, 0, entry.size),
  1 -> 0 occurrences) reds all seven collapse assertions and nothing else;
* M2 collapse on size rather than on emptiness (guard 1 -> 0) reds only the two
  "a WAL holding a frame still counts" assertions — which is what proves a STATE
  was masked and not a FILE;
* M3 widen the mask to every sibling (_WAL_SIBLING 2 -> 1) reds only the two
  scope assertions (an appearing zero-length .db, an appearing -journal);
* M4 have the entries writer re-stat instead of persisting key.entries reds both
  recorded-triple assertions and three of MC-3's own entries cases — and its log
  shows the miss line naming state.db-wal in diff=, the instrument accusing the
  input this fix exonerates.

The serve lifecycle is driven end to end through real connections rather than
asserted from a docstring: WAL on disk, connections held, cache settled, last
connection closed (SQLite unlinks), consult -> match; then the next boot's open
lays it back down empty, consult -> match. Closing the fixture's own holder is
not enough, and why is a finding: snapshot._build_snapshot_uncoalesced opens the
chat SessionDB via _default_persona_session_db and never closes it, so every
full build leaves a live connection behind.

M1's first run caught the obvious reopen case being VACUOUS — settling with the
WAL present and consulting with it present again matches under any keying at
all. It now writes its key while the database sits closed and WAL-less and
consults only after the open, and the docstring records why.

Focused suites: the five core-cache files 103 passed / 0 failed; the four
WAL-adjacent files 109 passed / 0 failed. Expect ONE demote on the first boot
after this lands — the recorded triple changes — and it is not a failure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(stream): MC-4 / P6 — the stale-first core goes to whoever declares it paints, not to whoever attached first

EG-3.1 serves the persisted core immediately, labelled stale, so the operator
sees the last projection instead of an empty canvas for the length of a full
build. Measured on the live launcher 2026-08-18 it was a RACE and it lost two
boots in three: `take_stale_first_core` was one-shot per PROCESS, a boot runs
TWO `stream_frames` generators, and the one that attaches first is the hub
producer started by `runtime.office.subscribe` — 0.1-0.2s before the launcher
asks for anything — whose `office_patch_sink` discards every row that is not an
`office_actor`. The one paint the design exists to deliver was taken and thrown
away.

Three changes, and the brief's shape was wrong on the second:

1. `stream_frames` takes `wants_stale_first`, and both production call sites
   state it. P6 proposed passing it "from serve_office_subscriptions"; the
   office lane does not call `stream_frames` at all — it is a SUBSCRIBER of the
   shared hub, not a producer. `stream_frames` has exactly two production
   callers (`_cmd_stream`, `serve.py::_stream_source`), so the discriminator has
   to live where the ROOM is known.
2. `serve.py::_room_wants_stale_first` derives the hub's answer from its
   subscriber tables at producer-build time, mirroring `_accepted_fold_entities`
   — with the OPPOSITE operator, written down at the site with its reason.
   Intersection is right for a promotion, which must be safe for everyone fanned
   the frame; union is right for an extra frame a non-painting sink merely
   discards. One painter is enough; a room of office-only sinks answers False.
3. `_stale_served` is gone. The one-shot is now the subscriber's — structurally,
   because `stream_frames` asks once at its head — and what still bounds a
   re-paint is the ARMED LANE, whose window is the boot: it closes at
   `note_full_build_completed`. `_lane_armed` is NOT widened.

Plus the hazard P6 named and today's code still had: the stale frame is yielded
at the head and the budget check returns immediately after it, so a
`--max-frames 1` request could be answered with a STALE core. The launcher's
forced-refresh lane scans that stdout for a `type == "hydrate"` line and applies
what it finds through `applyForcedSnapshot`, past its own sequence gate — so
"force a refresh" meant "re-paint what you were already unhappy with". Refused
in `stream_frames` (`_is_one_shot`) rather than in `_cmd_stream` as the brief
directed: it is an invariant of the frame BUDGET, so the generator owns it and
it holds for every caller rather than only the one that parses `--max-frames`.

The default is `False` — the safe direction — and an AST pin asserts both
production callers state it anyway, plus that no third caller has appeared.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(stream): MC-4 / P6 — a boot build that takes thirty seconds says so every five, instead of looking wedged

Measured on the operator's launcher 2026-08-18 (investigation A-x2): the boot
build took 29,560 ms and the lane emitted NOTHING for the whole of it. The
watchdog fired `stream_teardown cause=liveness_deadline` 0.67 s before the
authoritative frame arrived; that frame went to a retired request and was
discarded with no receipt; the launcher respawned, bought a second full build,
and the result landed as a same-offset duplicate. Three cores for one paint. A
delta batch's build has heartbeat through itself since `_full_core_batch_frames`
shipped — the BOOT build, the longest one any consumer ever waits on, was the
one lane that stayed silent.

The boot build now runs on `_SnapshotBuildJob` and the generator yields the same
`activity={"kind": "snapshot_build", "state": "busy"}` liveness on the cadence
while it runs. The offset is `None`, not 0 — `heartbeat_frame`'s own contract:
liveness without a position must not be stamped 0, which every watermark-gated
reader would take as a cursor at the head of the log. The build receipt is
preserved byte-shaped, with `waited_ms` from `job.elapsed_ms` (measured ON the
build thread, because the generator's wait polls at 100 ms and would round every
build up by that much).

The two wait loops SHARE `_build_with_liveness` — the worker, the poll, the
cancellation probe, the cadence, the activity block. What differs (which frame
the build becomes, which receipt it bills, which watermark it advertises) stays
at each call site: folding those in would have needed a discriminator per
difference, which is how one loop becomes two loops wearing one name.

**A defect in the brief's own shape, caught by reading the code.**
`_SnapshotBuildJob.run` called `build_snapshot(build_info=...)` WITHOUT
`accept_inflight=True`, which `hydrate_frame`'s inline build has always passed —
the serve prewarms a build right after `ready` and the boot hydrate is allowed
to ride it. Moving the boot build onto the job as directed would have made every
boot wait for the prewarm and then pay a SECOND full build, visible in the field
only as a second `snapshot_build_core role=led` line with the receipt still
reading `reason=hydrate`. The job now carries the flag, and a gate asserts on the
argument because the cost is invisible in the frame.

**The `max_frames` decision:** boot liveness does not count toward the budget,
and is suppressed outright for a one-shot. Read
`mission_control_bridge.dart::_loadSnapshotFromStreamHydrate` (read-only,
2026-08-18) to choose: it scans the one-shot's stdout for a `type == "hydrate"`
line and silently returns null when it finds none, so a counted heartbeat would
make a forced refresh no-op with no receipt. The rejected alternative — suppress
only, count when present — would leave the lane most exposed to a command
timeout as the only one that goes silent for thirty seconds. The budget counts
CONTENT; the tail loop's own heartbeats still count, because by then a core has
been delivered.

Golden-neutral by construction and asserted as such: a heartbeat is emitted only
once a full interval has elapsed with the build still running, and the committed
fixtures are produced by instantaneous builds at the 5 s production cadence. All
14 files under tests/fixtures/stream_frames/ are byte-identical.

Five suites drove sub-second cadences and took `next(frames)` as the hydrate.
That assumption is now ORDER-DEPENDENT — green alone on a warm build that beat
the interval, red in a batch run where it did not — so they route through one
shared `drain_boot_liveness`, which identifies boot liveness by its activity
block rather than by position and pins the null watermark for every caller.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(tests): MC-4 — the inventory gate asks git what this repo owns, and the office settle waits for the hydrate instead of for a frame

Two checkpoint-reddening defects, both mine, both from the MC-4 commits.

1. THE INVENTORY GATE WALKED THE VIRTUALENV.
`test_the_pin_covers_every_production_call_site_there_is` used `rglob("*.py")`
with two string exclusions. Measured: 10,112 files found, 7,121 OPENED and
AST-parsed on every run, 5,802 of them third-party code under `.venv-ci/`
(~51 MiB). Two independent defects, not one:

* CORRECTNESS. The claim is "every production `stream_frames` caller in THIS
  repo". A vendored package defining anything of that name would red the gate
  for a reason nobody here owns, and the message would send the reader hunting
  a caller they cannot edit. The docstring said "outside `tests/`"; `.venv-ci/`
  is outside `tests/` and is exactly what it did not mean.
* IT HUNG THE CHECKPOINT. A virtualenv is not a stable tree — it can be written
  while it is read — and the full run timed out inside this walk, blocked on
  opening a file under `.venv-ci`.

The scope now comes from `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard`.
Both halves are load-bearing: tracked-only would go quietly VACUOUS in the
window an author is adding a caller not yet `git add`-ed — the gate reporting
success on a set missing the file it exists to catch — and `--exclude-standard`
is what removes the vendored trees. This is NOT the hand-typed-denylist defect
MCF-2 recorded: there is one authority, `.gitignore`, already the repo's own
answer to what is its own code, and a new vendored directory is visible either
way — ignored and out of scope, or unignored and loud in `git status`. A
denylist would admit it silently. A git failure raises rather than falling back
to the walk, which would restore the old behaviour when nobody was watching.

Files opened and parsed: 7,121 -> 1,292 (5.5x fewer; 28.3s -> 12.0s as context
only, per ruling #60 the assertion is the count). Same answer both ways.

Two kills, because the scope and the inventory are two claims (C30): a real
third caller added to a tracked production file reds it; and a planted
git-ignored file (under `.pytest_cache/`, outside `tests/`, so it is not
excluded twice) calling `stream_frames` must NOT red it — reverting the scope to
the walk reds that one, with `.venv-ci` paths in the failure message.

2. THE OFFICE SETTLE WAITED ON A PROXY THAT ARM 2 INVALIDATED.
The coordinator's first checkpoint failed at
`test_unsubscribe_stops_delivery_against_the_real_producer`. It is NEITHER a
delivery regression NOR a deadline that lost a race, and both framings would
have led to a wrong fix.

`_settled_subscription` waited on `frames_delivered >= 1` as a proxy for "the
mandatory re-hydrate has landed" — exact only while the hydrate was necessarily
a generation's FIRST frame. Arm 2 ended that: the boot build now emits liveness
on the cadence, this fixture runs at 0.25s, and the office sink turns a
heartbeat into no notification at all. So the settle returned while the producer
was STILL BUILDING, the test's write landed before the hydrate was built, was
absorbed into it, and reached the sink as one `runtime.office.resync` instead of
the `runtime.office.patch` awaited.

Proven by holding the boot build, which reproduces it deterministically: peer
methods `[]` at settle, `['runtime.office.resync']` at the deadline AND three
seconds past it. The patch was never coming, so widening the deadline would have
fixed nothing and hidden this.

The fix synchronises on the EVENT rather than on a count that used to imply it:
the fixture records the frame types each producer generation yields, and the
settle waits for the hydrate to have been produced AND delivered (its 1-based
position in that list is exactly the delivered count that means "the sink has
run for it", the pump being FIFO). A new case pins it, holding the build on a
`threading.Event` released by evidence — that liveness was actually emitted —
so a build too fast to heartbeat cannot make it pass vacuously. Reverting the
settle to the old proxy reds that case with `['heartbeat']`, which is the
mechanism itself.

Goldens byte-identical, fence unchanged, no production code touched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(tests): MC-4 — drop a scope assertion that could not fail for the right reason

Self-review of the gate I had just reworked. It carried
`assert len(sources) < 12_000` as a "scope" check. Measured against its own
mutant, it was worthless: the filesystem walk it replaced returns 10,112 files,
comfortably under that bound, so the assertion passed just as happily on the
defect it was written to catch — an always-green check wearing a gate's clothes,
plus a magic number needing re-tuning as the repo grows.

Removed, with the reasoning left at the site so it is not re-added. The scope
claim is carried by the two assertions that actually discriminate and that both
red under the revert-to-walk mutation: the planted git-ignored probe must not
enter the inventory, and no virtualenv path may. Re-verified after the removal —
mutant still reds, 8/8 green restored. The 7,121 -> 1,292 file-open count stays
a measurement for the record rather than a threshold to defend.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
perf(core_cache): MC-8 / P12 — the graveyard leaves the walk, with the reader argument written where the exclusion lives

`deleted_archive/` is 18,804 of the operator's 23,107 fingerprint entries: 81 %
of every ~300 ms walk, paid four to five times per boot, and since MC-3 also
81 % of every ~3.4 MiB `entries.json` write-back. MCF-20 measured that the
encoding was not the lever (a compact text form saves 4 %); the CLOSURE SIZE is,
which is why this lands before anyone judges that write-back cost.

THE EXCLUSION IS THE EASY PART. THE ARGUMENT IS THE STAGE.

Every other name in `_EXCLUDED_STORE_ENTRIES` earns its place with "the runtime
rewrites it". This one is excluded because the PROJECTION has no reader for it —
a claim about a reader set, and a claim about a reader set rots the moment
someone adds a reader. So the whole of it is written at the constant: the grep
that establishes it, that the claim is repo-scoped (C14), and the obligation
that whoever adds a projection reader for compaction batches removes this
exclusion in the same commit.

THE MCF-12 CORRECTION IS NAMED, NOT OMITTED. P12 was first written as "zero
readers" and that is false:

    harness_doctor.py::_event_log_report
        -> events.py::event_log_health
            -> events.py::_archived_event_slices
                -> reads deleted_archive/*/manifest.json

The harness doctor does read these manifests. The exclusion is still right, and
the load-bearing word is "projection": this walk is the input closure of the
read-model build, and an operator-invoked diagnostic that builds no core and
consults no cache is not made an input by reading a file. Stating the exception
is what stops the next audit finding the doctor and concluding the constant is
wrong.

STRONGER THAN THE RULING NEEDED, so it is recorded: no current code WRITES the
tree. `deleted_archive_dir()` has exactly one non-doc caller in the repo and it
is the reader above; both archivers (`archive_task_events`,
`compact_archived_task_events`) were retired at S54. It is a graveyard of a
retired feature — immutable, so it contributes a constant to every key it
appears in.

The name is promoted to `paths.DELETED_ARCHIVE_DIRNAME` and IMPORTED rather than
re-typed, per the set's own rule (the rule MCF-2 paid for: a hand-typed
`"drain_state.json"` against a writer that said `dispatch_delivery_drain.json`).
The residual paragraph is updated to say the addition did not extend it — and
its count is corrected from "Four" to "FIVE", which was simply wrong (`locks` +
`snapshot.json` + a trio is five). A residual list exists to be counted against
the set; one that miscounts invites the reader to think a name is handled.

Two forward references updated in the same commit, both of which this stage
falsified: `build_input_fingerprint`'s class-1 promise of a subtree "without a
name list to fall behind" now states its one exception and where the reason
lives, and `entries_path`'s "which P12 removes" becomes "done", with the
pre-P12 measurement left standing as what justified it.

FIVE GATES, SIX KILLING MUTATIONS, EACH ASSERTION WATCHED FAILING

* count, both directions (M1 revert -> reds; M2 over-broad exclusion of a real
  store subtree -> the +1 assertion reds, which a count-of-zero cannot tell
  apart on its own);
* digest across a REWRITE of a graveyard file — a change the count is
  structurally blind to, so a half-applied exclusion that stopped counting but
  kept stat'ing passes the count case and reds here (M1);
* top-level only: a `deleted_archive` NESTED under another store subtree still
  contributes (M4, a name filter at every depth -> reds, and reds nothing else);
* the excluded name is the one the PATH HELPER produces (M5, hand-spell the
  literal beside the import and move the owner's value -> reds);
* `entries.json` carries no graveyard path (M6, have the entries writer re-walk
  the store for itself -> reds).

The fixture takes its baseline BEFORE the graveyard exists, deliberately. M3 is
why: "keep the directory entry, skip its contents" is the most plausible
half-fix there is, and against a baseline that already had the directory it
would survive every case. It reds the count gate only — and the digest gate
survives it, which is reported rather than smoothed over, because the digest
gate's kill is M1.

No log token added, no wire change. ONE `reason=fingerprint_mismatch` demote is
expected on the first boot after this lands: the closure changed, once.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(snapshot): MC-8 / P10 — an orphaned office says whether the workspace was deleted or never recorded, and says "unknown" when the ledger cannot prove it

`_office_parity_warnings` worded every orphan "which no longer resolves" — a
sentence that PRESUMES the workspace once did. The live field case had never had
a workspace record at all: 135 events for `ws_office_patch_test`, one
`office.surface.created` and 67 actor upserts, and zero
`workspace.created`/`deleted`/`archived`. An operator told "no longer resolves"
goes hunting the deletion that removed it, and there was none.

THE REASON IS DERIVED WHERE `orphaned` IS DERIVED. `classify_orphaned_office_workspace`
(pure, in `office_models`) is called from `_offices_summary` on the line after
`orphaned`, from the realm list `build_snapshot` has ALREADY read, and rides the
office ROW as `orphan_reason`. `_office_parity_warnings` reads it off the row
rather than recomputing it. That placement is the point:
`OfficeStore.workspace_resolves`' docstring exists to say this predicate and this
warning "cannot answer differently", and a reason computed at the warning from
its own inputs would be a second derivation free to drift from the flag it is
explaining.

THREE REASONS, BECAUSE A NEGATIVE HERE IS WEAKER THAN A POSITIVE

* `workspace_deleted` — a hit in a realm's `deleted_workspace_ids`. A tombstone;
  proof.
* `workspace_never_recorded` — a miss, and nothing makes the miss uninformative.
* `unknown` — not optional and not a shrug. Two shapes reach it: a ledger AT
  `DELETED_WORKSPACE_LEDGER_CAP` has been evicting its oldest entries, so an id
  that fell off is not "never recorded" and must not claim to be; and with no
  realms at all there is no ledger that could have recorded anything, so a miss
  carries no information whatever.

A CORRECTION TO THE STAGE'S PREMISE, recorded at the function rather than
smoothed over. The brief had the cap as the only thing that makes a negative
unprovable. It is not: `WorkspaceStore.delete` appends the tombstone under
`if realm is not None`, so a workspace deleted while bound to no realm — or to a
realm row that had already gone — is deleted with NO ledger entry written
anywhere and reads here as `workspace_never_recorded`. That window stays narrow
for one reason worth knowing: the same cascade `rmtree`s the office subtree, so a
deleted workspace normally leaves no surface to warn about at all, and an orphan
that survives a delete needs that removal to have failed. Widening past the
ledgers means an event-log read per orphan inside the build, which no warning in
the parity section currently pays for. Named residual, not a silent one.

THE CODE TOKEN DOES NOT MOVE. `code` stays `orphaned_office` for all three;
`reason` is a new FIELD. The code is what a census greps and what the launcher's
`warningCodes` reads, so `orphaned_office_never_recorded` would silently zero
every existing count of the condition and break the parity chip without any
consumer erroring.

ADDITIVE ON THE WIRE, confirmed read-only in the launcher: warnings are parsed by
`warning['code']` key lookup with no exact-key-set comparison
(`mission_control_snapshot.dart`), and office rows read `json['orphaned'] == true`
and ignore unknown keys. NOTHING CHANGED IN THE LAUNCHER. No test in either repo
pinned the old detail wording.

SIX KILLING MUTATIONS, EACH ARM WATCHED FAILING SEPARATELY

* N1 collapse the detail map onto the never-recorded sentence -> ONLY the deleted
  case reds; N2 collapse it the other way -> ONLY the never-recorded case reds.
  Two arms of one discrimination are two claims, and each is asserted against
  literal discriminating phrases rather than against the module's own map — which
  would have passed under exactly this mutation.
* N3 drop the cap arm -> the full-ledger case reds.
* N4 drop the no-ledgers arm -> the no-realms case reds.
* N5 put the reason in the code token -> the token case reds AND the parity
  catalog's producibility gate reds; two independent witnesses for one rule.
* N6 make `_offices_summary` filter archived rows out of the set it was handed ->
  the resolving-workspace case reds. Aimed inside the projection because the gate
  drives it directly, so a mutation of `build_snapshot`'s call site could not
  reach it.

Two of these gates failed on their first run — the detail assertions probed
tokens the sentences do not contain, and the two-orphan case expected both rows
to classify the same way when only one was tombstoned. Fixed in the tests, and
the second is now the sharper claim: two orphans, two different reasons, one
shared code.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office_store): MC-8 / P10 — an office is not minted for a workspace no record resolves, and the refusal is typed

`ensure_surface` authored a default surface for ANY id that passed `_safe_id`.
That is how a leaked test context minted a LIVE office in the operator's runtime
root — one `office.surface.created`, 67 actor upserts, a `revision 67` actor file
— for a workspace id no verb ever authorised and no `workspace.created` event
ever named. Arm 2 made the wreckage describable. This is the door.

THE ORDER IS THE CONTRACT, and the middle step is the one that matters

  1. `_safe_id` — an unusable id is a caller error, not a store-state question;
  2. the `surface_exists` short-circuit — **the refusal guards CREATION, never
     reading**;
  3. the refusal — before `office_lock` and before any write, the same
     discipline `WorkspaceStore.delete`'s cascade follows.

Step 2 is not a detail. `archive_orphaned_surface`'s entire precondition is
`workspace_resolves() is False`, and the projection and parity warning read
through here too. A refusal placed above that line would make the live orphan
UNARCHIVABLE by the one verb that exists to archive it — the operator's only exit
closed by the fix meant to protect them. It has its own gate and its own kill.

CALLER WALK — six callers, each read rather than assumed

* `upsert_actor`, `update_surface` — INHERIT the refusal. This is the ruled
  behaviour change and the path the field leak took.
* `archive_actor`, `restore_actor`, `resolve_conflict` — reach `ensure_surface`
  only after `get_actor` / `actor_exists` has proven the surface is there, so
  they take the short-circuit and are UNAFFECTED.
* `workspace_template._copy_office` — the one the brief flagged as interesting.
  UNAFFECTED, and provably so rather than by luck: the CLI create verb creates
  the workspace record and only then copies content ("Office/board content copies
  AFTER the workspace exists", `hermes_cli/harness.py`). Pinned in both
  directions, so a future caller that clones before creating gets a named failure
  instead of a silent orphan.

WHERE IT SURFACES — the brief's expectation corrected

The brief expected the typed code to reach the RPC envelope. It cannot, and
adding a handler would have been a production catch that can never fire.
`runtime.office.upsert` and `…surface_update` each pre-check
`store.surface_exists` and return `ERR_NOT_FOUND` / `workspace_not_found` before
the store is asked to author anything; `agent_create` does the same. So no RPC
handler was added, and `serve_rpc`'s docstring says why at the guard.

The reachable lane is the CLI/argv one — which is exactly the lane that docstring
used to bless ("lazily create the office, which is right for the CLI: a human
typed `--workspace` and can see what they made"). That reasoning is retired in
the same commit rather than left to contradict the code beside it.

There it needed real wiring, not just an exception. `WorkspaceUnresolved` is an
`AgentRuntimeError`, so without a taxonomy row it falls to the catch-all and an
operator refusal is reported as `internal_error` at exit 1 — the identical defect
the neighbouring `ArchiveUnreadable` row was added to fix. It now maps to its own
`exc.code`, exit family 3 beside `workspace_not_found` (same operator cure, same
exit, no client branch to relearn), with `safe_details` carried through.

FIXTURES: 21 SEED SITES ACROSS 13 FILES, AND WHY THAT IS THE FINDING

Every office suite here seeded itself by calling `ensure_surface` on a bare
constant — i.e. through the hole. That is not incidental. The fixtures had been
modelling a store shape production should never have been able to produce, which
is a large part of why the hole survived three reviews of this area. They now
create the record they always implied, through one shared helper
(`tests/agent_runtime/office_seed.py`) rather than 21 copies, so a suite cannot
drift back by seeding some other way. It is deliberately NOT a conftest fixture:
ambient setup would hide the precondition again.

`_seed_orphan` is the interesting one. It can no longer walk through the door it
tests, so it now creates the record, seeds the office, and UNLINKS the record —
which is also the more faithful model, since that is how an orphan actually
arises in the field. `WorkspaceStore.delete` is not used: its cascade `rmtree`s
the very office subtree the file exists to examine.

SEVEN KILLING MUTATIONS, EACH CLAIM ISOLATED

* P1 restore the lazy mint -> the `raises` reds (nothing refuses);
* P2 raise after `_write_surface` -> the DIRECTORY assertion reds, by its own
  message;
* P7 emit the create then refuse without writing -> the EVENT assertion reds.
  P7 exists because P2/P3 cannot isolate it: both write before they raise, so
  the directory assertion reds first and the event claim is never reached. "It
  refused" and "it refused before doing anything" are different claims and each
  now has a mutation of its own;
* P4 drop `include_archived=True` from `workspace_resolves` -> the archived case
  reds while the live one stays green;
* P5 move the refusal above the `surface_exists` short-circuit -> the idempotence
  gate reds and nothing else does. The mutation most likely to be missed, and the
  one that would break the live store today;
* P6 delete the taxonomy row -> the envelope gate reds at exit 1 /
  `internal_error`.

Three of the mutation receipts were WRONG before they were right, and G6 caught
all three rather than a green run hiding them: two token expectations could never
reach 0 (a 12-space guard line contains the 8-space token as a substring; the
`include_archived=True` spelling also appears in a docstring) and one injected
raise was indented for the wrong block. Fixed by aiming at the added token
instead of the removed one.

`archive_orphaned_surface`'s refusal predicate is UNCHANGED — `workspace_resolves`
is shared and gained a caller, not an edit — so the operator runbook's dry-run
step still answers exactly as before. Fence `test_office_class_key_one_fence.py`
byte-unchanged (`1b0b0e82f4…`); stream goldens untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(readiness): MCF-16 — a readiness READ stops rewriting the credential store, so the build stops moving an input it never declared

The snapshot's `agents_readiness` pass resolved a runtime provider per persona
purely to learn whether one resolves — it discards the resolved dict and uses
only whether it raised. That resolution reached `CredentialPool.select()`,
which under `STRATEGY_ROUND_ROBIN` with more than one pooled credential
rewrites the whole credential store to advance the cursor. `_save_auth_store`
has no content comparison anywhere and stamps `updated_at` on every call, so
two logically identical writes still produce different bytes.

`auth.json` is read by that pass and is NOT in `build_input_fingerprint`'s
closure (class 4 stats profile.yaml / config.yaml / dirs per profile). So a
credential change on an otherwise-quiescent store is indistinguishable from the
build's own self-perturbation and lands as a false cache HIT — cached
tool-visibility/readiness served as authoritative, the missed-input direction
the cache module itself calls its worst failure.

Shape taken: give the readiness path a selection that does not persist.

- `CredentialPool.select_without_persisting_rotation()` — a named entry point,
  not a flag defaulted at a call site. It performs the identical selection
  INCLUDING the in-memory rotation, so the strategy is not silently degraded to
  "always the first"; only the write-back is skipped. It deliberately does not
  suppress cooldown clears or token refreshes: those carry a real state change
  and their write is honest. The defect retired is a write with nothing to
  write.
- `resolve_runtime_provider(..., persist_pool_rotation=True)` threads the choice
  to every pool selection resolution can reach (the main pool and all three
  custom-pool branches, through one `_select_pool_entry` chokepoint), so a
  caller cannot half-suppress the write by landing on a different branch.
- `probe_runtime_provider()` is the readiness/visibility entry point;
  `_compute_provider_issue` routes the real resolver through it, extending to
  every provider what the codex branch beside it already did for refreshes.

Shapes NOT taken, argued at the seam so the next reader knows they were
considered: making `_save_auth_store` change-only retires the class for every
caller but moves the credential write boundary, and belongs in its own change
with its own mutation evidence; closure inclusion is wrong before that, and
even after would need a field-selective digest excluding `updated_at` — a
parsed digest, not a stat mask, because unlike a frameless WAL (genuinely
content-free) `auth.json`'s bytes change on every write, so masking mtime/size
or hashing the whole file still flips.

Gates (tests/agent_runtime/test_readiness_credential_store_quiescent.py, 5
cases), each assertion with its own killing mutation, all verified red then
restored byte-exact:

1. a readiness pass leaves the store byte-identical — killed by restoring the
   persisting selection; the vacuity pin (exactly one non-persisting selection,
   zero persisting) killed separately by stopping the probe reaching a pool;
2. the non-persisting path still rotates in memory — killed by making it also
   skip rotation;
3. a real consumer still rotates across a fresh `load_pool` — killed by gating
   the round-robin write off;
4. a genuine credential state change still persists — killed by a no-op
   `_persist`;
5. a real write still stamps a fresh `updated_at` — killed by adding a content
   comparison to `_save_auth_store`, which is what keeps that separate shape
   from merging into this one silently; its "logically identical" pin killed
   separately by making `write_credential_pool` non-idempotent.

`agents_readiness` is the largest section of the build, so this pass is on the
hot path. No timing claim is made or asserted here.

Fixtures use inert marker payloads under the per-test sandboxed HERMES_HOME,
and every assertion compares ids or digests so no store content can reach a
test log on failure.

author: nekwo
message:
perf(core_cache): H2 — the orphaned-surface graveyard leaves the walk, and the near name that must NOT stays in it

`paths.office_surface_archive_root()` is `store_root()/office_archive`, the
top-level tree `office_store.archive_orphaned_surface` renames a whole orphaned
office surface into via the operator's `harness office archive-surface`. The
runtime writes it, it grows without bound against MAX_FINGERPRINT_ENTRIES (the
destination helper appends `-2`, `-3` ... slots on re-archives), and no
projection reads it: `list_workspaces()` enumerates `office_root()`'s children,
and this tree is deliberately a SIBLING of `office_root()` precisely so an
archived surface stops being projected. So it is not an input to the read-model
build's input closure, and it is now excluded from the store-root walk.

Done in MC-8's shape, not by re-typing a name: `"office_archive"` is promoted to
`paths.OFFICE_ARCHIVE_DIRNAME`, the path helper uses it, and `core_cache`
IMPORTS it. That is the rule the set already runs on — it shipped once with a
hand-typed `"drain_state.json"` against a writer that said
`dispatch_delivery_drain.json`, so the exclusion named a file that had never
existed while the real one sat inside the key.

The reader-grep was re-run fresh rather than trusted from a brief, and every hit
is accounted for at the constant, split into the two trees one underscore apart:
`office_archive/` (this one, one writer chain and no reader) and
`office/<ws>/archive/` (`paths.office_archive_dir` — per-workspace archived ACTOR
placements, READ by OfficeStore on the actor-listing seam and every
archived-actor lookup, a projection INPUT that STAYS in the walk). Getting that
pair the wrong way round is a missed input, which this module calls its worst
failure, so it has its own gate.

STATED, not hidden: this does not stop the archive GESTURE flipping the key. The
surface is moved OUT of `office/<ws>/`, which is fingerprinted, so the move
itself is a real input change and should flip it, exactly once. What leaves the
closure is the graveyard's CONTINUING contribution -- its entries, its walk cost,
its unbounded growth, and any churn inside it afterwards. Expect ONE benign
`reason=fingerprint_mismatch` on the first boot after this lands.

The residual paragraph was RE-COUNTED rather than assumed: this addition is an
import, not a literal, so the literals are still `locks` + `snapshot.json` + the
`read_model.db` trio -- five, unchanged. The `build_input_fingerprint` class-1
docstring's "ONE stated exception" is now two, and `DELETED_ARCHIVE_DIRNAME`'s
"alone among this module's inline names" was falsified by this commit and is
corrected in it.

Gates (5 new cases, each watched failing against its own mutation): the real
archive verb's output is absent from the stat set; churn inside the archived
surface does not move the digest; the per-workspace actor archive is STILL in the
closure; only the TOP-LEVEL name is excluded; the excluded name is the one the
path helper resolves to.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(snapshot): H2 / MCF-27 — every led build closes the chat SessionDB it opened, so the WAL stops being present mid-session

The build bound `session_db = _default_persona_session_db()` into a local and
dropped it, and `status.build_status` did the same. Each call left one live
SQLite connection behind for the life of the process, and a serve does many
builds: one per led rebuild, one per forceFresh gesture, one per hydrate.

That is a cache-correctness defect, not housekeeping. SQLite keeps the `-wal`
sibling on disk for exactly as long as a connection is open and unlinks it when
the last one closes, and the read-model cache's fingerprint stats that file. The
leak is therefore WHY the chat WAL was present mid-session at all, and why
"which build in this process wrote the sidecar last" decided whether the next
boot could hit the cache (MCF-15's asymmetry, whose symptom MC-3b masked
correctly while this cause stayed).

Both call sites share the acquisition, so ownership became a scope --
`snapshot.persona_session_db_scope` -- acquired on the build's OUTERMOST frame
(inside `runtime_resolution_scope`, where the acquisition resolved its scope
before) and threaded down as a required keyword-only argument, so the section
cannot re-acquire and cannot leak. The None arm is explicit, not incidental:
`open_chat_session_db` answers None BY CONTRACT and every consumer types the
handle `Any | None`, so `contextlib.closing` over a bare None was not available.

WHERE THE BRIEF WAS WRONG: it named `_build_snapshot_uncoalesced` as the binder,
as MCF-27 does. That function is a two-statement wrapper; the binding was in
`_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope` one frame down, and `status.py` had the same
wrapper/body split. The wrapper pair is what made a scope cheap instead of a
220-line reindent.

Closing here is key-NEUTRAL, and only because MC-3b landed: `SessionDB.close`
drains the token queue and attempts a TRUNCATE checkpoint, and SQLite unlinks the
WAL when the last connection goes, so an absent WAL and a frameless present one
must key identically -- which is exactly what
`core_cache._wal_without_frames_is_content_free` guarantees. That dependency is
stated at the site. The key itself cannot be poisoned: `build_snapshot` stats the
input fingerprint BEFORE calling the builder, so the release happens after the
key was captured.

The external-surface floors in the two S27/S29 reachability gates moved one name
over -- `status.py` no longer imports `_default_persona_session_db` (still live,
called by the scope) but `persona_session_db_scope`. Both gates red'd on this,
correctly, and their own assertion messages ask for the departed consumer to be
named in the file rather than the list patched silently; it is.

Gates, each watched failing against its own mutation: a led snapshot build closes
what it opened, counted; the status site likewise, with its own kill that leaves
the snapshot case green; a build whose acquisition answers None completes AND
reports no release failure; a handle whose close raises does not cost the frame
but IS reported; and a led build leaves the chat database at rest so the next
consult matches (in the fingerprint suite, where the WAL lifecycle helpers live).

The None-arm case pins the LOG record, not merely "the build completed" -- under
the unconditional-close mutant the build still completes, because the release is
guarded, so a case asserting only completion would have been vacuous. Caught by
running the mutation, which is the only thing that catches this class.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(core_cache): H3 / C22 — the channel table's reverse gate can finally see a token spelled with its field

Found while retiring `entries_io` through the C22 table, and it is its own
defect rather than a detail of that retirement.

`test_every_token_the_table_names_is_one_a_writer_emits` resolved only BARE
spans (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$`), so a row naming its token as `reason=entries_io`
was invisible to it — and that is the spelling C22 exists to index, since the
whole filing was "three `reason=` vocabularies on one logger, two of them
colliding". Consequence: a row for a RETIRED reason survives forever, which is
"a census instruction that returns zero forever" — the exact defect this
direction's own docstring says it exists to prevent.

MEASURED, not argued. With the `entries=false` writer deleted, re-adding its row
spelled ``reason=entries_io`` left all eleven cases green; the identical row
spelled ``entries_io`` reddened this one. Same row, same token, opposite verdict
on the spelling alone.

The fix resolves both spellings through one `_named_token` helper. `ok=`,
`stale=` and `entries=` are excluded by name because they are the lane's BOOLEAN
fields — resolving them would make the gate demand a writer for `true`. That is a
fact about this lane, so it is listed rather than pattern-matched.

Committed on its own so it can be reverted independently of the MCF-21 change
that found it, and so the retirement that follows rides a gate that has been
watched fail. Anti-vacuity for the helper itself is pinned in
`test_the_parsers_are_reading_something`: both spellings must resolve to one
token, and a boolean field must resolve to none.

Green against the table BEFORE the retirement too — no existing row named a dead
`reason=`-spelled token, so the widening found no collateral.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(core_cache): H3 / MCF-21 — the write-back becomes one generation, published by one pointer replace

`write_back` landed three files through three independent `os.replace` calls.
Each was atomic ALONE and the TRIO was not, so "these three describe one build"
was held up by two ad-hoc binding guards rather than one rule — and MCF-21's
judgement was that a FOURTH file would make a third guard, so the moment to
decide was before that.

THE SHAPE, AND WHERE THE RECORDED ONE WAS WRONG

MC-3 recorded "write `serve_read_model.next/`, `os.replace` the directory". That
is not implementable and the brief was right to overrule it. Verified here
rather than taken on trust: `os.replace` cannot replace a non-empty directory
anywhere (POSIX `ENOTEMPTY`), and on Windows — the primary platform — it cannot
replace a directory AT ALL, empty or not (`PermissionError` / `WinError 5` for
both cases). A directory can only be renamed onto a name that does not exist, so
the only directory-swap shape available is rename-away-then-rename-in, which has
a window with NO live generation and is refused.

So the trio is written into a fresh `gen-<stamp>/` that nothing points at, and
the write-back LANDS when `live.json` naming it is replaced through the module's
one atomic writer. One atomic act publishes three files.

WHAT RETIRED, AND THROUGH WHICH CHANNEL

The entries write used to sit deliberately outside the pair's `try`, so a failed
diagnostic left a usable cache and receipted `entries=false reason=entries_io`.
A published generation missing a file is now unrepresentable, so that arm and
its token are gone from the writers and from the C22 table. The retirement was
watched fail in both directions of `test_core_cache_channel_table.py` (see the
commit before this one, which had to make the reverse direction able to fail at
all).

WHAT DID NOT RETIRE, AND WHY

`core_sha256` stays. The swap retires one of the two things it caught — a
half-replaced pair — and cannot touch the other: bytes that changed AFTER a
generation was published. MCF-14's tamper pin drives exactly that, and it now
tampers inside the live generation.

`entries_unbound` stays, re-aimed. Cross-generation mixing is unrepresentable,
but position is still not provenance inside a published generation, and the
alternative to refusing is a receipt that NAMES FILES an operator will go and
investigate, computed against a stat set that is not this pair's.

LEGACY LAYOUT: the benign-demote arm, chosen deliberately

A store with no pointer demotes `absent`. It does NOT adopt the flat trio — not
because the judgement could not vet it, but because keeping a second resolution
alive means a pointer that is ever lost silently falls back to whatever flat
trio is on disk and can serve an arbitrarily old core as authoritative. The cost
is one cold start per store; the first successful write-back reaps the flat
files. NOTE FOR THE FIRST BOOT: `absent` is deliberately unlogged, so the
transition shows as NO demote line, not as a `reason=` line.

GATES — each impossibility its own killing mutation, all watched fail

  core write fails -> nothing published      M1 (pointer first)     RED
  sidecar write fails -> nothing published   M1                     RED
  entries write fails -> nothing published   M2 (restore old arm)   RED, entries arm ONLY
  staged-but-unpublished -> OLD generation   M1 / M3 (newest-wins)  RED
  crash residue inert and reaped             M3 / M4 (drop reap)    RED
  the surviving guard still convicts         M5 (drop core_sha256)  RED
  channel-table parity, both directions      M2 / M6                RED
  failed landing changes nothing             M7 (raise through)     RED
  a pointer cannot escape the cache dir      M8 (any name)          RED

M2 is the one that proves the design changed rather than the docstrings: it reds
`[entries.json]` and leaves `[core.json]` and `[sidecar.json]` green.

Focused suite 175 passed (core_cache set + stale-first routing + office state
patches); 246 passed with the snapshot consumers added. Every mutation restored
byte-exact from a snapshot taken first, verified by sha256, restore in the abort
path. Fence unchanged. Live canary revision 67.

author: nekwo
message:
docs(harness): MC-9 — the investigation doc stops ending at a plan nobody can tell ran

This report was the MC line's authority and it ended at §4, an ordered plan, with
no record that any of it executed. A hermes-side reader looking for "what happened
to the cache that never hit" found twelve proposals and nothing else — and three of
its own sentences had been falsified by the stages it proposed.

WHAT IS APPENDED (§5) — promoted, not re-derived

The FINDINGS LOG in the launcher brain (`plan-eg-weakness-escalation-ledger.md`)
was written incrementally as each stage landed, precisely so this closeout would
copy rather than reconstruct. §5 carries all 55 rows: the sixteen stages with their
commits, the per-stage findings with their proof sentences, the field measurements
as dated receipts, and the open rows a hermes reader inherits.

Two of those rows matter more than the rest here, because without them §2 reads as
if a residual `fingerprint_mismatch` were inherent:

  MCF-14 — the story on offer ("the store legitimately advances between boots") was
  FALSIFIED. Boot A's last write-back and boot B's own both recorded the same offset
  and the same entry count, with a mismatch demote between them.

  MCF-15 — the real residual cause, and it is NOT among §2's ranked causes: an
  absent WAL and a present-but-empty WAL are keyed as different facts and are the
  same fact. Proven by the WAL's creation time landing 4.15 s AFTER the consult that
  missed.

That gap is the strongest argument in the document for why the investigation
discipline mattered, so it is stated as such rather than smoothed over.

CORRECTED IN PLACE (dated, original wording preserved underneath)

  §1 A2 — "never_converged did not fire, and cannot fire at boot" is FALSIFIED
  (MCF-17): it fired at 11:00:21.370 on a forceFresh-gesture boot, which makes five
  write-backs. The paragraph's reasoning is sound for the boot shapes it observed
  and is kept as the record of what the evidence supported.

  §1 A3 — `_build_snapshot_uncoalesced` is the WRAPPER (MCF-46). Every section
  described there, and the bind behind the SessionDB leak, live one frame lower in
  `_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope`. Two existing AST gates walk the wrapper for
  assignments in a function that has none.

  §3 P4 — the open "JSON or compact text?" question is SETTLED by measurement
  (MCF-20): 159 vs ~153 bytes/entry, a 4 % saving. Encoding is not the lever; the
  size of the closure is, which is P12.

§§0-4 are otherwise untouched. They are the record of what was believed and
measured on the day, and a correction is never an erasure.

Citations are `file::symbol` throughout (C25) — this document has already been
bitten by 55 stale line-number references.

Docs only; no code, no tests, no behaviour change.

message:
test(agent_runtime): MCF-47(i) — the dead-locals gate stops walking a two-statement wrapper

`test_the_named_dead_locals_are_not_bound_anywhere_in_the_builder` resolved
`_build_snapshot_uncoalesced` and collected `ast.Assign` targets from it. That
function became a WRAPPER when the SessionDB acquisition moved to the build's
outermost frame — one `with runtime_resolution_scope(),
persona_session_db_scope() as session_db:` and one `return
_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope(...)`. Zero assignments, so the bound set was
empty and the intersection was empty for a reason unrelated to the seeds. The
gate could not have failed: reintroducing all ten mission-lane seeds in the
body left it green. Sixth vacuous-gate appearance, and the same MCF-27 defect
the sibling `test_the_lookalike_live_locals_survive` was re-aimed for — missed
here because this gate names a FUNCTION rather than a source segment.

Re-aiming at `_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope` would reproduce it at the next
refactor that moves a section one frame over, so the scope is the MODULE: no
surviving code in `agent_runtime.snapshot` may bind one of the ten names. That
is where the guarantee lives and is strictly stronger than any single-function
walk — a seed reintroduced in a sibling function was previously invisible.

Binding is now read in every form a seed can return in (plain/annotated/
augmented assignment, walrus, `for` and comprehension targets, `with ... as`)
via a shared `_bound_names` helper; `ast.Assign` alone would have let `for runs
in ...` back in silently. And the walk carries an ANTI-VACUITY witness: it must
resolve `agents`, a local the module demonstrably binds, so a walk that resolves
nothing says so instead of passing. Aiming `_bound_names` back at the wrapper
now trips that arm — the mistake that created this finding is caught by the gate
itself.

defect-class gate) reintroduced in `_build_snapshot_in_runtime_scope`, the OLD

fix(hermes_cli): MCF-47(iii) — the archive_unreadable hint stops sending operators to the wrong tree

`_error_hint("archive_unreadable")` told the operator to repair the undecodable
copy "under store/office_archive/". The error is raised from reads of
`paths.office_archived_actor_path` (office_store.py ~652 and ~736) —
`office/<ws>/archive/<actor>.json`. `store_root()/office_archive` is a DIFFERENT

(`archived_path.parent.relative_to(paths.store_root())`), asserting the hint
names `office/<workspace-id>/archive/` and does NOT name `office_archive` — so

another plausible-looking tree.

(`"archive" in hint`) still PASSED — blind, as it had been all along — while the
