author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): PA-1 step 0 answered NO — the dispatch tile knew WHO it briefed and WHAT it said, never WHERE the answer went

The premise check first, because it gated everything: does `target_session_id`
ride the trace wire today? It does not, and the answer is not a grep — it is
four chokepoints, each of which alone would have been enough to drop it:

  * `_agent_chat_dispatch_fields` emits exactly `{dispatch_target,
    dispatch_order}`, both read off the INVOCATION;
  * `progress._SAFE_PROGRESS_KEYS` carries no session-id key at all (only
    `session_id_present`, a bool);
  * `persona_chat_history._trace_entry` projects those same two dispatch keys;
  * `operator_channels._TOOL_DETAIL_STR_FIELDS` merges those same two.

Derived by AST over the four key sets rather than by token, because the trap on
this surface is spelling: `dispatch_store` HAS a `target_session_id` column and
`dispatch_delivery` renders it into delivery PROSE, so the field exists in the
store and is legible to a human reading the reply — which is exactly the shape
that reads like a wire field and is not one. A field in the store is not a field
on the wire.

So this is the additive half. `_agent_chat_dispatch_thread_fields` reads the
relay's RESULT — the thread is resolved downstream of the invocation, so the
started event cannot know it — and emits ONE new key,
`dispatch_target_session_id`, through the allowlist, the trace entry and the
tool-detail merge. Nothing existing changes shape: `target_label`, `summary`,
`dispatch_target` and `dispatch_order` stay byte-identical.

Two things it deliberately does NOT do.

It does not name the target's `persona_instance_id`, which the stage offered.
That id is a mutable, re-stamped binding pointer, and naming it in an open
request is precisely what broke launcher chat switching on 2026-07-24; the
launcher's open path is session-keyed by design. A wire field whose only
plausible consumer is the harmful one is not worth emitting, so the plan is
narrowed here rather than followed.

And it stays silent on the detached lane. `agent_chat_send(wait=false)` returns
a null `session_id` BY CONSTRUCTION — the child turn resolves its thread long
after the sender's turn ended — so a background dispatch carries no thread field
and any console link over it stays inert. That is a stated absence, not an
oversight: the waiting lane is the default (`wait` defaults true) and it is the
lane that can answer.

The result arrives as a serialized JSON string on a live relay and as a dict
from an in-process caller. Both doors are read, which is the same pair
`_is_error_result` already opens for this exact tool.

Proof — all five new assertions watched RED against the reverted implementation
before they were trusted: the payload carries the thread from both result
shapes; a detached dispatch and a refused relay carry none; a non-dispatch tool
whose result happens to hold the same keys gets nothing; prose or an over-long
value in the id slot is DROPPED rather than truncated, because truncating hands
the console a wrong session to open. The sink re-asserts the id shape at the
redaction boundary, and the pair survives the started/finished merge onto the
tool_call the launcher reads. `tests/agent_runtime/` green: 6033 passed,
1 skipped.

author: nekwo
message:
docs(coverage-claims): MCF-78/MCF-75 hermes half — the guard that died on the 30th, the merge that broke its invariant on the 31st

A prose claim of coverage is the one thing no coverage tool contradicts. The
sweep note (launcher vault, `mcf-78-75-coverage-claim-sweep.md`) named eight
hermes citations. A reader built for the job finds **23 claim-sites** wrong, and
the two sharpest were not in the note.

**1. `env-determinism-audit.md` §7.2 — the invariant is not merely unguarded, it
is VIOLATED.** The section names four guards in
`tests/agent_runtime/test_env_determinism_audit.py`; `2154f05428` (2026-07-30)
gutted that file to a five-line retirement probe and took all four. One of them
was an AST sweep whose own prose said "one surviving in-body `SKILLS_DIR` is the
whole bug back". Replaying its exact logic: **0 offenders at `2154f05428^`, 11 at
`b9721809e6` and at HEAD.** That merge (2026-07-31, upstream) landed
`_index_installed_skill_dirs_by_name`, `_find_installed_skill_dir_by_name`,
`_backfill_optional_provenance`, `_read_hub_install_paths`,
`_index_active_skills` and `_recover_renamed_skill`, every one reading the
import-time-frozen constant instead of `_skills_dir()` — one day after the guard
that existed to red on exactly that was deleted. Stated in the doc; the code fix
is upstream-owned and is escalated, not smuggled in here.

**2. §7.3's REFUSAL has been inverted and nobody recorded it.** The doc refuses
to delete `hermes_cli/harness.py`'s `import os` because the exec'd parts "carry
no import block". `e887cdf265` (2026-08-01, "let each exec'd part declare the
names it actually uses") ended that: harness.py has **zero** `os.` uses of its
own and each part imports what it needs. The named guard was already gone, so
the change announced nothing. UNCOVERED SEAM stated: nothing asserts a part
imports the names it reads, and that failure surfaces on a live chat turn.

**3. The board sentence — the sweep's verdict is OVERTURNED.** The note ruled it
"STALE, seam now uncovered" on a grep for board.sentence returning zero. That
grep searched the DOC's vocabulary, not the seam's words. The sentence ships
from `runtime_hud.py:812` and IS pinned —
`test_board_agent_tools.py::test_hud_digest_present_when_open_cards_exist`
asserts `"MAY add a card" in block`, with two siblings pinning the absence
direction. What was true: the named id AND the path it named
(`_persona_chat_system_prompt`, tombstoned s61) both died in `c4a1fdef5c`. Doc 16
now names the real pin and adds a correction section stating the one hop that is
genuinely unpinned — `persona_commands.py:3183`, exec'd, so no test reaches it.

**Twenty-three sites fixed** across 22 files: repointed where real coverage
exists (`test_stream_patch.py:514/562` for the never-existent
`test_patch_coverage.py`; `test_send_path_runner_reuse.py:425-426` for
`test_runtime_resolve_cache.py`; `test_s56_config_block_removal.py:186/260` for
`test_s56_roster_gate_removal.py`; `test_docker_exec_privilege_drop.py` for
`test_uid_remap.py`; `test_snapshot_history_eviction.py:404`,
`test_chat_session_scope.py`, `test_home_override_scripts.py`,
`test_space_separated_name_still_normalizes`,
`test_named_custom_provider_wins_over_builtin_alias`); marked **deleted** where
the prose was recording a removal in the present tense; marked **not built**
where a shipped doc kept an unbuilt matrix. **Four named a real UNCOVERED SEAM**
and say so rather than falling silent: the skills-sync accessor bypass, the
exec'd-part import discipline, the HUD-to-prompt last hop, and
`runtime_provider.py`'s canonical-shadow branch (no case in that file defines a
custom provider named after a canonical one).

**The gate: `tests/test_coverage_claims_resolve.py`.** Four arms —
NAMED (`file.py::name`, AST not substring, plus the `::name` continuation form
the house docs use, which is how FOUR of the eight the sweep set out to fix are
spelled and why the sweep itself counted three), PATH, BARE, MEMBER (a
backticked bare function id resolved against a path in the same window — the
shape `agent_runtime_helpers.py:2802` used, which no `::` reader can see).
Corpus: md 119, py 3881, test files 2934; NAMED 47, PATH 198, BARE 140, MEMBER 3.

**It says what it CANNOT see, in the docstring AND in the failure message.** An
existence check proves a name resolves; it cannot prove the test asserts what
the prose claims. The launcher's sibling scores 33/35 and the two it misses are
exactly the VACUOUS pair. A gate that lets a reader infer semantic coverage is
this row's own defect one level up.

Kill proof, three ways, all watched failing first:
- Seeded `tests/agent_runtime/test_a_guard_that_does_not_exist.py` into
  `profile_runner.py:1563`. RED, naming it: `[PATH] agent_runtime/profile_runner.py:1563
  / claim : tests/agent_runtime/test_a_guard_that_does_not_exist.py / why : path
  ... does not exist`, with Levenshtein suggestions. Reverted byte-exact

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): the drag-drop create minted a chat pointer whose transcript root was never written

An operator drags a QA agent into the Mission Control office, messages it, and
every send comes back:

    UNKNOWN EXPLICIT PERSONA CHAT ROOT:
    persona_chat_personainst_qa_agent_03ba2049_67d5a1a6921f

That root existed in the persona-instance row (as BOTH default_chat_session_id
and session_id), in the create reservations recorded result, and in the serve
read-model. It existed in no SessionDB on the machine, and there was no mint
receipt for it.

**The refusal was right.** `mission-chat message` refuses any explicit
`session_id` naming no SessionDB row; that guards job is refusing
client-fabricated roots and it is untouched here. What was wrong is upstream of
it: `persona_chat_session_id_for` returns a bare `uuid4` string and creates
nothing, and the two mint fallbacks in `PersonaInstanceStore` handed that string
straight into `open_chat`.

**The structural shape.** Grep `_ensure_persona_chat_session(` before this
change: five call sites, ALL FIVE in
`hermes_cli/harness_parts/persona_commands.py`, ZERO in `agent_runtime`.
Chat-root durability was a CLI-lane concern, so the one-call create lane
(`agent_runtime.agent_create.perform_agent_create` — the lane the launcher
reaches over RPC) could not reach it. Not "forgot to call it": could not call
it, since the helper lived in a command part `agent_runtime` must not import.

And it never self-heals. `resolve_default_chat_session_id_for_instance` re-offers
a chat-shaped, own-instance pointer forever without asking the transcript store
whether it resolves — so the agent is born permanently undeliverable.

**The invariant, moved to where both transports meet it.** A
`default_chat_session_id` is never bound onto a persona instance unless its
SessionDB row already exists. `PersonaChatPersistenceError`,
`_default_persona_session_db` and `_ensure_persona_chat_session` move to the new
`agent_runtime/persona_chat_durability.py` (the CLI imports them back under
their old private names, so its four pre-existing call sites are unchanged), and
`add_instance` / `create_operator_chat` now route the root through
`_durable_chat_root` AT THE BIND ARGUMENT. The pointer cannot be bound without
that function having returned, so the ordering is structural rather than
remembered, and every future caller of `add_instance` inherits it.

The persona-id normalizers the ensure step spends (`_normalize_cli_persona_id`,
`_persona_id_from_instance_id`, `_normalize_cli_persona_or_template_id`) move to
`persona_assignments` with them — they were already pure functions of that
modules own primitives.

**Failing loudly, and leaving nothing behind.** A store that cannot persist now
refuses instead of binding a phantom: `perform_agent_create` answers the typed
`chat_session_persist_failed` shape the argv open-chat lane already spends, and
because `_durable_chat_root` raises on the way INTO `open_chat`, no instance row
exists to compensate. Both argv creates grew the matching arm. The mint sites
also assert bindability BEFORE the durable write — the ordering
`PersonaChatMintReceiptStore.mint` already learned — so a retirement or
sibling-steal refusal still leaves no titled thread behind.

Kill-proofed both directions with `_durable_chat_root` neutered: the RPC row
fails naming the exact phantom ("no SessionDB row for it exists: every
mission-chat send to this agent will be refused unknown_chat_session, forever"),
and the create-then-message row fails with the operators own sentence,
`unknown explicit persona chat root: persona_chat_personainst_qa_agent_...`.

Known residual, NOT covered here: `persona_chat_continuity`s mint binds via
`open_chat` and creates the session row after, deliberately (its EARLY BIND
comment owns the argument). A SessionDB write failing in that window leaves the
same permanent phantom. It is receipt-keyed rather than free-running, and
inverting it would undo a documented fix, so it is named rather than changed.

10102 passed, 103 skipped, 1 failed — `test_xai_provider_labels.py`, a
pre-existing red on a provider-label map that loads none of the modules touched
here.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): the dispatch mint bound the chat pointer, then wrote the row it had already promised

`PersonaChatMintReceiptStore.mint` bound the instance's pointer at
`open_chat` and only afterwards wrote the SessionDB row. In the window
between the two the instance named a root no transcript store held —
the same phantom `persona_chat_durability` closed on the create lane in
63768819a3, and just as permanent, because
`resolve_default_chat_session_id_for_instance` re-offers a chat-shaped
own-instance pointer forever without asking whether it resolves. Every
later `mission-chat message` on it is refused `unknown_chat_session`.

Shape: RETRACT the bind, not invert the order. Two independent lines
killed persist-before-bind:

  * The EARLY BIND ordering is already pinned by tests, not defended by
    a comment as the brief for this lane wrongly assumed —
    `test_a_retire_that_lands_mid_mint_still_leaves_no_titled_thread`
    asserts no row of that source exists at all, and
    `test_the_mint_binds_before_it_creates_the_session_row` asserts
    `order == ["bind", "create_session", "title"]` outright. Inverting
    would have required weakening both.

  * Its premise is empirically false. A bare row carrying no meta and no
    title IS Mission-Control-visible: `persona_chat_history_summary`
    lists with `min_message_count=0`, admits on `source` alone, and
    `_infer_persona_id` reads the persona out of the very `system_prompt`
    the mint's `create_session` writes, so `_history_row` hands it a
    fallback title. Persisting first would have re-opened the titled
    orphan the early-bind comment owns.

This lane also cannot route through `ensure_durable_persona_chat_root`:
its `session_db` is the CALLER's handle (dispatch, relay and argv each
pass their own), so the shared helper would write the row into a
different database from the one this mint's own reader dereferences.

The receipt stays `reserved` through the failure on purpose — a same-key
retry resolves the SAME root and completes, which is what covers the
crash-in-window case no in-process retraction can reach.

Kill proof in four sabotage directions: fix removed (fails on the typed
error, not the phantom — so a narrower variant with the retraction alone
removed was run to name the phantom itself); identity drift, where the
write targets `root + "_drift"`, red in three separate gates, proving
they pin identity and not mere existence; the retraction's identity guard
dropped, caught reverting a binding it did not make; and the argv
`PersonaChatPersistenceError` arm removed, letting a raw storage
exception escape to the operator.

Suite: `tests/agent_runtime` + `tests/hermes_cli` clean-room, one failing
file — `test_xai_provider_labels.py`, which fails identically at
e79537b9fd and is not this change's.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): the refusal that wrote nothing told the operator to go check the runtime for wreckage

`perform_agent_create`'s `chat_session_persist_failed` arm — the refusal
63768819a3 added so a store that cannot persist a chat root stops binding a
phantom — answered `ERR_HANDLER_FAILED` (-32000) with no `rolled_back` field.

The launcher's taxonomy (`mission_agent_create_rpc.dart`) has no case for that
reason string, so it falls to code -32000 -> `handlerRaised`, and its parser
reads `data.rolled_back` off EVERY error frame with `== true` and a `false`
default — deliberately, as a fail-safe ("a missing or non-boolean field must
read as NOT rolled back, which is the safe direction"). Absent key, therefore
`rolledBack: false`, therefore `mission_control_page.dart` printed:

    Could not place QA Agent — the placement was refused and the roster row
    could not be undone. Check the runtime.

There is no roster row to undo.

**Inventoried, not assumed.** Real `runtime.agent.create` over
`serve_rpc.handle_request`, throwaway store root, chat store made
unacquirable, every path under the root diffed before/after. What the refusal
leaves behind is ONE empty file — `locks/agent_creates/<digest>.lock`, the
cross-process file lock every attempt takes, success or failure. No
`persona_instances/` directory. No office actor. And **no reservation receipt
in any state**: `reserve_agent_create` yields an unwritten record for a
brand-new key and names `mark_instance_minted` "the first durable write",
which this arm is reached before. There is no `reserved` state in that module
at all — `_VALID_STATES` is instance_minted/done/rolled_back — so the "a
`reserved` receipt becomes permanent litter" worry this lane started from
describes something that does not exist, and there is nothing here to sweep.

`rolled_back: True` is therefore the literal truth, not a courtesy, and it is
the sibling spelling: `compensate_failed_placement` and the `STATE_ROLLED_BACK`
replay arm answer with that exact key and type. A second vocabulary for
"nothing survives" would be just as true and just as useless — the client reads
`rolled_back` and nothing else. The operator now gets:

    Could not place QA Agent — the placement was refused and nothing was
    written.

The hermes half is sufficient: `mission_control_page.dart:2274` is the only
consumer of `MissionAgentCreateRefused` in the launcher, and the parser reads
the key before any reason/code branching, so no taxonomy case is needed.

**`next_expected` too.** It said "retry with the same idempotency_key". The
only client on this lane mints a fresh micros-stamped key per gesture, on
purpose — a re-click must mint a second agent — so that advice was unreachable
from it, and it implied the key carried recoverable state. It carries none:
nothing was recorded under it, so a same-key and a fresh-key retry are the SAME
operation. The client is right and the server's sentence was wrong, so the
sentence changed: "restore canonical persona chat transcript storage and retry
the gesture; nothing was recorded under this idempotency_key". The argv verb
overwrites `next_expected` with its own and is unaffected — but it promises its
reader "a refused create wrote nothing unless it says rolled_back: false", a
key this arm did not carry, so the two lanes read the same absence in OPPOSITE
directions. Stamping it makes that sentence checkable, and a hermes_cli row now
checks it.

Kill proof, five directions. Fix deleted: `KeyError: 'rolled_back'` on both the
signal row and the argv row. `"true"` as a STRING: the value gate fires
(`assert 'true' is True`) and the sibling-parity gate fires on the type
(`assert <class 'str'> is <class 'bool'>`) — the launcher coerces nothing, so a
string would have printed the orphan sentence again while looking correct from
this side. `False`: `assert False is True`. Old `next_expected` restored: the
string gate fires. And a sabotage that is not a deletion — the arm made to call
`reservation.mark_instance_minted` before refusing — is caught by the
durable-trace row on the reservations directory, which is what keeps the
`rolled_back: true` claim honest if someone later changes what this arm writes.

The parity witness needed a correction of its own: driven under ONE monkeypatch
scope the chat-store refusal stayed installed through the sibling call, that
call took the persist arm too, and the test compared the arm with itself —
green against a str-vs-bool drift. Split into two `pytest.MonkeyPatch.context()`
scopes it kills.

author: nekwo
message:
perf(agent_runtime): the watchdog billed 2.29h of CPU rebuilding for reads, because opening a SQLite file looks exactly like writing to it

`_scope_fingerprint` keyed the chat SessionDB and the running-work
`state.db` by a raw stat of `("", "-wal", "-journal")`. SQLite deletes the
`-wal` sibling on a clean last-close and re-creates it EMPTY on the next
open, so a poll landing while any process merely HELD the database open
read a fresh `mtime_ns` and a poll landing at rest read `absent`. A
database nobody was writing to flapped the fingerprint twice per open.

Each flap appends a synthetic `state.reconciled`, which `patch_coverage`
classifies UNCOVERED, which demotes the whole batch to a full core
rebuild. Measured on the operator's runtime over the 22.16h to 2026-08-21
09:06 (`profiles/base`): 2433 `snapshot_build reason=demote` against 35
hydrates, median build_ms 3083, max 37266 — 2.29h of CPU — and 1239
`state.reconciled`, 96.9% of every event appended in the window, at a
median 9.0s spacing. 3338 distinct fingerprints over 4597 reconciles
against a recurring at-rest anchor is that flip's signature, not a
write's: real writes do not come back to the same value.

The mask that answers this already existed and was already field-proven —
`core_cache._wal_without_frames_is_content_free`, landed as MC-3b for the
boot-cache lane on 2026-08-18. It had one caller. The other two lanes that
key the same database were never told: the stream watchdog above, and
`serve._runtime_state_fingerprint`, where the same flip keeps the
read-model cache permanently cold — the defect a 2026-08-09 analysis named
and nobody propagated the mask to. Promoted to
`core_cache.sqlite_fingerprint_triples`, THE authority for how a poll lane
keys a SQLite database, and adopted by both.

This is a narrowing, not a disabling, and it holds the same line the
turn-element exclusion beside it holds. A committed write still moves the
fingerprint within one poll by one of two paths SQLite's durability rules
leave no gap between: uncheckpointed, the `-wal` sibling is non-empty and
keyed in full; checkpointed, the frames are in `state.db`, whose own mtime
and size are the FIRST triple. The staleness SLO that live incidents
2026-07-25 (Chat History frozen ~36h) and 2026-08-11 (stuck running_work)
bought is intact, and their existing pins — `test_scope_fingerprint_
covers_head_home_session_db` and `..._covers_running_work_stores` — still
pass untouched.

`PRAGMA data_version` was evaluated first and rejected; the reasons are
recorded at `_scope_fingerprint` so it is not re-proposed as the obvious
answer it looks like. Measured on SQLite 3.45.3: its value is comparable
only WITHIN one connection, so the stateless per-poll shape returns a
constant and detects nothing; making it work means the stream process
holding a SessionDB connection open for its lifetime, which is the exact
shape of MCF-27, two days after MCF-27; and it is not checkpoint-immune
either — `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` with no data change bumps it. Against
this mask it differs on exactly one scenario of nine, and that one cannot
occur without a preceding commit both already report.

Kill proof, both directions. Reverting the mask reds three of the new
tests, the sharpest being end-to-end: six consecutive polls during which
the database is only READ produce `['delta' x 6]` where the assertion
wants `{'heartbeat'}` — the storm, reproduced in-process. Pinning
`_scope_fingerprint` to a constant (the cheapest wrong fix: it kills the
storm perfectly and re-freezes Chat History) reds six, including both
incident pins and the new `test_scope_fingerprint_moves_on_committed_
chat_write`, while the three storm tests stay GREEN — which is the proof
that the pair does the work and neither half alone would.

Field check after the next restart, greppable: `grep -c "snapshot_build
reason=demote" agent.log` was 2433/22.16h = 110/h, and `grep -c
'"type":"state.reconciled"'` over the events slice was 1239/22.16h = 56/h
with the runtime largely idle. Both should now track real event-less
writes only — near zero at idle, a handful per hour under active chat.
A reconcile rate that stays near 56/h means the residual flap is NOT the
WAL and the fingerprint diff is the instrument, not a second guess.

Suite: 911 files, 10120 passed, 1 failed — `test_xai_provider_labels.py`,

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): six more refusals sent the operator hunting wreckage, and one of them was hiding real wreckage by saying nothing

33b11d9516 stamped `rolled_back: True` on ONE arm of `perform_agent_create`.
The rest still carried no such key, and the launcher's parser reads
`data.rolled_back` off EVERY error frame with a `false` default — deliberately,
as a fail-safe (`mission_agent_create_rpc.dart`: "a missing or non-boolean field
must read as NOT rolled back, which is the safe direction"). So every remaining
refusal printed:

    Could not place QA Agent — the placement was refused and the roster row
    could not be undone. Check the runtime.

**Inventoried per arm, not assumed — and they do not agree.** Real
`runtime.agent.create` through `serve_rpc.handle_request` on a throwaway store
root, every path under `store_root()` diffed before/after, one arm at a time:

* `workspace_not_found` — ZERO paths change. It refuses before
  `reserve_agent_create` is entered, so it does not even take the
  `locks/agent_creates/<digest>.lock` its siblings take. `True`.
* `instance_retired` — one empty lock file. `add_instance` decides retirement in
  `assert_bindable`, above `_durable_chat_root`; the record is unwritten because
  all three on-disk states are handled above this branch. Inventoried against a
  REAL tombstone (create → retire → re-create), not a stub. `True`.
* `instance_invalid` — one empty lock file. Every `ValueError` `add_instance`
  raises comes from its validation prologue. Inventoried with a REAL collision
  (`dev` re-using `qa`'s placement id). `True`.
* `idempotency_conflict` — zero paths change. `_validate_scope` refuses only when
  the stored persona/workspace DIFFER, so what survives is provably another
  gesture's receipt. `True`.
* `reserved_instance_missing` — **the opposite answer.** This arm is reachable
  only from `record.state == instance_minted`, and that state is written by
  `mark_instance_minted`, the reservation module's own "first durable write". A
  receipt naming a roster row is on disk BEFORE the call and is still there
  after it (the call changes nothing). `rolled_back: True` here would have been
  the same lie the absent key was telling, pointed the other way. `False` — and
  `False` is also what makes the launcher publish `persona_instance_id` as
  `orphanInstanceId`, so the drop log NAMES the row instead of asserting one.
* `create_lock_unavailable` — this attempt wrote nothing, but the holder of the
  key's file lock may be between its mint and its placement right now and its
  receipt is exactly what "lock unavailable" means we cannot read. `False` is
  not a claim that something survived; it is a refusal to claim it did not.
* `reservation_corrupt` — the receipt EXISTS and will not decode, so it may name
  a minted row. `False`. This is the one arm on the whole method where "Check
  the runtime" is literally correct.

The three reservation codes came out of ONE `except` that spelled one payload,
so they now go through `_RESERVATION_ROLLED_BACK`, a table with the argument for
each code beside it. A code missing from that table gets NO key and inherits the
launcher's fail-safe: a fault nobody has inventoried must not inherit optimism.

**`phase` too.** The launcher documents `instance | placement | null` and hermes
only ever emitted `placement`, so `mission_control_page.dart` logged `phase=none`
for every mint-phase refusal. Its parser is `dataMap?['phase']?.toString()` — it
accepts any string and renders it verbatim — which is why the vocabulary is now
closed HERE as `PHASE_INSTANCE` / `PHASE_PLACEMENT` rather than trusted to a
client that validates nothing. The four mint-phase arms say `instance`;
`workspace_not_found` and the reservation faults keep `null`, and that is an
assertion in the parametrized row, not a gap: they are refused before either
half is attempted, so naming one would be a third false claim in a payload this
lane exists to make honest.

**The two unbind paths that disagreed** (`persona_assignments.py`, both exposed
by b912cce88a):

1. `clear_chat_session_binding` claimed "Every unbind … goes through here so a
   stale binding can never be cleared silently by one path and loudly by
   another". False since b912cce88a: `rollback_chat_root_bind` nulls the same
   two fields and emits no `chat_binding_cleared`. The sentence was CORRECTED
   rather than made true, because routing the retraction through the clear costs
   three properties it needs: it RESTORES the previous pointer rather than
   clearing (a later mint failing must not orphan a live conversation), it must
   not raise (it runs inside a failure handler that already holds a typed
   error), and it must emit `emit_persona_instance_patch` — which
   `clear_chat_session_binding` does NOT do, because `_event` only appends to
   the log. Routing through it would have traded a false docstring for a stale
   client, which is the defect the retraction's patch exists to prevent. The
   docstring now enumerates the exception and an AST gate counts the writers, so
   a THIRD path goes red instead of quietly re-falsifying the sentence.

2. `mode` was not restored. `open_chat` sets `instance.mode = "chat"` in the
   same breath as the bind; the retraction reverted the pointers and left the
   mode, so a retracted FRESH mint produced `mode == "chat"` with no chat
   pointer — precisely the half-state `clear_chat_session_binding` demotes,
   reached by the one unbind path that does not go through it. Confirmed live on
   a real failed mint: pointer `None`, `session_id` `None`, `mode` `'chat'`, and
   `persona_instance_summary` ships that mode on the wire.

   **Latent, with a real reader — not cosmetic.** The launcher decodes `chat` to
   `MissionAgentInstanceMode.chatHistory` (`mission_agent_instance.dart`) and its
   persona-best election ranks `chatHistory` ABOVE `configuredIdle`
   (`mission_instance_resolution.dart`), so a retracted mint out-ranks a
   genuinely idle sibling on the strength of a conversation never written. I
   could not construct a live break — the tier only decides between two
   CANONICAL rows for one persona, and the canonical-before-placement partition
   settles the common case first — so this is reported as latent rather than
   fielded. Every hermes-side reader I checked is safe:
   `operator_channels._channel_key_for_instance` gates on `session_id and mode`,
   `repair_missing_chat_session_bindings` skips rows with no pointers, and
   `ensure_for_personas` iterates per-PERSONA rows, not placements.

   `previous.mode` rather than a flat demotion, because this method restores: a
   row that already owns a live thread keeps `chat` beside the pointer being put
   back, and a row the bind CREATED takes the store default `configured`. `mode`
   joins the emitted patch field list for the same reason the pointers are in
   it.

Kill proof, both halves. **Fix deleted:** `KeyError: 'rolled_back'` on six RPC
rows and both argv rows; `ImportError: cannot import name
'_RESERVATION_ROLLED_BACK'`; `AttributeError: module 'agent_runtime.agent_create'
has no attribute 'PHASE_INSTANCE'`; `assert None == 'instance'` on all three
mint-phase rows; and on the store half `assert 'chat' == 'configured'` plus
`assert 'mode' in '{… "changed": {"default_chat_session_id": null,
"chat_session_id": null, "session_id": null, "updated_at": …}}'`.

**Sabotage, not deletion.** (a) `rolled_back: True` stamped on
`reserved_instance_missing` — the arm that genuinely leaves state — and the
INVENTORY row catches it, comparing the stamp against what it just read off
disk: "the refusal claimed a rollback while its reservation receipt is still
'instance_minted' on disk and still names 'personainst_qa_resv'". (b)
`"idempotency_conflict": 1` in the table: the dict `==` comparison PASSES,
because `1 == True` in Python — only `assert all(type(value) is bool …)` fires.
That is the Dart trap an earlier lane found, where `1 == true` is false, and it
is why every row pins the TYPE beside the value. (c) A third unbind path added
to the module: `Left contains 1 more item: {'forget_chat_quietly':
{'session_id', 'default_chat_session_id'}}`.

The argv verb overwrites `next_expected` with its own sentence — "a refused
create wrote nothing unless it says rolled_back: false" — which was an
instruction to read a key that six of seven arms did not carry. It is now
answerable in BOTH directions from this lane, and a parametrized hermes_cli row
checks it that way rather than against a constant `true`.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(tools): six skills functions kept reading the profile that happened to be live when the module was imported

MCF-90. tools/skills_sync.py keeps HERMES_HOME / SKILLS_DIR / MANIFEST_FILE
as module constants purely as an override seam, and reads the ACTIVE
profile through _hermes_home() / _skills_dir() / _manifest_file(). Eleven
call sites across six function bodies read the frozen constant directly, so
in a long-lived `hermes harness serve` they kept resolving against whichever
profile was live at import — every profile switch after that was invisible
to them.

_backfill_optional_provenance held both halves in ONE function: it computed
`dest` from _skills_dir() (live) and then rebased it with
_safe_rel_install_path(dest, SKILLS_DIR) (frozen). After a switch those are
two different homes, relative_to raises, and provenance repair skips the
skill in silence.

WHY THIS WAS INVISIBLE. An AST sweep forbidding exactly this lived in
tests/agent_runtime/test_env_determinism_audit.py. It died on 2026-07-30
(2154f05428, mission-lane removal S0-S12) as COLLATERAL — that module's
top-level imports were part of the lane being removed, so the whole 684-line
file was reduced to a five-line retirement probe and an unrelated invariant
went with it. The upstream merge b9721809e6 landed the eleven reads on

author: nekwo
message:
docs(agent_runtime): the clear that "leaves every launcher stale" ships the whole core, and the patch that would fix it never reaches a client

`clear_chat_session_binding` writes the row and emits only
`persona_instance.chat_binding_cleared`, never a `state.patched`, while the
sibling `rollback_chat_root_bind` emits the patch and says why. Read from the
source that is a read-model staleness bug: `mode` and the session trio all move
on `persona_instance_summary`, so every connected launcher should keep
rendering the pointer the store no longer holds.

Driven, it is not. `chat_binding_cleared` is deliberately outside
`COVERED_DOMAIN_EVENT_TYPES`, one uncovered event makes the whole coalesced
batch uncoverable, and the frame that reports the clear is a full-core delta:

  FRAME type=delta  patches=null  core present=True

The client re-hydrates in the same frame. Adding the patch changes nothing —
the promotion gate rejects the batch before the patches list is assembled, so
the frame is byte-for-byte the one above with a dead row appended. Identical
with `read_model.delta_patches` off, where the lane is a full core by design;
this path is flag-independent, and the retraction is not.

The demote is load-bearing, not an un-done optimisation. Completing the
symmetry with `chat_opened` — emit the patch AND cover the event — does promote
the batch, measured:

  FRAME type=patch  core present=False
  patches=[{entity: persona_instance, changed: {mode, lifecycle_mode,
            default_chat_session_id, chat_session_id, session_id, updated_at}}]

and that one row is everything the client would get. A clear also empties the
instance's `persona_chat_history` row (the projection keys chat rows by
`default_chat_session_id`; measured one row -> none), and there is no
`persona_chat_history` patch entity for that departure to ride. The promoted
frame drops it from every connected client for the rest of its session — the
exact failure the `chat_opened` note says the producer and the coverage entry
must land together to avoid.

So: no patch here, and the reason recorded where the next reader of the
asymmetry will hit it — in the method's docstring and beside the covered-event
set — as a checkable fact rather than an assurance.

The sibling's hardcoded field list stays hardcoded. It is not a delta claim,
it is a statement of current values folded as an idempotent merge, and the
always-three-fields form is what makes the retraction complete regardless of
which pointer the bind moved. Its gate was a substring probe over the
serialised payload, which passes for a patch that renames `mode` to `api_mode`
and drops both wire names; it now asserts the field list and the values.

No AST writer-set change: this adds no writer of `default_chat_session_id` or
`session_id`, so `test_only_two_paths_may_move_an_instances_chat_pointers`
stands unchanged. `test_the_two_unbind_paths_are_told_apart_by_what_they_emit`
keeps its source-level assertions and now points at the wire-level ones.

Kill proof, both live callers driven (`persona chat delete`, the reconcile
sweep):
* emit the patch as proposed -> two gates red (`state.patched` first in a batch
  asserted to hold one event; the source-level emitter assertion), and the
  frame still carries a core, proving the row unreachable;
* emit it AND cover the event -> three gates red, the chat-history one naming
  the drop: "a promoted batch drops the chat row from every connected client";
* sibling wrong-field-list (`mode` -> `api_mode`, so "mode" still appears in
  the payload) -> the old substring assertions PASS, only the new field-list
  gate fails, naming the missing `mode` / `lifecycle_mode`.

Suite: 912 files, 10163 passed, 2 failed — both pre-existing
(`test_xai_provider_labels` `assert 'xai' == 'xAI'`, and the known-flaky
`test_mcp_startup`).

author: nekwo
message:
perf(agent_runtime): every boot threw the persisted core away for a config file whose bytes had not changed in two days

Measured on the operator's runtime, 2026-08-21. Every Mission Control boot
demoted the persisted read-model core with

  snapshot_core_cache core_source=rebuilt caller=prewarm reason=fingerprint_mismatch
    inputs=2225 diff_scope=last_pair changed=1
    diff=X:\Eternia\.hermes\profiles\alice\config.yaml

and paid a full rebuild: build_ms=6467 on the 13:17 boot, agents_readiness
3266 ms of it, prompt_observability 1484, events 732. One entry out of 2225.

THE CONVICTING MEASUREMENT IS NOT THE TIMESTAMP

profiles/alice/config.yaml was, at the moment of the miss, byte-for-byte
identical to a backup taken 2026-08-19: same 23,255 bytes, same SHA-256
(5640867efbae858a...). Its mtime had moved repeatedly in between (13:17:35.330,
13:45:24.032), and its NTFS creation time moved with it, so the file is being
ATOMICALLY REPLACED - temp file plus os.replace - with a document that has not
changed a byte in two days. build_input_fingerprint keys every input on
(path, mtime_ns, size), so a content-identical replacement reads exactly like an
edit. The persisted core was unreachable by construction.

WHY THE FIX IS AT THE FINGERPRINT AND NOT AT THE WRITER

Stopping a needless write is the narrower fix and would be preferred if the
writer were on this repo's boot path. It is not, and that is instrumented, not
assumed. A tracer on os.replace / os.rename / open(w) / Path.write_text /
Path.write_bytes / os.utime / shutil.copyfile, wrapped around

  * a real agent_runtime.snapshot.build_snapshot() with personas bound to
    profile homes seeded from a structural copy of the operator's own config,
  * a full `harness serve --ndjson` boot (prewarm included),
  * and one-shot runs of harness snapshot/status/agents/personas/doctor/chats/
    board/office, profile list, auth status, config get, doctor,

recorded ZERO writes to any config.yaml. migrate_config was ruled out
separately: it stamps _config_version 23 -> 33 and is idempotent on the second
call, while the live file still reads 23. And on the live machine the 13:51:01
boot demoted naming the same file while that file's mtime did not move during
the boot at all - the rewrite happens outside the build, then every later boot
legitimately sees a changed input for a document that did not change.

So the writer is real, repeated, and not reachable from here. A cache that any
writer anywhere can invalidate by re-serialising identical bytes has no floor.
This gives it one, for every future writer of these files rather than for the
one that happened to be caught.

WHAT CHANGED

_config_input_is_content_keyed(): the second member of the family
_wal_without_frames_is_content_free() started - one input class whose stat
triple moves for reasons that are not content, masked at the line where it
enters the closure. A bounded read (1 MiB ceiling, over it the entry keeps its
stat triple) replaces mtime_ns with 63 bits of the file's SHA-256.

Four call sites, all named in the closure spec: per profile config.yaml and
profile.yaml (class 4), the pinned ambient config authority and the harness
root config (class 5). Not the active_profile pointer, not the store subtree,
not the skill roots.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT WEAKENED

  * A genuine edit still invalidates - including a same-length one, which the
    size field alone could not catch.
  * A genuine edit that PRESERVES mtime now invalidates too. That was a false
    HIT before this change and is a miss after it, so the key got stricter in
    one direction while getting looser in the other.
  * Appearance and disappearance are still content events: an absent path keeps
    _stat_entry's -1/-1 and a directory keeps _DIR_MARK, and neither is read.

COST, measured rather than asserted: 2*<profiles>+2 bounded reads, 22 files on
the operator's ten-profile home. 20 warm passes at the live file size: median
1.3 ms stat-only vs 9.9 ms content-keyed, +8.6 ms per fingerprint, against a
6467 ms rebuild avoided.

KILL PROOF (both directions, plus the never-invalidate sabotage)

Reverted to HEAD's core_cache.py, the new file reds 4 of 7:
  mtime_ns: 1787335168302709400 != 1787335168292711100   (size 126 both)
  a restart after a content-identical config rewrite still demoted the
    persisted core and rebuilt - assert 'rebuilt' == 'cache'
  an edit that preserved both mtime and size was served from cache - the key is
    still reading the timestamp, not the bytes
Restored: 7 passed.

Sabotage - make the class never invalidate (return FingerprintEntry(path, 0, 0)
unconditionally), which is the trivially-passing wrong fix and turns gates 1
and 2 green. It reds 5, led by the one that matters:
  a REAL config edit was served from cache: the fix did not narrow the
    invalidation trigger, it removed the input from the closure

WHAT THE OPERATOR CAN GREP AFTER A RESTART

Before, on every boot:
  grep 'snapshot_core_cache core_source=rebuilt' profiles/base/logs/agent.log \
    | grep 'diff=.*profiles.alice.config.yaml'
After an idle restart that expression finds nothing for that file, and
  grep 'snapshot_core_cache core_source=cache caller=' profiles/base/logs/agent.log
carries the hit instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(agent_runtime): the content key's seven gates were all green while it hashed only the first 64 bytes of the file

Found by sabotage, not by reading. 2f98eef3ee replaced the mtime component of
the cache fingerprint with a SHA-256 over the bytes for the config input class,
and shipped seven gates for it. Change the digest to cover a PREFIX instead of
the body

  keyed = int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(body[:64]).digest()[:8], "big") >> 1

and the result is 7 passed. Not one gate fires.

WHY THE SUITE COULD NOT SEE IT

The fixture BODY is ~120 bytes and the mutation BODY_SAME_LENGTH flips
deepseek-chat -> deepseek-chaT at roughly offset 40 - INSIDE the 64-byte
window. So every case was still measuring a byte the truncating mutant happened
to hash. What the seven gates prove is "the key reads BYTES instead of MTIME".
What they do not prove is "the key covers the WHOLE FILE". Those are different
claims and the gap is not academic: the operator's real
profiles/alice/config.yaml is 23,255 bytes, where essentially every real edit
lands past any plausible prefix window. A truncating regression, a partial read,
a buffered-read bug, or a future "hash the head, it's faster" optimisation would
each ship green while serving a stale cache for every config edit past the
prefix - which is the every-boot-rebuild defect 2f98eef3ee exists to prevent,
restored, invisibly.

GATE 6: THE DIGEST COVERS THE WHOLE FILE

Two cases, both driven at the live file's size with generated padding (23 KB of
hand-authored prose would be 23 KB of noise, and none of it is what the mask
reads):

  * an edit in the LAST line of a 23,302-byte config, with three anti-vacuity
    assertions run before anything is measured - same length, the differing
    offset is within 40 bytes of the end, and the leading 4 KiB are
    byte-identical so the case cannot pass for a head-of-file reason;
  * the same claim at its limit: ONE byte, the last content byte. This is the
    off-by-one a chunked read most plausibly makes (body[:-1]) and it passes
    every other case in the file.

Kill proof, against the body[:64] sabotage above:

  FAILED test_an_edit_at_the_far_end_of_a_realistic_config_moves_the_key
  FAILED test_the_whole_file_gate_still_reds_when_only_the_last_byte_changes
  2 failed, 9 passed

  AssertionError: a 23302-byte config was edited at offset 23275 - near its
  END - and its fingerprint entry did not move. The key is being computed from
  a PREFIX of the file, not the whole file: every edit past that prefix will be
  served from a stale cache.

Restored: 11 passed.

GATE 7: THE CEILING IS A BOUNDARY AND BOTH SIDES ARE PINNED

The same blind spot applied one function down. Gate 5 proved "far over the
ceiling falls back to stat" with a file 22 bytes over it, and said nothing about
WHERE the ceiling is - so every off-by-one in the guard shipped green. Added the
pair: exactly _CONFIG_CONTENT_MAX_BYTES stays content-keyed (AT the limit is
under it), one byte more falls back to the stat triple. Both assert through the
observable consequence the way gate 5 does - content-keyed means a
content-identical rewrite does NOT move the entry, stat-keyed means it DOES - so
they survive a refactor of how the bound is enforced. Three mutants, each caught
by exactly the right gate and by none of the pre-existing seven:

  entry.size >  MAX  ->  >=      1 failed (exactly_the_ceiling), 10 passed
  len(body)  >  MAX  ->  >=      1 failed (exactly_the_ceiling), 10 passed
  both bounds MAX -> MAX + 1     1 failed (one_byte_over),       10 passed

THE CEILING IS NOT WEAKENED and neither bound moved. It exists so a huge file
cannot make every fingerprint pay an unbounded read, and it still does.

COST, RE-MEASURED independently of the number in the docstring. 22 paths (the
ten-profile home: 2 * profiles + 2) at the live 23,255 B, 20 warm passes, median
of each: 0.78 ms stat-only against 6.74 ms content-keyed, i.e. +5.96 ms per
fingerprint. Same class as the +8.6 ms recorded at 2f98eef3ee, slightly under
it, and 0.09% of the 6,467 ms rebuild it buys back on every boot that would
otherwise demote.

Tests only. No production file is touched by this commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
chore(agent_runtime): the registry's deliberate "a crash leaves the file behind" has no floor, because the launcher's hygiene sweep makes every orphan a crash

serve_instances/ accumulates tombstones. Two records stand on the operator's
runtime (13856, 35080) while a third (21440) exited cleanly and removed its own,
so clean exit IS the norm - 14 serve boots in ~19 h left 2 records. The reason
they survive is not a bug in the registry: the launcher's boot hygiene sweep
taskkill /F's orphan serves, which is a crash by construction, and a crashed
serve is never given the chance to unregister. The deliberate design ("a
registry that could only be correct if every process died politely would be
wrong exactly when it matters") therefore grows without a bound.

SCOPE, STATED PLAINLY: THIS IS NOT A CORRECTNESS FIX

The leftover records are harmless. resolve_socket_target returns only rows
classified `live`, the launcher never reads the directory at all, and it is
excluded from every freshness fingerprint. This is tidiness plus forensics and
it is scoped that way - after register_serve_instance at serve boot, call the
prune the module already exposes and put its report on the service log.

THE MODULE'S OWN ARGUMENT AGAINST PRUNING, AND WHY BOOT SURVIVES IT

serve_registry's docstring is the design authority here and it argues against
pruning on the READ path:

  "Listing never prunes: an operator debugging 'why do I have four serves' must
  see the wreckage, not a registry that tidied the evidence away before they
  looked."

That rule holds and is not relaxed. What it protects is a READ from destroying
the evidence it is reporting. A boot is a different moment on both counts. It is
a WRITE moment - registration has just created a file in this directory - and,
decisively, the evidence is not destroyed but relocated: the report names pid,
boot_id, path, classification and classification_reason for every record,
deleted and kept alike, onto the service log correlatable by boot_id against
that boot's ready frame. Records leave a directory nobody reads for a channel
the operator already reads. The ruling is that boot-pruning survives the
argument; a listing that pruned still would not, and there is a gate for that.

Two details are load-bearing rather than incidental:

  * the prune runs AFTER registration, so this serve's own entry exists and
    classifies `live` before the sweep looks - the sweep can never be the thing
    that removes it;
  * the boot caller passes NO widened classification set. stale_dead_pid only.
    stale_recycled_pid names a live process the registry no longer understands
    and an operator must see it; `unknown` means a probe could not answer, and
    "I could not read this process's start time" is not evidence that it is
    gone. Deleting on a failed probe is how a sweep removes a RUNNING service's
    record, and this repo has already been bitten once by a recycled pid.

It logs only when it acted (or tried and failed). A line on every boot saying it
deleted zero files is the noise that trains an operator to stop reading the
channel this report needs to be seen on.

KILL PROOF - five mutants, each watched red, then restored to 22 passed

  A  boot does not prune at all (the pre-change behaviour)
     FAILED ...::test_a_provably_dead_record_is_pruned_at_boot_and_the_report_names_it
     AssertionError: a record whose pid is provably gone survived a serve boot
     1 failed, 21 passed

  B  the prune is widened to delete `unknown` too   <- the dangerous direction
     FAILED ...::test_boot_never_prunes_a_recycled_or_unanswerable_record[990003-unknown]
     AssertionError: a 'unknown' record was deleted at serve boot. Only
     stale_dead_pid may ever be pruned: unknown is the FAIL-SAFE direction and
     collapsing it into 'dead' is how a sweep removes the record of a service
     that is still running
     2 failed, 20 passed

  C  prune anything that is not `live` (recycled AND unknown both go)
     3 failed, 19 passed - both parameterisations plus the pre-existing case

  D  the prune runs but nothing is logged
     AssertionError: expected exactly one serve_instances_pruned line, got 0
     1 failed, 21 passed

  E  the prune moves onto the READ path (listing tidies the evidence)
     FAILED ...::test_listing_the_registry_still_never_prunes
     2 failed, 20 passed

Mutants B and C also redden the PRE-EXISTING
test_the_instance_file_exists_while_serving_and_is_gone_after_a_clean_exit, and
that is not noise - it is the widening's damage caught in the act. Under the
real probe a pytest process's own record classifies `unknown` (its command line
is not a hermes serve), so a prune widened to `unknown` deletes the running
serve's OWN entry mid-request. The failure the sabotage was predicted to cause
is exactly the failure an existing gate reports.

The classification tests drive a synthetic ProcessProbe rather than this
machine's process list - the registry takes one precisely so classification is
testable against processes that do not exist - and the seeded record carries a
DIFFERENT baseline from the one the classifier later observes, which is what
makes the recycled case real rather than asserted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): the core's offset was stat'd when the build FINISHED and its content read when the build STARTED, so it counted events it did not carry

Operator-visible symptom, measured 2026-08-21: dragging a QA agent onto the
office canvas and messaging it made the agent DISAPPEAR from Mission Control,
while a QA agent that predated the drop was untouched. Every store was correct --
instance JSON, office actor row, chat session, and the whole event sequence
(`office.actor.upserted` -> `state.patched` -> `chat_opened` -> `persona_chat
.projected`). Only connected clients lost it.

`_parity_envelope` called `events_watermark()` at the END of the build, and that
function stats the log live. The CONTENT above it is read across the whole build
-- `CachedEventLog` is pinned at the first read by its own point-in-time
contract, and every store section is read at whatever moment its projection
runs. So a write landing mid-build was COUNTED by the offset and MISSING from
the content.

That is unrecoverable downstream, and specifically not symmetric with the other
direction. `stream.py` resumes its tail from exactly this offset
(`offset = _resume_offset(hydrate)`), so the events the core skipped are never
replayed as deltas: the client folds the core, advances its watermark past them,
and whatever they created is gone until an unrelated full core happens by. The
asymmetry in the report is the signature -- a core built before the drop carries
the old agent and not the new one.

THE INVARIANT WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, IN THIS FILE, AND THIS CODE BROKE IT.
`build_snapshot`'s `accept_inflight` contract says the stream hydrate is safe
because "its `watermark.event_offset` comes from the snapshot itself and the
stream loop tails events from exactly that offset, so a core built one
build-duration earlier loses no event, it only delays it to the first delta
frame". That is only true if the offset describes the content. It did not --
and `accept_inflight` WIDENS the window, since a shared in-flight build can be a
full build-duration older than the caller that rode it.

`build_snapshot`'s cache write-back states the same rule for its own stat set in
as many words -- "PRE-build, deliberately: a stat set taken after the build would
absorb any write that landed while the build ran, and the next process would
then serve a core missing that write as authoritative". Two stats over the same
log for the same build, taken at opposite ends. This makes them agree.

The offset is now captured by `events_position()` BEFORE the first section is
read, so it is a LOWER bound: content may be newer than the offset, and those
events replay as deltas the client has already folded. Idempotent, and the
direction `_full_core_batch_frames` already takes. `captured_at` travels with
the position rather than being re-dated at the far end. Every other
`events_watermark` caller is unchanged -- the parameter is optional and only
the snapshot builder passes it.

Not a widened contract: the typed-unknown path (`event_offset: None` +
`event_offset_error`, never 0) is preserved key-for-key on both branches.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(agent_runtime): the boot cache's armed window ended at a build a cache-hit boot never runs, so the serve stamped its 14:56 core with every offset it saw after

An operator drags a second QA agent into Mission Control and messages it. The
new agent disappears from the canvas; the pre-existing QA agent is untouched.
The store is healthy the whole time — instance row, actor row, chat root, turn.
Nothing on the write side is wrong. The PRODUCER served stale bytes under fresh
offsets.

THE CHAIN

`core_cache`'s boot consult memo is keyed on the stat triple of the persisted
PAIR (pointer/sidecar/core) and on nothing about the store, which is sound only
inside the window its own docstring claims for it: "the window is a BOOT — it
ends at the first completed full build of the process". That clause was
vacuously false on exactly the boots the memo optimizes. A cache-HIT boot
completes no build through `build_snapshot`, so `note_full_build_completed` was
never called; the only full build such a boot DOES run is the shadow validation,
and that closed the lane on a DIVERGENT verdict alone. On an agreeing verdict
the window never ended, and every `build_snapshot()` for the rest of that serve
process was answered with the boot-time core.

`stream.delta_batch_frame` then stamps the drained batch's last offset onto
whatever core the builder hands back. The demote lane is the designated carrier
of everything the patch lane cannot express (`patch_coverage`: "The demote to a
full core is what carries it"), a design that assumes that lane is fresh. The
launcher applies a `delta` core wholesale when its sequence is ahead, so an
older core's complete `persona_instances` section replaces away an instance that
existed only via folded patches — while every entity that predates the core
survives. That asymmetry is the whole report.

THE EVIDENCE, and a correction to the history first reported

`profiles/base/logs/agent.log`, 2026-08-21: a cache hit at 15:24:04 carrying
`offset=89843335`, `snapshot_core_shadow ok=true` at 15:24:11, then at
15:33:35-15:33:48 four `snapshot_build reason=demote role=cache` frames stamped
89,849,656 / 89,849,871 / 89,851,071 / 89,851,462 — each printing its own core's
`offset=89843335` on the `core_source=cache` receipt beside it. Nine minutes of
frames claiming to be authoritative for offsets their content predates. The only
`role=led` frames that hour are at 15:52, after a `build_stamp_mismatch`.

`2f98eef3ee` (today's config content-key fix) did NOT arm this. The same shape is
in the log on 2026-08-20 — cache hit at `offset=89567980` 18:30:05, then
`reason=demote role=cache offset=89568195` 18:30:11, and the pair again at 18:38
— a day earlier. What that commit changed is the VERDICT: those boots ended in
`snapshot_core_shadow_divergence section=parity.event_log_bytes` about ten
seconds in, and a divergence already closed the lane, so exposure was ~10 s per
boot instead of the life of the process. The log only reaches back to 2026-08-20
10:56, so the honest bound is "at least a day older than the report, and
structurally as old as the lane (EG-3.1, 2026-08-17)". The disappearance is
newly OBSERVABLE, not newly caused: until `63768819a3` the drag-drop create
minted a chat pointer whose transcript root was never written, so the first
message was refused and the flow failed before the agent could vanish.

WHAT LANDS, AND WHY BOTH HALVES

1. `core_cache.shadow_validate` closes the armed window on EVERY verdict —
   agreement, divergence, and a build that raised. That build IS the process's
   own full build; excluding it is what made the memo's bound vacuous. A
   validation that could not run is not a licence to keep serving the core it
   failed to validate.

2. `stream._full_core_batch_frames` refuses to stamp a batch's offset onto a core
   whose own `parity.watermark.event_offset` is behind it: it closes the cache
   lane with a typed receipt (`snapshot_core_cache_lane_closed
   reason=core_behind_frame core_offset= frame_offset=`) and rebuilds once. The
   2026-08-20 frames landed INSIDE a window that was going to close anyway, so
   the root fix alone would not have refused them. This is `7204896978`'s
   invariant one layer out: that one pinned a build's offset to its own content;
   this one refuses a frame's offset over a core it did not build.

Neither of the shipped fixes covers this path and neither is touched.
`7204896978` repins a build's own capture; the launcher's `05a122a9a` guards the
SAME-offset convergence window, and these frames came through the strict-`>`
front door.

THE PERFORMANCE THIS DOES NOT GIVE UP

The memo is not disabled and the ~2 s cache-hit boot is unchanged: the riders it
exists for (prewarm, hydrate, hub, cli) all arrive within about a second and are
answered from the shared consult long before the background validation finishes
(6.5-7.6 s). What ends is the part that was never a saving — answering builds
issued minutes later with the boot-time core.
`test_the_memo_still_answers_a_boot_where_nothing_moved` counts reads of the
persisted pair (1 for 4 riders) and reddens under a landing that disabled the
memo instead of narrowing it; that sabotage was run and does redden it while
leaving the four regression cases green.

Post-boot demote batches now pay a real build again, as they did before EG-3.1.
The follow-up that would make them cheap HONESTLY is widening patch coverage so
fewer batches demote, not serving a core that cannot answer for its offset.

TESTS

`tests/agent_runtime/test_stale_core_under_fresh_offset.py` — six cases, written
after the fix and watched failing against current code. Every case asserts on
entity CONTENT, and two entities in every direction: the pre-existing one
survives (a producer that ships nothing would pass a new-entity-only assertion)
and a DELETION still reaches the client (a fix that pinned rows in place would
pass the rest). The regression case drives the real `stream_frames` producer with
the shadow window recorded rather than run, which is the production window the
frame guard exists for.

Suite: 914 files, 10187 passed, 0 failed (tests/agent_runtime + tests/hermes_cli,
-j 8).

author: nekwo
message:
perf(agent_runtime): a snapshot build's span and a registry probe round were only ever log prose, so "did that steal the turn's time?" could be argued but never counted

Two remedy candidates for chat-turn latency rest on correlation today, and
neither has an instrument that could settle it:

* snapshot builds interleaved every sampled turn (2.2-7.9s each, waits to
  9.4s) -- but the warm turn stayed fast WITH one running, which argues they
  mostly do not steal turn time. The only evidence either way is the
  `snapshot_build` / `snapshot_build_core` log lines, and a log line is a
  point in time: nothing anywhere holds a build as a SPAN that another
  measurement can be intersected with.
* the cold profile bootstrap sweeps `tools.registry`'s `check_fn` probes, and
  whether it sweeps MORE THAN ONCE per turn has only ever been read off
  repetition patterns in a shared, pid-less agent.log. No line carries a pid,
  so the attribution is a pattern match, not an identity.

So each one gets the smallest instrument that can answer its own question.

`snapshot_build_ledger` is a bounded in-process ring of the spans this process
LED, on `time.monotonic` -- the same clock a chat turn anchors on, so overlap
is an interval intersection rather than a wall-stamp subtraction across two
clocks. Only the leader records: a caller that rode somebody else's build paid
a wait, not a build, and counting both would double every coalesced build. A
build that RAISED is still recorded, because it occupied the process for that
span either way. And a process that has never led a build answers `None`, not
`0` -- "no builds overlapped" and "I cannot see builds from here" are
different facts, and a chat turn running in a CLI child would report the first
while meaning the second.

The registry counter is THREAD-LOCAL for the same reason the pid mattered:
`harness serve` runs concurrent chat turns in one process, and a module-global
counter would attribute one turn's bootstrap to whichever turn sampled around
it. Agent construction runs on the turn's own thread, so a thread-local delta
across that window is exactly what this turn probed. A round is one
availability pass in which at least one `check_fn` genuinely EXECUTED; a pass
served entirely from the 30s TTL cache costs nothing and is not a round,
because counting it would inflate the exact number the remedy decision turns
on, and inflate it in the direction that argues for the remedy.

Cost: two monotonic reads and a deque append per BUILD (which costs seconds),
and one thread-local read per availability pass. Neither counter is read here
-- the consumer is the turn record, next commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): the turn record's only TTFT clock starts 1,100 lines into the handler, so the seconds of cold bootstrap the operator actually waits through are invisible to every consumer

The operator reported "my messaging feels slow". Answering that for ONE turn
took four unstructured sources across two clocks: agent.log prose, the turn
record's wall stamps, the emitter's `ttft_ms`, and the launcher's dateless
local-time diag lines. Three of the four are not joinable by anything but a
human, and the cross-clock hand-correlation misread has now happened twice in
one day.

`ttft_ms` is the closest thing to an answer and it cannot see the problem. The
emitter that owns its clock is constructed AFTER the replay checks, the native
history load, `build_mission_chat_turn_context` and the prompt-observability
row build -- so on a cold turn, the profile bootstrap (tool-registry probe
rounds, plugin discovery, auxiliary-client probes) runs entirely before the
record's `started_at` exists. The warm turn skips that work; the cold/warm
difference was inferable only from log-line archaeology.

So the turn record gains one key, `phases`, and the schema goes to 3. Every
value is elapsed MILLISECONDS from a monotonic anchor taken at command-handler
entry -- the first statement of the handler, ahead of the capability bind and
the config load, because everything after it is admission cost the operator is
waiting through. `ttft_ms` is untouched and still means what it always meant;
these phases are a superset of it, not a replacement.

The rule that makes it worth having, and the reason it is enforced in the
writer rather than trusted at eleven call sites: A PHASE THE TURN DID NOT
REACH HAS NO KEY. Not `0`, not `null`, not present-and-empty. A zero is a
measurement, and a turn whose provider transport died did not measure an
instantaneous first token -- which is exactly what a defaulted
`provider_first_byte: 0` would report, the single most misleading value the
field could hold. Same rule one level up: a v2 record on disk is not migrated
and not rewritten, because "this turn predates phase spans" is a fact about
it, and same rule for the Stage 4 counters, where `0` is a real verdict
(`builds_overlapped: 0` acquits build contention for that turn) and therefore
must never be what "unobservable" looks like.

Marks ride the persists that already happen -- write-ahead, the failure
settles, native-commit, terminal. No new write, no I/O in this module. Each
mark that names a PERSIST is taken as that persist is ISSUED, so the block a
record carries is complete as of that record: a turn that dies before the
provider still leaves a write-ahead row that describes its own admission.

Two marks are placed exactly where they can be honest and no further:

* `provider_first_byte` in the emitter's `delta()`, the first site in this
  process to have seen a provider byte -- no provider-client surgery -- and
  guarded by a boolean so the cost stays per TURN, never per token. First mark
  wins is enforced in `TurnPhaseMarks` too, because the callback rides a
  worker thread and "the call site remembered to guard" is not a property
  anything can assert.
* `agent_ready` / `provider_request_started` bracket the ready-callback, which
  the runner invokes the instant the agent object exists and returns from
  straight into the conversation. Stated rather than glossed: prompt assembly
  inside `run_conversation` falls AFTER the second mark, so it sits inside the
  provider span. Closing that needs a hook in the provider client, which this
  stage deliberately does not take.

Stage 4 rides the same marks: `agent_init_cold` from the runner's own
`resident_actor_reused` receipt (ABSENT when the runner reported none, never
guessed), `registry_probe_rounds` as a thread-local delta across agent init,
and `builds_overlapped` as the count of LED snapshot builds whose span
intersects anchor -> `stream_done`. It measures whether cold init and build
contention are guilty. It does not fix either, and stages no remedy.

Cost: one small dict and ~11 monotonic reads per turn.

author: nekwo
message:
test(hermes_cli): the probe-round row cleared the process-wide check_fn cache to make its point, handing every later test in the run a cold re-probe of docker, playwright and sockets

`invalidate_check_fn_cache()` is a real API with a real caller (`hermes tools
enable`), and it is exactly the wrong instrument for a unit row: it drops the
TTL cache the WHOLE process shares, so every test that ran after this one in
the same session paid a fresh subprocess probe per toolset. Under the repo's
30s per-test cap that is not a slow test, it is a failing one, several files
later, for a reason nothing in the failing test could point at.

The row never needed it. The check_fn is a closure this test alone holds, so
its cache entry starts absent by construction, and the one place the row
genuinely needs an expiry it evicts that single entry by key. The round
counter is read as a DELTA around the passes under test rather than zeroed,
which is the same discipline the turn record itself uses and for the same
reason: a shared cumulative counter has no owner allowed to reset it.

`reset_probe_rounds_for_tests` goes with it — it existed only for the zeroing
this row no longer does, and a test helper with no caller is a reader kept
alive by nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(agent_runtime): the first drop of a persona type pays 1.9-3.2s of cold memo misses inside the create RPC, where the operator is already waiting and nothing can absorb it

Stage 3a of the mission-control agent-drop-latency plan, whose Stage 0 convicted
this cost with numbers off the operator's drop log rather than by argument:
`instance_ms` 1,906 / 3,203 / 2,858 ms for the first drop of a type, against
141 / 125 ms for a second drop of the same type seconds later -- and it COMES
BACK once the 15/30/60s TTLs lapse, which is what makes it memo-shaped rather
than a one-time boot tax.

Where it sits is why it hurts. `perform_agent_create` -> `add_instance` ->
`emit_persona_instance_create` -> `project_persona_instance_full_wire_row` ->
`persona_instance_summary` -> `resolve_tool_visibility`, all INLINE: the RPC
does not return until the wire row is projected, so every memo miss behind that
resolution -- the toolset lru, the 15s readiness memo, the 60s provider memo,
and a registry probe round per toolset past the 30s `check_fn` TTL -- is spent
inside the span the launcher is awaiting.

`runtime.persona.prewarm {persona_id}` runs that same resolution ahead of time
on a worker thread and throws the answer away. Every memo it fills is
process-wide, so the create that follows finds them warm. Additive in the
strongest sense: a new method rather than a changed one, no call site in the
create path touched, and a runtime nobody calls it on behaves exactly as it does
today.

It fills memos and NOTHING else -- no store write, no event, no minted id, no
lock -- and that is a property of the path rather than an intention. With
`session_id=None` the permission read returns before touching the store; the
chat-lane scoping is all pure reads; and the provider check already routes
through `probe_runtime_provider`, the named non-persisting resolver that exists
so a readiness read cannot move `auth.json`. Which is what lets the ack be
fire-and-forget: there is no half-written state a killed worker could leave, so
the verb needs no completion channel and no compensation path. A failure inside
the warm is swallowed and logged -- it warms caches or it does nothing.

ONE daemon worker, not a thread per call. The trigger is "call it for every chip
on every palette open", and N threads would each find the `check_fn` cache cold
and each run the full toolset sweep -- N concurrent docker/playwright probes,
the exact herd the memo exists to prevent, paid all at once. Serialising means
the first warm fills the shared cache and the rest are cheap. The in-flight set
makes a repeat call for a persona already warming ack `already_running` and
queue nothing, so the idempotence is visible to the client rather than merely
claimed.

Refusals are the CREATE's refusals -- code, reason and message borrowed from
`agent_create` rather than re-spelled, because one id must not get two verdicts
from the pair. The one reason this verb owns alone is
`profile_persona_not_prewarmable`: `runtime.agent.create` deliberately accepts
`profile:` ids (D-U1) and then resolves the wire row's visibility persona from
the freshly minted INSTANCE, so the memo keys are unknowable before that create
runs. Refused with its own reason because "send a different id" and "this id is
fine, there is nothing to warm" need opposite responses.

The gate is the mechanism, counted, not a millisecond budget: `tools.registry`'s
thread-local probe-round delta across the create is 0 after a prewarm. Its
negative arm is what makes that zero mean anything -- the same create with the
prewarm omitted, against a `check_fn` cache holed by SINGLE-KEY eviction, pays a
nonzero delta. Never `invalidate_check_fn_cache()`: that drops the TTL cache the
whole process shares and cost a lane two downstream failures yesterday
(c7dad2f3cd). The per-persona half is pinned separately on the readiness memo,
because the toolset lru key turns out to be persona-INDEPENDENT under the
unbounded default and an assertion on it only looks specific.
