author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): A2 — the handler learns who is asking, from the transport and never from the request

`RpcContext` gains a `caller`: what the transport PROVED, built in exactly one
place (`call_authorization.caller_for_connection`, called from serve.py's
dispatcher) out of the connection object the transport handed us. `params` never
reaches it, and there is no argument by which a request can name its own
identity — a request that could would be a request that authorizes itself.

It does NOT ride `connection_key`. That field's own docstring commits it to
being the SUBSCRIPTION identity, the name a teardown sweep and the office
subscription registry both index on; an authorization fact borrowing it would
quietly redefine a key two systems already key on, and the next rename would
break a system that never mentioned it. The caller REPEATS the key instead, so a
refusal can still name the connection it refused and Stage 1's device-record
lookup still has its join.

`authenticated` is READ rather than assumed. `ServeSocketServer` only enters a
connection into `_connections` after `verify_hello_proof`, so the pre-handshake
arm is unreachable from today's dispatcher — which is why it is asserted. A
future transport that hands the dispatcher a half-open connection gets `unknown`
instead of silently inheriting a guarantee it never made.

The default is `stdio_owner`, and that is the honest value rather than a
convenient one: an `RpcCaller` can only be constructed by code already inside
this process, so a context built with no arguments describes an in-process
caller — which is exactly what the `transport = "stdio"` default beside it has
always said.

No handler reads it yet. Proven end to end over the lane suite's real loopback
socket and real HMAC handshake with a probe method registered and removed in a
finally, because nothing on the shipped surface echoes its caller — correctly,
since a caller identity is the server's business and not a payload.

Chokepoint plan Stage A2.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): A3 — the front door starts asking, and the answer is yes to everyone who exists

Every frame on both transports now passes an authorization decision before a
handler runs. The policy is empty by design: the stdio owner and an
authenticated socket peer are both allowed every tier, so nothing observable
moves for the local launcher, the CLI, or the suites. What moved is that there
is now a PLACE where the question is asked — which is the thing gateway Stage 1
was blocked on, and which turns R11's per-device scopes into an edit to one
predicate rather than an architecture change.

The gate lives in `handle_request`, not in a wrapper `method()` composes. That
is the single point every frame passes through, so a method cannot be registered
around it and there is no per-method opt-out to forget; it also leaves the
handlers callable directly, which is what every unit test in this repo does, so
landing the gate rewrote no suite.

Ordering is deliberate. An unknown METHOD answers -32601 before the gate runs: a
scope refusal that varied by whether the name exists would let a refused caller
map the surface by watching the error code change. A malformed frame is still
the normalizer's refusal, so a caller who cannot spell a request is told that
rather than told it lacks a tier it never asked for.

Reads stay open to a caller that has proved nothing, and that is a line rather
than an oversight: a read tier is what an unplaced caller may still do, and
nothing on the read side mutates a level. Stage A5 gates reads — if it gates
them at all — on a device record, not on the absence of one.

The A3 promise is asserted directly rather than inferred from a green suite:
every context shape that exists in this tree, including the two that carry no
caller at all (the argv lane's probes, every unit test), is driven over every
registered method and asserted never to meet the gate's refusal. Beside it, a
caller kind nothing yet mints IS refused with the typed `scope_denied` the
launcher's decoders branch on — without that half, "allow everything" and "no
gate at all" are the same tree.

Chokepoint plan Stage A3.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): A4 — the coordinator gate is renamed to the advice it always was, and both retire doors carry one console identity

Three sub-decisions, landed together because separating them leaves the tree in
a state nobody can describe.

(i) `authorize_coordinator_action` becomes `review_coordinator_budget`, and
`CoordinatorAuthorization` becomes `CoordinatorBudgetReview`. The old name
claimed a job the code cannot do: the request carries BOTH the identity being
checked (`--requested-by`, argv) and the grant it is checked against (four
argv flags overriding the persona's autonomy), and `OPERATOR_ACTORS`
short-circuits on a NAME. Every input a caller could lie about is one the caller
supplies. What it actually is — a coordinator declaring its own restructure
budget so the runtime can ask a HUMAN to confirm — is now the module's own
first sentence, and is asserted structurally: there is no branch here that
answers `ok=False` without also answering `needs_operator_confirm=True`. It only
escalates; it never denies. No alias is left behind, so a grep for "who
authorizes an agent retire" no longer lands here. The MODEL is unchanged
(plan §4): whether a persona should spawn or kill at all is a different
question from where the check runs.

(ii)/(iii) The CLI's authorization identity is `CLI_CONSOLE`, a CONSTANT that
reads nothing off the invocation — deriving it from argv would rebuild the
self-declaration hole at the one door the machine owner types into. It is minted
in `_agent_retire_outcome`, which is documented as "the ONE retire the CLI
performs, whichever verb the operator typed" — so `harness agent retire` and
`harness persona instance retire` cannot drift apart a second time. The
asymmetry canon 06 recorded therefore disappears without giving `agent retire`
the coordinator review, which answers a different question. The create door gets
the same mirror, asked BEFORE the roster read so a caller who may not place an
agent is not handed a probe of which persona ids exist.

It allows unconditionally today, and that is honest rather than vestigial: the
operator at their own shell IS the console. The value is that the grandfather
clause is greppable instead of implicit in an absent check, that both retire
doors provably share one predicate with the RPC front door, and that the day a
non-console CLI identity exists the refusal is a predicate edit, not a new
concept.

The three call sites the plan flagged as located-but-not-read (`re_route`,
`update_profile`, `set_model`) were read: all three follow the identical
coordinator pattern and none reaches authorization by a different path, so A4
did not grow.

Verified, not assumed: the refusal path is exercised by patching the mirror on
`hermes_cli.harness` — NOT on `persona_commands`, which is exec'd into harness's
globals, so a patch on the source module would go green while the shipped path
ran unpatched.

Chokepoint plan Stage A4.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office): D10(iii) — the unaimed lattice starts at the world origin and climbs, and D10(ii) is reopened because it is a real gap

Operator ruling 2026-08-27: "it should do 0,0 xy — if something is there it
should move it up a bit higher so you can still see it", and a full grid step.

ORIGIN. `ORIGIN_X`/`ORIGIN_Y` were `-5.0` / `6.4`, chosen to match the office
canvas's own unaimed-drop band. That is a canvas convention; the ruling is that
the world origin is the more predictable answer for a placement nobody aimed.

DIRECTION. The scan was row-major and filled left to right, so a run of unaimed
placements marched off the side of the floor. It is now column-major, and
`slot_at` ADDS the row offset instead of subtracting it, so the second placement
stands one full `ROW_SPACING` above the first. It wraps sideways only after
`ROWS_PER_COLUMN` are stacked; the pigeonhole bound is transposed with it, so the
termination argument is unchanged. `COLUMNS_PER_ROW` is renamed `ROWS_PER_COLUMN`
because the wrap bound is now per column, and a constant whose name says the
opposite is how two repos begin disagreeing quietly.

THE CROSS-REPO FIXTURE was re-authored, not translated: the scan ORDER changed,
so shifting coordinates would have preserved geometry while silently changing
what each case tested. Every case was re-expressed against the new lattice and
re-verified against the live policy before writing, and a new case
(`occupied_origin_steps_up_one_full_row`) pins the ruling itself — a policy that
stepped sideways there would satisfy every other case in the file. The launcher's
copy and both MANIFESTs moved in the same landing (launcher `cf9443f9b`).

TWO THINGS I GOT WRONG, both caught by tests and both recorded rather than
quietly fixed, because the next person will reach for them too:

  * At the world origin the boundary case LOOKS spellable the obvious way
    (`slot + occupancy_radius`). It is not. Only the launcher's `Vector2` STORAGE
    is 32-bit — `occupancyRadius` is a plain `double` — so it stores `0.7` as
    `0.69999998807907104`, compares against a float64 `0.7`, and blocks where
    hermes stays free. Same cross-repo disagreement as at the old origin, new
    mechanism. The case keeps the float32-exact point, and `<` → `<=` was
    RE-MEASURED as still an equivalent mutant here rather than assumed.
  * The float64 off-axis witness had to be searched for again: at the old origin
    the subtraction itself rounded, at the origin it is exact. The witness moved,
    the squared value did not — it is a property of the radius, not of where the
    lattice sits.

D10(ii) IS REOPENED, and it is a gap rather than a scope call. The operator's
expectation is that skills set on the context panel apply to the next agent
placed from that persona. They do not: the panel writes `--skill` to the INSTANCE
(`persona.instance.update_profile` -> `skill_overrides`) while a new placement
inherits `persona.skills`, the TEMPLATE, read live. Nothing writes
`persona.skills` — it comes from config only, with no operator verb and no
launcher capability. Recorded in 06's Open rows; the verb is not built here.

Gates: `tests/agent_runtime/` 903 passed (the one failure is
`test_duplicate_helper_bodies` on another session's `gateway_identity.py`, not
this change); office layout policy 42; agent-create service 43.

author: nekwo
message:
docs(charsheet): W3 — the skill stops teaching a launcher field that no longer means what it said, and the seed line becomes a pinned contract

Three sections of `harness-charsheet-authoring/SKILL.md` described
`CharaDraftBinding.home` as the AUTHORING home. Launcher `9e17d05ad` (§13.24)
redefined that field to **a home the launcher OBSERVED the draft readable in**,
renamed the sealed family `CharaAuthoringHome` -> `CharaDraftHome`, and gave it
its one production writer — Studio's adopt door, stamping only from a
`HermesLaneHomeResolved`. `9b44617c5` (§13.25) then flipped
`mergeCharaDraftBinding`'s home arm to freshest-sighting-wins with an unknown
never clobbering an observed one. A skill still teaching the old meaning tells
an authoring agent the launcher stores the very fact the launcher's own doc
comment says nothing there can produce — and an agent that believes it will
trust a seeded home instead of echoing the one it resolved, which is the single
failure this skill's whole preflight exists to prevent.

What the skill now says, all of it re-taken at launcher `origin/main` rather
than from the plan's pre-W1 quotations:

- The preflight echo keeps its instruction and loses its false reason. Your
  transcript is still the only carrier of the home your turn resolved; the home
  the launcher may hold is a SIGHTING written by an operator's click, never
  something you emit.
- §13.22 is untouched and still taught: the `CHARSHEET-QA:` line carries no home
  and is not to grow one. §13.24 left that ruling standing on purpose, so the
  sentence says so instead of implying the two moved together.
- The Studio-project bullet names the one writer, the freshest-wins fold, and
  W1's new affordance — an already-adopted draft is offered the door again
  whenever the fold would learn something, which is how a moved draft is
  corrected.
- A new bullet on what a resume actually hands you: `last observed home: <path>`,
  or `last observed home: never observed by the launcher`, quoted verbatim
  because `MissionCharacterResumeSeed.message`'s own doc comment calls the
  spelling "a contract across two repos rather than launcher copy". A sighting
  goes stale; the seed's closing sentence already says not to trust it.

**The red-first is a test in this repo, because the gate §W3 names cannot be
one.** `verify_harness_skill_install.py --check` hashes the package DIRECTORY,
and `FIELD-NOTES.md` sits in it, so an append to the field notes alone reports
`DIVERGED` with the two `SKILL.md` copies byte-identical. Proved in isolation
before touching `SKILL.md`: `diff -q` said identical and the gate said DIVERGED,
printing `repo 44478 B | installed 44478 B` with two different hashes — the size
column is `source.stat().st_size` (SKILL.md alone) while the hash spans the
directory. Equal sizes beside unequal hashes is the signature of a sibling file,
not of the skill. So the owned observable is
`test_charsheet_skill_states_the_launcher_bindings_home_in_its_landed_meaning`:
it bans the phrase "authoring home" outright, pins the replacement positively so
deletion cannot pass it, and pins the seed spelling as the hermes end of the
cross-repo contract. Red observed first, naming the phrase and the line it stood
on (1 failed, 25 passed); a second, honest red followed when the quoted string
`never observed by the launcher` was markdown-wrapped across a line — a quoted
contract is a contiguous string or it is not the contract.

Gate (canonical runner, per AGENTS.md, not the plan's bare `pytest`):
`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent_runtime/test_persona_skill_policy.py` 26/26;
widened over the five agent_runtime skill files 117/117; the plan's
`python -m pytest` form 26/26 for parity. Install gate: DIVERGED before the
install, `refreshed from the repo: harness-charsheet-authoring`, `--check`
exit 0 after. The two live serve children were not signalled or restarted.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S0b — the install identity gets a door an operator can type, and the rename stops claiming it only loaded

Stage 0a shipped the service half and the wire half; this is the CLI half it
split off for scope. `harness gateway id` shows this runtime root's install
identity and `harness gateway rename <name>` sets the operator-facing name
without ever moving the id.

Two subverbs, where the plan wrote `gateway id --set-name`. Not taste:
`_add_stage42_global_args` gives a writer `--dry-run` and a reader the full
output set, and one parser cannot carry both truthfully — that helper's whole
docstring is built on "an advertised flag that does nothing is a WRONG ANSWER
believed, not an error seen". `rename` and not `set-name` because `workspace
rename` is the house word for this operation and `set_display_name`'s own first
line is "Rename this install".

The read never mints. `gateway id` routes at `read_install_identity`, and the
test probes the FILESYSTEM rather than the ack — the kill-mutation is routing it
at `ensure_install_identity`, which returns a perfectly plausible exit-0 ack and
has silently created an identity on a root the operator only asked about. Stage
4's install picker runs this against roots it does not own.

No authorization gate, and that is written into the handler block rather than
left as an absent check. The A4 mirror exists so two doors onto ONE service
function cannot answer differently; Stage 0b adds no RPC method, so there is one
door, and `CLI_CONSOLE` here would gate against a predicate that allows every
caller that exists with no wire twin to keep it honest. The record is not a level
and not a secret. When a paired device may rename an install, the door is a
`gateway.*` method with a tier declaration (Stage 1 / A5) and the gate goes
there, where the caller is something the transport proved.

Shipping the verb found one Stage 0a wart. `set_display_name` returned a constant
`loaded`, so a rename against a fresh root — which MINTS by its own documented
contract — reported the opposite of what it did, on the one module whose whole
contract is "state it, never infer it from absence". It now propagates the
load-or-mint outcome it already held. Nothing pinned the old constant; a new test
pins both directions.

`clean_display_name` becomes public because `--dry-run` has to print the string
that WOULD land, and the only way to get that without a second copy of the rule
is to ask the rule: a preview that echoes the raw argument shows a 500-character
paste at 500 and lands it at 64.

Typed states become exit families rather than tracebacks — `absent` 3,
`malformed_record` 1 and deliberately never a re-mint (those bytes may hold the
id a paired device names), `empty_display_name` 2, every other I/O reason 7 — and
the typed reason travels verbatim in the message so a greeting frame's `install`
block and the verb read as one spelling. Both handlers stamp the resolution
block: the identity is per store root, so a `gateway id` against the wrong root
returns a well-formed identity for a runtime the operator did not mean.

Remote-gateway plan Stage 0b.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S1a — the install grows a credential per DEVICE, and says out loud what hashing it does not buy

`serve_auth.py` mints one secret per runtime root and its whole meaning is
"whoever holds this is the machine owner". That was the right shape for a
loopback lane and it is the wrong shape for a listener another machine can
reach: it has no name to revoke, no tier to refuse, and no way to tell two
phones apart. `serve_gateway_auth.py` is the same discipline one field over —
root is an input, never raises on a read, the value never leaves the module —
minting one 256-bit token per PAIRED device, with a tier and a revocation.

Two files under `<store_root>/gateway/` beside Stage 0's `install.json`:
`devices.json` (the durable rows) and `pairing.json` (pending codes and the
failed-redeem counter, both disposable).

The pairing lifecycle is `gateway/pairing.py`'s, imitated rather than imported,
and the reason is scope rather than laziness: that store resolves through
`get_hermes_home()` and is keyed by (platform, user_id), and this lane's own
Stage 0 finding is that a home and a store root are provably different scopes
on this machine. What is worth reusing is its RULES, so they are restated with
the same numbers and — more usefully — with the same two CORRECTIONS it had to
make. The lockout is checked before the pending lookup, so it gates guessing
and not merely minting (#10195: checked after, a code already issued still
redeems while the lockout is armed, which is a lockout that protects nothing).
A successful redeem clears the failure streak, so isolated typos cannot
accumulate for the life of the store and trip a spurious lockout on one fresh
mistype. Both are pinned as tests rather than inherited as comments.

Two numbers deviate downward, both because the channel differs: the TTL is ten
minutes rather than an hour (the code is on the operator's own terminal, not
DM'd to a stranger who may read it in an hour), and there is no per-requester
mint rate limit, because the requester is the operator at the install's own
console -- which under Ruling A is the account-auth trace the tier descends
from. The cap on outstanding codes stays.

The honest part, written into the docstring rather than a commit message: the
stored verifier is `sha256(token)` and it is HMAC-key-equivalent. A scheme
where the server holds nothing usable is an ASYMMETRIC one; this is symmetric
because the plan of record specifies the same HMAC challenge-response the
loopback lane already speaks. So digesting the token buys exactly one thing and
not two -- the bytes a phone holds are not the bytes on this disk, so a store
read cannot recover an ISSUED credential -- and `devices.json` is exactly as
sensitive as `serve_auth_token`. Which makes the Windows ACL gap `serve_auth`
recorded and declined to fix finally this slice's to answer: it declined on the
grounds that the real control belongs with the transport that introduces the
exposure, and this is that transport. `icacls` narrowing is attempted and its
outcome is returned, never assumed.

The proof binds three things and each closes a different hole: the nonce (a
transcript is unreplayable), the port taken from each end's OWN socket (a live
relay's answer does not verify at the real service -- `serve_socket.hello_proof`'s
argument, copied deliberately), and the device id (a proof cannot be presented
under another device's name). Revocation is checked AFTER the proof so an
unauthenticated peer cannot probe which ids exist by watching the reason
change; the wire collapses every outcome into one rejection anyway.

29 tests. The two that would survive the obvious first cut and nothing else:
the plaintext code appears nowhere in `pairing.json`, and a device row whose
tier this build does not recognise reads as the LEAST privileged tier rather
than as the default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S1b — R1's encrypt ruling gets its hermes half, and TLS is confidentiality rather than a second identity

Ruling B rejected plaintext-plus-HMAC: the challenge-response already prevents
impersonation, so the whole question was ever confidentiality, and chat bodies
and media in the clear on shared WiFi is not defensible. `gateway_tls.py` mints
the option (a) mechanism — a self-signed per-install certificate whose sha-256
fingerprint is what the pairing payload carries and what the launcher will pin
through `badCertificateCallback` at Stage 2.

The R1 survey's findings are about the CLIENT half (the launcher owns a real
ES256 custody stack and zero X.509 machinery; `asn1lib`/`x509` are transitive
and imported by nothing; there is no pinning precedent to extend). This file
does not solve that and does not hide behind it — it produces the one value
that half needs. Two of the survey's conclusions are honoured directly. Its
bullet 3, that R1(a) bundles two lifts which are not the same lift: TLS here is
confidentiality and never authentication, a device is authenticated by the HMAC
proof one layer up, and a peer that completes a TLS handshake has proven only
that it can speak TLS. Its bullet 4, that two keypairs mean two revocation
stories and a pairing that can be half-valid: this certificate is the install's
ONE link identity, minted once and never rotated silently.

EC P-256, for one cryptographic reason and one that is not. Keygen is
instantaneous where RSA-2048 costs a visible fraction of a second on every cold
boot that mints, and this runs inside serve's boot path, which the latency
baselines already watch. And P-256 is the curve the launcher's
`SoftwareDeviceKeyStore` already speaks, so the day bullet 4 is actually taken
— derive the cert FROM the device key instead of minting a second identity —
the curve is not also a migration.

Ten-year validity, argued rather than defaulted: a certificate validated by
FINGERPRINT is not made safer by expiring, because the pin IS the trust
decision and an expiry is a second one that can only fire as a lockout on an
operator nobody warned. Rotation is an explicit verb when it is wanted, and it
re-pairs every device — `serve_auth`'s own sentence, that rotating a credential
under the clients holding it is a lockout and not a hardening.

Two orderings that are load-bearing and would otherwise look arbitrary. The key
is written before the certificate, so a process killed between them leaves "a
key with no certificate" — which reads absent and which nothing has ever pinned
— rather than "a certificate with no key", which would read absent too and then
mint a SECOND identity under a device that pinned the first. And a certificate
that exists but will not parse is a typed `error:malformed_certificate` that is
never overwritten, on the same asymmetry `gateway_identity._decode` documents:
those bytes may be the ones a device pinned.

`cryptography` needed no dependency work — pyproject already pins 48.0.1
explicitly (CVE-2026-39892 et al, capped below 49 by msal), and 48.0.1 is what
is installed. The ImportError arm is kept anyway and degrades to "the gateway
lane does not come up", never to "the gateway lane comes up in the clear".

10 passed, 1 skipped (the 0600 assertion, correctly, on Windows). The one that
proves the ruling rather than the code: a client trusting NOTHING — no CA, no
hostname check, exactly the launcher's coming posture — completes a real
handshake, and the digest of the DER it was handed equals the fingerprint this
module published.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): A5 — the tier stops being a declaration and starts being a refusal, and the grandfather is not widened to reach it

A3 landed the enforcement point with an empty policy and promised that turning a
device's scope into a refusal would be an edit to `authorize_call` rather than
an architecture change. This is that edit, and the promise held: `handle_request`
is untouched, `method()` is untouched, no suite was rewritten.

`RpcCaller` grows a `device` kind carrying `device_id` and `device_tier`, and
`caller_for_connection` mints one from the stamp a gateway handshake leaves on
its connection after the device's proof verifies. `authorize_call` compares that
STORED word against the verb's declared tier — which is Ruling A's "the tier is
client security auth" made mechanical: fixed at a pairing ceremony only an
operator at this install's own machine can run, read off the authenticated
connection, and unreachable from anything the request carries.

The device arm was added BESIDE `_CONSOLE_KINDS` rather than folded into it, and
that is the design rather than a diff-minimising accident. A local console's
authority is its KIND — there is one machine owner and holding the root token is
being it. A device's authority is a stored tier, because there are N devices and
they differ. Two callers whose authority comes from different kinds of fact
should not share a membership test; folding them together is how a set someone
widens for one reason silently widens for the other.

The structural guard is the half worth reviewing. A gateway connection with no
usable device stamp is `unknown`, never `local_console`. Today that arm is
unreachable — the handshake refuses a hello it cannot place — but the
fall-through it replaces would hand a REMOTE peer the machine owner's authority
the moment any future change let a gateway connection through with an empty
stamp, and the grandfather clause is about the machine owner rather than about
whoever reached a listener. The condition is `transport != "gateway"`, i.e. a
property of the LISTENER the peer arrived on rather than of anything the peer
said. Same reason `authenticated` is read before the stamp is: a stamp on a
connection that never passed its proof is a claim.

Read verbs stay open to `unknown`, and that line was KEPT rather than inherited
by omission — the temptation once real devices exist is to gate reads on the
device record too, and the reason not to is that nothing on the read side
mutates a level. An `admin` tier for the skills install sub-phase is still R11's
question and is still not answered by adding a constant here on the way past.

Receipts, run not inferred (`C:\Python312\python.exe -m pytest` — the venv has no
pytest): the new `test_serve_rpc_device_scopes.py` plus A3's
`test_serve_rpc_authorization.py`, `test_serve_rpc_caller_identity.py` and
`test_serve_rpc_method_tiers.py`, 43 passed; the agent create/retire/notification/
office RPC suites 100 passed. A3's own no-behaviour-change assertions are
re-asserted in the new file rather than assumed from their staying green: "we did
not break the grandfather" is a claim about THIS commit, not about the one that
made the promise.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S1c — the second door opens, the first one does not move, and Stage 0a's config keys turn out never to have existed

`serve_socket.py` grows three constructor arguments, all defaulted to what the
loopback lane has always done, and `serve_loop` binds a second
`ServeSocketServer` with them filled in. Same class, same accept loop, same
dispatcher, same stream hub, same drain. It is one implementation and not two
because the hardened parts here are precisely the parts a second copy would get
wrong: the accept loop that announces its own death, the pre-auth bound that
counts peers who have proven nothing, the two limiters and the rule that
server-state refusals never charge the auth one, the lingering close that keeps
a rejection frame alive.

The three seams: `port` (0 stays ephemeral; the gateway lane is usually pinned,
because an operator writes a firewall rule for it and a phone has to find it
again after a restart), `ssl_context` (None on loopback — local trust model
unchanged, a local process that could read the token file gains nothing from a
TLS layer), and `authenticator` (None means the per-root token, the code that
was inline here, moved and not rewritten). The gateway lane's authenticator
checks a per-device credential and is the only thing that ever stamps a
connection with `device_id`/`device_tier`, which is in turn the only way
`call_authorization` mints a `device` caller. Its `token_provider` is wired to
return None rather than left absent: a provider that handed back the root token
while an authenticator happened to be set would be a live fallback waiting for a
refactor to find it.

TLS is negotiated BEFORE the admission checks, and the cost is deliberate: every
capacity, throttle and drain refusal answers with a typed frame, and a frame
written to a socket the peer never negotiated is bytes it cannot read — refusing
first would turn every one of them into an unexplained disconnect. A TLS failure
charges the SILENCE throttle, not the auth limiter: it says nothing about
credentials, and charging it there is the mistake that once made a blocked
window extend itself forever.

TWO REFUSALS ARE WHAT MAKE THE TIER GATE REAL, and the second is the one worth
reviewing. `drain` is refused to a device even at `console` tier, because it is
not a level mutation the tier speaks about — it ends this process and
disconnects every other attached client, and a phone deciding that for the
desktop it is a guest on is the wrong default. And **the argv lane is
unreachable from a device at any tier**: `authorize_call` gates the METHOD lane,
while `{"argv": ["harness", ...]}` runs the CLI dispatcher where no tier
declaration exists. Without that refusal, a `read` device turned away from
`runtime.agent.retire` sends the same verb as argv and is obeyed — the gate
would be real and bypassable in one frame. It is a refusal rather than a second
gate because gating argv means deciding a tier for every CLI verb in this repo
and keeping that map correct forever, which is the duplicated-authority shape
this stack keeps retiring.

`ops_manifest` answers per transport for the third time and earns it again: the
gateway set is the socket set minus `drain`, so a device learns what it may ask
by MEMBERSHIP rather than by trying and reading an error, and the manifest
cannot disagree with the dispatcher because both read one tuple. `hello_ok` and
`version` stopped hard-coding `"socket"` and read the connection's own transport
— a device told it was on the local lane would then be advertised a verb this
connection refuses.

A `gateway` block rides `ready`/`hello_ok`/`version` on `socket.outcome`'s
standing rule that a block states its own outcome. The failure it guards is
specific and quiet: an operator sets the key, restarts, and the phone cannot
connect — and every way that happens (port taken, certificate unmintable, config
never read) looks identical without a stated reason. It carries the
`cert_fingerprint` a client pins, for the reason the build stamp beside it
exists: a client that must ask a second question to learn what it should have
pinned has a window in which it is trusting nothing.

**Stage 0a's config keys never existed, and that is a finding rather than a
rename.** Its receipts say `gateway.listen`/`gateway.port` were "declared, read
by nothing". The second half is what hid the first: `"gateway"` is ALREADY a
top-level key in `config_defaults.py`'s single dict literal (the messaging
gateway's), and a duplicate key there does not merge or warn — the later entry
wins and the earlier is discarded at parse time. A key nobody reads and a key
that is not there are indistinguishable from every angle except a reader's, and
becoming the first reader is the only thing that could have found it. They are
`remote_gateway.*` now, which is also the honest spelling: Stage 0a's own
comment said the two lanes must not be conflated, and two lanes cannot share one
key and stay unconflated. `test_config_defaults_has_no_duplicate_keys` walks the
module's AST — the loaded dict cannot show the defect, because by then the
evidence is gone — and it is checked non-vacuous against the exact shape that
shipped. `listen` is a HOST STRING and boolean `true` is refused: an operator
opening a LAN port should have to say which interface.

The reference client (`ServeSocketClient`) learns TLS with fingerprint PINNING
and a `device_hello`, because it is the shape the launcher's Stage 2 connector
mirrors and the pin belongs in the reference rather than only in a test — without
it the encryption stops an eavesdropper and stops no impostor, and
`cert_fingerprint` would be a field nobody uses.

Receipts, run not inferred (`C:\Python312\python.exe -m pytest`):
`test_serve_gateway_lane.py` 17 passed — real `serve_loop`, real TLS, real pin,
real HMAC over a real paired credential; `test_gateway_listen_config.py` 16
passed; `test_config_defaults_no_duplicate_keys.py` 2 passed;
`test_serve_socket_lane.py` + `test_serve_socket_child_e2e.py` 59 passed
unchanged. The byte-identical claim is asserted DIRECTLY rather than inferred
from those staying green: two steady-state boots, one with the second door open,
compared field by field on `ready` and on a loopback client's `hello_ok`, with
volatile fields dropped by NAME so a field that starts varying for a real reason
breaks the test instead of slipping through it. The first attempt failed on
`auth.token_file` minted-vs-present, which is boot ORDER and not this lane — so
the test now warms the root and discards that boot, and says why.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S1d — the pairing code gets somewhere to be spent, and the one frame that carries a secret carries it once

S1a minted codes and S1c opened a door that only accepts credentials. Between
them sat a ceremony with no second half: an operator could print eight
characters and a phone had nowhere to spend them, which would have shipped a
device tier no device could ever enter. `redeem_pairing_code` had exactly one
caller, and it was a test.

A hello carrying `pairing_code` instead of `device_id` redeems it and the
connection is admitted as the device it just created, with the minted token
riding the `hello_ok` that was going to be sent anyway. One round trip rather
than pair-then-reconnect, and three properties are what make that safe enough to
do in one: the link is already TLS with a fingerprint the operator handed over
out of band, so the token is unreadable in flight and undeliverable to an
impostor; the code is one-shot, deleted before the token is minted, so a replay
finds nothing; and a failed redemption collapses into the same `bad_proof` as
every other credential failure and charges the same limiter, so the 40-bit code
space cannot be ground faster than the device-id space.

The token reaches the greeting through a ONE-SHOT slot on the connection that
`_pairing_block` reads and clears on the next statement. That is a function
rather than an inline expression on purpose: the clear has to be unconditional
and unmissable, because a `getattr` that read without clearing would leave a
secret on a long-lived object for the life of the session and the bug would stay
invisible until somebody logged a connection. `SocketConnection.payload()` — the
block that renders a connection to an operator, to a log, and to every other
attached client — has no field for it, and a test asserts the token and the code
appear nowhere in a `connections` frame taken on the very connection that was
just paired.

A hello carrying BOTH a code and a device id is refused rather than resolved to
either. A handshake with two credentials in it is exactly where a downgrade
lives, and the server does not get to pick which one it liked.

Neither door accepts the other's credential, and both directions are pinned: the
root token is refused on the gateway lane, and a pairing code is refused on
loopback.

Stated plainly because it exceeds the brief's letter: the brief scoped the
listener to "ONLY device-tier hellos", and this adds a second, narrower hello.
The argument for doing it anyway is that the alternative is a credential nobody
can obtain and a `harness gateway pair` whose output is decoration — a bigger
defect than the extra surface, and one that would have to be fixed before any
phone could be built against Stage 5.

23 passed in `test_serve_gateway_lane.py` (up from 17): the six new ones cover a
code becoming a credential that works on the NEXT connection, one-shot reuse,
wrong codes, the two-credential frame, cross-lane refusal, and the token's
absence from the connections block.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S1e — the pairing ceremony gets an operator door, and R3's two halves come out of one mint

`harness gateway pair`, `harness gateway devices list`, `harness gateway devices
revoke <device_id>`, beside Stage 0b's `id` / `rename` in the same subtree,
because they all answer questions about THIS machine's runtime root.

R3 as ruled — QR plus typed-code fallback, CLI-first — so one run prints both:
the eight characters an operator reads onto a phone by hand with the host:port
beside them, and the payload a phone scans. From ONE mint, which is the whole
point: a code shown as text and a code shown as a QR that could disagree would
be two ceremonies wearing one name. `qr_payload` is a STRING rather than a
nested object, because what a QR encodes is bytes and handing over the exact
bytes removes the chance that two renderers serialise one object differently and
only one of them scans.

The endpoint block SAYS WHICH SOURCE ANSWERED, because the three are not equally
good and an operator reading a port needs to know whether a listener is on it.
`live` is the running serve's ownership sidecar — which now carries the gateway
host/port/fingerprint, because that is the only place an EPHEMERAL gateway port
exists at all: the registry entry carries the loopback port and the `ready` frame
goes to a launcher rather than to a terminal. `config` is what the next boot will
use. `unknown` is the lane being off — and it is a NOTE rather than a refusal,
because a code minted against a lane nobody is listening on is still a valid
code, and an operator who does not know that will blame the code.

`pair` ENSURES the identity and the certificate rather than reading them, on the
precedent `gateway rename` set: pairing a root that has never booted is a
legitimate thing to do, and a `pair` that could not produce a fingerprint would
print a payload with a hole where the trust decision goes. A certificate that
cannot be minted is a refusal, never a payload with a null in it: that would tell
the phone to trust whatever certificate answers, which is R1 undone by a field.

Two exit codes were added to the shared table, documented in it the way
`duplicate_desk` and `cancel_unsupported` document theirs. `pairing_codes_pending`
and `pairing_locked_out` are both family 6, because the operator's next MOVE is
to WAIT — for a code to be redeemed or expire, for a lockout to lapse — and
neither is a fault: nothing is broken, nothing needs repairing, and the identical
command succeeds later unchanged. Two codes, one family, on this table's own rule
that the family is the next move and the code is which precondition.

`devices revoke` says `takes_effect: "next_handshake"` in its ack rather than
leaving an operator to discover it. A revocation somebody believes is immediate,
applied to a device that is attached right now, is the gap between what they
think they did and what happened; closing an in-flight session is a separate
decision (they can drain) and inventing it here would make `revoke` a verb that
disconnects people. `--dry-run` is on `revoke` and NOT on `pair`, which is the
one deviation from `rename`'s flag reasoning and has its own: a dry run of `pair`
would print a code it did not mint, and eight characters nothing will accept is
worse than no preview.

The handlers live in `harness_parts/gateway_commands.py` rather than in
`harness.py` — not for length, but because the credential wiring is the part that
must not be got wrong and it reads better beside a module docstring that can
carry R3's ruling and the no-authorization-gate argument. That argument is
Stage 0b's, unchanged and restated: these verbs have ONE door, no `gateway.*` RPC
method exists for them, so there is no wire twin that could answer differently —
which is the exact condition the A4 mirror exists to prevent. Imported lazily the
way `serve` already is, so `harness --help` does not pull in the certificate and
device-store modules.

15 tests, driving the real argparse tree through `args.func` because a handler
nothing routes to is a verb no operator can run. The three that would survive an
obvious first cut and nothing else: the scanned payload equals the printed
fields field-for-field; the code appears on stdout and nowhere in `pairing.json`;
and a `--dry-run` revoke is asserted against the STORE rather than the ack, since
the kill-mutation returns a perfectly plausible exit-0 having revoked a device
the operator was only asking about.

Cross-repo: this changes hermes' argparse tree, which the launcher pins.
Regeneration and its suites ride the next commit.

Note on hygiene: a concurrent session holds uncommitted work in `harness.py`.
Only this lane's hunks were staged — built as a patch against HEAD and applied
to the index — so no foreign hunk is in this commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
docs(gateway): the handshake prose said contract 2 and msg=nonce; the code has said 3 and bound the port since the relay defence

Two comment blocks — `serve_socket.py`'s module docstring and `serve.py`'s wire
summary — described the hello proof as `hello_contract` 2 over `msg=<nonce>`.
`HELLO_CONTRACT_VERSION` is 3 and `hello_proof` has computed
`HMAC(key=token, msg="v3|<dialled port>|<nonce>")` since the port binding landed
to close the live-relay hole. So the prose was wrong in both halves at once.

Found the only way this kind of drift ever is: somebody built a client against
it. The launcher's socket client (Stage 2, launcher `527940a0e`) is the first
consumer of this handshake in six weeks, and a client that trusts these
paragraphs computes a proof over the wrong message and is refused `bad_proof` —
which is the least debuggable failure available, because it is byte-identical
to holding the wrong credential. A comment that is merely out of date costs a
reader a minute; this one costs a client author an afternoon and points them at
their credential handling.

Both blocks now name the real derivation, both say that `hello_proof` is the
authority and this is a description of it, and both record what they used to say
— so the next reader who finds a client failing on `bad_proof` has the
historical wrong answer in front of them rather than having to rediscover that
the docs once disagreed with the code.

This also discharges the primary plan's §7 honest bound, which named exactly
this ("`hello_contract` current value — canon says v3; `serve_socket.py`
docstring shows the v2-era frame — confirm at Stage 2 client authoring"). It was
confirmed at Stage 2 client authoring, and the docstring was the one that was
wrong.

Prose only. No literal, no behaviour, no test moved.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(persona): S1 — the persona template learns to hold skills, and an omitted flag is a refusal instead of a clear

`harness persona set-skills` closes the half of the skills cascade nobody could
reach. The only skills door was `persona instance update-profile --skill`, which
writes ONE agent's `skill_overrides`; a placement made later inherits
`persona.skills`, and no operator verb wrote `persona.skills`. So "set the
skills, then place a new agent from that persona" was broken by construction,
not by a bug.

The verb is `persona set-model`'s twin on purpose — same store-row write target,
same `persona_not_persisted` refusal for a config-only catalog id, same
`profile:<name>` resolution, same supersede clock. Two of those are now the SAME
CODE rather than the same shape: `_template_write_store_target` and
`_parse_issued_at_arg` were extracted and `set-model` rewritten onto them, so a
second spelling cannot drift from the first.

The write lands on the AgentStore row because that is the record the runtime
reads: `ensure_persisted_personas` merges `{**catalog, **stored}` and a store row
wins wholesale, so the config `skills:`/`skills_remove:` merge is already dead
for every persona in live use. A config write would be a write nobody reads.
Minting a row for a catalog-only id would freeze every OTHER field of that
persona at its write-time value, so that case is refused and names the reason.

Absent is never a write here. `--skill` keeps the tree's `action="append",
default=None` spelling so an omitted flag stays distinguishable from `[]`, but at
the template tier — the root of the cascade — absent has nothing to inherit from,
so it is a typed `nothing_to_write` refusal rather than a write of `[]`. That
collapse already shipped once at the instance tier (`list(args.skills or [])`)
and cleared every skill of every renamed agent; the refusal is what keeps a
transport-mangled argv from doing it to a template. `--skill "   "` — present
flag, every value dropped by token safety — gets the same answer for the same
reason. `skills_override_issued_at` is its own field so a model write and a
skills write can never supersede each other.

Evidence: 14 tests in tests/hermes_cli/test_persona_set_skills.py, every one
driving the real argparse tree and probing the row FILE on disk rather than the
command's own reply. Three registered killing mutations, all KILLED with the
observed red quoted in the docstring: pts-s1-absent-becomes-clear
(`assert 0 == 2`), pts-s1-store-write-dropped
(`assert ['seeded-skill'] == ['alpha', 'beta']`), pts-s1-stale-write-applies
(`assert 'applied' == 'superseded'`). A live probe on an isolated
`agent-runtime-probe-*` root ran the verb end to end and re-read the changed row
off disk; ack and clock are pasted in the field notes.

author: nekwo
message:
test(persona): S2 — the operator's sentence runs end to end, and the agents that already exist are told apart from the one placed next

The verb S1 shipped is only worth what the placement lane does with it, so this
slice proves the sentence the ruling was written from: set skills on the
persona, place a new agent from it, and the agent has those skills.

Four cases, all driving the real CLI through the same argparse tree into
`perform_agent_create` — the function `runtime.agent.create` answers with — over
a workspace and office surface seeded in the per-test isolated root:

- a NEW placement with `--skill` absent carries the just-written template set.
  The create ack says `inherited: true` with `assigned: []` (the D11 shape,
  deliberately not the list), so the carried set is read where the runtime reads
  it — through `apply_instance_model_overrides` — and the new row is asserted to
  still hold `skill_overrides = None`, because an absent flag must leave the
  agent INHERITING rather than pin it to a copy;
- an instance placed BEFORE the write follows it afterwards. This is the case
  the plan's §7 listed as ASSUMED ("no persona record cached across the store
  write") and it now passes for the offline lane;
- an instance carrying its own overrides is untouched. The override is written
  through `persona instance update-profile --skill` — the door the launcher's
  skills sheet actually submits — so the two tiers are proven against each other
  through their real doors instead of against a poked dataclass;
- the placement lane and the roster row both see the write, which is why S1
  needed zero read-side changes: `ensure_persisted_personas` returns the store
  row's skills and `snapshot._agent_summary` projects them.

No production line changes here, so the changed-line mutation runner selects
nothing — `--base HEAD --list` prints `mutation candidates: 0 (cap 12)` — which
is its design and the reason this slice registers no claims. The integration
tests are the evidence.

One thing the writing found: `agent create --skill` hard-gates on resolution, so
the overridden-instance case could not be built by placing with an unresolvable
id at all. The three skills doors validate ids with three different strictnesses;
that stays the named adjacent gap it already was.

message:
docs(gateway): Stage 1 graduates into canon, and the row that said the config keys were "declared" is corrected to "never existed"

Canon 03 grows §1.1 — the gateway listener as a table against the loopback lane
(host, link, credential, transport tag, caller kind, ops, argv), the device hello
and its derivation, the pairing hello, the collapse of every credential failure
into one reason, and the fact that neither door accepts the other's credential in
either direction. §2 records that `ops` now answers three transports rather than
two, and that the tier is a refusal with a paired device on the other side of it.
Two invariants added: a listener beyond loopback is opt-in and TLS-only (a
certificate that cannot be minted means the lane does not open, never that it
opens in the clear), and a credential appears in exactly one frame, once.

§1's handshake paragraph is corrected in the same pass — it was the third place
saying `hello_contract` 2 over `msg=<nonce>` — and now says out loud that
`hello_proof` is the authority and that this prose has been wrong before, so the
next reader debugging a client refused `bad_proof` has the historical wrong
answer in front of them.

**The Windows firewall note lands in canon rather than in a plan**, because it is
the one operational fact that will bite an operator on day one and it is
unlearnable from the code: the prompt names the PYTHON interpreter rather than
`hermes`, Private is the answer a LAN pairing needs, and an operator who
dismisses it gets a listener that binds successfully and is unreachable — `ready`
says `listening` and is telling the truth. A pinned `remote_gateway.port` is what
makes a firewall rule writable in advance; an ephemeral one cannot have it. It is
labelled UNDRIVEN, because nobody bound a non-loopback interface during this work.

The plan gets its receipts, its deviations and — the part worth reading — its
honest gaps: no second machine, no phone, no QR ever scanned, no live serve
driven by hand, `icacls` reported but not asserted, and the primary plan in the
launcher repo still describing Stage 1 as unbuilt (deliberately not written by
this lane, because a sibling session was landing Stage 2 receipts into that same
file).

The chokepoint plan's A5 row goes NOT HERE → LANDED, with the two things the
design did not anticipate. The structural guard: a gateway connection with no
usable device stamp is `unknown`, never `local_console` — unreachable today, and
the fall-through it replaces would have handed a remote peer the machine owner's
authority the moment any future change let an empty stamp through. And the duty
it inherited: the tier gate covers the METHOD lane, so the argv lane had to be
refused to devices outright, or the gate would be real and bypassable in one
frame. §4 said "whether the argv lane should exist" was not that file's question;
whether a DEVICE reaches it turned out to be.

Field notes carry what a later session cannot re-derive, and the first entry is
the one that generalises past this lane: **"declared, read by nothing" is the
exact condition under which a config key that failed to load is
indistinguishable from one that loaded and nobody consulted.** Stage 0a's
`gateway.listen`/`gateway.port` were a duplicate key in one dict literal and were
discarded at parse time; being their first reader is the only thing that could
have found it. Also recorded: that the handshake prose drift surfaced only
because somebody finally built a client against it, and two repo-hygiene events

author: nekwo
message:
fix(gateway): the stage42 flag gate could not see the new handlers, and one of the flags it then reported was genuinely a lie

Two findings from one red test, and only one of them is the test's own blind
spot.

**The real defect:** `harness gateway devices list` registered the `sort`
control and nothing sorts. `list_devices` returns one deterministic order
(created_at, then device_id) and the handler passes it straight through, so an
operator typing `--sort name` would get the unsorted answer with no signal the
flag was ignored — a WRONG ANSWER believed, not an error seen, which is the
exact failure `_add_stage42_global_args`' docstring is built around and the
reason `--filter` and `--watch` were removed in 2026-07. The control is dropped
and the help now says "oldest first", so the order is stated rather than
implied.

**The blind spot:** `_stage42_lane_sources()` is a hand-written list of the
files that could legitimately honor a stage42 flag, and Stage 1's handlers live
in `harness_parts/gateway_commands.py` — a real imported module (like
`serve.py`), not one of the exec'd parts. The analysis is a static call graph,
so with that file unscanned it could not see `_print_stage42` at the far end of
a one-line wrapper and reported all fourteen presentation flags on the three new
verbs as unhonored. Adding the file is precisely the maintenance the list exists
to need: the docstring above it explains why scanning all of `hermes_cli/` is
the wrong fix (an unrelated command's identically-named flag would stand in as
the reader), so a new handler home is a line here, deliberately.

Worth stating that the gate was RIGHT to be loud in both cases. Twelve of the
fourteen rows were noise from the blind spot and one (`dry_run` on `revoke`) was
too — but `sort` was real, and a gate that had quietly resolved the wrapper
would have shipped it.

`tests/hermes_cli/test_harness_cli.py` 58 passed; the two gateway verb suites 30
passed.

Honest gap, NOT this lane's: `test_harness_json_root_observability.py` is red at
HEAD on `_cmd_persona_set_skills`, a verb a concurrent session added in
`9cfb63769e`. Confirmed red at that session's own `f515d6bbfe` in a clean
worktree before claiming it — the same discipline the A1 wave used on the three
manifest pins it found rotted. The three `harness gateway` verbs pass that gate;
they route through `attach_root_observability` because the credentials are per
STORE ROOT and a pair run against the wrong one mints a code for a runtime the
operator did not mean.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S3a — mission chat gets a method lane, and the key it dedupes on turns out to have been there all along

Stage 1 refused the argv lane to devices, correctly and load-bearingly: the
tier gate lives on the method lane, so an argv lane open to a device makes
every tier declaration bypassable in one frame. But mission-chat has no
methods — it lowers to argv — so the refusal quietly closed the one thing the
gateway is for. A paired device could place an agent and could not talk to it.

So the two chat-turn verbs are ported to the method lane, which is the
direction runtime-rpc-call-half.md already had, and the scope is those two and
not the argv surface. The local stdio lane does not move.

The door lands one step lower than runtime.agent.retire's. Mission chat has no
perform_* function: its service IS the argparse handler, and the one existing
second door onto it (dispatch_delivery) reaches it by building a namespace.
This one builds argv, which the worker dispatches through the same argparse
tree a local send uses — so a remote turn and a local turn are the same
execution rather than two implementations that agree today.

Tier is console, honestly rather than conveniently. A chat turn is not a level
mutation, but it runs an agent with tools, and a softer tier for it would be a
door around console — the read device refused runtime.agent.retire could ask
an agent to retire one. A new `chat` word would also have refused every
already-paired console device the very thing R11 says it may do, because the
device arm is an equality against the stored word and not an ordering.

The correction this stage rests on: the plan says mission-chat send has no
server-side dedupe, re-verified as "no turn_request_id anywhere". The grep was
right and the conclusion was wrong. Mission chat has carried exactly-once as
client_message_id plus the per-session turn journal since the 2026-08-24
incident, already answering idempotent_replay with the committed reply. So
turn_request_id is not a second key — it is passed to --client-message-id
unchanged. The new receipt covers only the window the journal cannot: the
journal's first write happens inside the chat-root lease, after a worker is
already running, and the RPC lane must accept before that.

The ack is an accept, not a reply, and that is forced: the method lane is
answered inline on the reader loop, whose own comment names chat turns as the
reason the pool exists. The turn rides the existing per-request frame lane; no
second streaming transport is invented. And it rides it as an _ArgvRequest, so
is_chat_turn is derived from the same _CHAT_TURN_COMMANDS shapes and
held_by_chat_turns counts an RPC turn exactly as it counts a local one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(gateway): S3b — the remote chat turn is made to hold a drain open, and the settle it does on the way out had to move

Twenty tests over the new lane. The one that earns the stage is the drain
hold: serve's contract is that a supervisor never recycles this process while
chat_turns > 0, the ledger is keyed at the ARGV boundary, and a turn that
arrived on the method lane and did not join it would be invisible to exactly
the protection it needs. It joins — held_by_chat_turns reads 1 and
chat_turn_request_ids names the server-minted id — because the RPC accept
builds the same _ArgvRequest an argv send does.

Exactly-once is asserted where it would fail vacuously: the dispatch counter
counts EXECUTIONS, and it is 1 across two sends of one turn_request_id, both
when the retry arrives after the exit and when it arrives while the first turn
is still running. The second is the case the turn journal alone cannot answer.

Writing the drain test found a real defect in the first draft. The settle sat
between the inflight pop and the exit frame, and the drain monitor polls the
pending set — so a request that was out of inflight and had not yet emitted
was a window in which the drain could complete and close the lane under its
own exit frame. Reproduced as a lost exit. It settles first in the finally
now, before the pop, where the monitor still counts the request.

The four manifest-literal pins across three office suites learn the two new
names in the same commit as the methods that grew them, per the S5 lesson.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(persona): S1 follow-up — set-skills says which runtime root answered, instead of joining a backlog it was born into

`test_harness_json_root_observability` reddened on `_cmd_persona_set_skills` the
moment S1 landed: a JSON-emitting harness verb that states no runtime root. The
gate exists because a wrong root returns a well-formed EMPTY answer, so an
envelope that cannot say which root it came from cannot be trusted when it is
empty.

The tempting fix was the wrong one. `persona set-model` — the verb this one is
deliberately twinned with — is listed in that test's LEDGER, so copying its
precedent would have meant adding one more name beside it. But that LEDGER maps
every entry to `_BACKLOG_REASON`: it is a debt list, not a justification, and the
gate's whole purpose is to stop NEW verbs shipping into it. The recent verbs
(`agent create`, `agent retire`) attach the block instead, and so does this one
now — all four payload sites, refusals included.

The refusals matter as much as the ack here, for the reason the create and retire
verbs already record: a `persona_not_found` answered out of the WRONG root
refuses exactly as plausibly as one answered out of the right one, and this verb
writes the template every later placement inherits.

Found by another session's run at hermes HEAD, not by mine — my S1 verification
ran the persona and create/retire suites and never reached this cross-cutting
gate. Recorded because the miss is the useful part: a new JSON verb needs the
whole-repo gates, not just its own neighbourhood.

claims re-checked and unaffected.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(gateway): the receipt claimed it never carried the id, and the launcher acceptance is what proved otherwise

Two questions got conflated in one comment. The KEY is a digest — the filename
and the field — because a client-chosen string must never become a path
component; a remote device can send `../` or two hundred characters. That is
not the same as saying the id is absent from the file, and it was written as
if it were.

It cannot be absent. The ack is recorded verbatim so a replay is byte-identical
to the accept the client saw, and an ack echoes the turn_request_id the client
itself sent and is waiting for. Digesting the key and echoing the ack answer
different questions; conflating them means either an unsafe filename or a
replay that returns something the client did not send.

The hermes test passed because it stored an ack with no id in it — which is
not a shape this lane ever writes. It now uses a hostile id, asserts the file
landed under its digest inside the receipts directory and nowhere else, and
asserts the ack round-tripped intact. Found by the launcher acceptance
asserting the wrong half against a real serve.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office): the climb went DOWN the screen — D10(iii)'s sign was wrong, and only a live capture could say so

The ruling was "if something is there it should move it up a bit higher so you
can still see it". `948aea9b80` changed `slot_at` to ADD the row offset, on the
reasoning that adding makes rows climb. It does not. The office canvas renders
+y DOWNWARD — measured on a live Stage C capture, ~32 px per world unit with
world y increasing toward the bottom of the window, cross-checked against two
actors of known position. So every extra placement stacked BELOW the last: the
exact opposite of the ruling, shipped under a comment asserting the opposite.

fixed correctly and which stands. Flipping the sign as well was a second change
nothing asked for, and it inverted the behaviour the first change existed to
produce.

Every test agreed with the bug, and would have agreed with either sign: they
assert against `slot_at`, so they pin the lattice's self-consistency and say
nothing about which way is up on screen. That is not a gap to close by adding a
test — no unit test in either repo can see the canvas — it is the argument for
the visual proof that found it. Two placements on a live level, one above the
other in world coordinates and one below the other in pixels.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S6a — the peer store, and the code discipline stops being the device ceremony's private property

Stage 6 needs a second credential store under `<store_root>/gateway/`, and the
first thing that became clear writing it is that the eight characters an
operator reads off a terminal are the same eight characters in both ceremonies.
Not similar — the same. Same alphabet, same TTL, same pending cap, and, the part
that matters, the same thing a guesser is grinding against: one listener, one
32^8 space, one failure budget. Two lockout counters would mean the lockout
gated half the guessing, which is to say it gated nothing.

So `gateway_pairing_codes.py` is the RULES, once, over one `pairing.json`: the
salted digest, the expiry sweep, the failure streak, the constant-time match.
What it does not share is what a code redeems INTO — every pending entry carries
a `kind`, and `match_pending` will only match against the kind that was asked
for. A device code presented on the peer hello is refused at the lookup rather
than by two files a refactor could merge, which is the plan's "device-tier and
peer-tier credentials are never interchangeable" enforced where it cannot be
argued away.

The functions take an already-read state dict and mutate it in place; none of
them opens a file or takes a lock. That is what lets both redeems stay ATOMIC —
"delete the pending entry and write the row" under ONE hold of the directory
lock, exactly as Stage 1 shipped it. A module that owned the lock too would have
forced a second acquisition between the halves, and a crash in that window burns
a code for nothing.

`gateway_peers.py` is the store proper. A row is
`{peer_install_id, display_name, endpoints, cert_fingerprint, secret_verifier,
approved_at, last_seen, revoked, revoked_at}`, and three of those names are
deliberately NOT the device row's: the two stores sit in one directory holding
rows of a similar shape, and a row copied between them by a script, a merge or a
hand edit must decode to nothing rather than to something that works. The proof
prefix is `pwv` against the device lane's `gwv` for the same reason.

The honest limit is restated rather than referenced, because a security note one
indirection away is a note nobody reads: the verifier is HMAC-key-equivalent,
and anyone who can read `peers.json` can answer a challenge as that peer. What
differs from the device lane is worth saying plainly — both installs store
`sha256(secret)` and USE it as the key, so the plaintext exists only for the one
frame that carried it. That is what makes the edge symmetric (either install can
dial the other with the row it holds) and why `peer_proof` has one spelling
where the device lane needs two.

`store_file_io` grows four more helpers, and they moved for the same reason the
first three did on 65f6194b4c: the peer store is the device store's sibling, and
a sibling restating the JSON read, the atomic 0600 write, the cross-process lock
and the UTC stamp is the exact group the duplicate gate would have named next.
Nothing was rewritten on the way; `serve_gateway_auth` keeps its private names
through alias imports, so its call sites and its 29 tests read unchanged. The
lock now takes a PATH rather than a root, and both ceremonies pass the same one —
they read-modify-write the same `pairing.json`, so two lock files would be two
names for a mutual exclusion that has to be one.

Green before landing, since this moved shipped bodies: duplicate-helper gate,
serve_gateway_auth, gateway_identity, gateway_tls — 60 passed, 1 skipped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(gateway): S6a — 37 tests on the peer store, and the one that matters most builds a device row and proves it is inert as a peer

Two claims carry the file. The first is that a device credential and a peer
credential are never interchangeable, proved at the STORE and not only at the
wire: a device pairing code refuses to redeem as a peer, a peer code refuses to
redeem as a device, and — the case a reader would actually worry about — a
device ROW written verbatim into `peers.json` does not decode to a record at
all, because the credential sits under a different key and the row is named by a
different id field. The wire suite proves the same rule over a real socket; this
one proves the layer beneath, so a wire refusal is never the only thing holding
it up.

The second is that the rate-limiting state is shared while the credentials are
not, and both halves are asserted rather than described: three outstanding codes
across the two ceremonies exhausts the cap for BOTH, and five failed PEER
redeems lock out the DEVICE mint. That second one is the test that would have
caught the design going the other way — two counters look correct in every
per-ceremony test and mean an attacker locked out of one simply grinds the
other with a fresh budget.

The proof gets the treatment its three bindings deserve: a port that differs, a
nonce that differs, and a proof minted naming install B presented as install A —
with A genuinely paired and holding the same secret, so the refusal is the
binding and not a missing row. There is also the collision case the `pwv`/`gwv`
prefix split exists for, constructed deliberately: a device proof computed over
the very bytes a peer holds still does not verify as a peer proof.

Plus the fail-closed sweep the handshake path is owed — a corrupt store
authenticates nobody rather than raising, a non-ASCII proof is merely wrong
rather than a TypeError unwinding out of the handshake, revocation is checked
AFTER the proof so ids cannot be probed by an unauthenticated caller — and the
endpoint coercion, which runs on data the other install sent before it has
proven anything: bounded, typed, deduplicated, and a malformed row dropped
rather than failing a pairing an operator is standing there waiting on.

One test was wrong on the first run and the store was right: it minted four
codes expecting the third to survive. The cap is three.

37 passed.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S6b — a peer is a caller KIND with an allowlist, and the canon's exclusion stops depending on anybody remembering it

Canon 06's remote-connector table has said since it was written that the peer
tier is "deliberately excluded: agents never mint or retire agents on another
install; a remote OPERATOR does". Until now that was a sentence in a document.
This is the sentence as code, and the shape it took is the decision worth
recording.

The obvious build is a third tier word — add `peer` to TIERS, declare it on the
verbs a peer may call, compare. It loses on what happens when the registry
GROWS: a tier comparison admits every future verb that happens to declare the
matching word, so the day somebody registers a new read method, every paired
install on the LAN can call it and nobody decided that. A membership test admits
nothing it was not edited to admit, which makes widening the peer surface a
visible line in a diff with a reason attached. So `PEER_METHOD_ALLOWLIST` is
`{peer.ping}`, and create/retire are absent from it not because anyone left them
out but because EVERYTHING is absent unless it is there.

The Stage 3 note that the device arm is an equality "deliberately" is kept
exactly as it was, and the asymmetry is now explicable rather than incidental: a
device is a client of THIS install whose operator chose how much of the surface
to hand it, so a stored tier is the right question. A peer is another RUNTIME,
whose own agents drive it, and "how much of my runtime may another runtime's
agents reach" is a different question with a different answer shape.

The arm's POSITION is load-bearing and easy to get wrong invisibly. The read
arm returns ok for every caller including `unknown` — A5 kept that deliberately
— so a peer evaluated after it would inherit this runtime's entire read surface:
the office core, the subscribe lane, every read verb not yet written. The peer
arm therefore runs before it, and there is a test that asserts exactly that
against real read-tier verbs, because no console-verb test can see it.

`authorize_call` grows an optional `method`, and the asymmetry is intentional:
every other caller kind is decided by tier alone, so requiring the argument
everywhere would rewrite call sites with no use for it (the A4 CLI mirror asks
"may the console run a console verb", a question with no method in it). A peer
arriving with no method name is REFUSED — absence of a name is absence of a
decision, and absence of a decision is never an allow.

`peer.ping` declares `read`, and the in-file argument for why that is not a lie
to device or console readers is the longest comment in the diff: the tiers map
answers what a call WANTS, never what a connection HOLDS (canon 03 §2), so the
honest answer for a verb that reads no store and mints no id is the same one
`runtime.office.get` gets. The allowlist NARROWS the peer lane; it does not
widen this row. Inventing a third tier word only one caller kind can hold would
put a value in the map every existing reader must be taught to ignore.

The handler touches no store, and a test proves it by breaking root resolution
outright and calling it anyway. It echoes the install id the TRANSPORT proved,
which answers "is my credential still the one you know me by" — a real question
no client-side check can settle.

The five manifest literals grew `peer.ping` in this commit rather than the next
one, which is the S5 lesson: those pins were red for weeks the last two times a
method landed without them.

18 new tests; 122 in the three pinned suites.
