author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S6c — the peer hello, and the rule that keeps two credentials apart turns out to be a counting rule

Four hellos now reach the gateway listener — a device credential, a device
pairing code, a peer credential, a peer join code — and one function tells them
apart. The first draft of that function was a chain of `if` branches, which is
how the Stage 1 version was written when there were two, and writing the third
branch made the defect visible: a chain answers a malformed frame by picking a
winner. "A code beats an id", "a peer beats a device" — every such rule is one
refactor away from picking the MORE privileged one, and the flip would be
invisible in review.

So `_credential_kind` counts. Exactly one credential field named is a
credential; zero or two is a refusal, and the refusal looks like every other
credential failure on this lane. The one pair that is not two credentials — a
join frame carrying `peer_code` AND `peer_install_id`, where the code is the
credential and the id is the name being claimed under it — is spelled out as an
explicit allowance rather than hidden inside a precedence, so the counting rule
stays intact for the combination an attacker would actually try.

The derivation is separated three ways, and each way closes something. The
`pwv` prefix against the device lane's `gwv` means a device proof does not
verify as a peer proof even if the two credentials were somehow the same bytes
— which the store suite constructs deliberately rather than assuming impossible.
The install id in the message is what stops A's proof to B being replayed as B's
proof to A: without it, one symmetric secret over one nonce would produce the
same bytes in both directions and a relay that bounced one back would
authenticate. And the port binding is Stage 1's, unchanged.

`_is_device` became `_is_gateway`, which is a rename and not a behaviour change
— and the reason it matters is that the refusals it guards (`argv_lane_unavailable`,
`op_not_available_on_gateway`) were ALWAYS keyed on the door rather than on the
device stamp. So a peer inherits both for free. "For free" is a claim about code
nobody re-read, so both are asserted over a real socket; the argv one in
particular is what makes "agents can never mint peers" hold against a remote
caller, since the peer verbs are CLI verbs and the argv lane is the only way a
CLI verb is otherwise reachable over the wire.

`ServeSocketClient` grew two hellos and lost three copies of the same fifteen
lines: the `server_hello` read, the frame check and the contract check were
restated per hello, and a fifth copy is how one of them eventually stops
checking the contract. `_challenge` is that half, once, and the three existing
hellos were folded onto it rather than left beside it.

25 new tests over the real `serve_loop`, real TLS, real HMAC: the join in one
round trip with the asserted facts landing bounded on the row, a device
credential refused on the peer field and a peer credential refused on the device
field, a frame naming both, a device code refused as a peer code and the
reverse, a revoked peer, an unpaired install indistinguishable from a wrong
secret, and `peer.ping` answering over the listener with the peer credential
while `runtime.agent.retire` is refused `scope_denied` on the same connection.

One test found a real behaviour worth keeping rather than a bug: `dial_peer`
READS this root's install identity and will not mint one. Minting an id as a
side effect of an outbound call would mean the name a paired install knows this
one by could be created by something nobody thought of as a write — and an id is
the one value in this lane that must never be quietly re-minted. The test that
caught it is now the test that pins it.

49 passed across both gateway lane suites.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S6d — the ceremony gets its four verbs, and R5's "both sides" turns out to be enforced by there being no verb that does it alone

`peers pair` on install A, `peers join` on install B, plus `list` and `revoke`.
The property R5 asks for — every edge explicitly approved on BOTH sides — is not
a flag on a row and not a confirmation prompt. It is that neither half of the
ceremony can be performed by the other install: A never learns B's address until
B dials, and B cannot mint a code in A's store. There is no verb that pairs an
install without a human at each end, which is a stronger guarantee than an
approval field, because a field can be set by whatever wrote the row.

"Agents can never mint peers" is written into the module docstring in two parts,
because only one of them is closed structurally and saying otherwise would put a
false claim in the file an auditor reads first. The REMOTE half is closed
completely: there is no `gateway.*` method for any of these, so the method lane
has nothing to call, and the argv lane — the only other way a CLI verb is
reachable over the wire — is refused outright to every gateway connection. No
caller on that listener, at any tier, on either lane, can mint a peer anywhere.
The residual is local: an agent with shell access on this machine can run these
verbs exactly as it can read `serve_auth_token` or edit `peers.json` in an
editor. Every tool-using agent already holds the machine owner's authority. So
the accurate claim is "no agent on A can cause B to trust it, and no remote
caller can mint a peer anywhere" — and an agent that has already taken over the
machine its operator is sitting at was never a case this ceremony could fix.

`peers` is a subtree beside `devices` rather than more verbs inside it: two
stores, two questions ("which phones may reach this install" against "which
INSTALLS has an operator approved an edge with"), and folding them would make a
list that mixes a phone and a workstation and needs a `kind` column to be
readable — a discriminator standing in for the two verbs the tree already has
room for.

Three guards keep an operator from pasting one ceremony's payload into the
other's verb, and the first fires before a socket opens: a peer payload names
`peer_code` where a device payload names `code`, so a device payload handed to
`join` is refused for its shape and told exactly what it is. The store's kind
split and the wire's counting rule are the second and third.

`join` refuses three things rather than papering over them: a payload whose
`install_id` the far side turns out not to have (something else is on that
address — the row is NOT written), a `hello_ok` with no `peered` block (the code
did not redeem, and a row written on hope is a row whose every dial fails), and
any dial failure at all as family 7 rather than family 2 — a listener that is
not up yet is exactly the condition where the identical command succeeds five
seconds later, and calling that an argument error tells the operator to change
something correct.

`revoke`'s ack says it is ONE-SIDED, which is the fact that distinguishes it
from `devices revoke`: a peer edge holds a credential at both ends, and a
revocation that reached across the wire would be one install writing into
another's credential store — the authority R5 says an install never has over
another.

The join's happy path is deliberately not faked here. A version of it that
dialled this same root would pair an install with itself: green, and describing
something that cannot happen. That proof belongs to the two-roots acceptance.

23 new tests; 38 across both pairing-verb suites; the CLI tree suite still 58.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(gateway): S6e — the acceptance the plan named: two isolated roots, both operator verbs, and a ping across the edge

Two real `harness serve` children, each with its own runtime root, its own
install identity, its own certificate and its own credential store, neither able
to read the other's disk. Then the ceremony in the order an operator performs
it: A mints, the code crosses because this test carries it exactly as a human
would, B joins over a pinned TLS link, both stores record the edge, and A dials
B for a `peer.ping`.

Child PROCESSES rather than two `serve_loop` threads, and the reason is the
whole point of the acceptance. A runtime root is resolved from the environment
and an environment is process-global, so two serve loops in one interpreter
would race over `HERMES_AGENT_RUNTIME_ROOT`: whichever booted last owns the
ambient value, and every later re-resolution inside the FIRST serve answers for
the SECOND root. A test built that way would pass while proving the opposite of
what it claims. Two processes make the isolation a property of the operating
system rather than of nobody having called `store_root()` at the wrong moment.

The step that matters most is step 5, and it is the plan's Stage 6 risk line
made checkable: A dials B at an address it learned from `peers.json`, because
that is the only place it could have learned it. B's serve registry is on a root
A cannot read — a cross-machine registry lookup is not stale here, it is
impossible — and B's port is EPHEMERAL, so the number exists in no config file
either. The only path from B's kernel-assigned port to A's dial is the endpoint
B asserted at join time, which is exactly the mechanism the plan specified.

Also asserted, because they are the claims a reader would otherwise take on
faith: the two certificates differ (a fingerprint pinned for one install cannot
authenticate the other); the two one-owner locks are per-root and did not
contend; both stores hold the SAME verifier for one edge; and the secret appears
in neither operator's ack, checked against the stored digest rather than against
the substring "secret", because scrollback is what an attacker over a shoulder
actually reads.

Step 6 is the exclusion at the door an agent on another install would really
reach: the same connection that just pinged is refused `runtime.agent.retire`
with `scope_denied`. Step 7 revokes from B and shows A refused at the door with
A's own row untouched — one-sided, because B could not write into A's store even
if it wanted to.

The honest bound is stated in the module docstring rather than implied: ONE
machine. Every listener binds loopback, which is a config value and not
different code, but "A reached B across a LAN" is unproven and stays Stage 1's
gap.

2 passed in 29s.

message:
docs(gateway): Stage 6 graduates into the canon, and the roster that said TEN had been twelve since Stage 3

Canon 03 gains §1.2 — the peer hello beside the device one: the row shape, the
`pwv` derivation and why the dialer's own install id is in the message, the
counting rule that refuses a frame naming two credentials, the allowlist and why
its arm runs before the read-tier arm, the four verbs, and the endpoints-from-
the-record rule with the acceptance that proves it.

Two corrections made in passing rather than filed. The lane table's credential
and caller-kind rows described a door with one kind of caller behind it; they
now name both. And the `rpc` roster said TEN and listed ten while the runtime
had twelve — Stage 3's `runtime.chat.*` pair reached the manifest and four
literal pins but never this table. It is thirteen now, with the two missing rows
restored and the correction dated in place, because a table that quietly grows
by one is a table nobody can tell was wrong.

The tier section gains the paragraph that keeps the map honest: `peer.ping`
declares `read` and a read-tier device may genuinely call it, because the map
answers what a call WANTS and never what a connection HOLDS. The allowlist
narrows the peer lane; it does not widen that row.

The plan's Stage 6 bullet becomes six receipts, and the notes below it carry
seven deviations with the argument for each — the largest being that "peer tier"
in §4 shipped as a caller KIND with a membership test, on the grounds that a
tier comparison admits every future verb declaring that word while a membership
test admits nothing it was not edited to admit.

The field notes carry what only the build could know: that the shared
`pairing.json` is not tidiness but the only design where a lockout gates
guessing rather than minting; that a symmetric secret needs the install id bound
into the proof or A's answer to B relays as B's answer to A; that the acceptance
had to be two PROCESSES because two threads would have passed while proving the
opposite; and the transcript of the ceremony as it actually ran, with the
verifier absent from every printed ack.

Eight honest gaps, and two of them are worth the operator's attention: "agents
can never mint peers" is closed structurally against remote callers and NOT
against a local agent with shell access, which is stated rather than glossed;
and two roots on one machine both display the hostname, so a `peers list` shows
identical names with only the install id discriminating.

author: nekwo
message:
test(gateway): S6c follow-up — the folded challenge check reordered two refusals, and the new order is the defensible one

Folding four hellos onto one `_challenge` moved the contract check ahead of the
nonce check, and the socket lane's parametrised refusal row caught it: a
`server_hello` carrying `hello_contract: 2` and no nonce used to be refused for
the nonce and is now refused for the contract.

The row moved rather than the code moving back, and the argument is that the new
order is right. A `server_hello` at a contract this client does not speak is a
frame it does not know how to READ. Complaining that a field is missing applies
this contract's field rules to somebody else's frame — and would report "no
usable nonce" for a frame carrying a perfectly good nonce under a name contract
2 happened to choose. The contract is the thing that decides how the rest of the
frame is interpreted, so it is the thing to check first.

The claim the test actually makes is untouched and still asserted: zero bytes
sent to a peer that does not speak this contract, in every case. And a row was
ADDED rather than only edited — a greeting with the right contract and a short
nonce, refused for the nonce — so the reordering is pinned as two sequenced
checks rather than one check that quietly replaced another.

58 passed in the socket lane; 161 across the office/parity/chat suites.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S7a — @install/target, and the rule that keeps every send ever written local

R4 adopted at its recommendation. The grammar's first property is the one that
matters: a target with no `/` in it never reaches the peer resolver, so
`unqualified = local` is a fact about the parser rather than a default somebody
chose — and there is no config, env var or roster lookup that can make a bare
`dev` mean another machine.

The qualifier is a PREFIX because the target half already owns a leading `@`
(instance handles), and a suffix form would put two meanings on one character
in one string. Inside the qualifier the sigil is optional and normalised away,
so a model that writes `@workstation/@personainst_x` out of habit is not
refused for punctuation.

Resolution refuses rather than guesses, and one refusal is Stage 6's own field
note #4 turned into a test: `display_name` defaults to the hostname, so two
roots on ONE machine really do collide, and a name matching two rows comes back
`ambiguous_peer_install` carrying both install ids instead of resolving to
whichever the store iterated first. Ids outrank names everywhere. A revoked row
refuses with its own reason — `dial_peer` would refuse it too, but reaching the
verdict before any work starts is what makes it cost no attempt.

24 tests.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): H1 — a draft records the home it was made in, and the one fact the launcher called unproducible gets a producer

`characters start` now writes `hermes_home = str(get_hermes_home())` into
`draft.json` beside `authored_by`, and the three payloads that carry
`authoredBy` republish it as `hermesHome` — the `start --json` summary,
`status --json`, and every `list --json` draft row. A launcher can observe
which homes it can currently READ a draft in; it could never learn where the
draft was AUTHORED, because nothing recorded it. Now the draft states it.

Unconditional, unlike `authored_by`: there is no caller to withhold it and
nothing to guess. `drafts_dir()` has already resolved `get_hermes_home()` two
statements before the data dict is written and the directory was just created
under it, so the draft IS sitting where the key says. That is hermes stating a
fact about its own filesystem, not a consumer slicing a profile name out of a
path it was handed — the derivation ban binds readers of a home, never the
authority recording where it put the file.

`SCHEMA` stays 1, and the comment that rules the question is extended to name
both provenance fields rather than leaving the argument half-quoted: neither is
copied into the installed manifest, and no consumer must read either to be
correct. Absence is `null` and never `""` — the path-field rule this payload
was already cleaned to follow.

`harness characters backfill-home [--json]` fills in the drafts that predate
the field, and it is a verb rather than a hook on purpose. On LOAD would turn
`characters list` — the launcher's cached polling read — into a disk writer
that races any concurrent mutation for the rest of time. On next MUTATION never
reaches the dormant drafts that ARE the backfill population, and hides a
provenance write inside every unrelated receipt. The verb is bounded to the
moment an operator chose it, and its receipt is the evidence.

Two rules inside `CharacterDraft.record_home()` are load-bearing, and both were
proved by planting their negation and watching the pin red:

  * It never rewrites. A copied or backed-up draft carries its ORIGINAL home,
    and that is the field being honest — "where hermes recorded it" is not
    "where it sits today". Stamping unconditionally reds four tests, including
    idempotence, and would silently rewrite provenance on every run after the
    first.
  * It does not go through `_save()`, which stamps `updated` with "now". The
    drafts this reaches are dormant exhibits whose timeline — and whose
    mis-attributed `authored_by` — is the evidence we keep them for. A
    `_save`-routed write reds exactly the two "left as I found it" pins.

The receipt names directories beside ids because two drafts really can carry
the same `id` (a copy keeps the id inside its own `draft.json`), and an id-only
receipt could not say which directory was written.

WHERE THIS CORRECTS THE PLAN IT WAS CUT FROM. The plan ruled the hermes skill
UNTOUCHED — "no SKILL.md edit → no install-hash cycle owed". That reasons
correctly about the new FIELD, which needs no teaching because `start` writes
it automatically, and not at all about the new VERB in the same strip:
`test_charsheet_skill_documents_exactly_the_characters_verbs_hermes_has` builds
the live argparse tree and pins the skill's verb table to it as a set, in both
directions, precisely so a grown verb cannot land undocumented. The table row
is here, the cycle is owed, and the field notes record the half-right ruling so
the next planner does not inherit it.

Not done here, deliberately: no event at `start` (the draft became
self-describing, not push-announced), nothing in the installed manifest,
nothing on the `CHARSHEET-QA:` line, and the backfill has NOT been run against
any live home — that is its own operational strip, separate so the receipts are
an operator's decision rather than a side effect of landing code.

Gate: scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/test_charsheet_draft.py
tests/hermes_cli/test_harness_characters_cli.py — 181 passed, 0 failed
(168 before this strip; 13 new). Plus, because the verb touched the skill:
tests/agent_runtime/test_persona_skill_policy.py,
tests/agent_runtime/test_skill_publishability.py,
tests/agent_runtime/test_s22_vestigial_parser_flags.py,
tests/agent/test_charsheet_spec.py — 137 passed, 0 failed.

feat(gateway): S7b — the peer surface widens by one verb, and who is asking stops being something a caller can type

`peer.agent_chat.execute` is the second name in PEER_METHOD_ALLOWLIST, and the
widening carries its reason beside it: canon 06 excludes minting and retiring
agents on another install, and a chat turn is on the permitted side of that line
— B runs one of ITS OWN agents, in its own chat store, under its own admission,
and B's operator sees the turn like any other inbound agent message. The whole
level stays excluded.

The security posture is a signature. `normalize_peer_chat_execute` takes
`peer_install_id` as a keyword-only ARGUMENT, never a params key, because the
handler reads it off `context.caller` — a value only an authenticated peer
connection produces. A caller that types `peer_install_id`, `requested_by`,
`install_id` or `caller` gets them all ignored, which is a test rather than a
claim. A correlation token arrives by the other route on purpose: it is
correlation, never identity, and the two facts must not share a door.

Two things the code forced. A non-peer caller is refused with
`peer_identity_required` rather than `scope_denied` — the chokepoint DID admit a
console caller, and it is the verb that has no provenance to run under; a
console client already has `runtime.chat.message`. And the reservation scope
carries the proven install id, because `turn_request_id` is minted on the OTHER
install: two paired installs can legitimately pick the same one, and a replay
answered out of the wrong receipt would hand install C the ack for install A's
turn.

Manifest pins updated in this commit, all ten of them (S6b's lesson). One was
already RED at HEAD: the notification lane's `all(startswith("runtime."))`
assertion has been broken by `peer.ping` since 6775911bbc and nobody ran the
file — re-measured on a stashed tree before editing, corrected to the two
declared families rather than to something permissive.

38 tests on the new lane; 99 across the chat-turn, peer-lane, stream-parity and
notification suites.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S7c — the drain's remote leg, and R8's "converges to dropped" turns out to mean the opposite of what the sender needs

The dispatch row lives on the SENDER, unchanged: written first, settled by
`record_completion`, forged into the sender's chat by the drain. What changes is
one key on the spec — a spec carrying `remote_install_id` is performed by a
peer-tier call instead of by a child process, and the two legs meet again at the
completion, which is the only thing the rest of the lane reads.

The plan says "the drain/executor performs the target's turn"; the code says the
DRAIN tells the sender and the SUPERVISOR performs the turn, so the leg lands
beside the spawn it replaces. Putting it in the drain would have given one
dispatch two owners and put a minutes-long network turn on the 5s loop that also
forges deliveries.

**The R8 deviation, argued in `dispatch_store.REMOTE_UNREACHABLE_REASON`.** R8
says an offline target converges to `dropped`. `dropped` is a DELIVERY state and
means the sender was never told — which is backwards for the one case where what
the sender most needs is the sentence "the other machine is not answering", and
a dropped row is indistinguishable in Activity from a dispatch that evaporated.
So the CAP is R8's, spelled from `MAX_DELIVERY_ATTEMPTS` rather than a second
number, and it converges to a terminal `error` completion that IS delivered,
carrying `peer_unreachable` on the row, in the event and in the sentence.

Transport retries; an answer settles. A dial that failed ran nothing, so it
costs an attempt; an install that ANSWERED with a refusal — unknown persona,
admission, revoked — settles immediately, the same fail-fast rule the delivery
side applies for the same reason (eight identical retries end with the operator
reading "attempts ran out" instead of the verdict). Deterministic refusals about
the peer STORE — unknown name, ambiguous name, revoked row — are answered at
send time, before a row exists.

Retrying is only safe because `turn_request_id` is derived from the dispatch id
rather than minted per attempt: a dial that dies after B accepted presents the
same key, and B's reservation replays instead of running the agent twice.

Two smaller things the code forced. `peer_store_root()` is NOT
`paths.store_root()` — the runtime root resolves through `HERMES_HOME`'s
config, `persona_profile_context` flips that process-globally, and both the send
and the supervisor thread live inside exactly that window; a peer edge belongs to
the install, so it reads under the head home like every other background-work
store. And `ServeSocketClient.set_timeout` exists because R8's bounded DIAL and
the turn's wall budget are different questions on one socket.

author: nekwo
message:
test(gateway): S7d — two roots and a turn between them, and the acceptance found two bugs the unit lane had agreed with

Three tests on two real serve children, reusing Stage 6's `_Install` rather than
growing a second harness. What is proven: the ceremony, the `@install/target`
grammar resolved on A against A's own `peers.json`, `peer.agent_chat.execute`
dialled A→B over B's listener and authorized as caller kind `peer`, the turn's
frames read back to their exit, and B answering `unsupported_persona` /
`unknown persona dev` at exit code 2 — out of ITS OWN empty roster, which is the
proof that the argv reached B's real mission-chat handler in B's runtime. Plus:
the same request id replayed on the real wire, `runtime.chat.message` still
refused `scope_denied` to a peer, a genuinely stopped B converging to
`peer_unreachable`, a revoked edge refused before a row exists, and the
credential absent from every printed surface.

Two bugs it caught, both invisible to a unit test:

**The serve stdout event is `line`, not `stdout`.** Only the ERROR stream is
named after itself (`serve.py:1784`). The reader guessed, collected nothing, and
reported every remote turn as "no reply payload" — and the unit test was GREEN,
because its fake emitted `"stdout"` too. A fake that spells the wire itself can
be wrong in the same direction as the code it tests. Now a named constant, read
BY the fake, with a grep fence against the one line in serve that decides it.

**A replayed accept carries no frames, and waiting for them is a hang.** B's
per-request frames go to the sink of the connection that asked, so when the
retry posture WORKS the retrying socket gets an ack and then silence — the
success path of the property was the thing that hung, for the full 180s. The leg
now settles a `settled` replay from the receipt, says plainly that the answer is
in the thread on the other install, and treats an unsettled one as still-running
and retries.

Honest gaps, stated in the file: one machine (every listener binds loopback,
Stage 1's gap inherited), and no model turn on B — these roots are fresh and
this suite has no provider, so the forge into A's chat is the unit lane's proof
and not this file's.

`_Install.python` grew `*args`, variadic and defaulted, so Stage 6's snippets
behave byte-identically.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S5 — a phone declaring less stops costing the desktop beside it its patch lane

R10 recorded the consequence and assigned the fix here: `accepted_fold_entities`
is the INTERSECTION over every subscriber in the room, so one narrow client
demotes everybody to a full core. Correct while a fan-out could deliver exactly
one shape of a frame — and the shape is what changed.

A batch the room disagrees about now ships as ONE `fold_variants` envelope
carrying the promoted patch and the demoted core together, and each
subscription's pump resolves it against its own declaration on the way to its
own sink. The producer promotes at the UNION; the demotion moves from the room
to the subscriber. No extra build is paid: the core inside the envelope is the
one the intersection rule was already making for everybody.

The gate is a set containment rather than a second coverage rule.
`batch_required_fold_tokens` is `batch_is_patch_coverable` re-expressed as the
set it tests, and the equivalence is pinned over the real event vocabulary
against nine declaration shapes rather than restated in a docstring — the two
would otherwise drift, and every homogeneous test would keep passing while they
did.

Single-subscriber behaviour does not move, and that is a property of two lines
rather than a promise: with one declaration the union and the floor are the same
set, so the split branch has no input that reaches it. Pinned twice — at the
gate (no core is built, proven by monkeypatching the snapshot builder to raise)
and end to end against a real serve_loop.

Two things the wire says differently. The per-connection `subscribed` ack now
answers with THIS client's accepted set, because a joiner can no longer narrow
it; for one subscriber that is the same value, so the byte-pinned launcher
capture does not move. The hydrate keeps echoing the intersection, deliberately:
one frame fanned to N subscribers can only honestly carry the floor, and a
subscriber handed a patch above that floor can fold it by construction.

`test_a_subscriber_declares_what_it_can_fold_and_the_ack_says_what_was_accepted`
asserted the OPPOSITE and the inversion is the fix, not a relaxation: read as a
product sentence, the old assertion said a phone may cost a desktop its patch
lane.

The envelope never reaches a wire. It is resolved at the last moment before each
sink, and a subscriber that declared nothing resolves through the historical set
exactly as the coverage gate reads it — so a lane that never learned to declare
degrades to what it always had rather than to a shape it cannot parse. The
office push lane declares explicitly for that reason.

Acceptance, real serve + two real socket clients + a real event log: one office
write, one producer, one build, two answers — desktop patch 407 B, phone core
7,968 B (19.6x on a test store; the field core is ~1 MB). An uncovered batch
still reaches both as one core.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S5 — a reconnecting client is sent the tail it missed, not the projection it already holds

Stage 2 recorded this gap in its own field notes and left the client half
built: `{"op":"subscribe","lane":"stream"}` took no resume parameter, the hub
restarts its producer so a rejoin's first frame is a hydrate, and the launcher's
remembered watermark could only ever feed its own `>`-gate — it paid for the
~1 MB core and then dropped it. On a desktop that is a rebuild nobody times. On
a phone it is the R7 line: a megabyte on every foreground resume, over WiFi, on
a battery, which is why the plan names watermark resume as the mitigation to
ship BEFORE any snapshot diet.

A resume is now the journal's tail from the client's own position, expressed as
ordinary v2 `patch` frames chained `base_offset`→`watermark`. No new fold
contract, no new frame type, no second projection: a resumed client folds the
same rows it would have folded had it stayed connected.

**The empty span is the point.** A phone that backgrounds for ninety seconds on
a quiet runtime comes back at a watermark that IS the tail, and the honest
answer to "what did I miss" is nothing at all — zero frames, where it used to be
a full core.

The half that took the real thinking: a honoured resume must NOT restart the
producer. A restart re-baselines the room, so a resume that restarted would hand
the client the very hydrate it just proved it did not need and charge every
other subscriber a fresh core for the privilege. `restart_producer=False`
already existed for the office lane, and its docstring names the precondition —
the joiner must not be NARROWING what the room may promote, because a producer
whose floor was frozen at build time keeps emitting BARE patches inside that
floor, and a joiner that folds less answers them with re-hydrates.

So the room is read LIVE, once per drain pass, instead of once per producer
(`stream_frames(fold_room=…)`). The next pass sees the narrowed floor and splits
instead. That also retires a wart the old comment had to accept: a LEAVE could
not re-widen a running producer without restarting it and charging everyone a
core; re-read, a leave re-widens for free. The window that remains is one drain
pass wide — a batch already GATED when a declaration lands can still go out bare
— and it costs one resync and cannot lose an event, because the client's
`base_offset` gate refuses a patch it cannot chain. Written into
`_accepted_fold_entities` rather than left for a reader to find.

Every refusal is NAMED on the ack — `patch_lane_disabled`, `journal_unreadable`,
`journal_truncated`, `watermark_ahead_of_journal`, `backlog_exceeds_cap`,
`span_not_foldable`, `span_without_patch_rows` — because a resume that silently
fell back is indistinguishable from one that worked and cost a megabyte, which
is the false-all-clear class this workstream exists to retire. The full hydrate
is the correct answer in every one of those cases, and it is what arrives.

`journal_truncated` needed a new primitive. `iter_from_offset` is a TAILER: it
skips a slice whose file is missing and yields what remains, which is right for
a tail and exactly wrong for a resume, where a skipped slice is a silent hole in
a span the client is about to fold as contiguous. `resume_floor_offset()` walks
BACKWARDS and answers the start of the earliest slice from which every later one
is present, so a hole raises the floor above it rather than being averaged out.

One assertion the measurement moved. The first draft claimed deleting the live
slice makes the floor `None`. It does not and cannot: once the file is gone, the
bytes that would say how much it held are the bytes that are missing, so the
floor cannot tell "deleted with content" from "not created yet" — and refusing
the latter would make a brand-new install the one runtime that can never resume.
What DOES catch it is the tail, and the test now pins that and names the bound
it leaves.

The ack carries `resume` ONLY when one was asked for, so a subscribe that
predates this parameter is answered byte-identically and the launcher's
byte-pinned `subscribed.json` capture does not move.

Numbers: a two-event span is 429 B against a 7,406 B hydrate on a test store;
the empty span is 0 B. Acceptance runs a real `serve_loop` with a desktop
holding the room open while a phone backgrounds and foregrounds on a NEW
connection — no hydrate is manufactured for it, and the next write arrives as a
patch chaining onto the exact offset it came back with.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve): an argv request now reads the home the serve was booted onto, not whichever persona a prewarm last mirrored into os.environ

Measured 2026-08-27 on the operator's screen. The launcher's serve child was
booted onto profiles\alice and ran its boot actor prewarm over every placed
persona at 20:56:06-20:56:14 — four instances bound to the profile launcher-qa,
the first bind held 11.25 s. A concurrent `harness characters status --draft
20260827-150945-7ba0cb` on the serve's argv lane resolved
profiles\launcher-qa\characters\.drafts and reported a base-authored draft as
nonexistent. Nothing was wrong with the draft; the request was asked to read the
wrong disk.

The mechanism, and the correction to the one we set out with. The prewarm has no
bind site of its own: it builds an AgentRunRequest and rides
ProfileAgentRunner._execute_agent_run, the same body a real chat turn uses,
which enters persona_profile_context with the os.environ mirror on. So the plan
of "make the prewarm bind scope-locally" had nothing to switch, and turning the
mirror off for prewarm_only requests is not sound either: mcp_admission runs its
registrar on a thread it starts itself (mcp-admission) and the cold path from
there spawns. A ContextVar crosses neither a thread nor a spawn, so that mirror
is the only channel by which an admitted MCP server learns which persona home it
serves. Drop it for the prewarm and the prewarmed actor stops byte-matching the
turn that was meant to inherit it — 3 s paid to build something acquire() then
rebuilds. The mirror stays.

So the fix goes to the consumer, where this repo has put it twice already:
core_cache's HC-1 note and chat_live_log's "HERMES_HOME trap" both reach the
same conclusion — resolving through the head is necessary and not sufficient,
because its first authority is a ContextVar and the bleeding thread has none —
and both answer with capture-once at a declared boot instant. The argv lane
simply never got its capture. serve_loop now takes get_hermes_home() beside
capture_fingerprint_home(), the instant that provably precedes every persona
scope in the process, and _run binds it per request through the new
profile_context.process_home_scope. A ContextVar out-ranks the env var in
get_hermes_home()'s ladder, so this lane wins without taking the global away
from the lane that needs it. Chat turns arriving on the same seam are unharmed:
their own persona_profile_context nests over this scope, so only their STARTING
home changes — from whatever another lane last left in the environment to this
serve's own.

Deliberately the runtime home, not the head: under the launcher's
HERMES_HEAD_HOME those are different directories on purpose, and an argv request
belongs to the runtime one.

Red first. test_argv_request_answers_the_serve_home_while_a_persona_bind_holds_
the_env drives the real serve_loop with a dispatch that resolves
agent.charsheet.draft.drafts_dir() — the same four-frames-deep reader the
incident hit — while a thread holds a persona bind with the mirror live. Before
the seam existed it answered
...\profiles\launcher-qa\characters\.drafts instead of ...\profiles\alice\...,
which is the incident verbatim.

Named residue, so the next slice does not assume otherwise: only HERMES_HOME is
pinned; HOME has no context-scoped hook and HERMES_AUTH_HOME's mirror carries
the head auth home rather than a persona's; a subprocess spawned from inside a
request still inherits ambient os.environ. Other unbound threads in this process
remain passengers on the mirror — this fixes the lane that was measured, not the
class. Field notes appended to the charsheet-authoring FIELD-NOTES.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve,mcp): the silent request was a pool with no workers left, and the alternating admission was a wake with no registration

Two defects the W6 Stage C walk measured and could not explain. Both have a
mechanism now, and both mechanisms reproduce in a test rather than needing the
live serve caught in the act.

THE SILENT `characters list`. The request pool is four workers wide and
`harness stream` is an argv request that never returns, so each one holds a
worker for its whole life. The only thing that ever released one was
`{"op":"cancel"}` — sent by a launcher that came BACK. A client that died, or a
socket session that simply closed, left its stream running forever:
`_release_subscription` is the disconnect path and says "A client left.
Unsubscribe it, and do NOTHING else", while `request_control`'s own module
docstring states the opposite as the contract — the stream handler "must release
its worker when its consumer disconnects". Nothing implemented the disconnect
half, and the cancel branch had already priced it: "four watchdog cycles exhaust
the entire serve pool with abandoned streams". So `_on_connection_closed` now
reclaims the departed connection's streams, and nothing else: read-only,
infinite, cooperative — the one shape the cancel path already calls the sole
safe exception. Chat turns and mutations stay uninterruptible.

WHY IT LOOKED LIKE A TRANSPORT FAULT, in two halves. An argv request emits no
frame until its HANDLER writes one, so a request queued behind a full pool is
byte-identical on the wire to a wedged one and to a dead service; the loop now
emits `request_progress` with a `queued`/`running` state on the lane that asked,
once a request has produced nothing for `_REQUEST_SILENCE_SECONDS`. And the
anti-silence liveness pump — written to satisfy the launcher's "no frames for N
seconds" watchdog — only ever emitted to stdout, so an attached socket client
read literally nothing while the pump ran. The drain path had already learned
this and broadcasts through `_broadcast_lanes` with the reason written down; the
pump was left behind. It broadcasts now.

THE 3/0/3/0 MCP ADMISSION. R2 keeps transports warm and tears the registry scope
down per run, so a server can be cached with `session is None` and no registered
tools. `_live_mcp_sessions` called that COLD and handed it to
`register_mcp_servers` on the written belief that it "has dedicated wake handling
for exactly that case". It has a wake and no REGISTRATION: the name is already in
`_servers`, so `new_servers` is empty, so it fires a fire-and-forget
`_signal_reconnect` and returns `_existing_tool_names()` — a stale list of tools
it did not register. The registry stays empty, the honest re-read finds nothing,
the turn admits ZERO and runs with no MCP surface — and the nudge lands a second
later, so the next turn admits everything, and is also the only turn that can
park it again. Two turns doing opposite things is what makes it alternate rather
than settle. `_default_registrar` now wakes parked servers itself — nudges all,
then waits on ONE bounded budget so N servers reconnect in parallel and the
admission cannot outrun its own `connect_timeout_seconds` — and routes whatever
comes back through the warm path. Whatever does not falls through to cold
exactly as before: this widens nothing.

Red-first, and the planted defects are named in each file. The serve tests
observed the real red: 20s of frames carrying no request id at all, and a socket
`recv` timing out with the serve busy. `test_a_parked_server_is_treated_as_cold`

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S8a — a picture gets a name that is its bytes, and the path stops being the only thing a client can hold

A chat image reaches an operator as a `MEDIA:<absolute path>` line inside the
message TEXT. There is no media field on any chat record, no blob store under
the runtime root, and no content address for a binary file anywhere in this
repo. So a launcher rendering a message from a runtime on another machine
reaches for `File(path)` and paints "Not on this machine".

`agent_runtime/media_handles.py` is the other end of that. A handle is
`sha256:<64 hex>` over the CONTENT, so a client cache keyed on it needs no
invalidation protocol; the grammar check runs on the raw argument, so a
path-shaped one is refused before any `stat`, `open` or `Path()` happens — there
is no traversal surface because there is no step that turns caller input into a
path. The lookup can only answer with something the derivation already put in
the set.

The scope is DERIVED, not registered. It is rebuilt from the chat live-log
mirror — the greppable projection of the transcripts that already exists — so
there is no second copy of the fact to drift, and the digest memo is keyed on
`(path, size, mtime_ns)` so a rewritten file mints a new handle rather than
serving the old one's bytes.

Two bounds beyond reachability, both argued in-file. `MEDIA:` is a line the
MODEL writes, so reachability alone would make `MEDIA:~/.ssh/id_rsa` an
exfiltration primitive: the extension allowlist makes that unrepresentable, and
the honest cost is that video and PDF are not in the namespace at all — the
largest MEDIA-delivered artifact on this machine is a 1.1 GB MP4. And the cap is
5 MiB because `gateway/platforms/api_server.py` already answered this exact
question for this exact protocol; measured here first: 428 Stage-C screenshots,
median 351,423 B, largest 2,146,781 B, whole image corpus topping out at
2,722,628 B. Nothing needs ranging, so none is built.

Verified against the live corpus rather than only fixtures: 46 mirrors, 17
declarations, 6 artifacts, and the largest handle is hash-equal to
`sha256sum` of the file on disk (1,138,544 B).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S8b — the fetch family lands, and the tier is the row where the one-line rule does not decide it

`runtime.media.index` and `runtime.media.get`, both `console`, plus the nine
manifest pins the set-plus-integer rule makes a same-commit obligation and a
real-serve acceptance over TLS.

TWO verbs and the second is not a convenience. A chat image reaches a client as
a `MEDIA:<absolute path>` line inside a message body, so the only pointer the
client holds is a PATH — and a path is what this lane refuses. Something has to
carry a client from what it holds to a handle it may spend, and the alternative
was rewriting every stream frame's text server-side: moving the stream contract
for every client on every lane to solve a problem only a remote one has. So the
index answers with the artifacts in scope, each carrying the reference the
client already rendered AND the handle it may send. A path travels out — it was
already ours to see — and never in.

The tier is `console` for both, and this is the row where "a level MUTATION is
console, everything else is read" does not decide it. Neither verb mutates
anything. But the read arm is deliberately open to `unknown` — a caller the
transport authenticated and could not place — and that is exactly the caller who
must not be able to pull files off the disk; handing over raw bytes is an
EGRESS, not a read of the level. A `read` device is a viewer of the level, not a
subscriber to every proof screenshot on the machine. `test_serve_rpc_media.py`
proves the ordering rather than asserting it: the derivation is monkeypatched to
explode, and an unknown caller never reaches it.

PEER_METHOD_ALLOWLIST was NOT touched, so Stage 6's iterated registry test
excluded both verbs the moment they registered — the exclusion holding by
construction, which is what that test asserts about the rule rather than about
two names. Cross-install media stays an open row.

The acceptance runs the real `serve_loop` with the second listener up, a real
TLS handshake with a real certificate pin, and a real HMAC over a real paired
credential: a `console` device indexes, joins on the reference, fetches, and the
received bytes are sha256-equal to the file on disk. The refusals are proven on
the same wire — the artifact's own absolute path sent as a handle, a traversal
string, a guessed digest, an over-cap artifact answered with the cap NAMED, a
`read` device refused the whole family, and an unpaired caller whose connection
is dead before the dispatcher exists.

One gate caught a real duplicate: `media_handles`' mtime helper was
`repo_context._safe_mtime` under another name, so it is folded onto a new
`paths.safe_mtime` and repo_context now calls the same authority. The gate was
right; the fold is the fix it prescribes.

hermes tests/agent_runtime: 6921 passed, 2 skipped before this commit's own
suites; the media three add 44.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

message:
docs(gateway): S8 canon and the survey that changed the design

Canon 03 gets §2.1 — the fetch family, why it is two verbs, and the sentence
that carries the security argument: a reference travels OUT and never IN. The
method table grows to sixteen rows, and the tier prose gets the row where the
one-line classification rule does not decide the answer.

The field notes carry the discovery step the brief made part of the stage, and
two of its findings changed what shipped. There is no media field on any chat
record and no blob store under the runtime root, so a client holds a PATH and
cannot compute a content handle — which is why the family is index + get rather
than get alone. And reachability alone is not a sufficient scope rule, because
`MEDIA:` is a line the MODEL writes: without an extension allowlist a model that
typed `MEDIA:~/.ssh/id_rsa` would have written an exfiltration primitive into a
chat log.

machine, every listener on loopback.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(atlas): a pose severed into slabs is one subject again, and auto stops raising on judgement calls

A live charsheet row died on "row 'walk-se' produced no sliceable strip in 3
attempts; last failure: frame 3 contains multiple separated subjects". Two
cached artifacts reproduce it exactly.

Measured, the briefed cause is wrong: nothing drew a seam and the chroma key cut
nothing. The keyed strip has exactly 8 connected components, one whole pose each.
The severing is ours. The gutter path crops a pose into a ~221px column, and
_isolate_slot_subject runs _erase_long_axis_lines on it -- a helper that deletes
thin rows spanning >=85% of the image as drawn floors/dividers. Sound against a
1774px strip; destructive against a narrow single-pose slot where the character's
own body spans the width. It deleted rows 426 and 450-451 and cut the pose into
three slabs 1px and 2px apart.

_merge_related_boxes had only the horizontal rule (overlap vertically, hairline
gap horizontally) for capes and props, so stacked slabs with near-total x-overlap
stayed three subjects. Add the mirror: h_overlap >= min_w * 0.45 and
y_gap <= max(14, min_h * 0.22), same fixpoint loop. Both artifacts now yield 8
frames, each one subject at full pose height.

Worth recording: the >=3 guard was catching the worst frames, not the defect.
Every frame in both artifacts was severed -- most into 2 slabs, which sailed
through as half-poses. The row that failed loudly was the lucky one.

Second, honor the contract. _validate_extracted_frames ran unconditionally, so
method="auto" -- documented in both call sites as the lenient last attempt that
never raises -- raised anyway, promoting one flaky roll to a dead row. It now
takes strict=, and extract_strip_frames passes strict=(method == "components").
Only the two judgement-call checks downgrade to a logged warning; wrong frame
count and empty frame still raise under both methods, because best-effort must
never mean installing blank cells. This also closes a door nobody had hit:
compose_draft_frames re-slices already-approved strips with method="auto".

The three "never raises" docstrings/comments were right about intent and wrong
about reality; they now say what the code does. No logic changed in pipeline.py
or orchestrate.py.

test_a_row_that_never_becomes_sliceable_fails_loudly needed NO adjustment: its
blank strip is all-magenta, which keys to nothing and still trips the HARD empty
check, so the gate's spirit holds unmodified.

Note the new tests live in tests/agent/test_pet_generate.py, which is skipped
unless HERMES_RUN_SLOW_PET_TESTS=1 -- that is where atlas coverage already lives,
but it means this guard does not run in a default suite.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(atlas): a drawn floor is a strip-scale fact, so stop asking a single-pose crop about it

Follow-up to 6015912064, which repaired the subject COUNT for a severed pose but
left the damage in place: the rows were still deleted, so accepted frames carried
transparent scanlines through the character, and compose re-slices saved strips.

_erase_long_axis_lines deletes thin rows spanning >=85% of the image, to kill
floors and panel dividers. That test means what it says against a ~1700px strip.
_isolate_slot_subject was running it on a ~220px single-pose crop, where "spans
85% of the image" describes the character's own shoulders, belt or outstretched
arms. It was deleting body rows.

Hoist the erase to strip scale: _isolate_slot_subject no longer calls it, and
extract_strip_frames calls it once on the whole strip at the moment it falls off
the clean path -- lazily, since it is a full per-pixel pass the happy path should
not pay for. Both slot-cutting routes consume that cleaned strip, so a genuine
floor is still removed, once, at the only scale where the question is answerable.

Chose caller-hoisting over the two alternatives. An explicit erase_lines= flag
would be dead weight: both callers of _isolate_slot_subject are slot-scale, so
every call site would pass False forever. An aspect/width threshold would be a
magic number guessing at what the caller already knows for certain. This is the
caller deciding -- it just decides once, at the top, while the strip still exists.

Measured on the two cached artifacts, interior transparent rows inside each pose
bbox: _81776461.png 12 rows across 5 of 8 frames -> 0; _76c03b99.png 15 rows
across 4 of 8 frames -> 0. Frame 3 of the first listed rows 426, 450, 451 -- the
exact rows named when the mechanism was first diagnosed.

Worth recording: the defect was not only scanlines. When the erased row falls
near one end of a pose the smaller slab drops below the keep threshold and is
discarded as noise, so the pose loses its head and the frame closes up around the
loss -- undetectable by a hole check. A synthetic frame came out 23px shorter
than its neighbours with no scanline at all, so the test asserts uniform pose
height too.

The floor-erase behaviour this must preserve had NO coverage; it has two tests
now. The seam fixture from the previous commit keeps its merge coverage but its
docstring no longer implies the live mechanism was a provider seam -- it was
ours. A genuine keyed seam remains possible, which is why that fixture stays.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(atlas): a wide band is a floor only where it crosses background, not wherever it is thin

21e3dc13b6 hoisted the line erase to strip scale and closed with a corollary: if
a provider draws the same wide feature at the same height in all eight poses, we
erase it and are right to. A compose run produced exactly that within the hour
and we were wrong to. The installed sheet had transparent scanlines in the two SE
rows and nowhere else.

Measured on the source strips: idle-se has wide-row runs (485,489) and (522,613);
walk-se has (386,390) and (394,429). In both, the thin band that got erased sits a
few rows above a thick band that did not -- one continuous silhouette, not a line
near a body. At a diagonal the chin/shoulder contour aligns across all eight
poses; head-on it does not, which is why only the diagonals can produce this. The
s-row control has a single 85-row run and no gaps.

So coverage-thinness cannot discriminate a floor from anatomy: they are the same
measurement. The discriminator is what the band is embedded in. A drawn floor
crosses the BACKGROUND between poses; aligned anatomy has body directly above and
below every column, being the silhouette's own widest row.

_erase_long_axis_lines now locates a band by width exactly as before, then erases
only columns whose local vertical context (3px) is empty, judged against the
ORIGINAL mask -- if context were read from the partly-erased image, the first
column cleared would make its neighbour look like background and the erase would
unzip along the row. Measured separation: idle-se 1320/1342 columns body-context
(98.4%), walk-se 1857/1871 (99.3%), a synthetic drawn floor 0/1664 (100%
background-crossing). The populations do not overlap; this is not a tuned
threshold.

Chose this over the segmentation-only design (erase as mask, crop frames from the
unerased strip) because that one was measured not to work: a floor touching the
feet makes the whole strip ONE component and the slot crop ONE component, so
nothing is detached and the floor survives into every frame. It would trade a
scanline for a bar across every cell.

Accepted residue: a floor's stub under a pose's own feet has body above it and is
kept. It merges into the pose it touches and bridges nothing, so segmentation is
unaffected. That is the price of never cutting anatomy again.

Real data, interior transparent rows inside the pose bbox: idle-se 4 rows in all
6 frames -> 0; walk-se 4 rows in all 8 frames -> 0; pose heights unchanged, no
beheading. Both walk-se cache artifacts from the earlier commits still yield 8
whole-pose frames with 0 scanlines.

The floor guard is rewritten to test the PURPOSE rather than the mechanism: the
floor must stop welding the row into one blob (components 1 -> >=8) and clear the
gutter between poses, not delete every floor pixel -- which is no longer true and
should not be.

message:
docs(realm-sync): realm-skill-delete staged plan — surveyed, rulings adopted, ready to build

Fable-scoped 2026-08-28: skills currently have NO deletion propagation in
realm sync (pull auto-adopts anything the realm holds that is missing
locally, and reinstalls the canonical set from repo source). The plan lifts
the deleted_workspace_ids tombstone precedent onto skills: an additive
skill_tombstones ledger on the realm record, enforced at pull (archive the
adopted canonical copy), publish (never emit a tombstoned slug), and the CLI
(skills delete / skills restore). No backend or git-host involvement: the
GitHub App mints repo-scoped write tokens before bytes exist, github.com has
no pre-receive for App pushes, and the behind-fence -> pull-applies-ledger ->
publish-filter chain closes the hole client-side on every lane, local realms
included. All seven rulings adopted as recommended (R-D = LWW v1, S4 gated
off); the operator's why-not-just-delete challenge is answered in §3.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(realm): S1 — the skill-delete ledger, and why a slug needs a record where an id needed only a set

Workspaces have had a first-class delete since deleted_workspace_ids: a
bare-id set, written at one store chokepoint, carried in the realm JSON so a
member's surviving copy neither lingers nor republishes it. Skills had
nothing — delete one locally, pull, and the realm's still-published copy walks
back in through the promotion door as promote_new.

This is that guard lifted to skills, with the one place the lift cannot be
verbatim spelled out: workspace ids are freshly minted, so a bare-id ledger
can never block a legitimate re-creation, while skill slugs are re-creatable
NAMES. So the entries are records (SkillTombstone: slug, deleted_at,
deleted_hash) and the block is absolute until an explicit verb lifts it —
deleted_hash is receipts, never an authority to auto-admit a same-name
package.

- Realm.skill_tombstones, additive at schema_version 1 (a bump refuses every
  older member's realm load); bounded by SKILL_TOMBSTONE_LEDGER_CAP=200.
- RealmStore.tombstone_skill / restore_skill, the two write chokepoints, with
  the set_skill_selection discipline (validate, save(emit_event=False), then
  realm.updated with a change code; dry_run returns the would-be realm).
- Typed refusals through SkillTombstoneRefused, WorkspaceDeleteBlocked's
  shape: skill_slug_invalid, and skill_installer_owned because every pull
  reinstalls CANONICAL_SHARED_SKILL_IDS from repo source — a ledger entry for
  one of those loses that argument on every pull, so the door names the real
  delete lane instead of minting a tombstone that silently does nothing.
- store.skill_tombstoned is the ONE match rule (exact slug, or a categorized
  slug's bare child name), mirroring _skill_slug_selected: the selection and
  the tombstone must agree about what a name means, or a slug can be
  simultaneously "selected" and "not the thing that was deleted". Tombstoning
  prunes the slug from skill_selection through that same rule; restore does
  not re-add it.
- skill_promotion._validate_slug gains its public name (validate_skill_slug,
  private alias kept for in-module callers) so a delete and a promotion share
  one alphabet rather than re-spelling it.

Enforcement (pull archive, publish filter) is S2; the operator verbs are S3.
A tombstone minted today already travels in the realm JSON and already blocks
nothing — that is deliberate staging, not a half-built fence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(realm): S2 — the delete reaches the copy git cannot see, and the fence closes at three points

A push already deletes the bytes: publish is a full-subtree replace, so the
deleter's push removes the file and every member's pull removes it from their
clone. What git cannot reach is the ADOPTED copy in each member's canonical
skills root — not a git file — and that copy rides the member's next publish
straight back into the realm. S1 minted the instruction git absence cannot
carry; this stage is the three places that obey it.

- Pull, inbox half: the mirror drops a package the ledger blocks from its
  desired set, so a stale publisher's copy is pruned exactly like a removed
  one and the promotion loop never sees it — a tombstoned slug can never
  auto-adopt. Reported as SkillSyncSummary.tombstoned (additive key; the
  launcher sheet is absent-tolerant per the store_drift precedent).
- Pull, canonical half: _apply_skill_tombstones ARCHIVES the local package to
  .archive/<ts>/<slug> rather than deleting it. The workspace twin
  hard-deletes; this lane cannot, because "never delete — archive" is the
  skills root's own standing invariant and a skill package is always
  operator/agent-authored content, i.e. always evidence. It also makes
  restore-with-content a two-step verb instead of a data-recovery incident.
  Per-slug isolation, installer-owned skipped with a typed warning, and the
  provenance sidecar left in place (provenance is history, not liveness).
- Publish: _skill_artifacts drops a tombstoned slug beside the selection
  filter. Normally redundant — the pull already archived the copy — but a
  package re-materialized out of band must not travel, and the comment carries
  the chain that argues no server-side hook is needed: sync_behind refusal →
  pull → ledger → archive → the retried publish cannot include it.
- Status + sidecar gain the ledger as receipt rows, read back
  absent-tolerantly.

Two places the plan was wrong about the code, followed the code:

- Filtering the mirror by TOP-LEVEL package would take a category's innocent
  siblings with it (the mirror's only notion of a package is rel_parts[0],
  which for a categorized skill is the category dir). _subtree_package_slug
  answers with the same package-shape rules the promotion door and the
  publisher use, and the filter is per package.
- Walking the ledger to find canonical dirs is a SECOND spelling of the match
  rule. The canonical half walks the publishable packages and asks
  skill_tombstoned instead, so the archive and the publish filter cannot
  disagree about what a name means.

And one ordering fix the plan half-anticipated: pull_realm_sync's realm is read
before the overwrite loop that rewrites the realm JSON, so the skill lane now
re-reads it. Without that, a freshly arrived tombstone would be mirrored,
adopted and archived inside one pull.

Verified two-HERMES_HOME against a bare repo: A publishes 'doomed', B adopts
it, A deletes + publishes, B's pull archives B's live copy (resolver misses,
ledger carries A's own deleted_hash), and B's next publish carries no
skills/doomed path. Transcript and the pre-existing .gitattributes pull
collision it surfaced are in the field notes.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(realm): S3 — the delete becomes a verb, and the receipt names every realm the name reached

S1 built the ledger and S2 made it bite on pull and publish, but nothing could
mint a tombstone except a Python one-liner. This is the operator surface: two
verbs, typed refusals, and receipts that are data rather than prose.

`hermes harness skills delete <slug> [--realm ...] [--dry-run]` resolves the
target realms, records the tombstone at the store chokepoint, archives the local
canonical package, and prunes the realm's inbox mirror.
`hermes harness skills restore <slug> --realm <id>` lifts exactly one ledger
entry and — because R-C keeps content out of it — names the archived copy and
the promote command that re-admits its bytes. `realm skills show` gains the
additive `tombstones` array, the same rows the sync status envelope and the
sidecar already carry.

Four places where the plan's §4 text and the code disagreed, and the code won:

- **"currently publishes the slug" (R-E) is two different questions.** Mode
  `all` publishes whatever the canonical root HOLDS, so such a realm publishes
  the slug exactly when a local package is covered by it — otherwise a bare
  `skills delete ghost` would tombstone every mode-`all` realm on the box for a
  name nothing has. Mode `selected` NAMES the slug, which is a standing
  statement that holds with no local copy. Resolved the way `_skill_artifacts`
  resolves it, because that is what publishing means on this machine.
- **`archived_to` / `deleted_hash` cannot describe a bare-name delete.** The
  match rule is one-to-many by construction (an entry `foo` covers a top-level
  `foo` AND a categorized `bar/foo`), so the receipt carries an `archived` array
  as the truth and keeps the two scalars as the single-package convenience.
- **`selection_pruned` is a list, not a bool** — a bool cannot say WHICH
  selection entry a bare-name tombstone took, and R-F prunes through that same
  one-to-many rule. `refreshed` rides beside it so a repeat delete is legible as
  a refresh rather than reading like a first write.
- **the inbox mirror is unlinked, not archived.** Never-delete protects AUTHORED
  content; the inbox is a byte-faithful cache rebuilt from the subtree on every
  pull, and the mirror already unlinks a package the realm stopped publishing.
  The canonical copy is the authored one, and that is what gets archived.

`skill_unknown` stays a warning inside a successful envelope (§3): a tombstone
records INTENT, so naming a realm explicitly records one even with no local copy
— reported as the distinct `skill_no_local_package`, because "nothing was
archived" and "nothing was written at all" are different answers. Restore reads
`restored` from the ledger BEFORE the write and asks for the EXACT slug, since
that is the entry the store removes; a bare-name entry that merely COVERS the
slug gets its own `skill_still_tombstoned` warning rather than being silently
left standing under a receipt that says "restored".

Two helpers got their public name (the `validate_skill_slug` / `_validate_slug`
idiom S1 established) so the CLI re-spells nothing:
`store.skill_tombstone_matches` — the match rule asked in the direction this
verb must ask it, holding a candidate entry slug with no ledger yet, and the
same rule the SELECTION uses by S1's design — and
`realm_sync.skill_tombstone_rows`, so one ledger has one receipt shape.
`skill_slug_invalid` / `skill_installer_owned` join the exit taxonomy at
family 2: the fault is in the request, and the installer-owned door names the
constant plus the repo source rather than a ledger every pull would overrule.

25 CLI cases, all driving the real argparse tree through `args.func`. Live smoke
against a scratch LOCAL realm in a throwaway HERMES_HOME — delete, `realm skills
show`, publish (the subtree loses the package), restore, re-restore — with the
transcript and the running record in the field notes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

operator watched 18 minutes of tool rows with no images, read the silence
as a freeze, and got no cards at the end -- while the pipeline itself had

author: nekwo
message:
fix(charsheet): the QA crop follows the poses, not the even slots

`characters thumb` wrote a 272x724 crop of `walk-e` attempt 1 with half a
character in it. The strip had two boundary rules and the QA surface was
reading the wrong one: `pipeline.frame_cell` divided the strip width by the
frame count, while the real extraction (`atlas.extract_strip_frames`) has
always been content-aware precisely because even slots are wrong on real
strips. On that 2172x724 8-frame row the first pose spans x 66-298 and the
even boundary falls at 272, so the crop stopped 26 columns into the body and
the cut edge stood as a 205px column flush against the frame's right side.
Six of the eight frames were severed.

`atlas.frame_x_bounds` now exports the frame boundary as a value, running
`method="auto"`'s own order: gutters merged down to the frame count, thin
severs at the expected boundaries when poses touch, even slots only when
there is no content to read. `frame_cell` crops the SOURCE at those bounds,
so an operator still sees the provider's pixels rather than keyed, isolated
and re-fitted ones. The strip is decoded once. `extract_strip_frames` is
untouched. Full strip height is kept, and the docstring now says why the
asymmetry is deliberate: a frame boundary can be read off the pixels, a
subject's top and bottom cannot.

Four existing tests asserted the defect - two spelled `round(width / frames)`
into a size assertion, two cleared the console budget only because the old
cell was a whole slot wide. Size assertions cannot see this class of defect,
so the new tests read pose mass per column, on a fixture built from the real
strip's measured pose ranges and on the shipped strip itself.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): thumb --square, so the hero card shows the whole frame

The console card is a fixed 1:1 centre-cover square (SKILL.md 13.17, ruled: the
card is not moving) and a character cell is taller than it is wide, so the
default QA crop renders there as a torso zoom. Stage 4a of the turn-efficiency
plan fixes it from the hermes side: `--square` pads the FINISHED crop onto a
square field of the same flat dark backdrop (side = the longer edge, cell
centred) via a new `pipeline.pad_to_square`, one step after
`upscale_on_backdrop` and downstream of the content-aware frame geometry, which
it does not touch.

The pad is the one step in the looking procedure that cannot remove a pixel; it
runs last so nothing already keyed or NEAREST-upscaled is resampled again, and
it takes the upscale's own backdrop because a second ground colour in one
picture reads as a second image.

Both budget booleans are weighed on the PADDED output, because padding raises
the pixel count and the file a consumer decodes is the padded one. A square crop
can therefore be refused at the default scale where the bare crop of the same
cell passes; the refusal names the padded size and the escape, since arguing
about the unpadded size would be arguing about a file nobody asked for. The
write ceiling is checked before the square field is allocated.

Filename gains `-sq` so both shapes can sit in `thumbs/` at once; the payload
gains `square` unconditionally (a consumer choosing where to draw cannot infer
the shape from a filename, and the default is a shape too). Default stays tall:
a compare pair's panes align on today's shapes.

Measured on the real 2172px 8-frame walk-e strip: bare 508x1448, square
1448x1448, margins 470px each side, the interior window byte-identical to the
bare crop, margins pure QA_BACKDROP, content h-centre 724.0 against an image
centre of 724.0.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): the payloads name their own next verb

Stage 4b of the turn-efficiency plan. Measured cause: the fire-imp one-shot
spent `characters --help` plus six per-verb `--help`s working out which verb
came next and how to spell it, and every one of those is a full API round-trip
that re-sends the whole turn context — 60-120k prompt tokens each, late in a
heavy turn. The verb table answers all of it, but only for a caller that has the
skill in context, and the persona that ran it did not.

So the payloads answer it themselves. `next` is `{verb, cmd}` — a COMMAND, not a
verb name, because a bare name still costs a `--help` to turn into a command
line, which is the round-trip being removed. Spelled with the `hermes`
entrypoint the skill teaches rather than `python -m hermes_cli.main`: both
resolve, but the long one is noise in every trace row and the operator trace
truncates at 500 chars.

Three arms, and each reads STATE rather than a plan:

* `start` -> `turnaround`, except a draft started without `--base-image` (the
  CS-5 repair shape), which is pointed at `base --image <image>` instead —
  `turnaround` refuses without the anchor, and a hint naming a verb the draft
  would refuse costs exactly the round-trip this key exists to save. This is the
  one deliberate refinement over the plan's table.
* `approve-direction` -> `rows`, only when the approval ADVANCED the stage. A
  hint disagreeing with the `advanced: false` beside it is a payload arguing
  with itself.
* a failed `rows` -> `reroll-row --row <the row it died on>`, with the resume
  `rows --only <the rows that never landed>` as `alternatives[0]`. The rows come
  off the draft's own pending list — not off the error text, which is a grammar
  that drifts from the message — intersected with what the call asked for, so a
  caller who ran `--only walk-e` is never handed a resume naming rows they never
  wanted. `_characters_verb` grew an `on_error` hook for this, and the hook
  cannot break the refusal it rides on: if reading the draft fails, the flat
  error shape still travels.

Additive keys only (the payloads are ruled supersets, SKILL.md:206-208). A verb
with no next step OMITS `next`; a refusal with no pending-row story still
carries exactly `ok`, `error`, `draft`, `stage`, which is what a shipped
launcher panel parses. `compose`'s refusal already hands its verb in prose and
is left as it stands.

The failed-`rows` test drives a draftsman that returns a bare chroma field, so
`generate_row_strip` genuinely exhausts its three attempts and raises — stubbing
the raise would have tested the hint against a failure shape the code cannot
produce.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(process): the mission-chat lane waits 600s, every other lane is untouched

`ProcessRegistry.wait` clamped every requested timeout to TERMINAL_TIMEOUT
(180s) lane-agnostically. The 2026-08-29 charsheet turn-efficiency measurement
priced that: wait-polling was 12 of 27 API calls on the fire-imp authoring turn
(~690k of its 1.556M cumulative prompt tokens) and 8 of 13 on a lean staged
turn, because a generation verb runs 1-2 minutes per image and a 10-strip batch
runs 10-20 minutes. The agent that asked for 600s was silently clamped to 180.

The ceiling now comes from `wait_ceiling_seconds`: TERMINAL_TIMEOUT as before,
raised with max() to MISSION_CHAT_WAIT_MAX_SECONDS (600) only when the run's
terminal envelope scope names the mission-chat lane. Lane-scoped because the
plan names a blanket TERMINAL_TIMEOUT raise a non-goal -- no other lane's turn
budget was measured -- and reading the envelope's ContextVar makes "no other
lane changes" structural rather than conventional. A configured value above
600s is never lowered. The existing timeout_note is kept verbatim in shape.

The 1800s turn wall, not this clamp, remains the guard on a runaway wait.

Stage 3a of docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/charsheet-turn-efficiency-2026-08-29.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(process): process notify — fire the verb, end the turn, get the receipt on exit

An agent that fires a 10-20 minute generation had no exit-driven wake-up: the
only way to learn a background process finished was to keep asking, and every
ask costs a full re-sent context (~60-120k prompt tokens on a heavy turn). The
runtime already proved the shape this needs on the dispatch lane -- background
completes, a new turn arrives carrying the receipt -- but it watched persona
replies, not processes.

`process` gains `action: "notify"`. It records {turn_id, session_id,
persona_instance_id} plus the chat root in a durable drain file beside
processes.json (tools/process_notify_store.py, resolved through the one
background-work home authority the checkpoint and the dispatch store already
share). On exit, `_move_to_finished` reads the row and publishes the completion
onto the SAME completion_queue the serve delivery drain has always consumed, so
`dispatch_delivery.drain_background_completions` forges the delivery turn --
one delivery road, not a parallel one. Routing rides `origin_ui_session_id`,
the key that drain resolves a chat root from first.

The four edges, each pinned by test:
* already exited at notify time -> the completion is queued immediately, and an
  explicit notify outranks `_drain_should_skip` so an inline read cannot swallow
  the wake-up;
* never exits -> nothing is delivered and NO timer is invented; the turn
  wall/budget system is the guard, and an agent that prefers to block is bounded
  by the Stage 3a wait ceiling;
* duplicate notify -> idempotent by session id, one row and one delivery;
* the requesting persona instance retired (or the thread re-owned) -> the row is
  dropped with a logged line and the reaper survives, per the positive-ownership
  rule the delivery lane already holds. A store fault degrades to "nobody asked".

The delivered block is self-contained for the same reason
format_dispatch_delivery is: the turn reading it is a new turn.

Stage 3b of docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/charsheet-turn-efficiency-2026-08-29.md
(owner ruling R-2).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(process): an evicted notify promise is logged, never silent

The drain file's MAX_NOTIFY_ROWS ceiling evicted settled rows first and pending

an agent that ended its turn to wait for a receipt, so losing one quietly is the
exact failure class this lane exists to retire. It now leaves a WARNING naming
