author: nekwo
message:
docs(skills): charsheet SKILL.md restructured to a 19.7k head + six references

Stage 2 of planned/charsheet-turn-efficiency-2026-08-29.md. The measurement
that forces this: the fire-imp one-shot spent 26 of 36 tool elements on
rediscovery, repo archaeology, redundant probes and wait-polling, and the reply
contract it then violated sits at SKILL.md:604+ — in the tail two 300-line
read windows never reached. Length was not only a token cost; it defeated
consumption.

SKILL.md 51,924 -> 19,712 chars (794 -> 292 lines), in the plan's order:

1. A new turn-zero card: the skill is already in context (never re-read it or
   FIELD-NOTES.md from disk, never `--help` a verb), this is not a repo task,
   the entrypoint is bare `hermes`, HERMES_HOME is already rebound so never
   export it, ONE preflight pair run ONCE, the wait cadence, and the batch
   patterns the fire-imp run got right (ten thumbs in one command,
   `approve-direction --all && rows`).
2. The verb table, moved up.
3. The reply contract — MEDIA / CHARSHEET-QA / clarify chips — compressed to
   the shapes plus one-line reasons, now in the first half of the file.
4. Refusal reading and the handedness operative rules, tightened.
5. Pointers to references/, each with its when-to-open trigger.

The wait-cadence bullet is written against the process-exit delivery build
landing concurrently (notify-and-end-turn preferred, `timeout: 600` when
blocking anyway) and carries a bracketed note so the text stays honest if that
build is reverted.

Zero canon loss, proved line by line: 698 of the old file's 700 non-empty lines
appear verbatim in the new package. The two that do not are deliberate —
line 36's `hermes` == `python -m hermes_cli.main` equivalence, dropped from the
head per the plan because agents copied the long spelling into every trace row
and preserved verbatim as a restricted-shell footnote in
references/homes-and-migration.md; and the `sprite` table row's "see below",
now "see above" because the rule it pointed at moved into the turn-zero card.

Six references beside the file, all verbatim moves:
homes-and-migration (the three-probe preflight + migrate-home lore),
payloads-and-growth (stage refusals, attempt numbering, payload shapes,
add-state), looking-procedure (with the FIELD-NOTES provenance paragraph that
used to head the file and invited the disk read), handedness (the measurement

feat(realm-sync): office store drift in status envelope

author: nekwo
message:
docs(planned): realm-sync writes that never reach a live projection

Read-only investigation of a reported realm-pull projection failure on the
operator's machine. The reported premise is falsified with three independent
measurements (sidecar last_pull=null, newest realm.sync.pulled is 2026-07-19,
and the instance's own office events carry the launcher's g-place/g-office
gesture correlation ids) -- the agent was created locally and published
outbound, not pulled.

The same read proved four real defects and stages them:
- apply_office_pull's WRITE_REMOTE arm writes raw JSON and emits nothing while
  its ARCHIVE arm goes through OfficeStore and does emit (office_sync.py:414 vs
  :443);
- _delta_touches_workspace returns False for realm.sync.pulled/.published, so
  the office subscribe lane is never resynced by a realm sync
  (serve_office_subscriptions.py:329-342, early return at :457);
- the parity drop SAMPLE is FIFO-capped at 50 and starved by by_design records,
  so the live 'projection drops 1' (session_not_in_db) chip carries no rows;
- two live serve children share one store, the older owning the socket.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-sync): the realm pull's adopt arm emits, like its archive arm always did

H1 of docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/realm-pull-live-projection.md.

apply_office_pull built an OfficeStore and used it only for reads: the
PullAction.WRITE_REMOTE arm and the surface arm were raw atomic_json_write
calls, so a pull that ARCHIVED a desk (store.remove_actor) reached every live
consumer and a pull that GAVE you one reached none — no office.actor.upserted,
no state.patched, nothing for the office subscribe lane or the patch fold.

Neither existing store verb could take the write: upsert_actor renumbers the
revision, re-canonicalizes the actor key, and spends three fences that exist to
refuse LOCAL authoring intent (the duplicate-desk one documents the pull as
deliberately outside it); update_surface refuses a workspace with no local
record, which is exactly the workspace a pull delivers. So this adds two verbs
that write a peer's record verbatim — adopt_remote_surface / adopt_remote_actor
— under the store's lock and through the store's emitters, the shape
resolve_conflict(take="remote") already uses.

Preserved and tested: the adopted revision is the REMOTE's, updated_by records
the sync (hash-neutral — office_content_hash excludes it), and the baseline
stays keyed off the remote content hash so the next pull is still a NOOP.

The class-key carve-out (task #33) MOVES with the write and stays open: its
entry in the one-fence witness is re-keyed to adopt_remote_actor and the
liveness test now pins both halves — the pull routes to the carved-out verb,
and the verb is still unfenced.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-subscribe): a realm sync touches every workspace on this runtime

H2 of docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/realm-pull-live-projection.md.

_delta_touches_workspace answered True on two shapes — an office.* event naming
this workspace, and a state.patched whose office scope is this workspace. A
realm-sync watermark matches neither: realm.sync.pulled's payload is
{realm_id, changed, artifacts}, so it fell through the loop to return False and
office_patch_sink returned without pushing a runtime.office.resync. The event
whose own docstring says it exists "so stream / read-model consumers refresh"
refreshed every consumer except the one that owns the office canvas.

Adds the third arm: an event type in a declared realm-sync set returns True
unconditionally. A sync is scoped to a REALM and this function is asked about a
WORKSPACE — the payload cannot answer, and the module's stated rule for a
question it cannot answer is the conservative arm ("A resync is recoverable; a
dropped change is not"). It is the ruling None already gets, spelled as an
explicit True so the reason is legible.

Widening the payload with workspace_ids was rejected at the arm: the EventLog
has a 4 KB payload cap, a many-workspace realm would blow it, and a truncated
list is a silent drop — the failure class this arm exists to refuse.

The set is declared, not a "realm." prefix, and a test reds if it is relaxed:
realm.activated / workspace.activated fire on every operator realm switch and
must stay scoped away.

fix(parity): reserve drop-sample slots so a by-design flood cannot starve anomalies

author: Tony Arena
message:
feat(doctor): the placement census learns to see desks, four faults apart

DL-H1 of the launcher repo's
docs/mission_control/planned/office-desk-litter-cleanup.md.

The census was structurally blind to desk litter and could not have found it
by looking harder. Its join is actor-level and instance-keyed, and it skips a
class-keyed actor by construction ("A class-keyed actor answers no roster
question") — but a desk minted by materializeAgentDesk carries the persona
CLASS id and no binding, so it lands in exactly the actor the join skips while
its agent lands in the instance-keyed one. The pairing is persona-level and the
storage is actor-level; nothing was reading across that gap. A kind:desk item
riding a live instance-keyed actor — the shape MEASURED on the operator's store
on 2026-08-30 — was counted as a healthy `placed` row.

So the sweep is over ITEMS, joined per workspace on persona_id, and it files
each live kind:desk item into exactly one of four reasons:

  agent_missing            no live kind:agent item for the persona in the
                           workspace. The retire seam's own litter:
                           archive_actors_for_instance archives only actors
                           BOUND to the instance, and the desk actor is bound
                           to nothing.
  agent_scope_stale        agent items exist, and every one is bound to an
                           instance no live roster row backs — the store-side
                           shadow of the launcher's projection scope drop.
                           Overlaps orphan_actors on purpose: that row names
                           the actor, this one names the desk left standing.
  persona_retired          no live row and no retirement tombstone names the
                           persona at all.
  desk_kind_agent_binding  the item is structurally an agent's — a live
                           instance binding on its actor, or an agent-shaped
                           item_id.

The fourth is kept OUT of the first by design, and that separation is the point
of the stage rather than a nicety: the two have opposite cures — one wants a
re-place, the other a reap — and conflating them is what cost the lane its
first day. The classifier tests the live instance binding BEFORE the id,
because a binding is a fact and an id is a spelling; the id test is positive
(an id must carry an agent marker) so an unreadable id degrades to the absence
buckets rather than over-claiming, and the desk marker beats the agent marker
so desk-<agentItemId> — what the materializer mints for every desk on every
store — is never read as mis-kinded.

State discipline is inherited whole, not re-argued: every bucket is a statement
about ABSENCE, and a file that will not decode is what absence is
indistinguishable from, so one unreadable file anywhere keeps the WHOLE census
at unknown with desk_litter None — never [], never a partition of the readable
remainder. Litter raises the census to notice and never past it: nothing
mis-renders, so needs_fix stays off for a store whose only fault is furniture.

Roster cost, as the plan priced it: ONE new key in finding_counts. No new
section — section_health, findings and the CLI's detail_sources already carry a
placement_census row each — so the four-hand-maintained-rosters weakness stays
open and is not worked here. schema_version 5 -> 6.

The reap is NOT here. DL-H2 is gated on this census's LIVE numbers plus
operator consent, and its item-prune arm is additionally gated on the live run
proving the mixed-actor shape exists at all.

Tests written after the implementation and each watched red first by reverting
the line it claims to cover — ten mutations, ten reds, including one that
caught a vacuous assertion: the widowed fixture's `notice` also has an unplaced
row behind it, so the health pin moved to the mis-kinded fixture where litter
is the sole cause. Fixture stores are built through OfficeStore verbs and the
real create service, never hand-written JSON.

Live proof is the operator's, and only the operator's: the store this census is
gated on is on a Windows machine this lane cannot reach.

author: Tony Arena
message:
fix(office-sync): a pull MERGES the tombstone ledger — a peer that never heard of a key cannot erase it

`adopt_remote_surface` wrote the peer's `archived_actor_keys` verbatim, so
the one lane that rewrites a live office from outside this machine could
delete the ledger half of the resurrection guard — the half
`classify_three_way_pull(..., locally_archived=)` reads. The archived FILE
survived, which is how the fence's OR-semantics papered the hole over.

Reachable, not theoretical: publish records the LOCAL hash as the baseline,
so an install that archives a desk and publishes reads as `unchanged` on its
next pull, and one peer folder edit later the classifier says `take_remote`
over that install's own ledger.

`merge_archived_ledgers` unions the two, peer order leading so a local subset
re-hashes to the remote's exact list (a converged pull stays a no-op), and
local-only keys landing on the cap-surviving tail — this store is the only
witness to a resurrection it alone archived. Cap and dedup unchanged.

Realm-actor-lifecycle wave, Track C1 (audit M4).

author: Tony Arena
message:
fix(office-sync): the pull's archive arm reports a typed outcome per key, and keeps the baseline for a delete it could not take

The arm was `try: remove_actor(...) / except Exception: pass` with the
`baseline.pop` OUTSIDE the try — the repo's known "best-effort lane discarded
its outcome" class, and here the discard is not a missing log line. Dropping
the baseline entry for a row that is STILL LIVE re-classifies it on the next
pull as a local ADD (`_local_state` reads a missing baseline as `new`), so a
delete this pull could not take comes back as a desk it offers to publish to
the realm — and no count anywhere said so. The fenced sibling beside it has
named its held-back keys since the day it was written.

`OfficeArchiveOutcome` is one row per key the arm REACHED: `archived`, or
`archive_failed:<ExceptionClass>` — the class, never the message. It rides
`OfficePullSummary.archive_outcomes` beside `delete_fenced`; `archived` is
that list's success count by construction. The loop still survives one bad
file; only the silence is gone. The baseline entry now leaves WITH the row and
only with it, so the next pull re-decides ARCHIVE_LOCAL and retries.

Track H-H3 closes this class across office_store; this is the pull-side
instance. Realm-actor-lifecycle wave, Track C2 (audit M5).

author: Tony Arena
message:
fix(realm-sync): office publish ships the scan it gated on, not a second walk of the directory

`_office_publish_scan` computed `scan_actors` for the refusal gate and then
built the artifact list from a SECOND `actors_dir.glob("*.json")` — two
authorities over one publish, and the glob is the one the gate cannot speak
for. It walks the directory again, later, and ships whatever is there: a
create landing between the two walks travels to every peer as a file no local
reader ever decoded.

One walk of `scan.actors` now yields both facts — the artifacts and the
persona ids the placements require — with the file named by
`office_actor_path` from the key inside the record, which is the same
authority `_write_actor` spends. Behaviour-preserving on any store where the
two agree, which is every store the office writes; pinned so it stays that
way.

Realm-actor-lifecycle wave, Track C3 (audit M6).

author: Tony Arena
message:
fix(office-store): the retire lane's two reads join the completeness discipline, so an empty failure list is a claim again

`archive_actors_for_instance` and `archived_actor_keys_for_instance` were the
last office lanes still spending `list_actors` — the view that drops a file it
could not decode and reports the remainder as complete. Both feed a retire ack
whose own docstring calls an empty `office_archive_failures` the positive
claim that every bound actor is off the level, so a bound desk behind an
undecodable file made that claim false in the one direction nobody could see.

The prune keeps surviving the bad file — a prune must not die on one — and now
files the shortfall as a failure row of its own, `actor_key: None` because the
key that could not be decoded is exactly what naming one would invent.

The replay's EVIDENCE read refuses instead: a short list there is not a
smaller truth but a different claim ("not archived by this instance" is the
one thing the empty list rules out). `agent_retire`'s `except Exception: []`
around it stays — the office projection is never authoritative for a
retirement — but the fault now rides the same `office_archive_failures` list,
so the empty list and the all-clear stop looking alike.

Re-anchors `d2-replay-hides-the-failures-it-can-now-have`, whose source line
this change moved.

author: Tony Arena
message:
docs(office): task #33's carve-out becomes the D3 ruling, and the neighbour that IS fenced says why

D3 (operator, 2026-08-30): the realm pull's adopt arm STAYS UNFENCED. A pull is
replication, not authoring — every fence in this store refuses LOCAL authoring
intent, and a pull has no operator behind it to offer consent, so fencing it
would mean refusing to hold a fact a peer already published with nobody present
to take the override. What #33 named as one hole was three: the two real ones
are closed (C1's ledger merge, C2's typed archive outcomes) and what is left is
a disposition, not an open question. The carve-out entry, `adopt_remote_actor`'s
docstring and the witness message all say so.

The asymmetry nobody had explained: `resolve_conflict(take="remote")` writes a
peer's row into the same directory and IS class-key fenced. Same input class,
opposite dispositions — because the discriminator is authoring INTENT, not the
row's provenance: that arm is an operator gesture whose whole content is the
decision to adopt the peer's copy, it has an override to hand them, and its
refusal points at a real next move. Recorded where a reader meets the
difference.

The witness's positive half stops resting on a spelling. It grepped
`apply_office_pull`'s source for `adopt_remote_actor(` — and the
behaviour-preserving extraction one commit ago reddened it while the property
never changed, which is this repo's measured "a gate asked of the source is a
gate on a spelling" class. It now drives a real pull and records which verb the
WRITE_REMOTE arm reaches; the negative half stays a source walk, correctly.

Also reconciles `patch_coverage`'s must-stay-absent argument for
`office.actor.conflict_resolved`: it cited the bypass-the-chokepoint reasoning
H1 (`f810bd2ac`) already discharged for the pull arm. The live reason is that
`resolve_conflict`'s adopt arm emits no actor patch for a covered batch to
ride. Making it emit is a follow-on.

Realm-actor-lifecycle wave, Track C5.

author: Tony Arena
message:
docs(office-sync): the ledger merge states its propagation direction, and the case it cannot yet tell apart

The union is what makes the direction total: a key entering this ledger on ANY
store travels — kept by the union, carried into the realm by the next publish,
read as `locally_archived` by every member that pulls afterwards. Writing a
key here is REALM-WIDE intent, not a local note, and it is one-way (no
un-tombstone syncs).

The consequence recorded rather than guessed at: a RECEIVER-SIDE REPAIR archive
— evicting a desk whose instance never existed on this machine, the
realm-pulled orphan — is indistinguishable in this list from an authored
delete, and the union exports both. Live on 2026-08-30: the Mac ledger holds
`personainst_neko_supervisor_agent_9682caf4` from such a repair while the actor
is alive and correctly linked at its Windows origin, which has not yet pulled.

The union stays as staged — losing tombstones is the worse failure, and this
case matches operator intent. The typed split (authored tombstone vs local
eviction that mints no realm-visible one) belongs with the delete lane that
picks between the two verbs, Track A1's hermes half.

Realm-actor-lifecycle wave, Track C1 addendum.

author: Tony Arena
message:
docs(office): runtime.office.remove gains its fifth case, and the verb says whose intent it carries

The scope enumeration beside the RPC table listed four things a placement verb
cannot reach — an authored desk, a class-keyed actor, a folder taxonomy, a
realm-sync sidecar — and read as exhaustive. It was missing the case the
launcher's operator could not delete at all: a realm-PULLED placement, whose
actor key is placement-shaped because the peer minted it with the same mint, and
whose `persona_instances/` row this install never held because a pull adopts
office actors and never instances. `runtime.agent.retire` refuses that
`not_found`, terminally by invariant 1; `runtime.office.remove` needs only the
surface and the actor file, so it is the verb that reaches it. The launcher now
routes on that FACT rather than on the shape of the key (launcher Track A1).

The same paragraph gains the intent semantics the routing rests on, ruled
2026-08-30: an operator-clicked delete is AUTHORED intent, so the tombstone and
its realm-wide propagation are correct on whichever machine the click happened.
A DIAGNOSTIC eviction — doctor remediation, dispatch step, census cleanup — is
the case that must never mint a realm-visible tombstone, and it gets its own
local-only mode rather than borrowing this one.

author: Tony Arena
message:
test(mutation-claims): a claim is anchored to its symbol, and survives the block moving

H-H14. `symbol` was decorative: `find` was matched against the whole file, had
to occur there exactly once, and nothing ever asked whether the named symbol
existed. Two costs, both measured on the C-slice, which needed three manual
re-anchors inside one nine-commit slice — a moved line and a two-level dedent
each rotted a live guarantee into a configuration error that had to be retyped
by hand.

The anchor now resolves the symbol first (dotted path, `Class.method`, a module
constant, `module` for the whole file) and requires `find` to be unique INSIDE
it, then splices the mutant at that offset instead of at `str.replace`'s first
occurrence. Inside the symbol, a block that was re-indented still anchors: the
registered bytes are re-matched with every line shifted by one constant and the
replacement follows the block to its new column. Relative nesting is fixed by
construction, so an extraction out of a nested `try` re-anchors and a re-NEST
does not — and a re-anchor is printed rather than applied in silence.

A stale symbol is now fatal, with the repair in the message. The first one it
caught is in this commit: `r1-create-stops-fencing-the-supplied-placement` named
`_parse_request`, a function `agent_create.py` has not had for months, while its
guarantee sat in `normalize_agent_create`.

Four claims registered on the new lanes; all four watched red (KILLED) against
their tests. The 66 pre-existing claims resolve unchanged under the new anchor.

author: Tony Arena
message:
feat(office): a diagnostic repair evicts locally; only an authored delete tombstones

AX7 (§AX Q1/Q2, operator ruling 2026-08-30). `remove_actor` writes two things
and only one of them crosses machines: the archive copy stays here, the
`archived_actor_keys` entry is what `adopt_remote_surface` merges on a realm
pull. So the ledger write is the assertion about the REALM, and everything that
calls `remove_actor` was making it — including repairs nobody authored.

The split is on INTENT, not origin and not id shape. An operator-clicked delete
is authored on whichever machine the click happens, and its tombstone
propagating is the point — that is what makes the delete survive a peer that
still holds the row. A doctor remediation, a dispatch step or a census cleanup
targets THIS install's projection; minting realm-wide intent from one deletes
the placement everywhere to fix a local display. The live case:
`personainst_neko_supervisor_agent_9682caf4`, archived rev 3 on the Mac by a
dispatch-ordered repair while still active rev 2 at its Windows origin.

- `remove_actor(record_tombstone=False)` / `harness office actor-remove
  --local-only`. Default unchanged in every byte, so the launcher's delete, the
  RPC verb and the flagless CLI keep authoring.
- Archive-never-delete is NOT what the mode trades: the archive copy is written
  either way and `actor-restore` works after both, pinned.
- Both the `--help` and the ACK say which mode ran — an
  `office_actor_local_eviction` warning, and a `local_eviction` default reason
  on the domain event, because the two runs are otherwise one invisible byte
  apart.
- The doctor's A4 remediation (`b4d3e13b3`, today) now names the `--local-only`
  form and says out loud what dropping it means. A report answering "what is
  wrong with this install" must not quietly author realm-wide deletes.

`office_sync`'s pull-side archive arm deliberately keeps tombstoning: it is
replicating a delete the peer's operator authored, and the local ledger entry is
that delete's record here.

Three claims registered, all watched red (KILLED); the A4 claim re-anchored onto
the rewritten string.

author: Tony Arena
message:
refactor(doctor): the four section rosters become one declared table

H-H1. A doctor section was added by editing four hand-maintained lists of
one set — `finding_counts`, `section_health` and `findings` in
`run_harness_doctor`, plus `detail_sources` in the CLI printer — and only
`section_health`'s key set was pinned, so a section added to three of the
four was counted and verdicted while rendering no operator line at all.
That is the shape the derived-verdict rework already fixed once by hand.

`DOCTOR_SECTIONS` now declares each section once: its name, its probe, where
its report lands in the payload, and the counts it contributes. All four
rosters derive from it — the CLI imports `doctor_detail_sources` rather than
re-typing the fourth copy. The None-not-zero counting rule is applied in one
place for every count in the table instead of being re-typed per entry, and
the probes share one `_DoctorProbeContext` signature so the table can hold
them (the `include_worktrees` branch moves into the worktree probe, where the
declined-observation argument belongs).

Payload is byte-identical: the snapshot probe now returns `rows` + `build`
and the table publishes them to the two keys they already occupied.

Tests (written after, each watched red by reverting the line it covers): a
synthetic section added to the TABLE and to nothing else reaches all four
rosters; an unexamined section's count is `None` from the same row; the
two-keys-from-one-probe publish; and the CLI detail line rendering for a

author: Tony Arena
message:
feat(office): the store records what an item was MINTED as (H-H12)

The desk-litter classifier's bucket-4 clause asked a SPELLING. It parsed the
``item_id`` for the launcher's three minting conventions — ``<persona>_<kind>``,
``desk-<agentItemId>``, the bare instance id — none of which anything enforces,
so a launcher rename would have silently reclassified every mis-kinded agent as
a widowed desk. That is this repo's own gate rule broken inside a classifier: a
POSITIVE claim ("this was an agent") resting on how somebody spelled a string.

``OfficeItem.minted_kind`` is the store's own record of the answer. Stamped by
``_stamp_minted_kinds`` inside ``upsert_actor``'s lock, keyed on ``item_id`` and
STICKY thereafter — an item already on record keeps what its first write gave
it, and only a genuinely new item is stamped from the kind it arrives with, so a
write can change what an item IS and never what it was minted as. A re-added key
carries it forward from the archive, the same precedence ``base_revision`` uses
one line down. It is never read off the payload: a value a client could send
would be the self-declaration the field replaced a spelling with.

``None`` — every item written before the field, every one adopted from a peer
that has not upgraded — is CANNOT SAY, never "no": such a desk falls through to
the absence buckets and is judged on whether its agent exists, which is the same
softer answer an unreadable id used to get. Not on the wire; no client decides
anything with it.

``_office_item_id_shape`` and its three ``ITEM_ID_SHAPE_*`` constants are
DELETED and tombstone-registered, per the wave's readability rule: a reader
whose only remaining effect is to be trusted about something it cannot know.

The migration consequence this stage was filed with is CLOSED, not accepted.
As first built the field rode inside ``office_content_hash``, so the first realm
status or publish after the upgrade would have reported every actor as locally
changed. ``_ITEM_HASH_EXCLUDE`` states the exclusion rule one level down, where
``_HASH_EXCLUDE`` (entity keys only) could not reach: a field that is not on the
wire and not rendered cannot be observed, so hashing it moves a hash with
nothing behind it — and a peer still decoding the field away would have
disagreed with this install over identical content, which is worse than the
one-time blip the row described. The filter drops the KEY rather than nulling
it, so the encoded payload is byte-identical to the pre-field one and no
existing hash moves at all. ``kind`` is content and is still hashed.

PROVEN. The store-level pins (stickiness, per-item keying, no client
declaration, resurrection carry-forward), the doctor-side classifier tests and
the tombstone-registry row all pass; the hash-exclusion pin was watched red by
dropping the items re-filter. The subject's earlier PARTIALLY PROVEN marker was
written when the Mac's wind-down killed the run before it reported.

author: Tony Arena
message:
feat(authorization): the console tier becomes a property of the VERB (Stage A6 / H-H13)

H-H13 as REWRITTEN by the plan's §AX: hermes 06:546-561 records that the
coordinator gate already landed at the RPC front door and explicitly supersedes
the scope-parameter design the plan's original H-H13 re-proposed. This is that
section's Stage A6 backstop and nothing else — the gate does not move, Ruling A
(b) still holds.

WHAT IT BUYS. The front-door check is a property of the DISPATCHER: it runs
because ``handle_request`` calls ``authorize_call`` before dispatch and because
``@method`` recorded the right tier. Both are one edit away from being wrong in
a way no service test would see — a method re-registered at ``read`` by a typo,
a future transport reaching a handler by another path, a refactor that moves
dispatch. ``service_backstop`` runs inside the two write verbs, whoever called
them and however they got there.

WHY IT IS NOT SELF-DECLARATION, which is the one way a second check could make
things worse: ``caller`` is an ``RpcCaller``, the services take their request as
a ``params`` dict, and no JSON a client sends crosses that line. The handlers
pass ``context.caller``, which only the transport builder mints; both CLI doors
pass the ``CLI_CONSOLE`` constant, which takes no arguments precisely so nothing
on the invocation can steer it.

Optional, per §AX. ``caller`` omitted is ``SERVICE_DEFAULT_CALLER`` — a spelled
VALUE, not an absent check — because Ruling A's own sentencing on option (c)
named rewriting ~60 grandfathered call sites as the reason (c) was not taken.
The asymmetry with ``authorize_call``, where ``None`` is ``unknown`` and
refused, is deliberate and documented at both ends: there ``None`` means a
transport failed to place a caller it was answering for; here it means no wire
was involved at all.

PROVEN. The subject carried an UNPROVEN marker because the Mac began its
machine-overload wind-down before the run; ``ccaa0485d`` was the retraction and
21/21 passed there, including the load-bearing
test_the_handlers_hand_the_proven_caller_to_the_service, which stubs the front
door to ALLOW and is the only observation of the second check on the wire lane.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(locks): the deadline is real on POSIX too, so HarnessLockUnavailable stops being a Windows-only fact

`_file_lock` computed a deadline on every platform and then, off Windows, took
a bare blocking `fcntl.flock(..., LOCK_EX)` that never consulted it. So one call
had two contracts: bounded on Windows, unbounded everywhere else. Every caller
that turns the refusal into a typed answer — `agent create`'s
`creation_in_progress`, the chat-turn reservation's `turn_in_progress`, the
persona chat mint — was Windows-only behaviour wearing a portable name, and a
stuck holder hung the process on Mac and Linux instead of refusing.

The two arms collapse into one. Each platform now supplies three primitives —
seed the byte range (a no-op under `flock`), try to acquire without blocking,
release — and the deadline loop above them is shared: poll at
`_RETRY_SLEEP_SECONDS`, re-raise an errno outside that platform's contended set
unwrapped, refuse `HarnessLockUnavailable` naming the budget when it runs out.
`LOCK_NB` is what makes the POSIX arm reach the loop at all.

Non-reentrancy is now uniform rather than accidental: a second acquisition from
this process opens a fresh handle, contends with the first, and refuses at the
deadline instead of deadlocking forever. Hermes 06:260-277 said the opposite
about POSIX and is corrected in this commit; H-H10 rewrites the rest of that
passage when the placement read moves inside the lock, which this stage is the
prerequisite for.

Three mutation claims registered, all verified KILLED: restore the blocking
acquire; refuse on the first contended attempt instead of spending the budget;
drop the non-contended-errno re-raise. Unwiring `_release` survives on POSIX and
the test says so rather than claiming a kill it does not have — closing the
descriptor releases a `flock`, which is not true of `msvcrt`.

Rebased onto the lifecycle batch (`76c6ade663`). Two corrections the rebase
forced, both in this commit because the gate has to be green at every landing
point: `hh6-posix-file-lock-ignores-its-deadline` named `_try_acquire` as its
symbol, which H-H14 (landed after this branch was cut) turned from decorative
into fatal — the selector's resolver walks definitions and not the branches of
a platform `if`, so that name has no anchorable node and every run aborted as a
configuration error. It is re-anchored at `module` scope with the arm named in
the label. The claim then SURVIVES on a Windows host, because the line it edits
is in the POSIX arm this interpreter never executes; the `mutation-claims` job
runs `ubuntu-latest`, which is where it fires, and the test docstring now says
so beside the `_release` non-kill the same test already stated.

Realm-actor-lifecycle wave, Track H-H6.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-store): the unaimed placement's slot is chosen inside the write's own lock

M10, closed. `perform_agent_create` resolved the layout policy OUTSIDE
`office_lock` and sent the answer as an ordinary position, because the lock is
not reentrant and wrapping the read would have deadlocked the write it was
meant to protect. That left a window: two creates that both omit a position and
race between their reads and their writes compute the same free slot, and the
second lands on top of the first.

`upsert_actor` gains `position_policy` — a hook it calls INSIDE the lock it
already holds, handed the workspace's live `ActorScan`, returning the point the
payload's single item is written at. The read and the write are now one
acquisition, so nothing can land between them. Proved by contending from inside
the hook: a concurrent `upsert_actor` refuses `HarnessLockUnavailable` rather
than getting in. That refusal only exists off Windows because of H-H6, which is
why these two stages ship in this order and rewrite one passage together.

The split of authority is the point. The store supplies the SET and the lock and
knows no lattice; `office_layout_policy` stays pure and store-free;
`agent_create.placement_slot_for` keeps the arithmetic and the exclusion rule —
skip the actor this create is about to write, without which an idempotent replay
walks one slot per retry. `resolve_placement_position`, which was the store-read
half, is DELETED rather than left beside its replacement.

rather than by convention, and a made-up origin cannot escape a later edit. A
multi-item payload is refused, not guessed at. The ack's `position` is now read
off the stored row, since this lane no longer holds the answer at all.

race as accepted); 01:116 and two docstring cites follow the rename.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(office-store): the store's best-effort loops report one typed outcome per key, in one vocabulary

Track H-H3 closes the "best-effort lane discarded its outcome" class inside
`office_store`, the way C2 closed the pull-side instance. The loops survive one
bad file on purpose — a prune must not die because one actor will not decode,
an office must not vanish because one conflict sidecar is mid-write — and each
paid for that survival in its own currency. `OfficeActorOutcome` is the one
currency: frozen, minting classmethods, one row per key the loop REACHED,
successes included, and a token that names the exception CLASS and never its
message.

`conflict_actor_keys` is the site that still genuinely discarded. It answered a
decode failure with `path.stem` and said nothing — and the stem is
`actor_file_token(actor_key)`, sanitised and truncated at 64 with a hash suffix,
so for a long key it is NOT the actor key and `office resolve-conflict --actor
<it>` finds nothing. Both readers hand these to an operator as keys to act on.
It becomes `scan_conflicts` returning `ConflictScan` — `ActorScan`'s shape for
the same question one directory over. The substitution stays; the silence goes.
A sidecar that decoded but carries no `actor_key` is recorded as the same guess,
because it is one. The two callers now spell `.keys`, so dropping the provenance
is a choice made in the open rather than a thin view's default — the discipline
AX5 is about to make general.

`archive_actors_for_instance` did account, but in two lists and two tallies kept
in parallel: any one could drift from the others in silence. All four ack keys
are now projections of the outcome list, and the counts are its lengths. The
returned dict is byte-identical, so `agent_retire`'s ack and the launcher's
`MissionAgentOfficeArchiveFailure` decode are untouched. `_unreadable_scan_
failure` is deleted into `OfficeActorOutcome.scan_unreadable`.

The outcome carries `error` beside the token, and the docstring says why: that
`class: message` string has ridden this store's retire ack to the launcher since
before the type existed, and dropping it to satisfy the token's purity rule
would take information away from an operator. The rule is about the TOKEN.

Two of the wave's older claims moved with the loop and are re-anchored
(s5, c4) — H-H14's "a reformat invalidates the gate" class again. Four new
claims registered; the selector ran ten of twelve at its cap and KILLED all ten,
and the two it capped out of (`hh3-a-resolved-sidecar-reads-as-a-live-conflict`,
`hh3-the-prune-ack-keeps-its-own-tally-again`) were verified KILLED by hand.

message:
refactor(office): the blank folder is filled where it is written, and scan_actors is the only actor read

Three stages, landed together because they overlap in `office_store.py` and
`test_office_store.py` and cannot be split by pathspec.

**H-H9 (M9) — the blank `folder` is filled at the WRITE boundary.**
`_normalize_item` persisted `""` for an item written without a folder, and one
stored value then meant two things: three readers compensated independently —
`office_layout_policy.item_folder` before scanning, the launcher's
`MissionOfficeSceneItem` at decode, and a third reader again. "Which folder is
this item in" had three answers derived three ways from a value that said
nothing. It is filled through `office_layout_policy.folder_for_kind`, the SAME
authority the scan's own fallback spends, so the folder written and the folder
inferred cannot disagree. The read-side fallbacks stay load-bearing and the
cross-repo fixture case `blank_folder_falls_back_to_kind` is unchanged: rows
older than this hold `""` on disk, and `apply_office_pull` adopts a peer's actor
files without passing through `_normalize_item`. What changes is that this store
stops MINTING the shape. Hermes 06 and the fixture README are corrected.

**AX5 — `list_actors` is DELETED.** The thin view returned `.actors` and dropped
`.unreadable`, so the arms that most needed the count were the ones that never
had to ask. The discipline then lived in PROSE: five separate comments across
`realm_sync`, `office_sync`, `office_class_key_guard`, `snapshot` and
`office_store`, each re-arguing to the next reader why THIS site spends
`scan_actors`. A rule re-argued at every call site is a rule the API is not
carrying. Every caller now spells `scan_actors(...).actors` and every one of
those comments is rewritten to argue the count rather than a dead symbol.
Dropping the count is still allowed and still usually right — it is now
something someone WROTE, and each site says why in one line.

The projection-cap guard in `_emit_actor_patch` — the worst of the set, because
its whole purpose is to notice incompleteness — gets the honest read: a scan
that is SHORT takes the same `refresh` demote a truncation takes. Truncation is
only one of the two ways the projection can be short;
`serve_rpc._office_projection` names the other beside its own cut
(`actors_unreadable`, "rows the platform took"), that number rides the office
row, and no `office_actor` patch can express it. Cost stated in the docstring: a
workspace holding one permanently-undecodable file demotes every write to a full
core, which is this lane's own named floor, paid on a store that is already in
an abnormal state.

**AX6 — the pull's actor-directory reader delegates instead of re-spelling.**
`_read_actor_dir` never took `self`, so it is lifted to
`office_store.read_actor_dir` and `office_sync._read_remote_office` calls it. It
was the third spelling of one walk-swallow-count, sitting in the one place where
disagreement produces a DELETION rather than a wrong number: a key absent from
the remote map is how the pull infers "the peer removed this desk". The pulled
directory also gains the per-class warning line the local ones have had, and the
log location becomes `<parent>/<name>` because every one of these directories is
called `actors` and the line now has two origins. One outcome the remote reader
had and the store did not is folded rather than dropped: a payload that decodes
fine and carries NO `actor_key` counts as unreadable, which is the safe
direction — `unreadable` is what fences this workspace's delete-shaped decisions.

PROOF STATUS, stated because this machine was wound down mid-verification.
H-H9 is proven: four focused tests, three mutations verified KILLED (drop the
fallback; fill unconditionally; ignore the kind). AX5 and AX6 are NOT yet
proven: import + `compileall` clean across `agent_runtime`, `hermes_cli`,
`scripts` and both test trees, every `list_actors` reference retired, all 78
mutation-claim anchors re-verified — but no pytest run completed against them.
The office/sync/snapshot suites are the ones that must go green before this
commit is landed on `main`. It is NOT landed.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(office): the conflict scan's filename guesses reach the operator

`scan_conflicts` has known since H-H3 which of its keys were invented from a
filename — a sidecar that would not decode, or one that decoded and did not
name its actor. `office_summary_row` had no field for it, so both readers took
`.keys` alone and handed an operator a token `office resolve-conflict --actor
<it>` may not find: the substitute is `actor_file_token(actor_key)`, sanitised
and truncated at 64 with a hash suffix, so for a long key it is not the key.

`ConflictScan.guessed_keys` is the derivation, projected from `outcomes` rather
than tallied beside them, and both call sites now take BOTH lists off ONE
`scan_conflicts` — a second read of that directory for the second list would be
two answers to one question, free to disagree.

`office_summary_row` gains keyword-REQUIRED `conflict_guessed_keys` under the
same never-silently-default rule `actors_unreadable` is declared under: a
caller holding no conflict scan says `()` out loud rather than claiming by
default that none of its keys are guesses. The row key and the warning's
`guessed` field are additive — an old launcher ignores them, and a row from an
older core reads as "cannot say", never as "raise".

The parity warning keeps ONE code (the `orphaned_office` rule: discrimination
in a field, or every existing census of the condition zeroes) and marks only
the guessed entries in its sentence. The CLI prints the guess list under
`--full` only, beside the keys it qualifies; the skinny row hands over a count
and no tokens, so it cannot mislead and is unchanged.

The four test call sites of the row builder now state `conflict_guessed_keys=()`
— which is the required keyword doing its job, not collateral.

reads as "the source had fewer desks", not "this machine could not open two of
its files". The COUNT is what the scan can honestly supply (`read_actor_dir`
keeps a per-class tally, not a path list), and the row names the SOURCE
workspace, because that is where an operator has to go.

Conditional, so a clean template stays warning-free and the `warnings == []`
contract callers attach to the create envelope still means something.

message:
feat(mutation-gate): a rewrite can ask which claims it is about to move, before it moves them

`changed_line_mutation_check.py --claims-for <symbol|path|path::symbol>` lists
every claim anchored there and exits. No `--base`, because the moment the
question is worth asking is before the rewrite that would produce a diff.

The gap, measured on the 2026-08-30 lifecycle merge: `a4-doctor-prescribes-
retire-for-an-orphan-retire-cannot-reach` and `ax7-the-doctor-goes-back-to-
prescribing-the-tombstoning-form` both anchor inside ONE function's remediation
string; the merge brief named only a4, and ax7 was found by the selector's own
configuration error rather than by review. Nothing was wrong with the selector.
The question "which of the 113 claims anchor in the symbol I am about to
rewrite?" simply had no answer short of reading the registry by eye, so nobody
read it.

Three query spellings because they are three real questions — this file, this
directory, this symbol — and a class reaches its methods' claims, since "I am
about to rewrite `OfficeStore`" is asked more often than any single method is.
The tail spelling (`agent_create.py`) is segment-aligned, so `create.py` does
not silently answer for `agent_create.py`.

refusing there and does. This lane is asked mid-rewrite, when some anchors have

useless exactly when it is needed.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(mutation-gate): the anchor and the splice finally agree about line endings

Found while building this batch, and RED ON PRISTINE `main` (`0c744aa586`) on
this host: `tests/scripts/test_mutation_claim_anchoring.py::test_the_mutation_
is_spliced_at_the_anchor_not_at_the_first_occurrence` fails with "holders.py
changed after the anchor resolved".

Two readers, one file. `_anchor_or_raise` read the target with `read_text`
(universal newlines — a CRLF file decodes with LF), and the mutate loop read it
with `read_bytes().decode("utf-8")` (raw, CRLF kept). Against any CRLF file the
anchor offset was therefore one byte short per preceding line, the splice's own
"did the file move under us" check caught the mismatch, and the run died as a
configuration error. The check was right; the offsets were wrong.

Not a test artefact and not Windows-only. `pathlib.write_text` is simply how
the test got a CRLF file cheaply on this host, and 25 tracked `.py` blobs carry
CRLF at this sha (the next commits normalize them) — a Linux checkout of one of
those is CRLF too, and a claim anchored in it would have hit exactly this.

One reader now, `_read_source`, returning the raw bytes AND the LF-normalized
text every offset in the module is measured in. LF is the only normal form
available: claims register their `find` with LF, so anchoring a CRLF file at
all requires it. The mutant is written LF and the original bytes go back in
`finally` either way, so a run never leaves a deliberately-CRLF file
normalized — asserted at the byte level in the new regression, which was
watched red against the two-reader version before this fix went in.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(mutation-gate): a diff that rewrote a symbol puts that symbol's claims on the hook

Two measured misses, one cause: SELECTION still read the anchor's own two
lines while everything else had moved to the symbol.

H-H2 (`0ecb921b9d`) rewrote 82 lines of `agent_create.py`, 41 of them inside
`_reply`, and git rendered the exact two lines the new claim
`hh2-the-one-reply-builder-stops-observing-the-revision` anchors on (1170-1171)
as unchanged CONTEXT. The claim registered FOR that slice was not selected by
its own landing diff, and the run was green while saying so. H-H14
(`2523bd440`) had already made anchoring symbol-scoped — the row asked whether
it covered selection too, and re-measuring says it did not: it covered the
splice.

A claim is a statement about a symbol's behaviour, so the diff that rewrote the
symbol selects it, whether or not the two lines carrying the needle survived
the rewrite verbatim. `module`-scope claims (2 of 113) keep line selection and
are pinned that way: their span IS the file, so widening them would select them
on any diff touching the module, which is not a claim about anything.

The widening is visible in the output — `(selected by symbol)` on the candidate
row. A gate that quietly puts more on the hook for reasons the reader cannot
reconstruct stops being read.

Second miss, same commit because it is the same predicate: `_changed_lines`
summed each hunk's `+` count, so a deletion-only hunk (`@@ -32 +31,0 @@`,
`range(31, 31)`) contributed nothing and every retirement wave selected zero
claims BY CONSTRUCTION while reporting `candidates: 0` — measured on the Z1
landing `4bf4387760` and filed there. A deletion now contributes the two
new-file lines its removed text sat between, clamped at line 1; with symbol
scoping, a deletion INSIDE a function reaches that function's claims, which is
what the row wanted.

MEASURED COST, since the cap is a runtime bound and this raises pressure on it:
against `origin/main` this branch selects 4 (the gate's own claims, in `run`
and `_symbol_span` — it is its own first customer). Replaying real bases, the
H-H store batch goes 6 -> 27 selected and the S2 landing 98 -> 104. CI's
declared cap is 20, so the next batch landing will have to raise it visibly or
split. The queue's open "batch landing exceeds the cap" row is now a decision
with numbers under it; it is NOT decided here.

The H-H2 case is pinned against the real blob at the real sha with the real
registered claim, both halves: the anchored lines still miss the diff, and the
symbol span still overlaps it in 41 places.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(mutation-gate): a claim can say which hosts it is about, and a skip says so by name

`hh6-posix-file-lock-ignores-its-deadline` mutates the POSIX arm of
`agent_runtime/locks.py`'s platform fork. RE-MEASURED before building:
`--base 36dc77c68d^` with that claim on this Windows host exits 1 with
`SURVIVED: hh6-posix-file-lock-ignores-its-deadline` — the mutated line never
runs here, so the claimed test passes over a mutant it cannot reach. A hand-run
on the gate host was permanently one known survivor away from green. That is
the gate's own failure mode with the signs reversed: not silence that looks
like success, but noise that gets learned as background and then covers a real
survivor.

Optional `platforms` on a claim row. Declared, and this host is not in the
list: `SKIPPED (platform): <id> (declared posix; this host is windows)`, by
name, on both lanes, never SURVIVED and never silent. `ubuntu-latest` is posix,
so CI enforces it exactly as before — the workflow needs no change.

The cap still counts SELECTED claims rather than runnable ones, so the number a
diff must answer for is the same everywhere; a Windows run squeaking under the
cap on skips would hand CI a refusal nobody local could reproduce.

Unknown claim fields are now REFUSED. `platform: "posix"` for `platforms:
["posix"]` is the typo this schema invites, and an ignored field means the
claim runs everywhere while its author believes it is scoped.

ON THE ROW'S OTHER HALF — "teach the resolver to descend a module-level `if`" —
the honest answer is no, and it is written at `WHOLE_MODULE_SYMBOLS`. `locks.py`
defines `_try_acquire`/`_prepare`/`_release` TWICE, once per arm, so descending
the branches would make both copies visible and an ambiguous symbol is refused
by design. There is no unambiguous node to anchor to. The claim stays at
`module` scope with the arm named in its label, its selection stays line-based
— which is what has been selecting and killing it on CI all along — and
`platforms` carries the part that was actually broken.

author: nekwo
message:
chore(line-endings): the 38 CR-carrying blobs become LF, and zero becomes the ratchet

`tests/agent_runtime/test_office_store.py` was CRLF on `main`, came back from a
Mac-side edit as LF, and turned a +149-line stage into a 2513-line whole-file
rewrite nobody could review. It was restored to CRLF so that landing stayed
readable — right for the landing, wrong as a steady state, because it left the
repo's endings a property of whichever host last touched a file.

THE CENSUS, byte-level at `0c744aa586`: 8862 LF blobs, 33 CRLF, 5 MIXED. The
queue row said "31 `.py`"; the measured number is 30 `.py` (25 pure CRLF plus
the 5 mixed) and 38 CR-carrying blobs in total once the 5 docs, 2 root
artifacts and 1 ledger are counted. The row was right about the class and off
on the count.

DELIBERATE KEEPERS: NONE. That is the finding, not an omission. Every one of
the 38 was a minority outlier inside its own directory — 2 CRLF against 64 LF
under `docs/agent-runtime-harness/archive/`, 5 against 122 across the whole
harness canon, 2 against 125 at the repo root — and the two root artifacts
(`.launcher_run.log`, `htasks_open.json`) arrived together in the
fork-foundation import `0ad80754fa` and have no reader anywhere in the tree.
Every Windows-only script (`*.ps1`, `*.cmd`, 6 of them) was ALREADY LF, so the
one argument for keeping CRLF on this platform is answered by the platform's
own files. The only place in this repo where bytes are a contract —
`tests/fixtures/office_layout/**`, `-text`, digest-matched against the launcher
— was already LF and is untouched, and is pinned by its own test here.

Per file: read bytes, `b"\r\n"` -> `b"\n"`, write bytes. Asserted before and
after that the decoded text is identical, that no lone CR existed anywhere in
the 38 (none did), that every `.py` still parses and every `.json` still loads.
Nothing else in these files changed.

TWO mechanisms, because they answer different questions. `* text=auto eol=lf`
stops the next accident at check-in — measured: with it in place, staging a
deliberately re-CRLF'd file silently normalizes it back. `tests/
test_line_endings.py` catches what attributes cannot see, which is every blob
ALREADY in the object store — precisely how these 38 sat there for months. It
reads the INDEX, never the working tree, because a contributor with
`core.autocrlf=true` has CRLF on disk by design and has done nothing wrong.
Red-proven by pinning one file `-text` to get past the attribute and staging it
CRLF; the gate named the file.

The keeper set exists and is empty. An empty exception set that is declared is
a decision; one that is absent is a gap.

Focused suites over all 18 normalized test modules: 582 passed. The 19th,
`tests/test_coverage_claims_resolve.py`, fails
`test_every_coverage_claim_names_a_test_that_exists` — verified IDENTICAL on
pristine `origin/main` in a separate worktree, so it is pre-existing and is
reported to the wave rather than folded in here.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(scripts): an advisory report for doc citations that no longer resolve

`scripts/doc_cite_report.py`. Not a gate, by ruling and in the code: it always
exits 0, and the docstring says why. It lands red on ~60 pre-existing cites,
and a gate that is born red is silenced, after which the next reader believes
it. Turning this into a gate is its own stage with a sweep budget, and it needs
the adjacency probe this deliberately does not attempt.

What it checks is whether a cite RESOLVES — the file is tracked, the line
exists, the sha is a commit on `origin/main`. It cannot tell whether
`office_store.py:444` is the line the sentence is about. Said plainly at the
top, because the rowed defect is cites landing on unrelated text and a green
line here does not deny that.

Noise control, measured rather than guessed: only tokens carrying `:N` count as
cites. Accepting bare path-shaped tokens gave 498 "dead path" rows over the
harness canon, almost none of them citations — `models.py` in a sentence,
`gateway/peers.json` naming a file in the runtime store, not the checkout.
`:N` is also exactly the class the queue row is about. Bare basenames are
resolved through the tracked-file index only when UNIQUE; 54 ambiguous ones in
the live canon are counted, not guessed, because picking one of three
`models.py` is how a report starts inventing findings. `.dart` and elided
`.../` paths are skipped as cross-repo.

Two sha classes kept apart, because the queue's own scar is the second one: a
sha that is not a commit here at all, and a sha that EXISTS but is not an
ancestor of `origin/main` — the pre-rebase-sha trap the queue warned about at
its round-five entry, where `d01e5f7bc … 7c35e3963` lived only in a local
reflog. A known false positive is named rather than filtered: this repo's docs
cite launcher shas, which are real over there and unknown here, and there is no
structural way to tell them from rot.

RUN ONCE, full output in the field notes. Live canon (60 docs, `archive/`
excluded): 538 line cites resolved, 6 paths that do not resolve, 0 lines past
end of file, 43 unknown shas (several are launcher shas), and 4 shas that exist
here but are NOT ancestors of `origin/main` — that last four is the real find.
Including `archive/`: 126 docs, 41 dead paths, 10 lines past end of file, 196
unknown and 123 non-ancestor shas, all of which is frozen copy and expected.

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): the suite's live-gateway escape ran from atexit, so the fence is not a fixture

Measured on this Windows workstation 2026-08-31 — tests/hermes_cli/
test_update_autostash.py ALONE reproduces it in 7s:

  test_cmd_update_skips_stash_restore_when_reset_fails
    -> main.py:9482 cmd_update -> update_cmd.py:3234 _cmd_update_impl
         atexit.register(_resume_windows_gateways_after_update,
                         {... "cold_start_if_installed": True})
  -- interpreter exit: every fixture torn down, every monkeypatch undone --
    -> schtasks /Query /TN Hermes_Gateway_alice   (the operator's REAL task)
    -> _cold_start_windows_gateway_after_update -> _spawn_detached
    -> Popen: python.exe -m hermes_cli.main --profile alice gateway run

That is the exact argv the 08-30 baseline caught leaving a read-only suite
run. The backend-spawn arm in tests/conftest.py already classifies it
correctly — and could not fire, because it is an autouse FIXTURE and the
caller was an atexit handler. HERMES_HOME had likewise been restored by
monkeypatch to the operator's real store, which is why the child came up on
profile alice rather than a tempdir.

Three layers, each placed where the escape actually went:

L1 root cause — autouse `_no_windows_gateway_pause_token` defaults
  `_pause_windows_gateways_for_update` to None for this directory, so the
  handler is never parked and no test reads the live gateway table or
  Scheduled Task. Five files here call cmd_update/_cmd_update_impl and only
  test_update_venv_health.py patched the seam. Same shape and same reasoning
  as the existing `_suppress_concurrent_hermes_gate`. Opt out with
  @pytest.mark.real_windows_gateway_pause.
L2 chokepoint — gateway_windows._spawn_detached is replaced at conftest
  import and never restored.
L3 backstop — the spawn primitives are wrapped process-wide (never undone,
  so collection, teardown, threads and atexit are all covered) and refuse a
  hermes-backend argv, the gateway.vbs/.cmd launchers, a mutating schtasks
  verb, and any spawn naming the operator's real store root.

The regression tests carry @pytest.mark.live_system_guard_bypass, and the
mark IS the claim: unmarked, the older autouse guard raises first and the
test would keep passing with this fence deleted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): the fence's real-store arm was over-wide, and the thing it over-caught is its own finding

hermes root" refusal fired 56 times on ONE command —

    X:\Eternia\.hermes\profiles\alice\node\agent-browser.CMD --version

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): two hermes_cli.main module objects, and the patches were landing in the wrong one

The biggest of the 39 order-dependent reds is one file:
tests/hermes_cli/test_skills_subparser.py deletes hermes_cli.main from
sys.modules, re-imports it to prove the parser still builds, and never puts
the original back. From then on the process holds TWO hermes_cli.main
namespaces — the orphaned first one, which every collection-time
`from hermes_cli.main import X` binding still reads, and the second one,
which is what `patch("hermes_cli.main.…")` reaches.

The stub therefore lands somewhere the function under test never looks, and
production runs for real. The `npm error code EJSONPARSE` in the 08-30
baseline output was not a mock misfiring — it was a genuine `npm run build`.
That also explains the shape of the whole class: green in isolation,
perfectly deterministic in a full run, because it depends on running after
one file rather than on timing, and alphabetical order does the rest.

Fixed as a class, not per caller: an autouse fixture restores the IDENTITY of
any module the session already had if a test replaced or dropped it. Newly
imported modules are left alone — lazy imports are normal. importlib.reload
is deliberately out of scope: it mutates the module in place, so identity
survives, and covering it here would only look like an answer.

Measured on the 8 modules the class hits: 16 failed -> 8 failed.

sys.modules row. So restoring sys.modules alone left the two spellings

import main as cli_main` binding — which is how the update tests and

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): the dashboard stayed in OAuth mode for the rest of the run

hermes_cli.web_server.app is a module-level FastAPI instance, so app.state is
ONE mutable dict for the whole session, and the auth middleware branches on
app.state.auth_required. The gate tests set it to True and stop there on
purpose — the assertion that a fail-closed public bind records the flag IS
the last statement — so every later test that authenticates with the legacy
session token gets a 401, because gated mode does not honour that token.

That is the second pollution class behind the 39. It reads as "the endpoint
broke", never as "the process has been in OAuth mode since three files ago".
Measured: test_dashboard_auth_gate.py alone reds 4 tests across
test_env_custom_keys.py and test_env_export_line_lifecycle.py — the same 4
the full run reports.

Restoring the whole _state mapping rather than the single key keeps it a
class fix: a future flag stashed on app.state is covered without a second
fixture, and tests that mean to change it still can — the change just ends
with the test that made it. 4 failed -> 47 passed on the 5 files involved.

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): reset app.state on the way IN, because monkeypatch tears down after us

Restoring app.state at teardown collided with the fixture that outlives every
fixture in this directory: monkeypatch is instantiated by the root conftest's
first autouse fixture, so its undo runs last, and
`monkeypatch.setattr(app.state, "bound_port", 9119, raising=False)` undoes
itself with a delattr. The teardown restore removed that key first and
monkeypatch's undo died with `KeyError: 'bound_port'` — one green test turned
into a teardown ERROR.

Resetting on the way IN leaves every pending undo intact and still gives the
guarantee that matters: no test starts on another test's app.state. The
baseline is the mapping as it stood the first time a test in this directory
saw the module, captured once.

web_server family + the auth files: 147 passed, 4 skipped, 0 failed, 0 errors.

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): sys.modules can hold a MagicMock key, and the guard must step over it

test_setup_openclaw_migration.py mocks importlib.util.spec_from_file_location,
so production's `sys.modules[spec.name] = module` files the module under a
MagicMock. Unpacking that key's rpartition yields nothing —
`ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 0)` — which turned
two green tests in test_state_db_guard.py into teardown ERRORs.

A junk key has no package attribute to repair, and policing junk keys is not
this guard's question, so it is skipped rather than crashed on.

author: nekwo
message:
test(dcw-h2): the xAI label test never provided the catalog it reads

The one baseline red that reproduced in isolation, and it is a fixture gap
rather than a defect. get_label("xai") has no _LABEL_OVERRIDES entry on
purpose — that IS the claim: xai takes its display name from the models.dev
catalog, xai-oauth takes its from the override table, and the bug being
guarded was the two collapsing onto one string.

The catalog reaches get_provider through agent.models_dev.fetch_models_dev,
which resolves HERMES_HOME/models_dev_cache.json and then the network. Under
the hermetic home that file does not exist, so the answer depended on the
host: a networked box got "xAI" from the catalog and passed, this workstation
fell through to the Hermes overlay whose name is
_LABEL_OVERRIDES.get("xai", "xai") — the lowercase id.

Seeding the real catalog record makes it hermetic without making it
tautological: the OAuth half still comes from production's override table, so
a regression that collapsed the two labels still reds here. The unused
`provider_label` import went with it.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(s4): the skill-tombstone ledger becomes a per-slug register, and realm pull unions it instead of adopting it

RD-11 upgraded R-D from "LWW acceptable" to UNION. `Realm.skill_tombstones`
and `Realm.deleted_workspace_ids` rode the pulled realm JSON's wholesale
adoption, so two members publishing concurrently silently dropped each other's
entries — a realm-deleted skill became publishable again. A union cannot drop
an entry; the worst a concurrent publish now does is delay one.

A union of ABSENCES cannot express a restore, so `restore_skill` stops removing
the entry and stamps `restored_at` on it. Entries become a per-slug state
register: a restore is a positive fact that wins the merge on its own
timestamp, a later delete replaces the whole entry, and the merge ranks by the
LATER of the two stamps — which makes "restore beats a stale delete" and "a
fresh re-delete beats an older restore" one comparison rather than two rules.
Equal stamps resolve to the DELETE: a restore that loses a tie is one explicit
verb away from being re-run, a block that loses one is a silent resurrection.

`store.active_skill_tombstones` is the ONE spelling of "currently blocks" —
the match rule, the receipt rows, and the two CLI verbs' before-the-write
questions all ask through it, so an open-coded `entry.slug == slug` scan cannot
acquire a second definition. `prune_settled_ledger` evicts settled history
before any live block, because the one eviction this ledger must never make is
a block: an evicted block is a resurrected skill. One rule, two shapes —
records at the store, raw JSON rows in the pull-time merge, which must stay
tolerant of a peer's unparseable stamps.

The ledger union is NOT gated on `server_id` (the authority-field half still
is): a local-only realm loses a tombstone exactly the same way, and the guard
is not about identity. `_pulled_artifact_bytes` now returns the source bytes
untouched when it reconciles nothing, so a no-op pull cannot report `changed`
on re-serialization alone.

Two of the plan's own premises failed re-measurement and are recorded in the
stamped plan doc: its "shipped S2 suite unchanged" is not achievable (that file
is S1, and three of its assertions pin the exact mechanism `restored_at`
replaces), and `deleted_workspace_ids` does have two lift sites in
`default_scope`. Built as ruled; the boundary is written at the merge site.

Seven mutation claims, all kills hand-proven.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): `characters auto` — one process drives the whole pipeline

Stage 5 of the turn-efficiency plan, ruled in this morning (R-3 -> YES, wave
ruling RD-10). The measured problem it answers: a one-message "make me a
character and drive it all the way" ask cost 27 API calls and 1.556M cumulative
prompt tokens, and twelve of those calls were the agent asking a blocked
pipeline whether it was done yet.

`hermes harness characters auto --draft <id> [--through <step>] [--json]` runs
turnaround -> approve-direction --all -> rows -> compose in ONE process and
prints a receipt as each stage lands. Measured on the suite's own fixture: 4
CLI processes become 1, 8419 B of output becomes 6814 B, 231 lines become 5,
and the two generation-bearing verbs that each needed a wake-up become one.

The receipts are the verbs' own payloads because they are the verbs' own
bodies: the four step functions were lifted out of the command handlers and
both doors now call them, so "the same payload the verb prints today" is a
structural fact rather than a copy waiting to drift. Each line carries a `step`
key naming its verb — without it a reader infers the verb from the payload's
shape, which is exactly the round-trip being removed.

Three things it deliberately does NOT do, all three load-bearing:

* It never overrides a handedness refusal. There is no `--accept-handedness` on
  this door, and its compose refusal carries no `next` hint, because the only
  hint available would BE the override — an autopilot nudging an operator to
  waive the mirrored-art gate unseen is the reason R-3 was gated at all.
* It does not restart what already landed. Read as a flat script the stage text
  is destructive twice: `run_turnaround` re-rolls every reference AND clears
  the approvals, and `rows` with no `--only` regenerates every approved strip.
  The plan comes off the draft's own `missing.turnaround` / `pending.rows` —
  the same two lists the 4b resume hint reads — so a reopened complete draft
  costs one step and generates nothing, and `auto` is the one-command repair
  after `reopen`. Every skip is reported with its reason; an autopilot that
  quietly does three of four steps is indistinguishable from one that did all
  four, to a caller that has ended its turn.
* It never emits the indented `emit_json` block. The framing IS the newline, so
  `emit_json_line` lands beside it in `cli_format` — same `to_jsonable`, same
  key order, no indent — and every line including a refusal goes through the
  one writer, flushed as it is written so `process log` shows progress mid-run
  instead of twenty silent minutes. The summary is always the LAST line.

Six mutation claims, all hand-killed: the pending-rows skip, the
missing-turnaround test, the break-not-return that keeps the summary, the
empty-plan refusal, the flush, and the encoder.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(chat-elements): a finished tool finds the call it belongs to, not the last one

Stage 6 of the turn-efficiency plan (bucket f), independent of everything else
in it. Measured on a live turn record 2026-08-28: with two tools of the same
name started concurrently, the stream emitter paired the finished events by
NAME and `pop()` — LIFO — so the elements came out CROSSED. Element [0]'s
`summary` named harness-charsheet-authoring while its `tool_input` named
eternia-launcher-workflow, and [1] the reverse; the same happened to two
`read_file` pairs in the same turn. The crossing is completed by the
carry-through rule beside it, where a finished payload's `tool_input` overrides
the started one — so the wrong input does not merely arrive, it wins.

The plan's fix reads "key by tool-call id, not arrival order". There is no
tool-call id at this sink: `_progress_payload_from_callback` is handed
`(event, tool_name, invocation, result)` and no identifier exists anywhere in
the callback contract. Minting one means changing the runner's signature and
every producer of it, which is not the small observability fix that was filed.

What DOES reach both events is the invocation itself — rendered by
`_attach_tool_io` to the `tool_input` block for most tools, and to
`command_full`/`command_label` for the terminal class, whose `tool_input` is
deliberately suppressed against the 4 KB event cap. So `_match_started_tool`
matches on `tool_input`, then on `command`, and only then falls back to arrival
order — FIFO now, not LIFO, because concurrent starts of one tool finish in
start order often enough that arrival order is the better guess, and LIFO is
the guess that was measurably wrong. A match is popped, so one start is settled
by exactly one finish; the orphan arm for a finish with no start is untouched.

Eight tests in a file named for what it pins, and four mutation claims, all
hand-killed: the identity match, the FIFO fallback, the pop, and the command
arm that carries the terminal class.

fix(dcw-h2b): the fence was installed process-wide and refused another directory's honest work

Installing the wrappers and refusing with them were the same act, and they
must not be. This module is imported the moment pytest COLLECTS anything under
tests/hermes_cli, and in a combined run that is the same process that later
runs tests/agent_runtime — whose e2e tests spawn real
`python -m hermes_cli.main harness serve` children ON PURPOSE, against roots
they sandbox themselves. Measured on 671ae4f9a7:

    pytest tests/hermes_cli/test_env_export_prefix.py \
           tests/agent_runtime/test_serve_socket_child_e2e.py -q
    -> 2 failed, GatewayFenceViolation on a legitimate serve child

and in the wave-close full run 6 failed / 5 errors across
test_serve_socket_child_e2e, test_gateway_peer_cross_install_chat_e2e and
test_gateway_peer_two_roots_e2e — every one green in isolation.

The wrappers stay permanent, because that is the whole reason the fence exists
outside a fixture. What is now scoped is the REFUSAL:

  * armed for the duration of each test under tests/hermes_cli, by an autouse
    fixture in this directory's conftest — a directory conftest runs its
    fixtures for its own items and no others, so the arming follows the running
    item's path without matching path strings, and without depending on
    collection order (agent_runtime happens to collect first; nothing should
    rest on that);
  * latched on permanently at pytest_sessionfinish, which is the window the
    escape actually used. Arming is a FLAG the installed wrappers read at spawn
    time, so it need not win a LIFO race against the handler _cmd_update_impl
    parked mid-test — it only has to be down before that handler runs, and
    session finish always is.

L2's _spawn_detached stub delegates to the real function while disarmed rather
than refusing, so the chokepoint is ours only where it is ours to close.

author: Tony Arena
message:
feat(realm-sync): unpublished changes gain a second exit — per-item revert to upstream

The sheet could say "1 actor removed" and nothing in the runtime could say
WHICH, so the only exit an operator holding local drift had was Publish. Pull
deliberately never clobbers local state (correct), which left an operator whose
local changes are noise with no exit at all — measured 2026-08-31 on the Mac
store: office drift `offices_changed 1, actors_removed 1`, the one item a
baseline actor the census archived locally and nobody ever meant to publish.

Two halves.

ITEMIZED DRIFT, one walk and one authority. `_board_store_drift` /
`_office_store_drift` now build per-item rows (`StoreDriftItem`: family,
container, item_key, kind) and the four existing counts are DERIVED from those
rows through a table. The count shapes are byte-identical — the launcher parses
them today — and `store_drift.items` is additive beside them. A row that is
counted is a row that can be reverted, by construction rather than by two loops
agreeing.

THE VERB. `hermes harness realm sync revert <realm> [--item F:C:K]... [--all]
[--dry-run]`, registered and wired exactly like publish/resolve (`--yes` gated,
root-observability stamped, RealmSyncError -> typed envelope). The transition
table is pure and total over (family x kind x upstream): removed -> restore
through the un-archive door then the upstream content; changed -> adopt;
added -> archive local-only, or ADOPT when the subtree does have the row ("no
baseline entry" says what THIS install last published, not what the realm
holds); no artifact behind a baseline entry -> the stale entry is dropped,
accounted; a container with no upstream -> refused, never deleted.

Three rulings hold every line:

* A revert NEVER mints a realm-visible tombstone (AX7 authored-vs-diagnostic).
  It archives through the `record_tombstone=False` lane, which `BoardStore`
  gains here as the office twin's parameter for the office twin's reason —
  `archived_card_ids` rides the published board def. Pinned by two tests and
  two mutation claims.
* Local-only: no git, no network, no credential. A missing clone — or a clone
  with no subtree for THIS realm — refuses typed `sync_repo_missing` rather
  than reading the absence as "upstream has nothing", the one misreading that
  would archive an operator's whole local office.
* Archive-never-delete stands, and the subtree passes the same `sync_admission`
  door every pulled payload does. An artifact that exists and will not decode
  is refused, never folded into absence — absence is what drives the two
  delete-shaped arms.

Baselines are realigned PER ITEM from the store's own post-write content, never
by re-recording the whole workspace: re-recording would zero the drift of every
row the operator did not select. Rows are processed before containers, because
a restored actor leaves the resurrection-guard ledger and that changes the
surface hash. `realm.sync.reverted` joins the two watermarks the office
subscribe lane resyncs on.

message:
docs(canon): the decision-close wave lands in the canon, and the never-sync posture is stamped superseded

Four domain docs, no code. Every claim below was re-verified against the tree
at `51b96505f0` before it was written; where a doc's own cite had drifted a
line, the cite moved with it.

01 — SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE.

- The skill-tombstone ledger's conflict posture was recorded as R-D's
  last-writer-wins v1 with the union "designed and gated". The union LANDED
  (`4a8d398268`, plan stamped SHIPPED `25dfcb897a`): `_UNIONED_REALM_LEDGERS`
  unions `skill_tombstones` AND `deleted_workspace_ids` on pull, each by its
  own rule, ungated on `server_id`. Both the §Skills posture line and the
  §Realms ledger paragraph now say so, and the §Open rows entry is struck
  CLOSED rather than dropped, so a reader who remembers the row finds its fate.
- `skills restore` no longer REMOVES the ledger entry — it stamps `restored_at`
  (RD-11), because an absence and "this member never heard about the delete"
  are the same bytes to a union. That makes the ledger a per-slug state
  register; the doc now says register, and says why.
- `harness realm sync revert` is new (`3e6d8c06f3`) and the canon had no exit
  from unpublished drift but Publish. Recorded with the itemization that makes
  it addressable (`StoreDriftItem`, counts DERIVED from the rows) and with the
  three properties an operator needs: `--yes`-gated, archive-never-delete,
  local-only.
