author: nekwo
message:
fix(tests): two gates that went blind, and neither of them was production

`main`'s red and the drain-accounting report are the same finding twice: a gate
measuring the right thing through an assumption that had quietly stopped
holding. Nothing under `hermes_cli/` or `agent_runtime/` changes here, and both
gates were red-first — the reachability one on `main` at `a4f8e62af7`
(1 failed, 2 passed, reproduced before anything was touched), the drain one by
a probe rather than by repetition.

1. THE FLAG CENSUS MISSED A THIRD READER SPELLING.
`test_every_harness_flag_has_a_reader` named six flags as advertised-and-
unreachable — `persona instance return`'s `--proof-id` / `--artifact-ref`,
`roots migrate`'s `--config` / `--root`, `workspace create`'s `--agent`,
`skills delete`'s `--realm`. All six are LIVE and every one still changes what
its verb does. `a3b48a06a2` removed no reader and killed no flag: it re-spelled
six one-line reads from `args.X` / `getattr(args, "X", ...)` onto
`list_flag_or_empty(args, "X")`, where the dest is a string argument and the
`getattr` runs one frame down inside `flag_binding._raw` against a variable.
The census read two spellings and that is a third. No flag deleted, so no CLI
contract change and no launcher fixture re-sync is owed.

The admitted class is narrow: only the readers `hermes_cli.flag_binding.__all__`
actually exports, read from the live module rather than hand-listed here (a
hand-maintained list of spellings is what produced this red); the argument index
from the live signature, so a reader that is not `(args, name, ...)` fails
configuration instead of being counted at a position it does not have; a
computed flag name REPORTED in the failure message, not skipped. A bare string
constant anywhere else still counts for nothing, so the vacuous-gate hole the
file's own docstring names stays shut — asserted in both directions, and
sabotage-checked whole-tree: cutting the real reader at `harness.py:2706` reds
the gate again on exactly `skills_delete_cmd.realms`.

2. THE DRAIN TEST RACED THE POOL; THE ACCOUNTING DID NOT REGRESS.
28 runs (5 parallel + 3 serial files, 20 of the two named tests) found zero
failures, so the mechanism was gone after directly. `requests_completed` counts
what completed DURING the drain, so `== len(exits)` holds only while all eight
requests are still in flight when the drain op is parsed — bought, until now,
with a 50ms dispatch sleep and a hope about thread scheduling. A probe letting
all eight land first makes the same assertion measure 0 against 8,
deterministically. The reviewer's `5 == 8` is that race caught part-way; it
wears FINDING B's numbers (`serve.py:2324` quotes them for the bug that was
FIXED) which is why it reads as a regression. The pop and the increment are one
critical section and the request enters `inflight` before `pool.submit`.

The precondition is now HELD: workers park on a barrier, the drain goes out, and
they are released on the `draining` frame — no wall clock either side. Sabotage:
capping `note_completed` at 5 reds it with the reviewer's literal numbers.

The abandon test's first cure was WRONG and the field notes keep it: waiting for
the `exit` frame before `shutdown` empties the pending set and the loop ends the
drain cleanly instead of abandoning it. The dispatch sleep is load-bearing; what
was raced is the 200ms grace it had to finish inside. Grace to 2s (the flake
policy's floor), monitor poll to 60s so widening the wait cannot hand the race
to the monitor. Costs the file ~1.7s.

Field notes, with every command and number:
`docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/main-reds-2026-09-02-field-notes.md`.

No production change, so `changed_line_mutation_check.py --base a4f8e62af7`
selects 0 of 252 claims (stated, not skipped). Lane A green: cite-adjacency
0 unwaived / 0 stale, CLI contract fresh at 189 paths.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(gates): nine rotted coverage claims, a preload nobody measured, and a test whose wall was the box's process table

Three rows. Two of the three premises were right that something was wrong and
wrong about why; both misreadings are recorded with the numbers that settled
them in
docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/claims-and-skill-ceiling-field-notes-2026-09-02.md.

1. test_every_coverage_claim_names_a_test_that_exists was red by NINE, not six.
   Three were broken by PUNCTUATION rather than by any test moving: a name
   wrapped mid-identifier across two doc lines, one elided with a trailing
   ellipsis, one written with a trailing glob star. Two were honest citations
   rotted by a later deletion -- test_projector.py and
   test_read_model.py::test_apply_full_rebuild_then_render_is_equivalent both
   existed at fac754194e^ and were deleted by fac754194e with the read model and
   the projector, checked with git show both ways -- and are annotated with that
   deletion rather than re-pointed, because the docs carrying them are records.
   One was a window mis-attribution in tests/scripts/conftest.py, whose member
   citation resolved against the only nearby path instead of the file the test
   is actually in (tests/scripts/test_mutation_claim_anchoring.py); spelling it
   in full fixes the gate and tells the next reader where to look. The rest are
   re-pointed at the surviving test.

   The row's SLOWNESS premise is FALSE and is corrected rather than implemented.
   Measured three times, same shell: collect_claims() 27.4 / 31.0 / 31.3 s;
   _unresolved() 1.0-1.2 s; the whole failure report for nine bad claims,
   every difflib call included, 1.2 s. The failure path costs 1.2 s more than
   the pass path, not minutes. What actually killed the file is pyproject's
   repo-wide --timeout=30 against a 31 s module-scoped fixture, so the gate
   only ever ran when someone remembered --timeout=600 -- the unrun-gate shape
   AGENTS.md built the push lane for. Declared as pytestmark
   pytest.mark.timeout(180) with the measurement beside it (proved to override
   addopts: a 35 s test under the marker passes). difflib IS the only per-claim
   cost (0.135 s per call over 3002 filenames) and was unbounded in the number
   of dangling claims, so _SUGGEST_BUDGET caps the nearest-name hints while
   every claim is still reported in full.

2. A required_preload skill's SIZE now has a declared ceiling.
   SKILL_SIZE_CEILINGS in agent_runtime/skill_install.py carries one byte budget
   per canonical id -- today's size rounded to the next KiB with the headroom and
   a one-line reason -- read by harness_skill_size_overages and failed by
   verify_harness_skill_install.py in the same verdict as the hash lane. A
   canonical id with no entry fails too: unmeasured is not within budget.

   The row's "SKILL.md + references" is also wrong and is not what shipped.
   skill_commands._build_skill_message inlines SKILL.md's body and lists the
   references/ files by PATH for skill_view to fetch on demand, so their bytes
   are not per-turn context. Pricing them would charge authors for the exact
   split the reference layout exists to reward. SKILL.md only: 22,449 B of a
   281,553 B charsheet package, 208,687 B of which is FIELD-NOTES.md that no
   turn has ever carried.

   RED FIRST, both directions. A ceiling planted at 20,000 B reds the real gate
   on the real tree ("preloads 22449 B ... over its 20000 B ceiling by 2449 B",
   exit 1). And the load-bearing test asserts the gate reds on a package whose
   two copies are BYTE-IDENTICAL after a repair, with
   harness_skill_hash_mismatches empty -- a size gate that only fired alongside
   a divergence would be the hash gate wearing a hat.

   The byte count also reaches the turn record: _resolved_skill_receipt gains
   skill_md_bytes beside content_hash. The hash says which bytes rode along,
   this says how many; None, never 0, when the skill did not resolve.

3. tests/hermes_cli/test_update_autostash.py stops timing the box.
   cmd_update on Windows called _pause_windows_gateways_for_update and
   _detect_venv_python_processes for real, and the latter runs
   psutil.process_iter(["pid","exe","name","cmdline","cwd"]) over every live
   process. Timed in one shell seconds apart: 7.46 s over 513 processes with
   cwd, 4.02 s without, 0.01 s for pid+name. That was 9.09 s of a 10.17 s file,
   in one test with no interest in the process table. Both seams stubbed in
   _setup_update_mocks, the same two the guard's own suite
   (tests/hermes_cli/test_update_venv_health.py) stubs, so no coverage moves:
   9.09 s -> 0.03 s, file 10.17 s -> 1.01 s. The original six-file batch timeout
   was NOT re-run; what is proved is the mechanism and its removal.

Proof: 190 tests green across tests/test_coverage_claims_resolve.py,
tests/scripts/, tests/hermes_cli/test_update_autostash.py,
tests/agent_runtime/test_persona_skill_policy.py, test_prompt_observability.py
and test_serve_boot_skill_install.py, in one run_tests.sh batch with no
hand-passed timeout (the claims file at 32.6 s); 160 more across the adjacent
receipt-shape files. doc_cite_adjacency and dump_cli_contract --check both
green. Three new mutation claims (w2-*), all three selected and KILLED by the
gate at the branch base.

Not done: the live shared install on this box was already diverged before this
branch (charsheet repo 22449 B vs installed 22875 B, i.e. another branch's copy
is installed) and was deliberately left alone rather than repaired from a
worktree that is behind main.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(replication): a dropped steering edge heals itself, and the create ack stops freezing its skills block

Two queue rows. They share a worktree and nothing else, but both are the
same shape of defect: a fact recorded once and then reported as current
forever.

1. A dropped replication steering edge never healed itself.

   Measured on the base sha before anything was written. Three pulls of a
   realm publishing a child whose `steered_by` names an unpublished
   parent: pull 1 mints and reports `steering_dropped`; pull 2 answers
   `kept_local` with an empty `steering_dropped`; pull 3 — with the
   parent now published AND minted here — still answers `kept_local`, and
   `steered_by` is still `[]`. The edge is gone for good.

   The chain: `apply_replicated_steering` drops the edge and, because
   `applied == instance.steered_by == []`, writes nothing; the local body
   then omits `steered_by` while the remote carries it, and the baseline
   holds the REMOTE hash, so `classify_three_way_pull` reads local
   changed x remote unchanged -> KEEP_LOCAL "unpublished". Phase two's
   input is `written`, and `kept_local` rows are not in it.

   Re-running phase two for every `kept_local` row stays REJECTED: it
   would clobber an operator's own re-steer, which is the one thing
   `kept_local` exists to protect. What closes it instead is a durable
   record of the drop (`paths.persona_instance_dropped_steering_path`,
   `{instance_id: {parents, remote_hash}}`, never synced, never
   published) plus one discriminator, `_healable_dropped_parents`: the
   row re-enters phase two only when the realm has not moved the body
   since the drop AND the local body is EXACTLY "remote minus the dropped
   edge". An operator re-steer differs somewhere the dropped edge cannot
   account for and is left alone.

   The ledger is REBUILT by the pass that ran phase two rather than
   merged, so a healed edge, a HELD row and a row the realm stopped
   carrying all clear themselves with no expiry rule; the two arms that
   return before phase two (an older peer's absent projection, an
   unreadable one) deliberately do not write it. Only `parent_absent` is
   recorded — a self edge and a cycle are refusals of the remote GRAPH
   and no arriving parent can repair them.

   Wire (additive): `steering_healed: [{key, parent}]` on
   `result["persona_instance_sync"]`, and a healed row is counted in
   `adopted` because a travelling field did move forward onto an existing
   row. `steering_dropped` now REPEATS while a parent stays absent, where
   before it was emitted once and then went silent — a drop announced
   once and then silent reads as repaired. The launcher's
   `AGENT LINKS DROPPED` note ("does not re-apply itself on the next
   pull") is now false for `parent_absent` and needs its own row.

2. `agent_create`'s `skills` block was the last mutable-row field replayed
   verbatim.

   `_reply` listed `skills` beside `persona_instance_id` / `placement_id`
   / `actor_key` as "the recorded decision". The block is a MIX:
   `inherited` is a statement about the REQUEST, but `assigned` is read
   BACK off `PersonaInstance.skill_overrides` (which `update_profile`
   mutates) and `installed[].installed_hash` names bytes the next install
   of the same id displaces. Both are observations, and the STATE_DONE
   arm handed a replaying client the assignment and the hash of the
   moment the key first completed — the same defect `position` /
   `revision` had before S4/S4b, one key over.

   Those two are now re-read (`_observed_skills`, and the new read-only
   `skill_install.installed_harness_skill_hash`) under a `skills_fresh`
   valve shaped exactly like `actor_fresh`; `inherited`,
   `installed[].skill` and `installed[].changed` stay verbatim, because
   re-deriving them would make the ack a second authority for what the
   key decided. The valve sits at the TOP LEVEL rather than inside the
   block: three tests pin the block's exact dict as the `inherited`
   contract, and a key added inside would have rewritten those pins in
   the same change that alters the behaviour they pin.

Red-first, each watched red before the production change: eight new tests
(six on the heal, two on the replay). One heal guard — the ledger entry's
`remote_hash` — is UNREACHABLE through the applier and is kept anyway on
the H3 `replicate_instance`-allowlist precedent, closed by a test that
calls the helper directly.

Gates: 23 mutation candidates selected against `origin/main` with
`--max-candidates 24`, 23 killed, exit 0 (10 new claims, `ir-heal-*` x6 +
`ac-skills-*` x4). Lane A green: `doc_cite_adjacency --exclude archive
--exclude planned` (0 unwaived, 0 stale), `dump_cli_contract --check`
fresh. Suites: 199 passed across the two changed files plus the five
adjacent ones; the eight `test_realm_*.py` files 211 passed.

Field notes: docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/replication-heal-field-notes-2026-09-02.md
Canon: 01 §Realms (the heal, and the receipt-audit correction), 06 (the
H3 gap stamped closed, and `skills_fresh` on the ack table).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve): a dial off the reader loop, a verdict nobody read, and four sweeps in one loop

Three queue rows. Two of them had a premise that did not survive being
measured, and the notes say so before they say what was done
(`planned/serve-small-batch-field-notes-2026-09-02.md`).

**1. `runtime.media.get`'s P4 proxy arm dialled a peer on the reader loop.**
The row said the arm is in `serve.py` — it is in `serve_rpc.py`; `serve.py`
owns the one line that emits what the dispatcher returned, which is why this
needed a seam and not an edit. The row said the stall is 5 s; `media_proxy`
has TWO timeouts and an install that accepts and then goes quiet held the
loop for 30 s more.

The fetch now runs on the SAME worker pool the chat lane uses, through a new
`RpcContext.spawn_reply` — `spawn_chat_turn`'s argument made general: a chat
turn hands the pool a whole request and acks, this hands it the TAIL of one, a
callable returning the frame the handler would have returned. A handler that
takes it returns `serve_rpc.DEFERRED` and the dispatcher's one job is not to
write that sentinel. `deferred_reply` carries `handle_request`'s own try/except
to the worker, because a raise there is a client waiting forever.

The frame did not move (byte for byte, refusals included — `_media_get_frame`
is lifted out so both arms build it from one body). The bound did not move:
`media_proxy`'s two timeouts stay the only clock, because a watchdog on the
reader would be a second one and the long-run lane's rule is that work is
bounded at its source. What moved is arrival ORDER, which JSON-RPC 2.0 §6
already requires a client to tolerate and which this lane's own clients do.

**2. A single-test run's cold import.** The row's attribution was wrong twice:
the AST walk is memoized on disk (1.11 s cold, 0.055 s warm), the real cost is
importing the 38 registrar modules (3.36 s), and it is reached at RUNTIME
through the wire-row projection, not at anyone's import. The stated failure —
crossing the 30 s cap — does not reproduce: the ten claim tests run 2.4–12.8 s
under the suite's own cap. **The nine `--timeout=180` claims should NOT drop**;
that cap is a hang detector and its last failure mode was the claim lane losing
its BASELINE and reporting no verdict at all.

What the measurement DID find: `personas.all_registered_toolsets` asked
`get_available_toolsets()` for a list of NAMES and paid one availability round
per toolset — every `check_fn`, so binaries probed and clients built — for an
`available` boolean it discarded. The key sets are identical by construction.
Interleaved A/B, 5 fresh interpreters each: **3.08 s → 1.65 s** median, and
**25 → 0** probe rounds on `perform_agent_create`'s own path.

That retires the counted half of persona-prewarm Stage 3a and W3-H1: two GATES
went vacuous and their anti-vacuity twins said so by becoming unsatisfiable —
the pair design working. Each file keeps the stronger single statement instead
(a create against a HOLED `check_fn` cache probes nothing) and keeps the
per-persona readiness gate that was always the honest witness. Whether the
prewarm's remaining three memos justify the stage is a row for its owner, filed
in the notes and not answered here; four docstrings are annotated rather than
rewritten, since the receipts they quote were true when measured.

**3. `_placement_census_report` was four sweeps in one loop.** The read and the
GATE stay — they must happen once, in order, for the whole census — and the
four questions after them become functions of the world they produce.
`_census_join_workspace` takes a `receipt_for` resolver rather than a store, so
the memo stays per-census and the sweep can be asked the retire question with
no archive on disk; `referenced` is returned rather than mutated through. One
of the six claims anchored in that function moved with its block and is
re-anchored by symbol to `_census_live_actor_bindings`; `--list` selects all
six.

Gates: Lane A green (16 cites followed this batch's line shifts; one stale
waiver deleted, one re-anchored, net 90). Mutation gate `--max-candidates 40`
against the fork point: 15 selected, 15 KILLED. Tests: 562 green across the
media, socket, gateway, cross-install, drain, doctor, agent-create, prewarm and
CLI suites.

Not done: no live two-machine shot for row 1 — the dial is parked in-process,
which proves the reader is free and not that a real switched-off install
behaves this way.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(tooling): a span rule, a block-nested anchor, a summary that contradicted itself, and two wrong premises

Five rows filed 2026-09-02. Two of them carried a diagnosis that does not
survive measurement; both are corrected rather than implemented, with the
numbers, in
docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/tooling-residue-field-notes-2026-09-02.md.

1. The adjacency probe pairs backticks LINE BY LINE (scripts/doc_cite_adjacency
   ._spans). The row is right and the mechanism is one step earlier than it
   says: dumped at the call site, the noise cites are ones whose SUBJECT WINDOW
   cut lands inside a code span, so the first backtick the window sees is a
   closing one and every pair after it inverts. 07|snapshot.py:437 read out as
   detect/downstream/instantaneous while its real subject
   _log_agents_readiness_split sat at 437-454.

   The variant that keeps this canon's ~90 hard-wrapped spans (carry into a line
   that is itself unbalanced) was built and measured and is WORSE: the window's
   own cut leaves both boundary lines odd, so the junk returns, and it kept
   07|stream.py:135-173 green on advanced/having/honest -- a cite pointing sixty
   lines from its emitter. Table in the field notes.

   Baseline 90 -> 75: 15 waivers retired (13 now pass on their real subject, one
   is an honest UNCHECKED, one stopped existing), 0 added. The rule surfaced 4
   findings the junk had hidden; all four were read one by one and answered in
   the canon, three of them real rot (main.py:5039 pointed at a bare `#:` line;
   stream.py:135-173 and its sibling :100-101 at a docstring and a comment sixty
   lines from what they claim).

2. A block is not a naming scope. _qualified_definitions descends through
   if/try/with/for/while/match/except with the SAME prefix, so
   serve_loop._drain_monitor -- a def inside a try inside serve_loop -- anchors
   by symbol instead of by outer-function-plus-prose. The WHOLE_MODULE_SYMBOLS
   note predicted that this would make locks.py's two platform arms collide; it
   does, the refusal is by design, and it is now pinned rather than predicted.
   All 283 claims still resolve under --base origin/main --list.

3. The straggler pass bills its collection. tests_collected was accumulated only
   in the pool's _on_done, so a file killed at 8 workers and passed at 1-worker

author: nekwo
message:
fix(runtime): five small rows, and three of them were the same blindness twice

Five rows filed 2026-09-02, closed together because two pairs share a mechanism.

1. `migrate-home`'s skipped arm has `backfill-home`'s asymmetry. Its own comment
claims "Every line names the DIRECTORY beside the id or slug"; the skipped line
printed `{kind} {id-or-slug} {reason}`, and could not have printed a directory
because `_relocate` never put one in the row. The live store holds an
id-collision pair (`<id>` and `<id>.backup-…`, one id inside both `draft.json`
files, already pinned), so two refusals list under ONE id and the source
directory is the only field that tells them apart — on the arm an operator has
to ACT on, because the entry is still sitting somewhere.

2. Three load-flaky tests in `tests/hermes_cli`. `test_mcp_startup`'s
`assert elapsed < 0.2` was a stopwatch reading of a claim a stopwatch cannot
make; it is now an event — the stub sets `entered`, blocks on a BOUNDED wait,
and sets `left` after it, so "the main call returned while discovery was still
parked" is the contract stated exactly and an inline regression cannot produce
it. Probed: rewiring `main.py` to discover inline reds `assert not left.is_set()`.
The other two were bounds-too-tight around sync that was ALREADY event-based,
and both carried a second hole — the six-worker rendezvous's own go-file
deadline (which the parent cannot satisfy until the slowest sibling arrives),
and an untimed `multiprocessing.Barrier` plus children left running on a failed
assert. AND THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG IN A WAY ONLY A RUN COULD SAY: 120 s bounds
under `pyproject.toml`'s repo-wide per-test `--timeout=30` can never report —
the box killed the test at 103 s with a thread dump where the message should
have been. Both declare `@pytest.mark.timeout(180)`, the pattern
`tests/test_coverage_claims_resolve.py` already settled on.

3. `test_serve_drain_accounting.py`'s concurrency check billed itself "a
live-fire check". Nothing in that file runs a real serve; every test drives
`serve_loop` through an injected pipe and sink. What it adds over the pin beside
it is CONTENTION — eight workers finishing at once against one counter — not
realism, and the docstring promised a second KIND of evidence that was never
there. Corrected in the test and in the module header.

4. Every reader-spelling census re-checked against `a3b48a06a2`. Six gates read,
three blind, and the two directions are different bugs. A POSITIVE gate that
misses a spelling goes false RED and says so (`858c12c7a0`'s six live flags). A
NEGATIVE gate goes false GREEN, silently, forever — and `test_s26` / `test_s27`
are that, each knowing exactly ONE spelling: s26 matched
`'getattr(args, "task_id"'`, s27 matched `"args.task_id"`, so each was already
walked through by the other's spelling BEFORE `a3b48a06a2` added a third door to
a wall that had two. The fourth was unnamed by the row: the BAN itself
(`_is_args_read`) recognised the spellings the readers REPLACED but not
`list_flag_or_absent(args, "x") or []` — the collapse re-committed one layer up,
which is the spelling this very fix created and the one the next handler will
reach for. Every census now derives its readers from `flag_binding.__all__` and
the live signatures, and the rule is written ONCE for the pair that shares it
(`tests/agent_runtime/namespace_reads.py`) because "three handlers each
re-derived it by hand" is the finding `a3b48a06a2` was about. Both directions
pinned: a bare string constant is not a read, or `test_s26`'s own docstring —
which says `task_id` several times — would make its gate unfalsifiable.

5. `hermes postinstall` as a SUBPROCESS. The monkeypatched seam cannot reach a
child, so the fence has to be in the derivation, and reading it showed the two
platform arms already disagreed: Windows read `LOCALAPPDATA` from the env and
refused when it was absent; POSIX read `Path.home()`, which falls back to the
password database. So an absent `HOME` meant "whichever home this box's passwd
file names", and a spawner that CLEARED its environment — which is exactly what
a hermetic one does — still wrote a durable shim into the operator's real
`~/.local/bin` with the run's throwaway `HERMES_HOME` baked in (measured on an
operator's Mac). The honest hermes-side fence is the Windows rule applied to
both: the environment is the sole authority, an absent variable is a refusal,
and the receipt names the variable that would have answered instead of naming
`LOCALAPPDATA` on a platform without one. Setting `HOME` in the child already
worked; UNSETTING it did not, and that was the whole gap. Both arms of
`TestShimInstallDir` now run on either OS rather than skipping the one that rots.

The `harness.py` edit moved `_cmd_characters_auto` five lines, so two cites are
re-anchored — the same refusal `eb1a2fe8e3` answered two days ago.

Proof: red-first on every claim; mutation gate 6 selected / 6 KILLED; Lane A
green with zero stale waivers; the three converted tests green under an
8-worker 64-file load that had previously timed one of them out (626 passed,
0 failed). Field notes at
`docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/runtime-small-rows-field-notes-2026-09-02.md`.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(characters): publish the payload key set, measured from the producers

The launcher/hermes character payload is a cross-repo contract with a
default-deny comparison on one side and an "additive is safe" habit on the
other, and no shared schema. Three field moves have landed blind and all three
were found by a person: `34a8dad32e` ADDED `handednessAccepted` (every
`bundle_character.dart` run threw on machines with hermes, and was silently
fine on machines without one, which is CI); `4659127eba` REMOVED `cardSafe`
without an alias (the launcher's reader kept asking and read every live crop as
unjudged); `a4f8e62af7` added the CONDITIONAL `sheet` slot, which a captured
snapshot cannot describe at all.

`characters payload-contract --json` publishes the KEY SET, so the two sides
disagree in a file the launcher commits and diffs instead of at runtime.

It is DERIVED, never declared: the module builds a throwaway character library
in a temp directory, installs two synthetic characters and drafts, calls the
real handlers with `--json` and reads key paths off what they PRINT. Reading
stdout is what puts the envelope (`ok`, `draft`, `stage`) in the contract —
`charaRowThumbFromPayload` reads two of those FIRST and neither is in
`row_thumb`'s return.

Two probes with different state vocabularies and direction schemes, because
some map keys are DATA: a naive path intersection kept
`directions.mirrored.w`, since 8-way and 4-way both mirror `w`. A map whose own
key set moved between the probes is reported as one dynamic key and its
children are dropped — nothing declares which maps those are, the disagreement
is the measurement.

Key paths only and never a value, so the dump is byte-stable despite temp
paths, `mtime_ns:size` revisions and clock-stamped draft ids.

The load-bearing test plants a key in each producer and removes one, requires
the dump to move, then restores and requires it to move back. Both directions,
because a removal is the worse half of the class and the row's title says only
"add".

`tests/fixtures/hermes_cli_contract.json` is regenerated here: a new subcommand
moves the argparse tree and the freshness gate is the reason that is not
optional.

author: nekwo
message:
test(env): one canonical venv outside every checkout, and the fence arm that was inert without it

hermes-agent had no canonical test environment, so `scripts/run_tests.sh` had
no interpreter and every wave hand-carried `HERMES_PYTHON=/c/Python312/...`.
Measured: 22 checkouts of this repo on this box (primary + 21 worktrees), and
ZERO of them have a `.venv`. The system interpreter the waves fell back to
carries `packaging==26.2` over the repo's pinned 26.0, `mcp==1.28.1` over
1.26.0 and `starlette==1.0.0` over 1.6.0 — three environments wearing one name.

The venv is therefore built OUTSIDE every checkout, from the LIVE install's
own `pip freeze` (minus its `-e ...#egg=hermes_agent` line, which resolves to
ONE checkout and would silently import the primary tree while you run a
worktree's tests). The freeze diff against the live venv is exactly pytest,
pytest-asyncio, pytest-timeout, setuptools, ruff, ty and pytest's own
iniconfig/pluggy. Nothing else moved; `packaging==26.0` is preserved.

The probe gains `$HERMES_TEST_VENV` and `$HOME/.venvs/hermes-test`, APPENDED
after `.venv`/`venv` so a checkout that pins its own environment — and CI,
which creates one — is unchanged. Every candidate goes through the existing
"pytest must be INSTALLED" check, so an absent one is skipped, not selected
and then failing every file. No machine-specific path is committed: a box
whose venv lives elsewhere links it into `~/.venvs/hermes-test`, and a new
test rejects any drive letter in the probe list.

Sibling defect, found while doing the above and fixed here: the gateway
fence's "would run hermes against the operator's REAL store" arm was INERT
under this very runner. `run_tests.sh` execs `env -i` without HERMES_HOME (on
purpose — conftest installs a hermetic home), the fence imports after that,
and `get_default_hermes_root()` therefore handed it the throwaway TEMPDIR.
Measured 2026-09-03:

    _REAL_ROOT under run_tests.sh : C:\...\Temp\hermes-test-home-g_quyxlh
    _REAL_ROOT under bare pytest  : X:\Eternia\.hermes

and a `hermes config get` argv aimed at the real store classified ALLOWED
under the runner, REFUSED under bare pytest. A directory minted milliseconds
earlier appears in no argv, so the arm could not fire and the three tests
driving it were asserting against it — the defence existed only on the path
nobody is told to use.

The root now travels as `HERMES_TEST_REAL_ROOT`, computed by the production
resolver before the env is dropped. NOT by forwarding HERMES_HOME (that would
put the live store back in front of every test — the hazard, not the guard),
and NOT under `HERMES_REAL_HOME`, which is a production variable (the OS-user
home an ACP child inherits) that conftest blanks per test. Explicit wins over
the fallback: under the runner the fallback names the session's hermetic home,
and treating that as forbidden would refuse tests for using their own sandbox.

Per operator ruling, `[dev]`'s pytest pin moves 9.0.2 -> 9.0.3 so the declared
pin, the canonical venv and what the waves ran are one version; `uv.lock`
regenerated (`uv lock` reported exactly `Updated pytest v9.0.2 -> v9.0.3`).

Verified from a worktree with HERMES_PYTHON and HERMES_TEST_VENV unset:
tests/scripts + the gateway files 192/192; full lane (agent_runtime, hermes_cli,
cli, state) 1100 files, 12715 passed, 1 failed in 1968.9s. The one red is
`test_web_server.py::test_no_single_field_categories`, pre-existing: the
single-field `charsheet` config category arrived in 0c9fb95410 (an ancestor of
this HEAD) with no `_CATEGORY_MERGE` entry. Rowed, not fixed — this diff is
about the test environment. A `test_worktree.py` 30s timeout under 6-way load
cleared on the runner's own 1-worker retry.

author: nekwo
message:
docs(gateway-peers): the peer row's two halves are named, and a test holds the line (S0b B-h)

`peers.json` holds two KINDS of fact and said so nowhere: credentials this
install decided, and copies of what the far install told us. R-IP14 makes that
split a rule — one authority per fact, every other copy a labelled cache — and
a label nothing checks is a comment, so it lands as two frozensets beside
`_row` plus a test that they partition its keys exactly. A field added without
being classified fails; that is the whole mechanism, because the alternative is
a new key nobody ever decides the authority for.

`PEER_ROW_TRUST_FIELDS` = peer_install_id, secret_verifier, approved_at,
revoked, revoked_at. `PEER_ROW_CACHE_FIELDS` = display_name, endpoints,
cert_fingerprint, last_seen. S2c's `peers_cache.json` is then a MOVE rather
than a re-derivation.

No wire change and no behaviour change. `note_peer_seen` keeps writing a cache
fact into a trust file on every verified hello — the honest residue, stated in
the docstring and left for S2c (R-IP12a) rather than half-moved here.

`serve_gateway_auth` and `gateway_identity` get one sentence each on the same
rule: `name`/`last_seen` are the device row's cache half, and an install's
`display_name` is what it calls ITSELF, published as a cache fact — the one
name a launcher shows is the account's device name, joined by install_id, with
this as the labelled offline fallback.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(harness): harness_core is the one declared toolset, and the lane finally reads it

S0a A1. Nothing on the harness lane read a profile's `toolsets:` key: the
shipped posture is `unbounded` and that branch resolved
`all_registered_toolsets()` — every toolset registered in the process — so Neko,
both devs and QA had byte-identical 79-tool surfaces with 17 hygiene-withheld
names on every turn, while three copies of a per-persona `toolsets` list were
consulted by nobody.

- `toolsets.py`: `harness_core`, a composite of 15 member toolsets (the fork's
  `agent_chat`/`board` plus the conversational core), and `expand_toolset_names`
  — a pure, registry-free expansion to member NAMES so the bounded lane's cost
  policy (which drops by name) still sees `browser`/`vision`/`file`.
- `agent_runtime/personas.py`: `declared_lane_toolsets` reads the persona's BOUND
  profile config through the same mtime-cached reader `profile_readiness` uses.
  Absent / non-list / empty / the bare upstream `[hermes-cli]` default resolve
  `harness_core` as `lane_default`; anything else is honored verbatim as
  `profile_config`; an unresolvable home is `profile_unresolved`; a YAML fault
  resolves narrow. `effective_toolsets` is now that declaration, which retires
  `AgentPersona.toolsets` as an admission input in ONE place.
- `persona_runtime` / `tool_visibility`: both permission modes start from the
  declaration. `unbounded` still bypasses the cost policy and the blocklist; it
  no longer bypasses the declaration. The preview gains `toolset_declaration`
  and `persona_toolsets_in_force: false` (additive — no schema bump, R-S0a-6).
- Canon 01 + 05 §4/§4c/§5, and the docstrings in `mcp_admission` /
  `persona_prewarm` that described the retired posture.

Measured on all four mission personas, HERMES_HOME=X:\Eternia\.hermes, no
profile edited: final_tool_count 79 -> 43, withheld 17 -> 0, model_tool_tokens
2142 -> 1149, source `lane_default`. `declared_lane_toolsets` imports no
`model_tools` (A6a): 88 ms first call, 1.2 ms warm, against 1.7-2.6 s for a cold
`import model_tools`.

feat(harness): the ratchet — withheld 0, requirement failures 0, count pinned at 43

S0a A3.

`admission_requirement_failures` precedence 1 was "admitted AND registered in
THIS process ⇒ no row", which made the STEADY state a failure: the CLI preview
process registers no MCP at all and the serve tears the run's registry scope down
after every admitted run, so "admitted, not currently registered" is what

the 1-3 `mcp_not_registered_on_lane` rows per persona was for a server
`--explain-mcp` listed as admitted with `denied: []`. Precedence 1 is now

both arms are asserted.

requirement failures / 1149 tokens for all four mission personas, with the
anti-vacuity arms: a declaration naming `kanban`/`feishu_*` brings all 17 withheld
back, an opt-in `spotify` moves the count by 7, the bounded cost policy still cuts
the expanded set, and the chokepoint and the preview agree byte-for-byte on

REGISTRY membership while a turn resolves them through `resolve_toolset` (static ∪

author: nekwo
message:
feat(harness): A6 fold-ins — skills accounting, and the two measurements the rows asked for

S0a A6.

A6a (toolset names without the registrars) shipped inside A1 and is measured:
`declared_lane_toolsets` answers from static `TOOLSETS` + the mtime-cached profile
YAML with `model_tools` never imported (asserted in a subprocess) — 88 ms first
call, 1.2 ms warm, against 1.7-2.6 s for a cold `import model_tools`. The tool
NAMES still need the registry, so the full manifest stays its own row.

A6b (prewarm re-measure) is a number, not a change: after A1, in a fresh
interpreter under a hermetic root, the first `apply_chat_lane_tool_scope` +
`resolve_tool_visibility` costs ~1030 ms (the registry import), and after it a
`warm_persona_memos(dev)` costs 8.5 ms while the warmed `dev` resolve (6.6-7.8 ms)
and an UNWARMED `backend_dev` resolve (7.5-9.9 ms) are within ~1-2 ms of each
other. Three runs. The plan's decision rule (delta >= 300 ms keeps the worker)
therefore points at retiring it — that is the orchestrator's call, and nothing is
retired here.

A6c (persona→skill seed): skills WAIT, with the reason. The mechanism is the same
store-wins merge as toolsets, but skills have a store-writing verb with a
supersede clock (`persona set-skills`) and the launcher's Skills console writes
through it, so for skills the store is the authority by design; a config seed that
won over it would reintroduce the two-writer problem. What ships is visibility:
`config.persona_skill_sources` and two new `harness agent list --json` keys,
`skills_source` and `catalog_only_skills`. Worth shipping on its own — against the
operator's live config four of five personas carry config `skills:` entries their
store rows do not have (`dev` alone has six), silently, with no surface saying so.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(realm-sync): the board pull unions its tombstone ledger, like its office twin

`BoardStore.adopt_remote_board` wrote the peer's `archived_card_ids` verbatim,
so a pull from a member that had never heard of a card THIS install archived
erased that card's tombstone — a deletion of the exact evidence
`classify_board_pull(..., locally_archived=…)` reads to refuse a resurrection.
`OfficeStore.adopt_remote_surface` closed the identical hole for
`archived_actor_keys` on 2026-08-30 (C1); the 2026-09-02 board event lane left
this one alone on purpose, because it moves a resurrection guard and that is a
decision about DATA rather than about events. Operator ruling 2026-09-03: the
board family takes the office's union.

Reachable, not theoretical, and the red-first test walks the exact path: publish
records the LOCAL hash as the baseline, so an install that archives a card and
publishes is `unchanged` on its next pull and one peer edit away from
`take_remote` over its own ledger. Before the fix the adopted def landed with
the peer's empty list and the tombstone was gone; after it, the id survives.

The rule moved to `sync_merge.py` rather than being copied a second time. That
module is already the shared home of `classify_three_way_pull` — lifted there
from `board_sync` on 2026-07-17 when the office family became its second
consumer — and this is the same lift in the same direction: the classifier reads
`locally_archived`, and this is the function that keeps that input alive across
a pull. `cap` is a required argument so each family keeps owning its own
`ARCHIVED_LEDGER_CAP`; `office_store.merge_archived_ledgers` stays as a
two-argument wrapper so every existing office caller and cite is unchanged.

Two tests, one of each kind. The union test was RED first (`assert [] ==
['card_0f7a317e…']`). The peer-order test was green at base — the verbatim write
happens to produce the peer's list — so it was falsified against the wrong port
instead: reversing the two arguments in `adopt_remote_board` reds it, which is
what it is for. It pins the property the union must not lose, since local-first
ordering would re-hash every converged board and hand the next pull a permanent
"unpublished" local edit over identical content.

`tests/mutation_claims.json`: the `c1-ledger-union-leads-with-the-local-list`
claim was re-pointed at the function's new home — `changed_line_mutation_check
--list` refused outright ("mutation source not found in
agent_runtime/office_store.py::merge_archived_ledgers"), which is the drift
AGENTS.md §Unattended reporting warns about, caught by the tool rather than by a
reader. Added `c1-board-pull-adopts-the-peer-ledger-wholesale`, the board twin
of the office C1 claim.

Canon: hermes 01 and 06 said the board family does NOT take the union, which is
now false in both. 07's three `office_store.py:NNN` cites drifted when the
function left that file (the cite probe went 0 -> 3 unwaived failures); they are
re-pointed at the true lines, and the prose cite at :57 — which quotes a

author: nekwo
message:
feat(persona): --inherit-skills, the door back out of a one-way write

`skill_overrides` has meant three things since the instance tier shipped and
only two of them had a door. A non-empty list is "exactly this set";  `[]` is
"NO skills", the pinned empty; `None` is "follow the persona template, live, at
every use" — and NOTHING wrote `None`. `--clear-skills` writes `[]`, which is a
different agent. So one Save at the Skills sheet's "this agent" scope pinned
that agent off its template permanently, and the template tier shipping on
2026-08-27 made it worse in proportion to its use: "fix the persona and let the
existing agents follow" silently skipped every agent the sheet had touched —
which is the ones an operator most recently cared about. Operator ruling
2026-09-03: a separate arm, the capability an arg, and the sheet SHOWS the state.

A separate argument rather than a third value on `--clear-skills` or a
`skills=None` sentinel, and that is the ruling rather than a taste call.
`skills=None` already means "the caller expressed no opinion" through every
layer — `flag_binding.list_flag_or_absent` exists to keep it that way, after an
empty-list collapse silently erased skill sets (S4) — so overloading it would
put the tri-state's third value on the one spelling that must keep meaning
"untouched". The three are mutually exclusive and two in one call raises at the
STORE, not at argparse, so `harness call` and the RPC lane get the refusal too.

TWO SEAMS HAD COLLAPSED `None` ONTO `[]`, and both are the reason this is not a
one-line diff. A door whose write nothing can observe is not a door.

* `_profile_patch_snapshot` stored `list(skill_overrides or [])`. That dict's
  only job is the `!=` that decides whether a field moved, so an inherit write
  off an emptied agent diffed to NOTHING and this chokepoint shipped no
  `state.patched` field at all — a connected launcher went on rendering the
  agent as customized until its next full snapshot. Red-first: the new
  `test_state_patches` case failed with `IndexError: list index out of range`,
  i.e. no patch was emitted at all, which is a sharper red than the one I wrote
  it for.
* the `persona_instance.profile_updated` payload spelled both states `[]`, so
  its readers could not tell "pinned to no skills" from "follows the template"
  either. Now `None` travels as `None`.

No wire field was added, because measurement said none was needed:
`persona_instance_summary` and `state_patches._persona_instance_wire_row`
already emit `skill_overrides` as `None`-or-list beside the RESOLVED `skills`,
and the live fixtures carry it (`patch_agent_create.json`,
`live_repro_snap.json`). The row's premise — "the roster row carries the
template's skills, not the instance's override state" — is true of the
LAUNCHER'S READER, not of the wire; the launcher half reads the field that was
already there.

Six tests, four of them adversarial: inherit resolves to the persona's set (not
just `is None` — a mutant that made the call a no-op would pass that alone),
`[]` and `None` are two states through the CLI, and each conflicting pair exits
2 with the store untouched. Two mutation claims added, one per collapsed seam.

Canon: hermes 06 gains a tri-state table under the D10(ii) section, and the two
places that recorded "there is no re-inherit door" as an open gap are corrected
rather than left to disagree with the code. Three `:NNN` cites in 01 and 05 that
my +1 / +8 lines pushed out of the probe's window are re-pointed at their true
lines (`characters auto`'s pair collapsed to one cite while I was in there).
No baseline row was added; the cite probe is 0 unwaived / 0 stale.

Verified from the w11-hermes worktree on the canonical venv:
`scripts/run_tests.sh` over test_persona_instance_update_profile_skills,
test_state_patches, test_persona_assignments, test_harness_cli_contract,
test_flag_binding_boundary, test_stream_patch — 204 passed, 0 failed. Lane A
green, contract regenerated (190 command paths, sha256 a220d7e7).

A red I did not cause, proven at base 368387ae0b by stashing this diff:
`test_persona_skill_policy.py::test_charsheet_skill_documents_exactly_the_
characters_verbs_hermes_has` — the charsheet skill's verb table is missing

message:
docs(canon): the office's warnings, realm sync's own section, and one unrun-gate principle

Three of the four canon leftovers the replication fold handed over, each RULED
by the operator on 2026-09-03. The fourth is launcher-only (the hand-copied
ratchet numbers) and lands in that repo's commit.

(1) THE PARITY-WARNING CANON MOVES INTO 06. `office_actor_conflict`'s `guessed`
field, `conflict_guessed_keys`, `actors_truncated` / `actors_unreadable` and
`office_actors_unreadable` were written up inside 07's honesty contract while
the subject they describe lives in 06, so "what warns, and why" cost two files
that were free to drift. 07 keeps the RULE — a list that was shortened is as
much a silent zero as a phase that defaulted — and now points at 06 §"The parity
warnings the office raises" for the instances. The rule is 07's; the office
facts are 06's.

(2) REALM SYNC GETS ITS OWN SECTION. It had outgrown being a subsection of
§Realms and workspaces: the ledger union rule, the per-half authorization
correction, drift and revert, and the whole instance-replication lane were all
sitting under a heading that is supposed to define the ENTITIES. 01 now has
`## Realm sync` with four sub-heads, and §Realms and workspaces keeps the data
(what a Realm and a Workspace are, the two ledgers as fields, publish modes,
workspace scoping) plus one forward pointer for "fail closed" — which half of
which verb that gates is a lane fact, not an entity fact. 06's adopt-arms
section gains a lead-in saying it holds what those two FAMILIES do on a pull,
and the lane is over there; 00-index's 01 row names the new home.

(4) THE UNRUN-GATE CLASS IS A PRINCIPLE, STATED ONCE. "An unrun gate is
indistinguishable from a passing one" had been the load-bearing argument in at
least three plans without ever being written down as a rule — which is the shape
it describes, a thing everybody relies on and nobody checks. It is now a named
section at the top of 07, argued from the conjunction (a green report is "it
ran" AND "it passed", and the reader sees only the verdict), evidenced by this
repo's own `6979bad59`, and carrying the three consequences the canon actually
acts on. The two places in `planned/serve-small-batch-field-notes-2026-09-02.md`

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S2 — introduce, credential expiry, an attested join, and a capabilities list

`harness gateway introduce` is a COMPOSITION of the two mints that already
exist, printed as one envelope a launcher POSTs as a backend pair-grant. No
third ceremony, no new store, no wire twin: `test_introduce_is_unreachable.py`
walks the method registry, the peer allowlist, the gateway ops manifest and the
tool registry and asserts the name is in none of them, with the argv lane's
refusal re-asserted beside them so the absence means something.

Four things came with it, each additive by construction:

* `gateway_capabilities.py` — R-IP16's four words, sorted, in a module that
  imports nothing so the serve and a cold CLI process read one tuple. Stamped on
  EVERY gateway-block outcome including `disabled`, because "does this build
  know the verb" and "is the LAN door open" are different questions and S3 asks
  the first over loopback argv. Two named pins moved deliberately
  (`test_serve_gateway_lane.py`).
* `expires_at` on both credential rows, classified TRUST — a peer that could
  push its own expiry out would hold a credential with no end. `None` means
  never and is what every manual `pair`/`peers pair` keeps minting, so no
  migration; `introduce` mints 30 days (R-IP15 as amended). Both verifiers
  refuse AFTER the proof, beside the revocation arm and for its anti-probing
  reason, with new typed outcomes `peer_expired` / `device_expired`; the wire
  stays collapsed. The stamp rides `hello_ok.peered.expires_at` so both ends of
  an edge lapse together rather than each deriving its own.
* Requester scoping (R-S2-4): the peer half is genuinely CHECKED — a code minted
  `for_install_id` refuses any other install as `invalid_code`, charging one
  failure and leaving the pending entry for the install it was meant for. The
  device half is a LABEL (`account_device_id`) and the docstrings say so, because
  hermes never learns an account device id at redeem time.
* `peers join --expect-fingerprint` refuses a mismatch BEFORE any dial (proved
  with a client that raises if constructed) and the TOFU path now announces
  itself as `fingerprint_attested: false`. `gateway id` gains `endpoints` /
  `endpoints_source` / `listener` / `capabilities`, with a wildcard bind
  enumerating interfaces via `_candidate_endpoints` — the same list a join
  payload advertises, so the two surfaces cannot drift.

`store_file_io.stamp_passed` is the reader half of `iso_stamp`, written once
because an expiry written by one module and read by another is exactly the pair
that drifts. It fails toward LIVE on an unreadable stamp: reading a corrupt one
as expired would refuse a whole store at the door with the wire collapsing the
reason.

Deviation from the plan, recorded: R-S2-14 allowed a new `agent_runtime/
correlation.py` "if the fence is not already importable without pulling
serve_rpc" — it is (`state_patches.normalize_correlation_id`), so both CLI sites
import that and no module was added.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S2c — the peer cache sidecar, five events, peer.announce, and one usable_peers predicate

Two files where there was one. `peers.json` is now TRUST only; everything the
far install is the authority for lives in `peers_cache.json`. `note_peer_seen`
moved with it — before this, the one thing the NETWORK wrote into a credential
store was a `last_seen` stamp, which is exactly the confusion S0b's frozensets
were added to make visible. "Can the network change this?" is now answered by
which FILE a fact is in, and no function in the cache writer set opens
`peers.json` at all (asserted byte-for-byte after every writer runs, including
`apply_peer_announce` with hostile payloads).

`peer.announce` is the fourth name on the peer allowlist and the only one that
WRITES. Three properties keep that acceptable, each structural: the row is
addressed by `context.caller.peer_install_id` and there is no parameter that
could name another install (a payload that names one is refused
`announce_names_other_install`); an announced fingerprint becomes a
`fingerprint_rotation` NOTICE beside the pin and never the pin, because a peer
that could nominate the certificate it is checked against could become a
different machine; and `revoked_you` is one-way, cleared only by
`_clear_revoked_you`, which is reachable only from the two functions that write
a credential.

`usable_peers` is THE predicate (R-S2-16) — not revoked, not expired, not
`revoked_you` — and the resolver, the directory matcher and `peers list` all read
it. `resolve_install_ref` is the matcher factored out so the send path and the
tool cannot disagree about which machine `@mac` is. Refusals now name three
states where there was one, and the hint lists usable refs only, so a spelling
the runtime prints is never one it then refuses.

`peers revoke` announces `revoked_you` BEFORE the local write (R-S2-15), pinned
with a fake that reads the store at call time: a peer we have already revoked
would be refused at our own door on the way back. A failed announce never blocks
the revoke; the ack says `announced: false`. `--no-announce` for the offline
case, and a dry run announces nothing.

Outbound pushes (`gateway_announce`, best-effort, off-thread, bounded at
peers x 2 x 5s): rename, post-boot endpoints/fingerprint, agent create/retire
(`roster_changed`), and revoke. Nothing loops — an inbound announce drops a
stale roster and never fetches one. `dial_peer` tries cache endpoints before
trust ones and pins the trust fingerprint on every attempt regardless; every
hello now carries this root's own name/endpoints/fingerprint so the far cache
refreshes without a re-`join`.

Five `gateway.peer.*` contracts, emitted from the writing process (the
`realm.sync` precedent) so a CLI join beside a running serve is visible with no
restart. Ids and counts only — no secret, endpoint or roster body, under the
4096-byte cap. `SURVIVING_EVENT_COUNT` 59 -> 64 in the same commit as the
emitters, per S55. The revision memo's one remaining job is a write that emitted
nothing (an editor, a pre-S2c binary): a stat on reads that were happening
anyway, seeded per process so a fresh CLI never claims a change it has no
baseline for.

Two bugs found and fixed while building, both worth naming:

* `_cache_row(**merged)` collided with its own positional `peer_install_id`, so
  the first write to a fresh row succeeded and every write after it raised
  TypeError into a best-effort `except` and silently did nothing. It takes a
  dict now, and the id is always the caller's.
* `store_file_io.store_lock` documents that it falls through WITHOUT the lock
  rather than raising. Right for the credential stores (ceremonies, one at a
  time); wrong for a cache whose writers are a handshake, a dial and an announce
  fan-out inside ONE serve process. Added `_CACHE_WRITE_LOCK` on top of it.

Deviations recorded: `tools/agent_chat_remote.py` lands here rather than in S2b
because the outbound announce is its first caller; and the allowlist grows by
`peer.announce` only, with `peer.roster.list` / `peer.thread.read` held for the
commit that registers them (the "every peer.* name is allowlisted" pin would
otherwise go red on names nothing serves).

Plan: docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/s2-introduce-directory-push.md §2 S2c.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S2b — the read-only peer directory, the far thread read, and the HUD's install lines

Since Stage 7 an agent on install A has been able to send to `@B/neko` and have
the reply delivered back. What it could not do was anything a person does before
and after sending: see who is on B, or read the thread it was just handed. The
dispatch delivery has been printing "Their thread: persona_chat_… (agent_chat_open
with this session_id …)" — a pointer that resolved to NOTHING on the machine that
received it. S2b makes that sentence true.

Two read methods join the allowlist (R-IP9), and both are narrow the way
`peer.media.get` is:

* `peer.roster.list` (tier read) — B PROJECTS, A never filters. A roster is not
  a list of rows, it is the answer to "who is addressable from this scope", and
  the scope rules are B's; handing over the raw instance list would be a second
  implementation of `addressable_roster` that drifts. `target` decides the
  workspace, answering the SAME question the send path answers, so a roster
  scoped one way and a send resolved another can't offer an unreachable teammate.
* `peer.thread.read` (tier console) — `target` is REQUIRED, and that is the
  security decision: with only a session id this would be a transcript reader.
  With it, the same lane guard the local `agent_chat_open` applies runs here,
  through one shared `read_chat_lane_tail`, because a second copy of that guard
  is a second place to widen it by accident.

§0.10's fact 1 — a transcript read inside the serve process has no precedent —
is handled by failing CLOSED: a scope refusal surfaces as `thread_unreadable`
carrying the reader's own word, and the env gate is never set. A peer door that
widened its own scope would hold more than the local tool does.

`agent_chat_installs` is the directory verb (44th tool; ratchet and inventory
RE-MEASURED, 43 -> 44 and 1149 -> 1177 tokens). With no argument it reads this
install's own two files and dials nothing; with one it makes exactly one call and
caches the roster. Rows are `usable_peers` verbatim, so what the tool lists and
what the resolver accepts cannot disagree — asserted both ways round.

`@install/` now works on `agent_chat_open` and `agent_chat_threads`. Far reads
require `session_id` (`remote_session_required`) because there is no shared
default thread across installs — the far side's default is its most recent thread
with anybody. `agent_chat_send` refuses a far `clarify_token` as
`clarify_token_not_portable` and names the route: the continuity that DOES cross
is the session id (R-IP10).

The HUD gains a STABLE `installs` field and R-IP11's residency note: a local
instance whose handle appears in a cached far roster renders "[also on @mac,
last turn there 3 min ago]". Every fact is read from two files — the block dials
nothing, and drops when no peer is paired, so the committed stream goldens' HUD
bytes are untouched. Matching is on the HANDLE, never the display name: a wrong
residency claim is worse than an absent one because an agent acts on it.

Named pins moved deliberately: the allowlist literal in two files (four -> six),
`test_harness_core_ratchet` (re-measured, not adjusted), the inventory count, and
the three regenerated inventory artifacts.

Plan: docs/agent-runtime-harness/planned/s2-introduce-directory-push.md §2 S2b.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): S2d — the serve's peer-directory door for its own launcher

Scope addendum for the Stage 3 launcher lane (its plan's §0.6 + S3-R13), and
the decisive measurement is theirs: **the launcher's hermes stream carries no
events.** Its hydrate core is `agents, boards, offices, persona_instances,
running_work, …`, its fold entities are `persona_instance, incident, office_*,
scope`, and hermes reads `event_log.tail(20)` only for parity warnings. So S2c's
five `gateway.peer.*` contracts reach a stream consumer, a snapshot and an
operator — and reach a launcher NEVER, however many are emitted. Canon 03
invariant 6 routes new server→client push over JSON-RPC notifications; this is
that lane.

`agent_runtime/serve_gateway_peers_rpc.py` holds the row builder, the
subscription registry and the fan-out. Three methods:

* `runtime.gateway.peers.subscribe` (read) — the directory AND the registration
  in one call, for `runtime.office.subscribe`'s reason: a read followed by a
  separate join is two reads of one truth with an unreported window between
  them. A caller with no push channel is REFUSED (a subscription that can never
  deliver is a promise nothing can keep) and pointed at `…list`.
* `runtime.gateway.peers.list` (read) — the same body, no registration, so a
  channel-less caller does not read the directory by subscribing to it.
* `runtime.gateway.peers.roster` (console) — the fetch-through. A launcher
  cannot call `peer.roster.list`: it is a PEER method and a launcher holds a
  DEVICE credential. So it asks its own hermes, which IS that install's peer,
  and the answer lands in `peers_cache.json` (cached BEFORE the reply, so the
  reply and the notification describe one roster).

The notification `runtime.gateway.peers.changed` is fanned out from the SAME
`_emit_peer_event` call site the EventLog append happens at — one write, one
process, one moment, so the two lanes cannot disagree about when. It carries the
WHOLE row, so a client re-renders from the payload and never fetches, and a
dropped frame costs one row's freshness rather than a resync. That is also why
this needs no watermark, no sequence gate and no re-baseline receipt: an office
patch is a delta and this is not, and inventing the three would guard a failure
this shape does not have. Rows are the `peers list --json` shape, because the
launcher greets by running that verb.

All three join `LOCAL_CONSOLE_METHODS`. S3-R13 says "stdio owner + local
console", which is a KIND and not a strength: the peer directory is the
operator's own map of their network — which machines they paired, what those are
called, the addresses they answer at — and `…roster` additionally dials on the
caller's behalf, so a remote caller could spend this install's peer credential.
A console-tier DEVICE holds a real credential of the right strength and is
refused anyway; that case is asserted by name.

Pins moved deliberately: `test_scope_use_methods` (the set is no longer only the
two scope verbs, so it pins the SCOPE half exactly and leaves the peer half to
S2d's own file), `test_serve_rpc_authorization`'s gate walk (a kind-restricted
read verb IS refused by the gate — the opposite of the plain read arm, and the
whole point of the set), and the literal method-set lists in the three office
files, which grew by all six names this wave adds.

Plan: launcher docs/mission_control/planned/s3-launcher-lane.md §1 S3-R13.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(gateway): the S2/S2b/S2c acceptance across two real serve children

Five tests on the two-roots harness, and one of them found the thing the plan
warned about.

* **S2's acceptance**: B runs `introduce` once, A joins from the envelope with
  the account's attested fingerprint, the device half redeems against B as a
  phone would. Both ends hold the SAME `expires_at` (~30 days), the device row
  carries `account_device_id` as a label beside its own minted id, and the
  greeting's `capabilities` list is asserted verbatim.
* **The scoping, over a real handshake**: a THIRD install spends a code minted
  for A and is refused with the same words a code that never existed gets — and
  the code survives, so the install it was for still gets its edge.
* **S2b, and §0.10 fact 1's proof**: a real persona chat thread is seeded on B,
  then read from A through `peer.thread.read` — so the transcript read happens
  INSIDE B's live serve, which had no precedent. A session outside that lane is
  `foreign_session` over the wire.
* **S2c**: B's revoke tells A `revoked_you` over the still-working edge, A's
  own credential is untouched, and A's next resolution refuses on that word
  before any dial. And a CLI join beside a running serve is visible to that
  serve with no restart, with `gateway.peer.recorded` on A's own log.

**The find.** The far thread read first came back `thread_unreadable /
chat_scope_unresolved` — the CORRECT failure (closed, typed, never an empty
page) for a runtime nobody told where transcripts live. Root cause was the
FIXTURE, not the door: `publish_chat_head_home` is a no-op for a process that
named no explicit head, and `_sandbox_env` set `HERMES_HOME` without
`HERMES_HEAD_HOME`, so no serve in this file ever published a chat-head pointer.
The Launcher always sets both. The sandbox now does too, which makes it model
the configuration that ships instead of one nothing produces — and the ambient
rung's fail-closed behaviour keeps its own test in
`test_peer_directory.py`.

`_json_line` replaces "take the last line": `_Install.python` concatenates
stdout and stderr, and a snippet that opens a SessionDB trips the SQLite WAL
advisory AFTER printing its answer.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(gateway): the peer-directory notification names the store that was WRITTEN

`publish_peer_event` resolved its own root through `peer_store_root()` while
every writer in `gateway_peers` already had one in hand. On this machine those
agree; the point is that they need not, and that is exactly the class of bug the
module's "store_root is an INPUT, never re-derived" rule exists to prevent —
several roots coexist here, and Stage 6's whole subject is two of them at once.
A notification that resolved its own root could describe a different store from
the one the write landed in.

So the root travels with the event: `_emit_peer_event(..., store_root=)` from
all seven call sites, through to `publish_peer_event`. `None` still falls back
to the head home's root, which is right for the one caller with no write in
hand — the subscribe handler reading its own directory — and the test pins the
distinction by exploding on `peer_store_root` only AFTER the subscribe.

The EventLog append is unaffected (per-process, not per-root).

author: nekwo
message:
perf(doc-cite): classify every sha cite in two git processes, not two per sha

The report's cost WAS process creation: 454 `git` spawns over the gated
harness canon, 46.2 s of a 46.2 s run, because each distinct sha paid
`cat-file -e` and then `merge-base --is-ancestor` at ~90 ms of Windows
spawn apiece.

`_classify_shas` collects the walk's shas and answers all of them twice:
one `cat-file --batch-check` peels every cite through `^{commit}` (and
hands back the FULL oid, which is what makes the second call expressible),
one `rev-list --stdin` with `^<base>` names the ones that are not
ancestors. Measured on the same corpus: 3 spawns, 2.5 s, output byte-identical
to the per-sha version. A base this clone cannot resolve still reads as
"offline" for every sha, as it did before — that failure mode is not this
change's to redesign.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(mutation-gate): a zero says WHY it is zero — the unregistered-source census

A registration-gated gate is silent in two unrelated situations and printed
the same `mutation candidates: 0` for both: the diff touched no production
source, and the diff touched several while nobody registered a claim for any
of them. CI skipped its install and its run identically. S5 landed in the
second state (`--base 748687daa3^ --list` -> 0) and read like the first.

Every run now prints `changed production sources: N (M carry no registered
claim)` and names the M, sourced from one `git diff --name-only` over
`*.py` outside `tests/`, deletions excluded. On a zero the workflow turns
that count into a run-page annotation, so the skip is legible without opening
the step.

Reported, never enforced, and a warning rather than a failure: whether a given
changed file MUST carry a claim is unruled and has no honest default, and a
gate that guessed would be switched off inside a week. `mutation candidates:`
stays the first line — CI's selector greps it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(tests): root the parallel-runner probes on themselves, not on the system temp

`tests/test_run_tests_parallel.py` hands the inner pytest a probe built under
`tmp_path`. With no ini file at or above it — the system temp has none —
pytest's rootdir falls back ABOVE the probe and the collection tree is rooted
over the shared temp directory, so the inner session walks every other test
process's hermetic home while those are being created and deleted.

Measured on the Windows dev box, the same probe both ways:
`python -m pytest --collect-only <probe>` cost 58.5 s and died with
`FileNotFoundError` on a sibling that vanished under the walk; 1.0 s with a
`pytest.ini` in the probe dir. The file itself went from timing out at 8
workers and passing only on the runner's 1-worker retry (185.8 s, 111.8 s of
it the retry) to 14 green on the first attempt in 72.3 s.

`_root_the_probe` writes an empty `[pytest]` section — a rootdir anchor,
not configuration — at the three sites that spawn an inner pytest, and a new
test reads the rootdir back out of pytest's own header so a version that
declined to honour the file would fail.

This is the root cause, and it is not the one the queue row named:
`HERMES_TEST_TMP_ROOT` also made the file green (52.7 s, measured) but by
giving the walk an emptier tree to walk, and it is an opt-in env contract. No
env decision is needed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
docs(testing): the 30 s per-test cap, and why raising a wait bound needs a marker

`pyproject.toml` carries `--timeout=30` for every test in the tree and
AGENTS.md never said so. A test whose own wait bound exceeds it CANNOT report:
pytest-timeout kills it first and prints a thread dump where the test's message
would have been, so the obvious repair for a wall-clock flake — raise the bound
— silently trades one bad failure mode for a worse one.

The rule and the three worked examples now live in AGENTS.md §Testing, beside
the note on why there is no gate for it: a scan for numeric wait bounds over
`tests/` flags 51 modules and nearly all of them are safety valves rather than
waits any test expects to reach. Telling a valve from a bound is semantic, and a
gate here would be born red and land an allowlist.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve_socket): a DEAD socket owner yields the lane, with a receipt (R-L2)

Measured on the operator's machine 2026-09-04: the launcher killed a serve
child and respawned without awaiting its exit, the replacement read
serve_socket.owner.json naming the corpse (pid 25672), answered lock_held_by,
and ran stdio-only for the rest of the session — no socket lane, and therefore
no LAN listener, which is how a toggle that had written its config correctly
produced a door that never opened.

The OS lock is not the stale part; the SIDECAR is. Both msvcrt.locking and
flock are released by the kernel when the holder dies, so a sidecar naming a
corpse cannot describe the current holder of a lock that is still held.
SocketOwnerLock now proves the pid before believing the file, and reports what
it found: took_over_from + owner_started_at on the block when it inherited a
proven-dead owner's lane, owner_started_at alone when it was refused by a live
one, and one service-log line (serve_socket_owner_takeover /
serve_socket_owner_stale) whenever the sidecar was anything but empty-or-ours.

Liveness is serve_registry.pid_alive — the same probe that classifies a
registry row stale_dead_pid, made public and imported rather than copied,
because two answers to "is that pid alive" are two answers that can drift, and
this is exactly the pair that came to disagree about pid 25672. The fail-safe
direction is the OPPOSITE of the registry's: a probe that cannot answer is
never read as a takeover.

A LIVE owner is refused exactly as before, byte for byte. The payload's three
original keys are unchanged and the two new ones are absent when unknown.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): the gateway block says WHY there is no listener (R-L1)

"No LAN listener" had four causes and one word. `remote_gateway.listen` off,
no runtime root, a socket lane that never came up, a listener that failed to
bind — the first three all arrived as `{"outcome": "disabled"}`, which is the
word for "the operator never asked for one". On 2026-09-04 the launcher had
just asked: it wrote listen + port correctly, respawned, the replacement serve
lost the socket-owner lock, and the greeting told it the feature was off. It
rendered `unsupported` and the operator got a grey switch.

`gateway_block_when_no_listener` splits them:

  error:root_unresolved  no root — the same word `auth` and `install` use,
                         so one frame tells one story
  disabled               the config is off. The default, forever
  socket_unavailable     THE CONFIG ASKED AND THE SOCKET LANE IS WHY NOT.
                         `reason` is the socket block's own outcome verbatim
                         (disabled | lock_held_by | error:<token>), `pid` and
                         `owner_started_at` name the process holding the lane,
                         `host`/`port` are the door that was asked for
  error:<Type>           unchanged, from start_gateway_listener

Config-off wins over socket-unavailable: `disabled` is the actionable answer,
while socket_unavailable on a runtime nobody asked to listen would send a
launcher chasing a lock for a door it was never told to open.

The block rides `ready`, `hello_ok` and `version` exactly as before — nothing
moved, one branch was added. Note that `socket_unavailable` can only ever
appear on `ready` and a stdio `version`: in that state there is no loopback
listener to greet on, which is why `ready` has to be complete.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(serve): two real serves, one killed — the successor takes the lane and opens the door

The operator's 2026-09-04 session, reproduced end to end against two real
`harness serve --ndjson` children and a real kill. This is the one claim the
in-process tests cannot make: the first serve holds a real OS lock, and it is
KILLED rather than shut down, so the owner sidecar it leaves behind is a
genuine leftover rather than a file a test wrote.

The successor must do two things and both are asserted: take the socket lane
over reporting `took_over_from` = the corpse's pid and `owner_started_at` = the
corpse's own `started_at` from the first boot's ready frame, and then actually
open the LAN listener the config asked for. Before this stage that second boot
read `socket: lock_held_by` and `gateway: disabled`, and an operator who had
just enabled the listener was told the feature did not exist.

`remote_gateway.listen` is written into the sandbox home's config.yaml rather
than monkeypatched, because the config read is half of what failed: the write
path was correct and the greeting still said off.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve_socket): a loser still names the FRESHEST winner, not the one it read first

The takeover rule needs the sidecar read BEFORE the lock attempt — that is the
only moment the previous owner's identity is still on disk. But the branch that
reports `lock_held_by` needs the opposite: the incumbent publishes its sidecar
just after it takes the lock, so a copy read before the attempt can predate the
very process that beat us. This restores the pre-takeover behaviour exactly by
re-classifying on the contended path, and keeps the read-first copy for the
receipt. Two reads, two questions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
