author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): the default route is the first candidate, and the probe asks the internet

R-D2. `_machine_addresses` connected its datagram probe to 10.255.255.255,
which asks "which of my addresses reaches 10/8" — so on the operator's Windows
PC the kernel correctly named a 10.97.7.100 adapter with no gateway and the
router-granted 192.168.1.203 came out THIRD. The probe now points at
1.1.1.1:53 (no packet is sent; connect on a datagram socket only fixes the
peer), so the kernel answers the question we meant.

Discovery order is no longer offer order either: `_address_rank` sorts the
default route first, then RFC1918 on its own /24, then other RFC1918, then the
rest of v4 (Hamachi/Tailscale-class overlays included — sorted by rule, never
filtered by adapter name), then global v6. MAX_CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS is applied
AFTER the sort, so a multi-adapter machine can no longer truncate away the one
address a LAN peer could have dialled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): one dial host for every payload writer, and never a bind

R-D1 and R-D3's payload half. `gateway pair`, `peers pair` and `introduce`'s
two nested payloads each took `_endpoint(root)["host"]` — the LISTENER'S BIND —
so a wildcard bind wrote the literal `0.0.0.0` into a QR payload, a join
payload and a backend grant. That is not an address: Windows answers
WSAEADDRNOTAVAIL and macOS resolves it to the dialler's own loopback, which is
how S4's hardware attempt produced `runtime_unavailable` on both machines with
nothing wrong with either listener.

`_dial_host(root)` is now the one answer to "which address do we hand out" —
the first of `_candidate_endpoints`, i.e. the default route after R-D2 — and
`_dial_target` wraps it with R-D1's refusal: a live-or-configured listener that
enumerates no address refuses `runtime_unavailable` with
NO_DIAL_HOST_SENTENCE, BEFORE the mint, so nothing burns one of the operator's
three pending codes. `unknown` is left alone, because `introduce` already
refuses it and `pair`/`peers pair` deliberately still mint with a note.

Both payloads gain `endpoints: [{host, port}, ...]` with `host`/`port` kept and
equal to `endpoints[0]`, so a scanner that predates the key reads the same
first candidate it always did.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): peers join dials the payload's candidate list in order

R-D3. `cmd_gateway_peers_join` dialled exactly one address — the payload's
`host`/`port` — and any failure was `runtime_unavailable`, so a far install
with three addresses got one chance at whichever one it happened to list
first. That is S4's 12:00:13 receipt: a healthy listener, reported unreachable.

The verb now walks `endpoints` in order and stops at the first `hello_ok`;
`--host`/`--port` still collapse it to one candidate (the launcher's redeemer
owns the ORDER and passes one per run). A dial failure is about the address and
moves on; a certificate that does not match the pin is about the identity and
stops the loop — for which `ServeCertificatePinMismatch` now names a condition
`serve_socket` already raised, as a subclass so every existing catcher and
`pytest.raises(..., match=)` stays true.

The refusal names every `host:port` tried with its exception class, and the
stored row holds the candidate that ANSWERED rather than the payload's first —
otherwise every later dial starts with a failure this run already proved.
`_clean_candidates` also drops a wildcard row an older far install might still
advertise, and a payload with no `endpoints` key is read as a one-row list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): a requester supersedes its own invitation

R-D5. MAX_PENDING_CODES is 3 across both ceremonies and every `gateway
introduce` mints TWO codes, so the launcher's 2s/8s/30s retry for one stalled
edge tripped the far side's cap on its SECOND attempt — `too_many_pending` →
`pairing_codes_pending` → the launcher's `refused`, which is S4's 12:00:16 and
12:00:24 receipts with both machines healthy.

`supersede_pending` drops a named requester's own earlier pending rows of the
same kind before the cap is counted — that ordering is the ruling, since
counting first would refuse the retry on the codes the first attempt made.
`mint_peer_code` scopes on `for_install_id` (which redemption checks) and
`mint_pairing_code` on `for_device_id`; an unscoped `pair` / `peers pair`
supersedes nothing, because there is no requester to attribute the earlier code
to and dropping one anyway would invalidate a code the operator is holding.

Not a hole in the cap: what stays bounded is how many DIFFERENT parties hold an
outstanding invitation, and a fourth requester still trips it — asserted on
both stores and through `introduce`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:

feat(gateway): the routing table names the dial host, and the probe ranks behind it

still answered the VPN: Private Internet Access installs 0.0.0.0/1 +
128.0.0.0/1, which cover every address and beat 0.0.0.0/0 on specificity, so
there is no destination that follows the default route while the tunnel is up.

The routing TABLE can still be asked the different question. `_default_route_address`
reads it with stdlib subprocess, one command per platform, two seconds, and
answers None on any doubt at all: `route print -4`'s row whose destination AND
netmask are both 0.0.0.0 (PIA's split-default rows carry 128.0.0.0 and are
rejected by that comparison, which is the whole ruling), lowest metric wins;
macOS `route -n get default` then `ifconfig <if>`; Linux `ip -4 route show

Its answer is kept like any other discovered address and takes rank 0, the
probe's keeps rank 1, and the /24 arithmetic below follows whichever came
first — so on a VPN'd machine "the default route's own subnet" means the LAN's.
When the table declines, the order is byte-for-byte D1's: this ruling only ever
promotes an address ahead of the probe's, it never removes one.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(mutation gate): a claim can say which commit its needle was derived at

A claim's `find` is a source SPELLING inside the anchored symbol. The loud
failure is impossible to miss -- a spelling that stopped occurring is a
configuration error, and S8b and the S5 landing both paid it. The quiet one had
no surface at all: a needle that STILL resolves after a semantic edit runs a
mutation nobody re-derived, and the run goes green on a guarantee that may no
longer be the guarantee.

Ruled 2026-09-04, and all three halves are the ruling, not a preference:

- ONE optional field, `derived_at`. The schema had to be taught the key --
  unknown claim fields are refused by design, so provenance was not something
  an author could have adopted on their own.
- NO backfill. Absence means "written before this schema" and says nothing
  about a claim's health; the rows that predate the field are not silently
  asserted to be fresh.
- A stale marker is a WARNING line in the report, never a failure. Staleness is
  a suspicion, not a defect, and a gate that refuses on suspicion is one that
  gets turned off.

The count is of commits to the FILE, not the symbol: a per-symbol read would
need the anchor resolved at the old commit to say something the report is not
entitled to say anyway. The line is a prompt to a human re-derivation.

Also re-derives the one claim this branch invalidated. R135.4 rewrote the
ordering barrier in `_cached_tool_names_for_toolsets`, so
`bwh3-registry-read-before-the-deferred-import-populates-it` stopped resolving;
the guarantee it pinned survives with a new mechanism -- the barrier is now the
plugin-discovery call -- so the claim is re-derived onto it, renamed to say
what it kills, and stamped with `derived_at` as the field's first user.

Red-first, four cases: the schema accepting the key, the warning appearing with
exit 0 IN THE SAME CASE (an implementation that refused would fail there), the
silence for a claim carrying no field, and the git read itself against this
repo's own history with no stub anywhere.

Found and NOT fixed (predates this branch, not mine): the gate is currently a
configuration error on `main` --
`iws-ws1-the-activate-events-free-ride-at-an-undeclaring-client` anchors
`"realm.activated": SCOPE_ENTITY,\n}` in `agent_runtime/patch_coverage.py`, and

author: nekwo
message:
feat(mutation gate): the bound is wall clock, and the count is only reported

Ruled 2026-09-04, the same ruling the launcher's discovered-extras count took
(`kRepoLaneWallBudgetSeconds`). `--max-candidates` was always a proxy for
runtime -- one baseline plus one mutant test run per candidate -- and the proxy
kept mis-reading the thing it stood for. Symbol-overlap selection raises the
count BY DESIGN, measured on W1-H3's own diffs at 6 -> 27, 32 -> 64 and
98 -> 104 against a cap of 20; and the same work selects wildly different
counts depending on the base, because on a push the base is `HEAD~1` and a
two-commit branch selects 2 and 2. Neither moves how long a run takes.

So `--wall-budget-seconds` is the bound, defaulting to 900 -- fifteen minutes,
the ceiling CI's own `timeout-minutes: 15` already enforced, said out loud
where a local run can read it -- and the candidate count is printed on every
run and never asserted.

Checked in two places, both load-bearing. Before the mutating phase, so a
refused run holds no lock (the property the cap refusal had, and the reason a
run that stops for being too big cannot strand the split-up runs behind it);
and between claims, never INSIDE one, because a run stopped mid-mutation would
leave a spliced file on disk, which is the one thing this gate may never do.

`--list` no longer refuses on size. Under the cap, a diff too big to run was
also refused the inventory -- the one thing it needed to know was the one thing
it could not ask.

The count line keeps a token after the number on purpose: CI's selector greps
`^mutation candidates: 0 ` WITH the trailing space to decide whether to install
the test environment at all.

CI passes `--wall-budget-seconds 600` with the reason beside the call site (a
checkout plus `uv sync` eat into the 15-minute job timeout, and a budget that
expires inside the gate stops with a report where the job timeout kills the
step and says nothing). README rewritten; the workflow/README pin repointed at
the new flag, still hand-typing neither number.

Red-first, three cases: the count reported and never refused; a spent budget
refusing before the lock with no command run and both cures named, budget raise
first; and `--list` never spending the budget.

Two existing cases changed hands rather than being deleted, because the
property under each survived the unit change -- the over-cap inventory case
becomes "prints both halves and refuses nothing", and the platform case's "a
skipped claim still counts toward the cap" becomes "still counts in the

author: nekwo
message:
fix(store): the secure writer grants DELETE, because a replace is a delete

R-D9. `write_secure_json` narrowed every store file to `<user>:(R,W)` after
each write. On Windows the rename inside `os.replace` needs DELETE on the name
it removes -- or FILE_DELETE_CHILD on the directory, which only Full control
carries. A directory under the user profile grants the user Full control, so
every test on every developer machine wrote its second file and passed. A
directory on any other volume inherits `Authenticated Users:(M)`, which has
neither, so the SECOND write raised PermissionError [WinError 5].

That is the whole of D3 run #1's 18:06:20 receipt: every peer handshake on the
operator's PC completed, dialled fine, and then failed to record its row --
for a week, on a store at `X:/Eternia/.hermes/agent-runtime/gateway`.
Reproduced at `X:/wt/acl_repro_d4h` before touching anything: write 0 ok,
write 1 `[WinError 5] ... '.peers.json.qtip3iur.tmp' -> 'peers.json'`.

The grant is now `(R,W,D)` and gives away nothing: the DACL names the file's
OWNER, and an owner always holds WRITE_DAC -- it could grant itself DELETE in
one icacls call. Withholding D bought no security and cost the store every
write after the first.

Two files need DELETE for one atomic replace, so `prepare_windows_replace`
does both before it:

* the TARGET, because a `peers.json` an older build already narrowed to
  `(R,W)` is on disk right now with no DELETE on it. Repairing it on the next
  write is what un-wedges those installs, rather than leaving them behind a
  writer that can no longer touch the file it must replace;
* the TEMP, because a rename deletes the source name from its directory, and
  the temp's ACL is whatever the directory handed down. A directory granting
  this user only `(RX,W)` hands down no DELETE, so the FIRST write fails there
  -- measured as case B of the same repro.

`gateway_tls._write_private` narrows-then-replaces identically and wedged
renewed keys on the same volumes for the same reason; it takes the shared
helper rather than a second copy of the reasoning.

Tests are new because `store_file_io` had none. They build their directory
under the REPO and strip its inheritance down to `(RX,W)`: a case written
against `tmp_path` lands in %TEMP%, inside the profile, and is green against
the bug -- which is exactly how the bug reached hardware. They also put
USERNAME back, because `scripts/run_tests.sh` runs under `env -i` and does not
forward it, so `narrow_windows_acl` answers `skipped:no_username` there and a
test of it would have been green because the code under test did nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway): a store this machine cannot write is its own refusal

R-D14. D3 run #1, 18:06:20: the code was granted, the dial reached
192.168.1.39:8765, the far install redeemed and returned the secret, and then
`record_peer` came back `permission_denied` from a [WinError 5] on
`peers.json`. That fell through `_REFUSAL_CODES` to `runtime_unavailable`, the
launcher's fulfiller maps `runtime_unavailable` to `no_route`, and the sheet
told the operator the Mac was unreachable -- a claim about the network, for a
DACL on a local directory, retried once a minute for four minutes to the
identical result.

So `permission_denied` / `unwritable` / `root_not_a_directory` leave family 7
and become `store_unwritable`, family 1, not retryable. The families encode the
operator's next MOVE, and these two conditions differ on exactly that: a 7 is
transient (an AV hold releases, a listener comes up, retrying is the cure),
while a directory's permissions are a standing verdict until a human changes
something. `root_missing` deliberately stays on 7 -- an absent directory is the
one condition the writer creates for itself on its next call.

The message names the file, because the OSError does not: it says
`'.peers.json.ntk1yca6.tmp' -> 'peers.json'`, two basenames that name no
directory an operator could go and fix. The verb knows which store it was
writing, so it is the one place that can print the absolute path, and it says
in words that the other machine is fine.

One helper, not four copies. Every verb on this lane that writes a store --
`pair`, `devices revoke`, `peers pair`, `introduce`, `peers join`, `peers
revoke` -- passes its store path to `_refusal`, which classifies. `peers join`
and `peers revoke` also catch a RAISED OSError, because those two store
functions run a cache touch and an event append after releasing their lock,
outside the `except OSError` that covers the write itself; both doors give the
identical code, message and exit, so an operator does not get two stories
depending on which line inside the store surfaced the same permission.

`reason` is `store_unwritable` on the wire rather than the store's own word:
the launcher renders this condition as one sheet sentence, and three spellings
would be three sentences for one fault. The raw word rides in the message
beside the OSError text, which is where "which failure was it" is read anyway.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(realm-sync): a workspace lift that reaches the other members

RULED 2026-09-04: a restore that never leaves this machine reads as a failed
restore. Under RD-11's set-union merge, `default_scope`'s two lift sites removed
the reserved local-default workspace's id from `deleted_workspace_ids` — and a
removal is an ABSENCE, which the union cannot tell apart from "that peer never
heard about this delete". The next pull from any member still carrying the id
put it straight back, so the lift stayed local until the 500-entry cap aged it
out (MEASURED 2026-08-31 by W2-H5, recorded in the merge's own docstring).

A lift is now a POSITIVE marker with a clock, the same shape `restored_at`
already gives a skill tombstone: `Realm.workspace_lifts`, additive at
schema_version 1, travelling in the realm JSON and merged per workspace id with
newest-transition-wins. The deleted-id union then SUBTRACTS the ids whose marker
is still live, so a peer that has not seen the restore cannot re-add them.

It is a state register, not a one-way flag. `WorkspaceStore.delete` stamps
`deleted_at` on an existing marker rather than dropping it — dropping it would
be an absence again, and a peer's surviving lift would out-rank the fresh
delete. So "a fresh re-delete beats a stale lift" is the same comparison as "a
fresh lift beats a stale delete", tie to the delete, and a lift is never a
permanent immunity to deletion.

Back-compat floor: absent or empty `workspace_lifts` reproduces the old union
byte for byte, which is exactly what an old member's realm JSON carries — the
degrade is to local-until-age-out, never to something worse.

RED FIRST: `test_a_pull_cannot_undo_a_lift_the_publisher_never_heard_about`
fails without the subtraction with `['ws_theirs', 'ws_default'] != ['ws_theirs']`
— the peer re-deleting the just-restored workspace, which is the defect.

One doc cite into models.py is re-anchored by the lines this added; the four
unwaived cite-adjacency failures are the same four as at base.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway peers): EHOSTUNREACH on-link is a permission, not a route (R-D20)

Measured on the operator's Mac 2026-09-04 20:19:25. macOS 15 Local Network
privacy had never been granted to the app responsible for the launcher's
process tree, so the kernel answered EHOSTUNREACH (errno 65) for every host
on the Mac's own /24 except the router -- on every port and on ICMP, with the
ARP entry for 192.168.1.203 resolved, in 177 ms because nothing was ever sent.
`peers join` reported `192.168.1.203:8765 (OSError)` under `runtime_unavailable`,
the launcher painted "Unreachable", and the operator was sent to the router for
a permission on their own machine.

The errno alone cannot carry that: the identical number against an address
nobody routes to really is a route failure. `classify_dial_error` asks the
second question -- is the host on a segment one of THIS machine's own
addresses sits on -- and only then spends the word. v4 reuses `_shares_24`
against D1's `_machine_addresses`; v6 answers from the address itself (link-
local by definition, unique-local by a /64 share, global never).

`local_policy` joins the family table at 2, not 7: the identical command does
not succeed later (thirty denials and zero prompts in 24 h on that Mac) and
every retry burns a pairing code. The refusal names the addresses and the pane;
the reachability note leads with the word so a reader can branch on it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): `characters thumb` crops a turnaround DIRECTION reference too

The launcher's QA card drew a tile through the whole turnaround stage — not
because a reference was unsafe to decode (it is generated on a square canvas
well inside both bounds) but because no verb published a VERDICT for one. The
crop verb was row-only.

`--direction <d>` is the second arm, and it is the SAME code: one `_finish_thumb`
weighs both bounds, keys, upscales, pads and writes for both kinds, so one
consumer rule ("inline only when both booleans are true") covers both. A
reference is one pose, so `frame`/`frames`/`row` are absent from its payload
rather than faked to 0-of-1, and `--frame` asked of a direction is refused
rather than silently answered with the whole picture. `pipeline.reference_cell`
is `frame_cell`'s "nothing to slice" counterpart, so every decode of a QA source
still happens in the module that owns pixels.

The payload contract measures both arms as two MODES of the thumb kind, so the
launcher reads one contract for the card's two arms; the planted-key test now
plants both producers, because a key union across modes proves nothing when only
one arm is moved.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): approve-direction reports the reference's measured facing

Approving a turnaround certified nothing about the direction it approved.
Measured on the live anime-girl draft: the approved `e` reference is a
west-facing profile (face offset -44.8) while all three `e` rows drawn from it
face east (+10.9 / +9.9 / +10.5) — one attempt, approved index 0, nothing
rerolled. The disagreement was there to be read at approve time and no surface
read it.

`pipeline.face_offset` is that quantity: the alpha-weighted horizontal centroid
of the top quarter of the subject's own bbox, minus the centroid of the whole
subject, keyed off the chroma field first (a measure that skipped the keying
step would return the centroid of the CANVAS — 0.0 for every picture ever
drawn). Signed, positive to the right of frame; `None` for a picture with
nothing on it, because "nothing to read" is not "it faces straight at you".

It rides on BOTH approval arms — `--all` is the path `auto` takes and the path
the anime-girl draft was approved through — in the payload and in the human
line. A measurement, not a gate: what a correct offset is for a given sector of
an unknown character is not something this code knows, and the front and back
views measure near zero legitimately.

feat(charsheet): status and list join the payload contract, behind a `{}` placeholder

Two of the four READ payloads the launcher decodes were outside the published

from the contract cost a person a re-run of the verbs to discover.

They were outside because every QA item in `status` hangs off a map keyed by

test(charsheet): a payload FLAG is admitted by a check, not by the author's memory

The class behind two repaired instances: a payload boolean whose guarantee lives
only in prose. `MAX_CARD_PIXELS`'s "can never drift" comment and `cardSafe` both
passed a green suite because every test asserted the predicate's ARITHMETIC and
none asserted a case where the documented guarantee and the implemented one
disagree. Both instances were fixed; nothing looked at the next one.

The gate has two halves, split along what each side is good at. The POPULATION
is measured — `build_flag_inventory` re-reads the same probe run the contract

print, so a flag cannot fail to reach the test. The ADMISSION is declared,
because it is a judgement: a Guarantee (naming the pure predicate that computes
it and a test where it DISAGREES with its neighbour) or Data (saying why there
is nothing to drift). Twelve flags today; an unadmitted one reds, and so does a
stale entry.

Proved by planting `plantedFlagBySuite` in `row_thumb`: red with it, green
without. The kind probes were refactored to return their raw documents so ONE

author: nekwo
message:
fix(gateway peers): the re-pair's revoked_you clear was taking the lock it was already holding

`redeem_peer_code` called `_clear_revoked_you` from inside its own
`with _store_lock(store_root):`. That helper writes through `_touch_cache`,
which opens the same lock, and the lock is not reentrant -- so a re-pair of an
install carrying `revoked_you` spent the whole ten-second budget contending
with the write it was describing. `record_peer`, the other credential writer,
always cleared after its lock closed; the redeeming half now has that shape.
The credential is captured inside the block and returned after it, and every
refusal path still returns from inside, unchanged.

Measured, and the mechanism is not the one `locks._file_lock`'s docstring
predicts: `_store_lock` is `store_file_io.store_lock`, which falls through
WITHOUT the lock rather than refusing. On Windows the nested acquire polls for
10.03 s and then writes unsynchronised; the POSIX arm takes a bare blocking
`flock` with no deadline at all, where a second open file description in the
same process never returns.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(stream lane): a refused subscribe leaves a line, not a silence (R-D26)

The serve logged `stream_attach` on every successful attachment and NOTHING on
any of the six refusals. On 2026-09-04 the Windows cockpit's stream to the Mac
died 7 ms after its subscribe and neither machine held a record of which of the
five denials it was -- the reason lived only in the launcher's memory and went
out with the connection.

`agent_runtime/stream.py` grows `log_stream_denied` beside its sibling, same
logger, same `key=value` style, INFO:

    stream_denied lane=stream reason=already_subscribed connection=conn-7 \
        client=cockpit transport=gateway tier=console at=precheck pid=28344

`serve.py` grows one `_deny_subscribe(sink, connection, lane, reason, **extra)`
that logs and then emits, and all six inline emits call it. Single-homing both
halves is what stops a seventh branch growing the frame and forgetting the line.
The frame is unchanged key for key -- the launcher's connector switches on
`event`/`reason`, and the parity and socket-lane tests pin the shape.

The line carries no device id: the connection key identifies the connection to a
reader of this process's log and to nobody else, which is all this needs.
`transport` and `tier` ride because "which door, at which tier" is the question
the field gap was about. `at` separates the two branches sharing
`already_subscribed` -- a stale attachment and a lost race are different
diagnoses and the frame cannot tell them apart.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(store lock): the deadline is the contract on both arms, and the block only runs locked

`store_file_io.store_lock` was a second copy of `locks._file_lock` carrying the
exact defect that module's docstring records having been rewritten to remove,
and worse in both arms. Windows polled `LK_NBLCK` to the deadline and then
`break`ed with `locked = False` and yielded ANYWAY, so a caller that lost the
race did its read-modify-write of `peers.json` ten seconds late and
unsynchronised -- silently, since the store, the return value and the wire all
read identically for a write that held the lock and a write that gave up
waiting for it. POSIX never reached a deadline at all: a bare blocking
`flock(fd, LOCK_EX)` that ignored `timeout_seconds`, where a second open file
description inside one process did not stall, it never returned.

R-D27. The body is now one line -- `locks._file_lock(path, timeout_seconds=)` --
rather than a third implementation of one primitive: that function already
TAKES a path, so the "the gateway lane may not re-derive a root" rule the
restatement was written for is not in play, and a second correct deadline loop
would be the copy that drifts next. One loop, both platforms: contention polled,
a real fault re-raised unwrapped, the deadline raising `HarnessLockUnavailable`,
and the block running only with the lock held.

Every caller audited. The seven that already turned a store they could not
write into a typed `StoreRefusal` catch the refusal beside the `OSError`;
`os_error_reason` names it explicitly and answers `unwritable`, which is what
it answered by accident before, so the CLI renders `store_unwritable` (family
1, D4h) with the lock's own sentence in the message. The two best-effort
writers (`note_device_seen`, `_touch_cache`) catch `Exception` and now SKIP the
bookkeeping instead of writing it unlocked. Nothing crashes where it previously
fell through.

Tests in D4h's file: a lock another holder owns refuses inside the budget and
never runs the block, a release lets the next caller in, the POSIX arm's
same-process deadlock is pinned POSIX-only with the reason on the mark, the
Windows arm is pinned with an elapsed FLOOR proving it polled to the deadline,
and `record_peer` under a held lock returns a `StoreRefusal` in the unwritable
family with `peers.json` still absent. Every case asserts on the error, not on
timing: the defect spent the identical ten seconds and then wrote anyway.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>

question — is any branch in this module unreachable today — could not be asked

`coverage==7.16.0` is pinned in pyproject's `[dev]` extra (uv.lock regenerated;

`scripts/unreachable_branch_report.py` is the measurement, and a REPORT by the

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): compose persists the colour table, and both payloads publish it

The launcher's swatch strip is blocked on a fact only this repo has. Sheets are
palette-locked — one table, derived from the approved references, that every
cell is quantized into — and that table reached no payload the launcher reads.
Deriving it there would decode a 1536x2080 WebP per character on a surface that
asks this process even for a cropped thumbnail, and would re-derive at read time
what the producer knows at write time.

`palette_table` measures it off the sheet being installed: the sheet's distinct
opaque colours ARE the locked table, and counting them adds the one thing the
palette image cannot carry — how much of the character each colour is — so a
strip's first swatches are its dominant colours rather than whatever order the
median cut assigned. Alpha is `ff` on every entry because the locked palette is
an opaque RGB table (the pipeline carries alpha separately, so grouping by RGBA
would answer thousands of entries for a 48-colour sheet).

`compose` writes it to `palette.json` beside the draft AND beside the install,
from one measurement. The two directories are different objects whose lifetimes
do not agree — the clobber guard exists because a slug can be owned by a
different draft — so neither can answer for the other.

Absent stays absent. A character composed before this field carries no `palette`
key at all, never `[]`: "nobody recorded a table" and "this sheet has no
colours" are different facts, and the launcher owes them different renders. A
malformed file is absence too — a colour table must not take `characters list`
down.

The payload contract now SEES the key: `status` and `list` are each probed with
and without a table on disk, so `palette` is recorded conditional rather than
meeting the launcher's default-deny key walk for the first time at runtime —
the `handednessAccepted` incident that module exists to prevent.

Red-first: reversing the sort kills `test_the_table_is_the_colours_in_
DESCENDING_pixel_count` and `test_a_third_colour_lands_where_its_coverage_puts_
it`; the order is asserted positionally and against counts recomputed from the
real installed sheet.

The two doc cites re-pointed are line shifts this commit caused in harness.py.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(charsheet): the 46 one-armed branches get a case, a deletion or a named reason

`scripts/unreachable_branch_report.py` found 46 branches in `agent/charsheet`
whose line ran every time and whose other arm never once won, and nobody had
triaged them. Each is now answered: a case that reaches it, a deletion where no
input can distinguish the arms, or a named case with the suite it belongs in.

46 -> 7, both runs green (before: 6 files, 408 tests, 235.6s; after: 7 files,
463 tests, 328.6s, both at -j 4). `palette.py`, `prompts.py`, `spec.py` and
`revisions.py` report zero one-armed branches and zero cold statements;
`pipeline.py` is down to one of each.

Two branches deleted, both provably indistinguishable rather than merely
uncovered:

* `palette.py:130`'s `if used:` — `getpalette()` reads out of the SAME palette
  object as `.colors`, so bytes imply a non-empty `.colors` and no bytes imply
  an empty `triples`. Both arms answered the identical list for every reachable
  image. `used` defaults to `{}` and the filter is unconditional.
* `pipeline.py:2400`'s `if global_med_w and global_med_h:` — reaching it means
  a row with >=2 boxes exists, every box is a `getbbox()` spanning >=1 pixel,
  and that is exactly what assigns both medians. Neither can be zero there.

`palette.py:91`'s `getcolors() is None` gets the `# pragma: no cover` its
identical twin in the same file already carries: the cap is the pixel count, so
nothing can reach it, and deleting the raise would turn it into a `TypeError`.

Three of the 46 were filed on a premise that did not survive re-measurement, and
the tests say so: the revision store's `keys()` guard is not reached "before
anything is written" (the constructor mkdirs the root) but by the root vanishing
under a live store; `_handedness_accepted` NORMALISES the round-two bare row
keys rather than dropping them; and `handedness_summary`'s one-armed arm is the
one that SKIPS the unjudged clause, not the one that writes it.

The report itself reds without a fix, twice over: 110 traced pipeline tests
cross the runner's 300s per-file cap and come back as "no tests ran", and the
obvious `HERMES_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT` seam is dropped by `run_tests.sh`'s `env -i`
fence. The cap now rides the argv, and both facts are pinned.

message:
feat(gateway): the address a far install actually reached stops being thrown away

D12, ruled 2026-09-05, hermes half. Every address this install publishes today
is an inference -- a routing-table read (R-D8) or a datagram probe (R-D2), and
the probe has already been measured wrong once with a VPN up. The one MEASURED
answer exists on every successful pairing and was discarded: the accepting
socket's `getsockname()` is the local address the kernel bound that connection
to, which on a wildcard bind names the single interface the packet arrived on.

admission refusal can close the socket before the frame is built) and parked on

bind address" held at a new door.

(the far side), each `connections` row (THIS install's launcher, which is the
consumer R-D7 actually writes for and which the row did not name), and the
`gateway peers join` ack, copied off the frame and never re-derived from the
candidate that was dialled -- a fabricated measurement would look like proof
and be an echo of the guess.

The loopback-vs-gateway greeting equality test now compares `reached_at`'s host
and drops its ephemeral port; nothing was waived and the volatile set is
unchanged. Two cites in docs 03 and 04 re-anchored for the insertion.

recorded in 03-transport-and-wire.md section 2. The launcher half (write it

author: nekwo
message:
fix(test runner): a --files slice past PATH_MAX is a list, not a filename

Asked to confirm CI's run history for the coverage-claim gate. It runs the job
and the job has never reached a test: all 8 matrix slices die 8 seconds in with
`OSError: [Errno 36] File name too long`, on every main push since 2026-08-04 —
55 failures and 0 successes in the last 60 runs.

`--files` hands the runner one colon-joined slice, ~380 files and ~30 KB, and
`_split_path_list` opened with `Path(raw).exists()` as a fast path for "the
argument IS one path with a colon in it". A joined list is not a path, and the
hosts disagree about how to say so: Linux's stat() answers ENAMETOOLONG past
PATH_MAX and pathlib does not ignore that errno, so the probe raises, while
Windows folds the same overflow into its ignored winerror set and answers
False. Green on every developer's box, fatal on every runner.

The probe now swallows OSError, with the asymmetry written at the site. The
test asserts both halves — the real over-PATH_MAX list, which is enough on
POSIX, and a forced OSError, which is what makes a Windows author trip here.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): --service — stdin EOF is the starter detaching, not the runtime stopping

The reader loop IS the main loop, so until now stdin EOF ended everything: the
pool joined, both socket lanes closed, the registry entry went. "The runtime"
was in practice a child of whichever launcher held the pipe, and closing that
launcher took it with them (F1).

`harness serve --ndjson --service` splits the two facts EOF used to conflate.
A stdio `{"op":"shutdown"}` received BEFORE EOF is still an ORDER and ends the
runtime exactly as it always has — which is what keeps the flag safe for Update
and Repair. EOF alone is an OBSERVATION: the loop logs `stdio_owner_detached`,
broadcasts it to attached socket clients, swaps the stdio frame sink for a null
sink, and parks the main thread on a stop event. Both socket lanes keep serving
throughout. When the park is released the SAME finalization runs, in the same
order, with the same exit codes — nothing is skipped and nothing duplicated.

Three things release it: `{"op":"drain","force":true}` over the socket (set
beside the reader's existing wakeup, at the same instant and for the same
reason), SIGTERM where the platform delivers one, and the stdio shutdown that
never reaches the park at all. The park's event is the mechanism; a half-second
re-check of the drain latch bounds a missed wakeup rather than stranding a
drained runtime forever.

`_FrameWriter` gains `detachable`, OFF by default: with it off there is no
`detach()` call site and the new BrokenPipeError branch is unreachable, so a
non-service serve raises on a dead pipe exactly where it always did. With it on,
a service does not die of its observer leaving.

`--service --no-socket` is refused at the CLI rather than accepted and degraded:
it asks for a process with no way in and no way out, since the socket lane is
the only lane a drain can arrive on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): a --service starter that loses the ownership lock exits 0 and serves nothing

F1's explicit requirement, and the hazard the flag would otherwise create. A
STDIO serve that loses the per-root socket ownership race keeps serving stdio —
it has an owner waiting on a pipe, and that contract is untouched. A SERVICE
that lost it has nobody: it was asked to be "the runtime for this root", there
already is one, and the only thing it could do by carrying on is become a
second execution process against the same store that nothing discovers, nothing
drains and nothing knows to stop.

So it names the winner and leaves, before the request pool, the registry row and
the ready frame exist — which is what "serves nothing" means literally.

Exit code 0, because losing this race is the ORDINARY outcome of two starters (a
launcher that respawned, a second launcher) and the caller's next act is to
re-read the registry and attach to the winner (RL-4). A nonzero code would read
as "the runtime failed to start" about a root that has a healthy runtime.

Both a frame AND a service-log line carry `serve_owner_exists`, with the
winner's pid and port off the owner sidecar: a starter that spawned us over
pipes reads the frame, and one that spawned us detached — the normal case — has
no stdout to read at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): service and starter_pid on the registry row, all three greetings and the ops manifest

An attach-first client decides whether to ATTACH to a running process or to
start one of its own, and it makes that decision twice: once from the registry
row, before it dials anything, and once from the greeting, after it connects.
Both now say whether closing the pipe would DETACH from a runtime that keeps
going or KILL it, and which process started it.

Always present, never inferred from absence — the rule `ready`'s other blocks
already follow, and it earns its keep here twice over. `service: false` says
"this runtime dies with the stdin it was started on"; an ABSENT key says "this
row/greeting was written by a hermes that predates service mode", which is the
launcher's condition for falling back to the stdio-pipe transport (RL-2). A
reader must be able to tell those apart.

`starter_pid` is read at BOOT and never again: a detached service is reparented
the moment its starter exits, so a parent read later names the reaper that
adopted it — and on Windows often nothing at all.

`ops_manifest` gains the same key on every transport, so the membership gate
does not depend on which door the client came through. The ops contract integer
is unchanged: this is an added key on an existing block, which is the
set-plus-integer rule that block already uses.

`serve connect --probe` lifts both to the top of its report — "is the thing I
just reached a durable service, and who started it" is the first question an
operator running that verb has — read off the hello it actually completed, so
it cannot disagree with the frame printed below it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(serve service mode): the lifetime, held at the seam

Ten tests on the real `serve_loop` with the real socket lane, driving it through
the two events that used to be one: a stdio `shutdown` (an order) and stdin EOF
(an observation).

What each arm holds:

- without `--service`, EOF still ends the runtime — shutdown frame, code 0,
  registry entry gone. The regression twin, first, because the flag is a lever
  and not a change of default.
- a service survives EOF and still EXECUTES: an argv request over the socket is
  answered by the pool the EOF path used to join.
- nothing more reaches the starter's pipe after the detach receipt. A parked
  service that kept writing into a pipe whose reader has gone is one full buffer
  away from blocking forever, and the failure would look like a wedged runtime
  nowhere near the write that caused it.
- a drain over the socket ends a service that has NOBODY attached — the state a
  closed launcher actually leaves behind, and the one where a missed wakeup
  would strand the process with no client to notice.
- a stdio `shutdown` before EOF ends it exactly as today, with no detach receipt.
- a `--service` lock loser exits 0 naming the winner and registers nothing,
  while a stdio loser still serves stdio.
- the published fields agree across the row, `ready`, `hello_ok` and `version`,
  on both values of the flag.

Red proof, both directions. Disabling the park: the three lifetime tests fail on
a missing detach receipt. Disabling the lock-loser exit: the file TIMES OUT —
the loser becomes exactly the extra stdio executor the branch exists to prevent,
parks, and never comes back.

The registry classification is deliberately not asserted here: a serve running
inside pytest has a pytest command line, so the registry answers `unknown`,
which is its fail-safe direction working correctly. Live classification is
proven where the process really is a serve — the child e2e file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
test(serve child e2e): the service lifetime against real spawned processes

Four arms on the file that already spawns real children, because two of their
premises cannot exist at the in-process seam: a stdin that was never a pipe (the
null device, closed at spawn — how a detached launcher starts a runtime), and
two processes contending for one OS lock.

(a) `--service` with stdin closed at spawn: the child says `ready` with
    `service: true`, writes a registry row that says the same to a client that
    has not connected yet, and then — after EOF — `serve connect --probe` finds
    it and classifies it `live`, an argv `status --json` over the authenticated
    socket exits 0, and `--drain` ends it with `drain_complete`, process exit 0
    and the registry row gone.
(b) a second `--service` starter loses the kernel's lock, emits
    `serve_owner_exists` naming the winner's pid and port, exits 0, and never
    emits a ready frame. One registry row survives — the winner's — and the
    winner still answers a probe on its original boot_id.
(c) a `--service` child whose stdio owner sends `shutdown` before EOF exits as
    today, with no detach receipt.
(d) without `--service`, closing the child's stdin still ends it.

`_spawn_serve` gains extra argv and a `detached_stdin` switch; its existing two
callers are unchanged. Sandboxing is the file's own — LOCALAPPDATA, HOME,
USERPROFILE, HERMES_HOME and the runtime root all under tmp_path — so no boot
here touches a live root or publishes the machine-global anchor.

A launcher attached to an IDLE runtime was told it was busy, forever. The
launcher holds two `harness stream` subscriptions; they are infinite by
design and never leave `inflight`, so `_liveness_pump` — which only ever
asked "is anything pending?" — emitted
`{"event":"busy","chat_turns":0,"long_runs":0,"pending":2}` to stdout and
to every attached socket client every five seconds, for the life of the
process. `_report_quiet_requests` had already learned to exclude those
requests and says why; the frame the launcher actually reads had not.

`_busy_frame` gains two ADDITIVE counts: `subscriptions` (the
`is_runtime_stream` subset) and `work` (`pending - subscriptions`).
`pending`, `chat_turns` and `long_runs` keep their exact names and
meanings, because the launcher decodes `chat_turns` and `pending` by name
and a supervisor that learned a renamed key would be one that stopped
reading the old one mid-upgrade. The pump emits only when `work > 0`;
`ping` still answers with all five counts, because silence is the pump's
rule, not the frame's, and a supervisor that ASKS needs to see the
subscriptions it is holding itself.

RL-13 of the launcher plan `local-runtime-ownership-and-retry-safety.md`
(§8.8). Pinned as DEFECT D in the request-silence module — the same seam,
the opposite failure.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(chat turn): the method carries the verb's whole operator surface

R-C8, the hermes half. The C5 field run measured a console send to the Mac
that never left the launcher:

    chat_turn lane=argv capability=mission.chat.message
        reason=methodUnavailable detail=args_not_carried:workspace_name

`normalize_chat_message` read eleven param keys and ignored the rest silently,
so the launcher — which decorates every console send with `workspace_name` —
could not prove the key would be honoured and fell to the argv arm, and argv to
a remote install is a designed wall rather than a fallback.

Seven keys now lower to the argv a local send would have used: `workspace_name`,
`provider`, `model`, `use_agent_default` (a flag), `clarify_token`, and a
NON-DEFAULT `surface_prompt` / `intent_hint`. The two defaulted ones are lowered
only off their default because the console sends the default word on every
ordinary message, and a remote turn must be the same execution as a local one
rather than a longer argv that means the same.

Every cap is the handler's own — safe_assignment_text's 120 / 240 / 4000,
safe_assignment_token's 120, _CHAT_PROVIDER_MODEL_RE's 200 — so the boundary
cannot hand the handler a string it silently truncates. The charset for
provider/model stays the handler's to enforce; a second regex here would be a
second place to keep correct.

`use_agent_default` with `provider` or `model` is refused at the DOOR
(ERR_INVALID_PARAMS, reason `model_override_conflict`). Over argv that rule is a
ValueError raised deep inside the turn, which on this lane would mean an
accepted turn — a client already holding an ack and a receipt keyed on its
turn_request_id — dying as a handler failure.

Unknown params stay ignored, pinned by a test: a client cannot be refused for a
key this runtime has never heard of, and that is precisely why the runtime has
to publish what it does hear (next commit).

CHAT_MESSAGE_PARAMS / CHAT_STEER_PARAMS are the single source the manifest is
derived from, and a test drives each normaliser through a recording mapping to
assert the advertisement equals the keys actually read.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): the runtime writes why it ended, and no reader mistakes it for a row

RL-16. A stale registry row said a runtime was here; nothing said why the one that
was here is gone. A closed console window, a logoff, an uncaught fault and a
`taskkill /F` all left the identical evidence, so the 2026-09-05 death of pid 33680
had to be guessed at — twice, and §8.8b struck its own §3 for it.

So a serve now writes `serve_instances/<pid>.ended.json` — `{reason, at, boot_id,
pid}` — on any end it can observe, through the same `write_json_atomic` helper the
row uses. Three mechanisms plus a floor: a Windows console control handler
(`SetConsoleCtrlHandler` via ctypes, all five events, installing cleanly on a
process with no console — RL-17 is about to make that normal), `SIGTERM`/`SIGHUP`
handlers that record and then restore `SIG_DFL` and re-raise so the process still
dies exactly as it did, and an `atexit` hook for everything else. The drain and
shutdown paths write inline rather than trusting `atexit`, because the drain's tail
can end in `os._exit`.

`TerminateProcess` writes nothing, and that silence is load-bearing: the launcher
words a stale row with no sidecar `ended=absent`. Nothing writes a placeholder for
an end it did not observe.

The directory now holds two file shapes, so the one scan the rest of the tree is
built on (`list_serve_instances` → `resolve_socket_target`, `harness serve
connect`, the boot prune, `harness status`'s `serves=`, the launcher's
`local_serve_attach`) filters the suffix; one test per reader, plus the two test
helpers in `test_serve_socket_child_e2e.py` that globbed the directory to mean
"the row is gone". Retention is a boot-time floor at the newest 20, because
nothing ever consumes a reason.

Nothing on the wire moved: no frame, no op, no argparse flag, no fixture.

Armed only from `_cmd_serve` (`record_end_reason=True`), the same injection
contract as `root_anchor` and `skill_install` — arming it mutates the HOST
process, which in a `serve_loop` unit test is pytest.

Red-first, and the reasons are proven against REAL spawned children, which is the
only honest seam for "what happens when this process is killed": nine arms in
`test_serve_ended_sidecar_child_e2e.py` (drained, shutdown_op, stdin_eof, ctrl_c
via a real `GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent`, no-console install under DETACHED_PROCESS,
uncaught, unknown_exit, the absence after `os._exit`, boot retention) plus 29 at
the seam. `ctrl_close` cannot be generated by any Windows API — the mapping table
is pinned instead.

message:
feat(serve): three ways an argv ends, and only one of them may be replayed

RL-24. `dispatch_argv` shared one `SystemExit` path between
`parser.parse_args(argv)` and `func(args)`, so a handler that called
`sys.exit()` after its effect reported `argv_parse_failed` — the one word the
launcher's stale-child fallback replays on a fresh CLI. Three exits now, each
its own type and its own frame: `argv_root_unsupported root=<word>` refused
before a parser is built (R-C11's runtime half — `hermes profile delete` is a
CLI verb this lane does not own, and an argparse `invalid choice` was
indistinguishable from a stale child), `argv_parse_failed` unchanged for the
parser's own refusal, and `handler_exit code=<int>` for a handler that exited.

Both new types subclass `SystemExit`, so every non-serve caller of
`dispatch_argv` keeps the process behaviour it had, and each frame is still
followed by the request's `exit` frame with the same code — a launcher that
knows only the middle word decodes all three exactly as it does today.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(gateway auth): one live device row per account device, and a floor under the dead ones

RL-23. The redeem wrote a new row per code and revoked nothing, so a launcher
re-pairing on a backoff left a live credential per attempt: five rows on this
machine for one Mac, fourteen on the Mac for this one, every one of them able to
open the door. A redeem whose pending entry names an `account_device_id` now
revokes every non-revoked row carrying the same label in the SAME write —
`revoked_reason: "superseded"`, `superseded_by: <new device id>`, both additive
— so no reader ever sees two live rows for one device and the old credential's
next hello answers `device_revoked`, which is the honest word.

An unlabelled row supersedes nothing: `harness gateway pair` names no device, so
treating the absent label as a key would collapse every manually paired device
into one. `prune_revoked_devices` gives revocation a floor — thirty days past
`revoked_at`, at serve boot beside the two `serve_instances` prunes, never a live
row and never a stamp it cannot read. `note_device_seen` and the verifier path
are untouched.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(serve): a service runtime keeps its own stderr, and its death names itself

RL-19. Since RL-17 the launcher starts the runtime with all three stdio
handles on DEVNULL — right, because a pipe nobody reads is a runtime that
blocks on its first full buffer — and the price was measured on 2026-09-06 at
09:09:18Z: a local hub stream went silent for thirty seconds, the watchdog
tore it down, and the runtime's side of that half hour did not exist.

So a --service runtime opens serve_instances/<pid>.stderr.log beside its own
registry row and its end-reason sidecar: line-buffered UTF-8, truncated per
pid, one header line naming pid/boot_id/build/start so a file read cold says
whose it was. The registry opens it (one writer for that directory), the
loop's stderr proxy mirrors every completed line into it, logging's root
handler is repointed if it was writing to stderr, and the handle becomes the
loop's original_stderr so the restore at unwind lands there too.

And one thing the redirect could not buy, found while proving it: an uncaught
exception out of a serve child prints no traceback on ANY channel — the
harness dispatch converts it to an error envelope the --ndjson serve never
emits, so a faulting child writes booting/root_anchor/ready and exits 1
having said nothing. serve_loop's uncaught arm now writes the traceback into
the file itself, beside the uncaught:<Type> the sidecar records.

Retention: prune_serve_ended floors both families at the newest twenty EACH —
pooled, twenty service boots would evict every reason a non-service serve
wrote. list_serve_instances ignores the third shape twice over (not a .json,
and named in _NON_ROW_SUFFIXES). A non-service serve is byte-identical: its
parent holds its stderr pipe and reads it as frames.

Red first: both modules against origin/main — ImportError on the unit module,
and the e2e's three arms on a file that did not exist.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(charsheet): a fake draftsman a spawned runtime can reach

RL-26. `characters turnaround|rows|auto` are the runtime's only long runs and
every one of them is a generation, so no sandboxed `harness serve` could run a
batch to completion without spending money: the package has ONE provider door
(`pipeline._generate_image`) and the only deterministic draftsman in the tree
was a `monkeypatch` that reaches nothing outside the process performing it.
The long-run acceptance proof stopped at exactly that gate.

`agent/charsheet/fake_draftsman.py` is the arm a spawned process can reach. The
Pillow drawing moves there out of the three test modules that each carried a
copy, and gains two things a fixture never needed: it reads the REQUEST (the
built prompt's numbered turnaround slots, its `LAYOUT: arrange the N …` count
and the row's frozen facing) instead of a `SheetSpec` nobody can hand a child,
and its strips grow with the slot count so a twelve-frame row is still
sliceable. A prompt that lost an anchor raises rather than guessing.

`pipeline._draftsman()` resolves which door a generation takes, at CALL time —
a serve started without the variable and a child started with it read two
environments. `HERMES_CHARSHEET_DRAFTSMAN=fake`, exactly that word, binds the
fake; anything else is ignored with ONE stderr line per value per process and
the real door stands. Unset is the default and the untouched path;
`_generate_image` is still a module global inside the resolver, so every
in-process monkeypatch still wins for its own process.

The seam is visible: `"draftsman": "fake"` rides every `characters` `--json`
result while it is armed — `_characters_emit`, `_characters_error` and the
autopilot's per-stage stream — and NO key at all when it is not, so an existing
reader sees byte-identical output on the door it has always used while a
sandbox that forgot to arm the seam reads as a paid run rather than a silent
one. No wire change, no argparse flag, no config key.

Tests: the door pinned by identity with the seam off; the fake with it on;
every other value refused; determinism (same request, same bytes, same
draftsman twice and across processes); every slot the request asks for; the
prompt anchors read from real built prompts; a full flow with
`imagegen.generate` booby-trapped; and a child e2e that spawns a real sandboxed
serve with the variable set, runs start → turnaround → approve → rows → status
down the argv lane, and proves no provider was called twice over — the child
holds no credential-shaped env var, and the bytes it committed for a row equal
what the parent draws from the same public function. Ten killing mutations
recorded, nine registered in `tests/mutation_claims.json`.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(charsheet): an occupied lock path is taken on both hosts, not just POSIX

`O_EXCL` against a path a DIRECTORY sits on raises EEXIST on POSIX and EACCES on
Windows. `_claim` caught only `FileExistsError`, so the identical draft refused
the identical generation with a typed `DraftBusy` on one host and an unhandled
`OSError` out of the middle of the verb on the other — the split
`agent_runtime.locks._file_lock`'s docstring exists to forbid, one package over.

The EACCES arm answers "taken" only when the path EXISTS. EACCES also means
"this process may not create files here", which is not a held lock: reporting it
as one would tell an operator to wait for a holder that does not exist and then
delete a lock file nobody wrote. That refusal-not-to-lie has its own test.

The errno is parametrized rather than left to the host, so a Linux runner
exercises the Windows arm and a Windows workstation the POSIX one; a second test
runs the same planted directory with nothing patched, so the real host is
proven to be one of the two arms.

author: nekwo
message:
ci: a red main push opens one issue, not a 56th unread email

Step (2) of the queue row. The repo has had no failure-notification
mechanism at all: nothing matched `failure()`, `github-script`, an issue
action or a webhook, and the only channel that existed — GitHub's default
pusher email — had fired unread on 55 consecutive red pushes while every
test slice died 8 s in.

`notify-main-red` is `needs: [all-checks-pass]`, gated
`failure() && github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`,
and upserts ONE issue titled `CI red on main` from `all-checks-pass`'s
existing `needs-json` output, so the issue names the failed jobs instead of
handing the reader a link to go read. One issue, reused: body rewritten and
a comment added per red push, closed by a human when main goes green.

`issues: write` at the job (nothing else), no secret, no external service,
and NO checkout — the job runs zero repository code, which is what makes it
safe in a workflow that also runs PR-controlled branches. `needs-json`
reaches the script through `env` and is read with `process.env`, never
interpolated into the script body, so a job name can never become script.

PROOF, and its limit. The script was extracted from the YAML and driven
against stubbed `github`/`context`/`core` with run 33969282189's real
failure set: no existing issue -> create (`tests`, `lint`, `e2e-desktop`
named); issue #42 already open -> update + comment, with a PULL REQUEST of
the same title correctly ignored; malformed needs-json -> a warning and the
issue still opens with the run link. `node --check` passes and the workflow
parses. What that does NOT prove is the job firing: its condition is a
failing push to main, so THE FIRST REAL EVIDENCE IS THE NEXT RED MAIN PUSH
AND IT MUST BE WATCHED — including that `needs.all-checks-pass.outputs.needs-json`
survives the hyphenated output name, and that the runner honours
github-script v9's `node24`.

message:
feat(serve): a prune names every row it removed and every one it refused

RO-3. `prune_stale_serve_instances` was this directory's one silent
writer: a boot deleted a registry row and said so only in the aggregate
`serve_instances_pruned` report, which is written only when the count is
non-zero — so "who removed the row for pid 43244, and when" (the
2026-09-06 field run's question) had no answer on any channel while the
neighbouring lanes each had one.

It now takes an `emit` sink and writes one `serve_registry_pruned` event
per row it ACTED on: `removed`, `refused` (a recycled or unclassifiable
row it deliberately keeps — the ruling's "and what it refuses"), or
`remove_failed`. A `live` row writes nothing, because that is this
boot's own entry on every boot and a line every boot is how a channel
stops being read. The words are the CLASSIFIER's, not a second set:
`reason` is `classify_serve_instance`'s classification verbatim and
`classification_reason` its finer word.

The serve passes `_service_log`, the sink it already owns, and the RL-19
stderr-log arming moves AHEAD of the prune so a `--service` runtime's
verdicts land in `<pid>.stderr.log` instead of the DEVNULL stdio RL-17
hands it. No wire contract moves, no new op, no manifest key.

author: nekwo
message:
feat(chat): a turn's terminal payload carries its own timing split

RO-7's producer half. The breakdown has been on the durable record since
`phases` landed, and on 2026-09-06 it answered the operator's question
exactly once — through a hand-written script that joined the launcher's
`[MissionChatTiming]` line to `mission_chat_turns/*.json` on the turn id.
That join said the extra seconds of a local turn were spent BEFORE the
provider, which is the opposite of what the launcher's line alone
suggested. An operator cannot write that script.

So `mission_chat_phases.turn_timing_block` projects seven of those
numbers — turn_context_ms, request_assembled_ms, provider_first_byte_ms,
responses_create_ms, stream_consume_ms, builds_overlapped,
resident_actor_reused — and the chat-turn commit copies them onto the
terminal payload under `timing`, from the same two instruments the
terminal persist writes in the same breath. That payload is the argv
lane's `--json` object and the served lane's `chat.final`, which is the
last frame carrying a payload under a `runtime.chat.message` request id
(its `exit` frame carries a code and nothing else).

The record's honesty contract travels with it: a phase the turn never
reached has NO key, a measured zero survives, and anything unreadable is
dropped rather than coerced. Strictly additive — no existing key moves,
RPC_CONTRACT_VERSION / OPS_CONTRACT_VERSION / SERVE_SCHEMA_VERSION do
not move, and both byte-pinned fixture families regenerate unchanged.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(machine roots): POSIX roots may contain spaces too; pin the migration host

Six tests in this file were red in every Linux slice of run 33969282189 and
green on Windows, for two independent reasons — one a real product defect, one
an unstated assumption in the tests.

The defect: `_ABS_PATH_RE`'s own comment says a whitespace-terminated pattern
truncates a spaced root and the migration then finds nothing to do — and the
POSIX alternative did exactly that. `/Users/tony/My Projects/EterniaLauncher`
was discovered as `/Users/tony/My`, a directory that does not exist, so
`_nearest_repo_root` walked up from the wrong place and returned nothing. On
the Mac of the multi-device program that is the ordinary case, not an edge
case. The POSIX branch now tolerates a space INSIDE a segment while keeping
its two-segment structure and refusing a segment that OPENS with a space, so
"budget / diff / stop" is still not a path.

The assumption: `${exe_suffix}` is host-relative by design — `.exe` on
Windows, empty elsewhere — so verifying a rewrite of a WINDOWS config only
round-trips on a Windows host. That is correct behaviour, and the fixture
config here is the live Windows profile, so the module now pins
`current_platform_key`. The pin is stated rather than hidden: a new test turns
it off and asserts the POSIX answer and that nothing is written.

Red-first: the two spaced-path cases failed before the regex change (recorded).
Killing mutations, all recorded 2026-09-06: (1) restoring the space-free POSIX
segment class reds the spaced cases; (2) letting a segment open with a space
reds `test_slashes_in_prose_are_not_absolute_paths`; (3) making `exe_suffix()`
return `.exe` unconditionally reds the host-relativity test.

Proof for the six original reds is the next CI run — the mechanisms were
verified here from `_absolute_paths_in` directly and from a forced-POSIX
`current_platform_key`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(cli gate): argv[0]'s separator belongs to the launcher, not to the host

on both hosts — a POSIX console script's path never carries a backslash — and

of only where they happen to be native. A new test states the rule.

seven "is the CLI" shapes answer True and all seven "is not" shapes answer

author: nekwo
message:
ci(tests): the sliced suite gets the history its gates read

`actions/checkout`'s default fetch-depth of 1 handed the eight test slices a
one-commit clone, and two shipped gates read this repo's history:

* `tests/agent_runtime/test_tombstone_registry.py` runs
  `git diff --name-only 4a21f0779..HEAD -- tests` at MODULE IMPORT. On a
  shallow clone that exits 128, and the raw `CalledProcessError` took the
  entire 4,300-line gate file down at collection — run 33969282189's slice 8,
  "1 error during collection", the file where no tests ran.
* `tests/test_docket_stage_claims.py` asks `git merge-base --is-ancestor` per
  cited sha. With no history every answer is "no", so the gate accused seven
  BACKED dockets of citing commits that never landed (slice 7). A gate that
  cannot tell "not an ancestor" from "this clone has no ancestors" produces a
  false accusation, which is worse than not running.

`filter: blob:none` is what keeps this affordable across eight parallel jobs
on a 20k-commit repo: both gates want commits and trees, not file contents, so
blobs are fetched lazily and only for the few `git show` calls the round-4
walk makes.

Proof is the next CI run — the checkout cost lands in the run's own timing
report, which is worth a look on the first green.

author: nekwo
message:
test(docket claims): the ancestry gate says when the clone cannot answer

`git merge-base --is-ancestor` answers NO for every sha in a shallow clone,
and this gate reads a run of NOs as "these dockets claim a landing that never
happened". In run 33969282189's slice 7 it therefore named seven BACKED stages
across two dockets — a false accusation, which is worse than not running.

A gate that cannot tell "not an ancestor" from "this clone has no ancestors"
now says which one it is looking at:
`_assert_the_clone_can_answer_ancestry` reads
`git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and fails with the cause and the cure.
Deliberately an assertion, not a skip — a checkout that cannot answer ancestry
is a broken environment for this file, and a skip is how this went quiet for a
month.

`test_ancestry_is_the_question_asked_not_existence` also probes HEAD~1 now:
the two existing probes (HEAD, and forty zeroes) both pass in a one-commit
clone, so the probe called itself real while seeing nothing.

Root cause proven, not inferred: a `git clone --depth 1` of this branch
reproduces the CI failure exactly — the same seven stages, verbatim — and with
this commit applied the same clone reds on the precondition instead, naming
the shallow checkout.

read as "nothing uncovered".

collects (1,153 tests deselected, so collection succeeded) and exactly one
test reds, naming the shallow checkout. Full local run: 1,155 passed.

future git problem from costing the whole file again.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(desktop-e2e): the running dot is the turn-is-running signal, not the background dot

sessionDotState resolves ONE dot per session and ranks isWorking above
hasBackground, so a session running a turn while holding a live
terminal(background=true) process paints "Session running"; the "Background
task running" label is by design unreachable until the turn goes idle. Three
E2E call sites polled the background label to learn that a turn had STARTED --
a wait only the turn ENDING can satisfy. Two of them are red on CI run
34051553815 (sidebar-states.spec.ts:215 and tile-unread-bug.spec.ts:61, first
attempt and retry); the third (sidebar-states.spec.ts:154) is green only
because its self-exiting `sleep 5` outlived the turn by a second or two, which
its own evidence screenshot from that run shows.

The primitive is not the wrong side. The ordering predates the one-primitive
collapse (87aaf87748 moved sessionDotState out of session-row.tsx, it did not
invent the ranking), the running/stalled dot is the only live-turn cue the
pane tabs and session tiles get, and a swap would let any background process
mask a stalled turn. So the specs move: each file gains a RUNNING_DOT_LABEL
that states the rule where the next author will look, and every "is the turn
running?" poll reads it. No timeout widened, no assertion loosened -- the
background-dot assertions stay where they belong, after the turn settles with
the process held by the sentinel.

The unit test is why this was writable in the first place: the existing case
is named "keeps background and unread states below active-turn states" but
passes isWorking: false, so it never exercises the ordering it names. The new
case states working-over-background, stalled-over-background, and background
only once idle. Killing mutation (hoist the hasBackground branch above
isWorking -- make the product do what the specs believed): 1 failed | 3
passed, only the new case red.

This does NOT by itself turn the Linux job green. The same run's page snapshot
shows the turn wedged on a terminal-command approval prompt for the sentinel
background command ("+ 6 commands", 27s elapsed on a background=true call, a
Run/Reject bar, and the running dot present in the sidebar), so no background
process ever spawns. That is a separate defect; the field notes carry the
evidence and what could and could not be ruled out from Windows.

author: nekwo
message:
fix(serve socket): the accept loop is woken, not raced out of accept()

`_close_listener` called `listener.close()` and nothing else. Windows aborts a
pending `accept()` in another thread on `closesocket`; Linux and macOS do not,
and `close()`'s `thread.join(2.0)` moved on regardless. So `accept_loop_exited`
— the field whose whole purpose is "the loop never stops quietly" — was stamped
by whichever platform happened to be kind, and CI saw it as a flaky.

The wakeup is a socketpair the loop selects on beside the listener, chosen over
`shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` (wakes Linux, `ENOTCONN` on macOS/BSD — a Linux-shaped
assumption replacing a Windows-shaped one) and over a self-connect (a wakeup
with side effects on the very counters these tests read). It is the one whose
test states the rule instead of the mechanism.

`bind()` creates the pair and sets the listener non-blocking, so the loop can
never park where `close()` cannot reach it; a `BlockingIOError` after a
readiness that evaporated is a retry, not an accept error. `_close_listener`
wakes first and closes second: one byte for a loop already waiting, then the
write end closed so the read end sits at EOF for a loop that has not arrived
yet. The accept thread closes the read end, being the only thread that ever
selects on it. `begin_drain()`'s listener close rides the same wake.

Red-first: `_CloseDoesNotWakeAccept` wraps the real listener and neuters only
its `close()`, giving POSIX semantics on any host. Without the wakeup it reds
with `assert None == 'listener_closed'`, the CI signature exactly. Killing
mutation: dropping the one `_signal_wakeup()` call reds it again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(machine roots): a POSIX root keeps the slash it is rooted at

`_root_pattern` split the root on separators and dropped the empties. A
drive-letter root carries its own anchor (`X:`) through that split; a POSIX
root's anchor is the leading slash, and it went out with the empty first
element, leaving a pattern that could only match from the `t` of `/tmp`.

Both readers were wrong on the second machine. `unmapped_absolute_paths`
matches at position 0, so a root the operator had just bound came back as
unmapped residue — the assertion still red on Linux CI after 854f0f2482.
`tokenize_text` searches, so it matched and replaced everything but the slash:
`repo_scope: /Users/tony/My Projects/EterniaLauncher` rewrote to
`repo_scope: /${roots.eternia_launcher}`, a token that re-expands to a doubled
root and fails verify_roundtrip. Measured both before and after.

The pinned `current_platform_key` is not involved: nothing on the residue path
reads it. The Windows/Linux difference was only ever `tmp_path`'s own shape,
which is why the new test uses a literal POSIX root and reproduces the
Linux-only failure on Windows. It asserts both readers, since they failed in
opposite directions; reverting the product line reds it. The existing sibling
needed no edit and goes green on Linux from the product fix alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: nekwo
message:
fix(root observability): the walk follows the emit into its seam

`test_ledger_does_not_rot` said `_cmd_persona_instance_open_chat` "no longer
emits JSON — remove it". It does. 13c1d67178, the R-C5 open-chat lowering, moved
the emit into `_emit_persona_open_chat_payload` so a serve's in-process caller
can take the row without redirect_stdout rebinding the process's stdout; the
scan counted direct calls only and read that transport refactor as a verb that
had stopped answering.

The row's platform premise does not hold either: this is red on Windows too on
unmodified main, so nothing about path case, os.sep or part-file resolution is
involved.

`_handlers()` now propagates emits/attaches/chat_scope from a handler's local
`_emit_*` callees, to a fixpoint. That seam is named by convention and is the
one the lowering introduced; following EVERY local callee instead would add
thirty handlers rather than three, twenty of them neither classified nor
attaching. Nineteen of those twenty remain after this commit and are handed back
as their own row — `_BACKLOG_REASON` says not to grow that list, and nineteen
classifications is not a line of this one.

Of the three the seam adds, two already carry ledger entries and the third,
`_cmd_usage`, was a real miss: it emits an account-usage envelope through
`_emit_usage_json` and states no root, so credentials under a different
HERMES_HOME answer zero lanes in a well-formed envelope. Stamped on both JSON

feat(build identity): a commit is not a build, so the row says which code

RS-6. RL-20's build-behind restart compared `build.commit` against the
checkout's HEAD, so on 2026-09-07 at 16:25:09Z a DOCS-ONLY landing drained a
healthy runtime and its replacement lost the socket lock for the rest of the
session. The runtime now states WHICH CODE it is running.

`agent_runtime/build_identity.py` is the rule, once: `NON_RUNTIME_PREFIXES`
(`docs/`, `tests/`, `.github/`) plus repo-root markdown (a path with no `/` in
it whose name ends in `.md`), and `code_tree_for` = sha1 over the sorted
(path, blob) pairs of `git ls-tree -r -z HEAD` after the rule, framed
`<path>NUL<blob>NL` and sorted by the path's UTF-8 bytes.

The `build` block on the ready frame, the socket greeting and the register row
gains `code_tree`, `code_tree_rule` (the rule itself, so the launcher applies
the one it was handed) and `code_tree_reason` (why a null is null). A non-git
source writes no digest and says `not_git:<source>`.

The two implementations are held to one answer by a byte-equal fixture hashed
on both sides; the launcher's copy is
`EterniaLauncher/test/fixtures/build_identity/code_tree_parity_tree.txt`.

9,257 tracked paths on this checkout.

`_defer_demote_build_for_active_turns` and both of the chat-actor prewarm's
